title: CHOREO: Every Humanoid Skill as a Trajectory
summary: Recent advances in humanoid robotics have produced diverse skills through reinforcement learning, motion imitation, and generative modeling. Yet these capabilities remain siloed because they are built around incompatible representations, interfaces, and controllers. We present CHOREO, a framework for training-free composition of heterogeneous humanoid skills. Our key observation is that, regardless of how a skill is learned, it can ultimately be expressed as an executable motion trajectory. Based on this observation, CHOREO converts each capability into SkillMotion, a unified representation that combines motion states, contacts, semantics, and boundary conditions. Skills are composed through direct continuation, cubic Hermite blending, or validated bridge motions, without retraining source models or updating models at test time. On Unitree G1 in MuJoCo, CHOREO organizes 2,950 admitted SkillMotion assets derived from heterogeneous sources and achieves 95.4\% sequence success across 130 multi-action tasks, including 93.8\% success on eight-action sequences. These results demonstrate that executable trajectories provide a scalable interface for accumulating and composing pretrained humanoid capabilities.

AI.tldr: CHOREO is a training-free framework that unifies heterogeneous humanoid skills as executable motion trajectories (SkillMotion) and composes them via continuation, Hermite blending, or validated bridges, achieving 95.4% sequence success on Unitree G1.
AI.motivation: Humanoid skills from reinforcement learning, motion imitation, and generative modeling remain siloed because they rely on incompatible representations, interfaces, and controllers. There is a need for a scalable way to accumulate and compose these pretrained capabilities without retraining or aligning their original frameworks.
AI.method: The framework converts every skill, regardless of learning paradigm, into SkillMotion, a unified representation encoding motion states, contacts, semantics, and boundary conditions. Composition is performed training-free through three mechanisms: direct continuation, cubic Hermite blending, and validated bridge motions, with no retraining of source models or test-time model updates.
AI.result: Evaluated on Unitree G1 in MuJoCo, CHOREO organizes 2,950 admitted SkillMotion assets from heterogeneous sources and attains 95.4% sequence success across 130 multi-action tasks, including 93.8% success on eight-action sequences.
AI.conclusion: Executable motion trajectories serve as a scalable interface for accumulating and composing pretrained humanoid capabilities, enabling training-free integration of heterogeneous skills.

title: D3DWA: Adaptive Weight and Prediction-Horizon for Dynamic Window Approach via Dueling Double Deep Q-Network
summary: The Dynamic Window Approach (DWA) is widely used for local navigation, but its performance depends strongly on parameters that are typically fixed before navigation. In particular, the appropriate prediction horizon can vary with local free space: longer horizons support efficient motion in open areas, whereas shorter horizons help preserve feasible motions in narrow or cluttered regions. This paper proposes D3DWA, an adaptive DWA framework based on a Dueling Double Deep Q-Network (D3QN), which jointly selects the DWA evaluation weights and prediction horizon from a continuous navigation state at every control step while retaining DWA's trajectory generation and collision checking. In eight simulated environments, including unseen layouts, D3DWA reached every goal. Real-robot experiments further showed that D3DWA completed all three tested configurations, including a constrained case in which the weights-only variant timed out. These results demonstrate the benefit of jointly adapting the evaluation weights and prediction horizon. Additional material is available at https://mertcookimg.github.io/d3dwa/

AI.tldr: D3DWA is an adaptive Dynamic Window Approach that uses a Dueling Double Deep Q-Network (D3QN) to jointly select DWA evaluation weights and prediction horizon at each control step from the continuous navigation state, while keeping DWA's trajectory generation and collision checking intact.
AI.motivation: DWA is widely used for local navigation, but its performance depends strongly on parameters that are usually fixed before navigation. In particular, the appropriate prediction horizon varies with local free space: longer horizons support efficient motion in open areas, while shorter horizons preserve feasible motions in narrow or cluttered regions. Fixed parameters therefore limit performance across varying environments.
AI.method: The paper proposes D3DWA, an adaptive DWA framework based on a Dueling Double Deep Q-Network (D3QN). It jointly selects the DWA evaluation weights and prediction horizon from a continuous navigation state at every control step, while retaining DWA's original trajectory generation and collision checking.
AI.result: In eight simulated environments, including unseen layouts, D3DWA reached every goal. Real-robot experiments showed that D3DWA completed all three tested configurations, including a constrained case in which the weights-only variant timed out.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the benefit of jointly adapting the DWA evaluation weights and prediction horizon rather than adapting them separately or keeping them fixed.

title: DeViGrasp: Robust Visual Mobile Grasping for Quadruped Manipulators under Degraded Perception
summary: Quadruped manipulators enable mobile grasping in complex environments, yet their whole-body control policies remain vulnerable to unreliable onboard visual perception. Existing methods are typically developed under relatively reliable observations and have not systematically examined how occlusion, segmentation-mask dropout, depth noise, and target-localization jitter affect grasp reasoning and target tracking. To address this gap, we introduce DeViGrasp-Bench, a benchmark for mobile grasping under degraded vision that incorporates controlled visual degradations, seen and unseen objects, multiple difficulty levels, and complex terrains, and evaluates task success, execution efficiency, and action smoothness. We further propose DeViGrasp-Net, a teacher--student framework that combines state-conditioned grasp reasoning with reliability-aware temporal target estimation. The privileged teacher attends to offline grasp candidates conditioned on object, robot, end-effector, and task states, while the deployable student fuses dual-view segmented-depth observations with current, memory, and recovery target hypotheses through Target Hold Memory and Temporal Memory Attention. DeViGrasp-Net outperforms VBC across degradation levels, unseen objects, and complex terrains, and surpasses an adapted DQ-Net across all evaluated degradation levels. Under the Difficult setting, it achieves a success rate of 62.3\%, improving upon VBC and DQ-Net by 16.1 and 4.3 percentage points, respectively; under the Hard setting, its margin over DQ-Net increases to 10.5 percentage points. Ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of grasp-aware supervision and reliability-aware temporal memory.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DeViGrasp-Bench to benchmark quadruped mobile grasping under degraded vision and proposes DeViGrasp-Net, a teacher-student policy achieving state-of-the-art robustness across degradations, unseen objects, and terrains.
AI.motivation: Whole-body control policies for quadruped manipulators are vulnerable to unreliable onboard visual perception, yet existing methods assume relatively reliable observations and have not systematically examined how occlusion, segmentation-mask dropout, depth noise, and target-localization jitter affect grasp reasoning and target tracking.
AI.method: DeViGrasp-Bench: a benchmark with controlled visual degradations, seen/unseen objects, multiple difficulty levels, and complex terrains, evaluating task success, execution efficiency, and action smoothness. DeViGrasp-Net: a teacher-student framework combining state-conditioned grasp reasoning with reliability-aware temporal target estimation. The privileged teacher attends to offline grasp candidates conditioned on object, robot, end-effector, and task states; the deployable student fuses dual-view segmented-depth observations with current, memory, and recovery target hypotheses via Target Hold Memory and Temporal Memory Attention.
AI.result: DeViGrasp-Net outperforms VBC across degradation levels, unseen objects, and complex terrains, and surpasses adapted DQ-Net across all evaluated degradation levels. Under the Difficult setting it reaches 62.3% success, improving over VBC and DQ-Net by 16.1 and 4.3 percentage points; under the Hard setting its margin over DQ-Net grows to 10.5 percentage points. Ablations confirm complementary benefits of grasp-aware supervision and reliability-aware temporal memory.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-aware temporal target estimation and state-conditioned grasp reasoning jointly yield robust whole-body mobile grasping under degraded vision, with DeViGrasp-Bench providing a systematic evaluation testbed.

title: ORDER: A Fictitious-World Benchmark for Domain-Adaptive Embodied AI
summary: Adapting language models to new domains via continual pre-training raises a basic evaluation problem: if the training corpus overlaps with what the model already knows, performance gains cannot be cleanly attributed to new learning rather than pre-existing knowledge. This matters most for knowledge-intensive, task-light (KHTL) robot deployments - pharmaceutical dispensing, hazardous-material handling, facility-specific protocols, where the physical task is simple but the governing rules are proprietary and safety-critical, and where extensive live testing is costly or unsafe. We introduce ORDER (Ontology-driven Decision-making for Embodied Reasoning), a benchmark built on a fictitious world: a 342,069-token synthetic corpus defining a self-consistent physics that cannot appear in any model's pre-training data. ORDER pairs a 500-question knowledge test (ORDER-BENCH) with a harder compositional task, ORDER-SPATIAL: ordering objects for safe manipulation across both familiar and entirely novel scenes. GPT-4.1 without adaptation scores below chance on ORDER-SPATIAL (Kendall's tau = 0.441), showing its priors actively conflict with the invented physics. After continual pre-training, small models improve substantially on both familiar and novel scenes alike evidence of genuine world-model induction rather than memorization. We then carry this through to a robot pipeline: models that answer the knowledge test well often cannot produce valid, executable plans without a further skill-adaptation stage, after which small, fully offline models outperform GPT-4.1 even when GPT-4.1 is given retrieval access to the same rules (Kendall's tau = 0.848 vs. 0.606), on a full perception-to-execution loop demonstrated on a simulated iiwa7 arm with human-in-the-loop correction. Throughout, ORDER-SPATIAL performance, not knowledge-test accuracy is what predicts real plan quality.

AI.tldr: ORDER is a synthetic, ontology-driven benchmark (342,069-token corpus, 500-question knowledge test, and a compositional ordering task) that prevents pre-training contamination, showing that continual pre-training induces genuine world-model learning, and that spatial-reasoning performance, not knowledge-test accuracy, predicts real robot plan quality.
AI.motivation: Continual pre-training evaluation is confounded: if the training corpus overlaps with model priors, gains cannot be attributed to new learning. This is critical for knowledge-intensive, task-light (KHTL) robot deployments (e.g., pharmaceutical dispensing, hazardous-material handling, facility protocols), where rules are proprietary and safety-critical and live testing is costly or unsafe.
AI.method: The authors build ORDER (Ontology-driven Decision-making for Embodied Reasoning) on a fictitious world defined by a 342,069-token synthetic corpus encoding self-consistent physics absent from any pre-training data. It comprises a 500-question knowledge test (ORDER-BENCH) and a harder compositional task, ORDER-SPATIAL, requiring object ordering for safe manipulation in familiar and novel scenes. Continual pre-training is followed by a skill-adaptation stage and full perception-to-execution evaluation on a simulated iiwa7 arm with human-in-the-loop correction, including a retrieval-augmented GPT-4.1 baseline.
AI.result: GPT-4.1 without adaptation scores below chance on ORDER-SPATIAL (Kendall's tau = 0.441), indicating priors conflict with the invented physics. Small models after continual pre-training improve substantially on both familiar and novel scenes, evidencing world-model induction rather than memorization. However, models strong on the knowledge test often fail to produce valid executable plans without skill adaptation; after adaptation, small fully offline models outperform retrieval-augmented GPT-4.1 (tau = 0.848 vs. 0.606) in the complete loop.
AI.conclusion: ORDER-SPATIAL performance, not knowledge-test accuracy, is the reliable predictor of real plan quality, and skill adaptation is necessary to convert knowledge into executable robot behavior.

title: Didactic knowledge or Clinical Cases? How Data Types Shape Medical Large Language Models
comment: This paper is accepted by NLPCC 2026 oral
summary: Medical large language models are commonly trained on mixtures of didactic data (e.g., textbooks) and clinical data (e.g., patient records), yet how these data types differentially shape model capabilities remains unclear. We address this issue with token-matched experiments that vary the didactic-to-clinical ratio and analyze how data composition affects performance, capability profiles, and error patterns across knowledge-intensive and clinic-oriented tasks. We uncover an asymmetric transfer across task types: clinical data improves clinic-oriented tasks while remaining competitive on knowledge-intensive ones, whereas didactic data mainly improves knowledge-intensive tasks. Error analysis suggests a knowing-doing gap, where improvements in knowledge recall do not reliably generalize to clinical reasoning. We further observe that modest amounts of clinical data yield most of the gains on EHR-grounded tasks, while the optimal mixture ratio varies with the knowledge and clinical reasoning demands of downstream tasks. These findings suggest that medical LLM data curation should be application-driven, with higher proportions of clinical data preferred for reasoning-intensive use cases.

AI.tldr: Token-matched experiments varying the didactic-to-clinical data ratio reveal asymmetric transfer in medical LLMs: clinical data boosts clinic-oriented tasks while staying competitive on knowledge-intensive ones, whereas didactic data mainly helps knowledge tasks, implying application-driven data curation.
AI.motivation: Medical LLMs are typically trained on mixtures of didactic (e.g., textbooks) and clinical (e.g., patient records) data, but how each data type differentially shapes model capabilities is unclear. The paper aims to clarify the effect of data composition on performance, capability profiles, and error patterns across knowledge-intensive and clinic-oriented tasks.
AI.method: Token-matched experiments varying the didactic-to-clinical ratio, followed by evaluation of performance, capability profiles, and error patterns across knowledge-intensive and clinic-oriented tasks.
AI.result: An asymmetric transfer emerges: clinical data improves clinic-oriented tasks while remaining competitive on knowledge-intensive ones, whereas didactic data mainly improves knowledge-intensive tasks. Error analysis indicates a knowing-doing gap—gains in knowledge recall do not reliably generalize to clinical reasoning. Modest amounts of clinical data yield most of the gains on EHR-grounded tasks, and the optimal mixture ratio depends on downstream knowledge and clinical reasoning demands.
AI.conclusion: Medical LLM data curation should be application-driven, favoring higher proportions of clinical data for reasoning-intensive use cases.

title: OJOx: Specification-Conditioned Demonstrations for Embodied AI in Construction
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Project website: https://ojox.ai
summary: Large-scale egocentric and whole-body human demonstrations are becoming a primary source of data for embodied intelligence. They record what people perceive and do, but rarely the external specification that gave an action its purpose. In construction that omission is consequential: skilled work is directed at project-specific configurations defined in a design model - configurations not yet present in the environment being observed. A mason's transferable competence is not the geometry of one wall but the ability to realise a new geometry from a specification. We introduce the specification-conditioned demonstration: a synchronised record of the physical state a demonstrator perceives, the intended state supplied to them by an external design, and the behaviour connecting the two. We present OJOx, a capture interface that realises this for construction - delivering design geometry to a headset, anchoring it in the physical workspace, rendering it into a demonstrator's stereo passthrough view, and recording that view synchronously with whole-body and hand motion. We report one fully instrumented session - a 33-component wall laid against a specification that changes while the work proceeds - and check the record against the physical scene through an external camera registered independently of the capture. Recorded sessions remain compatible with existing humanoid retargeting infrastructure and replay onto a Unitree G1 in simulation. The result is a data interface for testing whether embodied policies can learn not merely to imitate demonstrated actions, but to act toward specifications absent from their training experience.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "specification-conditioned demonstrations," a new data paradigm that synchronously records the physical state a demonstrator perceives, the intended state from an external design specification, and the behaviour linking them. It presents OJOx, an interface that delivers design geometry to an AR headset, anchors it in the workspace, and records it alongside whole-body and hand motion, validated on a 33-component wall assembly session and replayed on a Unitree G1 humanoid in simulation.
AI.motivation: Existing large-scale egocentric and whole-body human demonstration datasets capture what people perceive and do, but rarely the external specification that gave an action its purpose. This omission is especially consequential in construction, where skilled work targets project-specific configurations defined in a design model that is not yet present in the observed environment. The transferable competence of a worker (e.g., a mason) lies not in reproducing a specific geometry but in realising a new geometry from a specification, which current demonstration data cannot support learning.
AI.method: The authors formalise the specification-conditioned demonstration: a synchronised record of (1) the physical state a demonstrator perceives, (2) the intended state supplied by an external design, and (3) the behaviour connecting the two. They build OJOx, a capture interface for construction that delivers design geometry to a headset, anchors it in the physical workspace, renders it into the demonstrator's stereo passthrough view, and records that view synchronously with whole-body and hand motion. Validation uses one fully instrumented session—a 33-component wall built against a specification that changes during the work—checked against the physical scene via an external camera registered independently of the capture.
AI.result: A single fully instrumented 33-component wall assembly session was recorded under a dynamically changing specification and verified against the physical scene using an independently registered external camera. The recorded sessions remain compatible with existing humanoid retargeting infrastructure and replay onto a Unitree G1 humanoid in simulation.
AI.conclusion: OJOx provides a data interface for testing whether embodied policies can learn not merely to imitate demonstrated actions, but to act toward specifications absent from their training experience—shifting demonstration data from action imitation toward specification-conditioned competence.

title: An Affordable AI-Integrated Smart Cane for Multimodal Mobility Assistance of Visually Impaired Users
summary: Visual impairment affects over 2.2 billion people worldwide, yet conventional white canes cannot detect elevated hazards or provide semantic environmental context. Existing AI-assisted navigation systems typically rely on expensive hardware or cloud connectivity, limiting accessibility in resource-constrained settings. This paper presents an affordable (\$88 USD), fully offline AI-integrated smart cane designed for multimodal mobility assistance on an ultra-low-power Raspberry Pi Zero 2W. The system fuses RGB vision sensing with Time-of-Flight (ToF) distance estimation, pairing an INT8-quantized SSD MobileNet V1 model with distance-aware vibrotactile feedback and real-time audio alerts. To ensure operational robustness on constrained hardware, a multiprocessing architecture isolates sensor acquisition, neural inference, and haptic feedback into independent processes with fail-safe sensing support. Experimental evaluation across indoor mobility scenarios demonstrates a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.82 (precision: 0.85, recall: 0.81), a mean end-to-end latency of 330\,ms, and a peak power draw of 2.8\,W. A preliminary usability study with 12 participants (SUS: 78.5, NASA-TLX) demonstrated positive user perception and enhanced obstacle awareness. The proposed prototype validates the feasibility of deploying privacy-preserving, edge-native assistive intelligence for cost-sensitive mobility assistance.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an $88 fully offline AI smart cane running on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2W, fusing RGB vision with ToF distance sensing and INT8-quantized SSD MobileNet V1 to deliver distance-aware vibrotactile and audio alerts, achieving 0.82 macro-F1, 330 ms latency at 2.8 W peak power.
AI.motivation: Over 2.2 billion people have visual impairment, yet conventional white canes cannot detect elevated hazards or provide semantic environmental context. Existing AI-assisted navigation systems typically require expensive hardware or cloud connectivity, limiting accessibility in resource-constrained settings.
AI.method: An $88 fully offline smart cane on an ultra-low-power Raspberry Pi Zero 2W. It fuses RGB vision sensing with Time-of-Flight distance estimation, using an INT8-quantized SSD MobileNet V1 model with distance-aware vibrotactile feedback and real-time audio alerts. A multiprocessing architecture isolates sensor acquisition, neural inference, and haptic feedback into independent processes with fail-safe sensing support.
AI.result: Indoor mobility evaluation yields a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.82 (precision 0.85, recall 0.81), mean end-to-end latency of 330 ms, and peak power draw of 2.8 W. A preliminary usability study with 12 participants reported SUS 78.5 and NASA-TLX measures indicating positive user perception and enhanced obstacle awareness.
AI.conclusion: The prototype validates the feasibility of deploying privacy-preserving, edge-native assistive intelligence for cost-sensitive mobility assistance.

title: When Does Test-Time Physical Diagnosis Pay? A Frozen Policy Buys Evidence It Never Reads
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures
summary: When a robot faces unfamiliar physical conditions, a common approach is to collect evidence about what changed and adapt. For such diagnosis to improve behavior, six ordered empirical conditions must hold: a meaningful reference, identifiability of the physical condition, use of the acquired evidence, decision value, selection value over a fixed alternative, and safe realization. We test this chain in controlled and public environments. It holds end to end in our controlled environments. After transfer to unseen mechanisms, however, it breaks at evidence use. On decisions requiring the full trace, the frozen decoder does not change its choice. A linear model using only trace increments recovers the correct choice on mechanisms excluded from fitting, showing that the trace is informative but unused. The failure is concentrated at the richest evidence level: those decisions fall to chance, while decisions settled with lower-cost evidence remain correct, a split hidden by aggregate accuracy. The same chain can fail at other links in public environments. Successful physical identification therefore guarantees neither evidence use nor useful adaptation; evaluation should identify where the chain breaks rather than rely on recovery accuracy or aggregate performance alone.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a six-condition diagnostic chain for robot physical adaptation and shows it can break at the "evidence use" link after transfer, with failures masked by aggregate accuracy.
AI.motivation: Robots facing unfamiliar physical conditions typically collect evidence about what changed and adapt, but it is unclear whether such diagnosis actually improves behavior. The authors argue that effective diagnosis requires a specific ordered set of empirical conditions to hold, and that researchers currently rely on coarse metrics (recovery accuracy, aggregate performance) that cannot reveal where this process fails.
AI.method: The authors define six ordered empirical conditions: (1) a meaningful reference, (2) identifiability of the physical condition, (3) use of the acquired evidence, (4) decision value, (5) selection value over a fixed alternative, and (6) safe realization. They test this chain in controlled and public environments. To localize the failure, they compare a frozen decoder's choices on decisions requiring the full trace against a linear model using only trace increments, on mechanisms excluded from fitting.
AI.result: In controlled environments the chain holds end to end, but after transfer to unseen mechanisms it breaks at evidence use: on decisions requiring the full trace, the frozen decoder does not change its choice. A linear model using only trace increments recovers the correct choice on held-out mechanisms, indicating the trace is informative but unused. The failure concentrates at the richest evidence level: those decisions fall to chance, while decisions settled with lower-cost evidence remain correct—a split hidden by aggregate accuracy. In public environments, the same chain can fail at other links.
AI.conclusion: Successful physical identification guarantees neither evidence use nor useful adaptation. Evaluation should identify where the diagnostic chain breaks rather than relying on recovery accuracy or aggregate performance alone.

title: PAANI : On Device Visual Evidence Fusion and Explainable Guidance for River Robot Simulation
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 11 tables. Includes system and AI architecture diagrams, model-training results, qualitative evaluations, and Arduino UNO Q deployment measurements. Project code, trained models, ONNX artifacts, logs, and reproducibility documentation are available at https://github.com/immanuelihs/ASV_PAANI
summary: Mobile river monitoring robots must interpret obstacles and water boundaries that geographic waypoints alone cannot describe. On resource constrained platforms, converting imperfect visual predictions into timely and inspectable guidance is a distinct challenge. An object label or steering command does not explain which evidence supports a decision or when that evidence is unreliable. We present PAANI, an on-device perception to guidance architecture that combines a project trained YOLO11n detector and a custom MobileNetV3 Small semantic segmenter with timestamp aligned evidence fusion on Arduino UNO Q. Bounded tracking supplies object persistence, while an explicit corridor policy combines surface labels, accepted detections, urgency and mask uncertainty. Each final advisory exposes its contributing evidence and policy reasons. ROS 2 interfaces connect the local AI pipeline to a separate Gazebo vessel, localization and control testbed. Training uses 10,000 WaterScenes images for four-class detection and 1,127 MaSTr1325 images for segmentation, including 198 segmentation validation images. The selected FP32 ONNX models occupy 14.817 MB. Detector checkpoint test mAP at 0.5 IoU is 0.7388, while the separately evaluated rectangular ONNX export achieves validation mAP at 0.5 IoU of 0.7367. Segmentation ONNX validation mIoU is 0.9750. A five-minute UNO Q recording produced median and 95th percentile pipeline latencies of 467.8 ms and 580.3 ms at a configured 0.5 Hz cadence. The evaluation also identifies black input misclassification and a sampling rate mismatch that prevents the diagnostic apparent motion estimator from collecting sufficient evidence. These results support an inspectable and reusable edge robotics foundation while clearly distinguishing model accuracy and on-board execution from validated on-water collision avoidance.

AI.tldr: PAANI is an on-device perception-to-guidance architecture for mobile river monitoring robots, fusing a YOLO11n detector and MobileNetV3-Small segmenter with timestamp-aligned evidence fusion and an inspectable corridor policy on Arduino UNO Q, achieving mAP@0.5 of 0.7388 and mIoU of 0.9750 with median pipeline latency of 467.8 ms.

Training uses 10,000 WaterScenes images for four-class detection and 1,127 MaSTr1325 images for segmentation, including 198 segmentation validation images.

Detector checkpoint test mAP at 0.5 IoU is 0.7388, while the separately evaluated rectangular ONNX export achieves validation mAP at 0.5 IoU of 0.7367. Segmentation ONNX validation mIoU is 0.9750. title: EditWM: Event-Decomposed World Modeling with Incremental Correction for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: World models support autonomous driving by predicting the scene evolution associated with candidate trajectories. Driving dynamics differ in predictability, motivating a distinction between regular evolution and event-induced deviations that call for selective correction. We propose EditWM, a world model that decomposes future prediction into normal evolution and event-driven incremental correction in compact visual feature space. A trajectory-conditioned normal predictor provides the base forecast and is then frozen for correction learning. A correction decoder compares this forecast with observation history and planned actions, producing a bounded feature update whose contribution is regulated by a learned gate. The corrected future features condition trajectory scoring through candidate-specific cross-attention, linking world modeling to plan selection. At inference, EditWM uses only past and current observations, ego state, and candidate trajectories. Across all 12,146 NAVSIM navtest scenes, expert-trajectory-conditioned evaluation shows a 5.35\% reduction in future-feature MSE over Normal, with improvements in 83.54\% of scenes. The system achieves 91.05 EPDMS on a 100-point scale using the official EPDMS evaluator. These results demonstrate improved future-feature prediction and competitive trajectory selection when corrected future representations are integrated into planning.

AI.tldr: EditWM is a world model for autonomous driving that decomposes future prediction into a frozen normal-evolution predictor plus a gated event-driven correction module in compact visual feature space, improving future-feature prediction and trajectory selection on NAVSIM.
AI.motivation: Driving dynamics differ in predictability: most scene evolution is regular, but event-induced deviations require selective correction. Treating all future evolution uniformly is suboptimal, motivating a decomposition into base evolution and event-driven deviation.
AI.method: The model splits future prediction into normal evolution and event-driven incremental correction in compact visual feature space. A trajectory-conditioned normal predictor yields the base forecast and is then frozen for correction learning. A correction decoder compares the forecast against observation history and planned actions to produce a bounded feature update, regulated by a learned gate. Corrected future features condition trajectory scoring via candidate-specific cross-attention, linking world modeling to plan selection. Inference uses only past/current observations, ego state, and candidate trajectories.
AI.result: On all 12,146 NAVSIM navtest scenes, expert-trajectory-conditioned evaluation shows a 5.35% reduction in future-feature MSE over the Normal baseline, with improvements in 83.54% of scenes. The system reaches 91.05 EPDMS (100-point scale) under the official EPDMS evaluator.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing future prediction into frozen normal evolution plus gated event-driven correction improves future-feature prediction, and integrating corrected future representations into planning yields competitive trajectory selection.

title: Social Influence and the Allocation of Scientific Attention in AI Populations
summary: AI systems are becoming participants in the evaluation and use of scientific research. They encounter citation counts, download statistics and lists of popular articles developed around human readers, but the collective consequences of these signals for artificial readers remain uncertain. This paper adapts the Music Lab design to a market for academic attention. In the first experiment, 1,000 AI agents choose papers from the titles and abstracts of all 114 regular research articles published in the American Economic Review in 2025. The experiment has five independent-choice communities and five social-influence communities, each with 100 sequential agents. Only agents in the social-influence condition observe earlier selections within their community. Agents may select any number of papers. Social-information communities select 17.2 percent fewer papers per agent, concentrate their choices more heavily, and collectively cover 73 papers, compared with 90 independently. Between-community variation is greater under social information. In a second experiment with 200 agents across twenty social communities, randomly assigning papers five initial selections raises their subsequent selection rate by 45.55 percentage points (95% CI: 41.20 to 49.90). Choices have modest correspondence with external citations and little correspondence with download counts. The results show how a simple information rule shapes the volume, breadth and distribution of scientific attention in an artificial population.

AI.tldr: Adapting the Music Lab design to academic attention, 1,000 AI agents selected from 114 AER 2025 articles. Social-influence communities chose 17.2% fewer papers per agent, concentrated choices more, and covered fewer papers (73 vs. 90) than independent communities. Randomly seeding papers with five initial selections raised their subsequent selection rate by 45.55 percentage points. Choices showed modest correspondence with external citations and little with downloads.
AI.motivation: AI systems are increasingly participating in the evaluation and use of scientific research, yet they encounter attention signals (citation counts, download statistics, popularity lists) developed for human readers. The collective consequences of these signals for artificial readers remain uncertain, motivating a controlled study of how social information shapes AI-driven attention allocation in science.
AI.method: The study adapts the Music Lab design to a market for academic attention. Experiment 1: 1,000 AI agents chose papers from the titles and abstracts of all 114 regular research articles published in the American Economic Review in 2025, divided into five independent-choice communities and five social-influence communities, each with 100 sequential agents; only social-influence agents observed earlier selections within their community, and agents could select any number of papers. Experiment 2: 200 agents across twenty social communities, where randomly assigning papers five initial selections tested the effect on subsequent selection rates.
AI.result: Social-information communities selected 17.2 percent fewer papers per agent, concentrated choices more heavily, and collectively covered 73 papers versus 90 under independence. Between-community variation was greater under social information. In Experiment 2, randomly assigning five initial selections raised subsequent selection rates by 45.55 percentage points (95% CI: 41.20 to 49.90). Choices corresponded modestly with external citations and little with download counts.
AI.conclusion: A simple information rule—observation of others' choices—shapes the volume, breadth, and distribution of scientific attention in an artificial population, reducing per-agent volume, increasing concentration, narrowing collective coverage, and amplifying early-selection advantages through a strong social-influence effect.

title: Embedding Physics Priors in Robot Learning: A Survey
summary: The rapid progress of artificial intelligence is reshaping robotics and accelerating the adoption of learning-based approaches. While purely data-driven methods have achieved remarkable success in computer vision and natural language processing, robotics remains constrained by limited data, complex real-world interactions, and the need for reliable operation. These challenges have motivated the exploration of physics-embedded robot learning, which embeds physics priors into learning algorithms. By encoding the underlying physical laws and constraints, physics priors can complement limited data with robotics-specific inductive biases, potentially improving generalization, interpretability, and sample efficiency. However, the literature on physics-embedded robot learning remains fragmented across terminology, methodologies, and application domains, making it difficult to assess this growing body of work. This survey reviews physics-embedded robot learning across a broad range of physics priors, robotics applications, and machine learning models, from single-layer perceptrons to generative foundation models. We adopt a unified taxonomy that classifies existing approaches according to their physics embedding: physics-guided inputs, data, and representations; physics-encoded model architectures; and physics-informed training loss functions. Building on this taxonomy, we review methods for robot dynamics learning, trajectory planning, prediction, control, and estimation, together with the corresponding open-source software ecosystem. We identify key open challenges, and outline promising future research directions. Overall, we argue that physics priors provide a particularly relevant robotics-specific inductive bias, complementing rather than replacing data-driven learning, and paving the way toward more generalizable, data-efficient, and trustworthy robotic systems.

AI.tldr: This survey reviews physics-embedded robot learning, proposing a unified taxonomy that classifies approaches by how physics is embedded—via guided inputs/data/representations, encoded model architectures, or informed training losses—and covers methods, applications, software, and open challenges.
AI.motivation: Purely data-driven learning excels in vision and NLP but is constrained in robotics by limited data, complex real-world interactions, and reliability requirements. Physics-embedded robot learning embeds physics priors as robotics-specific inductive biases to improve generalization, interpretability, and sample efficiency, but the literature is fragmented across terminology, methodologies, and application domains, hindering assessment.
AI.method: A survey adopting a unified taxonomy classifying existing approaches by their physics embedding: (1) physics-guided inputs, data, and representations; (2) physics-encoded model architectures; and (3) physics-informed training loss functions. The review spans a broad range of physics priors, robotics applications, and machine learning models—from single-layer perceptrons to generative foundation models.
AI.result: The survey reviews methods for robot dynamics learning, trajectory planning, prediction, control, and estimation, along with the corresponding open-source software ecosystem, organized under the proposed taxonomy.
AI.conclusion: Physics priors serve as a particularly relevant robotics-specific inductive bias that complements rather than replaces data-driven learning, paving the way toward more generalizable, data-efficient, and trustworthy robotic systems. Key open challenges are identified and promising future research directions are outlined.

title: Learning 3D biophysical cell properties from 2D images and cell-population statistics
summary: Inferring 3D cellular properties from 2D microscopy is difficult when a reference instrument reports only population statistics rather than labels for individual cells. Here we develop a population-supervised framework that maps single 2D red-cell images to latent biophysical quantities and aggregates them to mean corpuscular volume, red-cell distribution width and mean corpuscular haemoglobin. The model combines shared local inference, a biophysically structured decoder for volume and haemoglobin, learned instance weighting and device-specific calibration. We formalise conditions under which aggregate observations identify restricted instance predictors, show why population agreement does not by itself identify single-cell properties or 3D geometry, and derive the dispersion penalty induced by subset mean matching. The development dataset comprises 390 specimens and 1,105 acquisitions across six devices, with reported Pearson correlations of 0.86--0.98 against a Sysmex analyser. The framework provides a testable route from 2D images and population supervision to 3D cellular biophysics without claiming explicit 3D reconstruction.

AI.tldr: A population-supervised framework maps single 2D red-cell images to latent biophysical quantities and aggregates them to match analyser-reported population statistics (MCV, RDW, MCH), achieving Pearson correlations of 0.86–0.98 across six devices, while formally clarifying what such aggregate supervision can and cannot identify at the single-cell level.
AI.motivation: Inferring 3D cellular properties from 2D microscopy is challenging when the reference instrument provides only population-level statistics rather than per-cell labels. Standard supervised learning is therefore unavailable, yet clinically relevant biophysical quantities such as mean corpuscular volume, red-cell distribution width and mean corpuscular haemoglobin remain desirable endpoints.
AI.method: The model couples shared local inference over single 2D red-cell images with a biophysically structured decoder for volume and haemoglobin, learned instance weighting, and device-specific calibration. It is trained under population-level supervision, i.e. matching subset means to reported aggregate values. The authors formalise conditions under which aggregate observations identify restricted instance predictors, analyse the limits of population agreement (it does not by itself identify single-cell properties or 3D geometry), and derive the dispersion penalty induced by subset mean matching.
AI.result: Evaluated on 390 specimens and 1,105 acquisitions spanning six devices, the framework reports Pearson correlations of 0.86–0.98 against a Sysmex analyser for the aggregated indices.
AI.conclusion: Population supervision offers a testable route from 2D images to 3D cellular biophysics without claiming explicit 3D reconstruction, provided the identifiability conditions and dispersion penalty are taken into account.

title: ReliCAD: From Uncertain LLM Generation to Reliable Parametric CAD Modeling
summary: Large language models have shown considerable potential for natural-language-driven parametric CAD modeling. However, a fundamental contradiction exists between their probabilistic generation and the deterministic requirements of CAD modeling, resulting in limitations in reliability, design-intent preservation, and geometric validity. Existing methods typically rely on large-scale annotated datasets, lack explicit modeling of design intent, and underutilize the deterministic capabilities of CAD kernels. To address these limitations, we propose ReliCAD, a unified framework that transforms uncertain LLM generation into reliable parametric CAD modeling. Through explicit design-intent modeling, ReliCAD converts user requirements into structured design specifications and explicitly models geometric relations, topological dependencies, and feature construction order. It then generates constraint-aware parametric instructions and invokes the CAD kernel through an Agent-ready API to perform geometric construction and constraint solving. ReliCAD further records runtime evidence and employs a verification-feedback mechanism to assess consistency between the generated model and the design specifications, enabling error localization and iterative repair. Experiments on the public HistCAD generation dataset and our multi-granularity CAD editing dataset demonstrate that ReliCAD significantly outperforms baseline methods, achieving 99.8\% validity rate and 0.8753 IoU. ReliCAD provides a verifiable, repairable, and generalizable approach to natural-language-interactive CAD modeling.

AI.tldr: ReliCAD is a unified framework that converts uncertain LLM generation into reliable parametric CAD modeling via explicit design-intent modeling, constraint-aware instruction generation, CAD-kernel invocation, and a verification-feedback repair loop, achieving 99.8% validity and 0.8753 IoU.
AI.motivation: LLMs show promise for natural-language-driven parametric CAD modeling, but a fundamental contradiction exists between their probabilistic generation and CAD's deterministic requirements, causing limitations in reliability, design-intent preservation, and geometric validity. Existing methods rely on large-scale annotated datasets, lack explicit design-intent modeling, and underutilize deterministic CAD-kernel capabilities.
AI.method: ReliCAD performs explicit design-intent modeling by converting user requirements into structured design specifications that explicitly model geometric relations, topological dependencies, and feature construction order. It then generates constraint-aware parametric instructions and invokes the CAD kernel through an Agent-ready API for geometric construction and constraint solving. Runtime evidence is recorded, and a verification-feedback mechanism assesses consistency between the generated model and design specifications, enabling error localization and iterative repair.
AI.result: On the public HistCAD generation dataset and a multi-granularity CAD editing dataset, ReliCAD significantly outperforms baseline methods, achieving a 99.8% validity rate and 0.8753 IoU.
AI.conclusion: ReliCAD provides a verifiable, repairable, and generalizable approach to natural-language-interactive CAD modeling, effectively bridging probabilistic LLM generation and deterministic CAD requirements.

title: Goal-driven Variant Categorization
summary: Process discovery rarely yields a single coherent process structure. For analysis, a common step is to cluster process variants based on structural similarity and then assign business meaning to the resulting groups. Since these partitions are not derived from the organization's goals, analysts must manually interpret and consolidate variants into business-meaningful categories. This judgment-intensive step becomes increasingly difficult as the number and complexity of variants grow. In this paper, we propose a goal-driven approach to variant categorization that reverses this workflow. We first author an organization's goal model that predefines the categorization axis. Each variant is transformed into a textual narrative describing its behavior, and a Large Language Model (LLM) interprets it in the context of the goal model and assigns the variant to the most appropriate category. LLM-based semantic reasoning connects low-level process behavior with analyst-defined business goals. We instantiate this approach end-to-end and evaluate it on three public logs differing substantially in scale and behavioral diversity. Goal-model guidance yields partitions that differ from those produced by unguided induction and respond to controlled edits to the declared alternatives, at the cost of authoring a goal model.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a goal-driven approach to process variant categorization that reverses the traditional workflow: instead of clustering variants first and interpreting them manually, analysts author a goal model that predefines the categorization axis, variants are converted to textual narratives, and an LLM assigns each variant to a business-meaningful category using the goal model as context.
AI.motivation: Process discovery rarely produces a single coherent process structure, so a common analysis step is clustering variants by structural similarity and then manually assigning business meaning. However, these partitions are not derived from organizational goals, so analysts must interpret and consolidate variants into business-meaningful categories. This judgment-intensive step becomes increasingly difficult as the number and complexity of variants grow.
AI.method: The approach is goal-driven and reverses the usual workflow. First, an organization's goal model is authored to predefine the categorization axis. Each process variant is transformed into a textual narrative describing its behavior. A Large Language Model then interprets the narrative in the context of the goal model and assigns the variant to the most appropriate category. LLM-based semantic reasoning thereby connects low-level process behavior with analyst-defined business goals. The approach is instantiated end-to-end.
AI.result: The approach is evaluated on three public logs that differ substantially in scale and behavioral diversity. Goal-model guidance yields partitions that differ from those produced by unguided induction and respond to controlled edits to the declared alternatives, at the cost of authoring a goal model.
AI.conclusion: Goal-model-guided LLM categorization can produce business-meaningful process variant partitions that are sensitive to the declared goals and alternatives, offering a feasible alternative to manual interpretation, though it requires the upfront effort of authoring a goal model.

title: AffordanceWAM: Affordance-Aware Joint World-Action Modeling for Robot Manipulation
summary: Generalizable robot manipulation requires predicting how a scene will evolve, identifying where interactions are feasible, and determining how to act. Action-labeled robot videos directly supervise control but are costly and limited in diversity, whereas egocentric human videos capture diverse interactions but lack robot actions and differ in embodiment and appearance. We introduce AffordanceWAM, an affordance-aware generative World Action Model that represents object-centric spatiotemporal affordance through Scalar Affordance and Affordance Heatmap, within the generated future World. This representation grounds visual prediction in task-relevant objects and interaction regions for action generation, and provides shared interaction targets across human and robot videos. Built on a pretrained video diffusion Transformer, AffordanceWAM uses separately parameterized World and Action Experts, coupled through Masked Joint Self-Attention, to jointly predict future RGB observations, Scalar Affordance fields, Affordance Heatmaps, and continuous robot actions under a unified flow-matching objective. Human videos supervise all three future-World streams, whereas robot trajectories additionally provide action supervision, enabling transfer without human action labels or retargeting. Experiments on RoboCasa, CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D, and real-world manipulation demonstrate consistent gains over RGB-only and robot-data-only baselines. Under fixed robot supervision, RoboCasa performance improves monotonically as affordance-annotated human video scales. These results support affordance as an effective interface for both vision-language-action learning and human-to-robot transfer.

AI.tldr: AffordanceWAM is an affordance-aware generative World Action Model that jointly predicts future RGB, Scalar Affordance, Affordance Heatmaps, and robot actions via a video diffusion Transformer with World and Action Experts, enabling human-to-robot transfer without action labels or retargeting.
AI.motivation: Generalizable robot manipulation requires predicting scene evolution, identifying feasible interaction regions, and determining actions. Action-labeled robot videos provide direct control supervision but are costly and limited in diversity, while egocentric human videos offer diverse interactions but lack robot actions and differ in embodiment and appearance.
AI.method: AffordanceWAM represents object-centric spatiotemporal affordance via Scalar Affordance and Affordance Heatmap within a generated future World, grounding visual prediction in task-relevant objects and interaction regions and providing shared interaction targets across human and robot videos. Built on a pretrained video diffusion Transformer, it uses separately parameterized World and Action Experts coupled through Masked Joint Self-Attention to jointly predict future RGB observations, Scalar Affordance fields, Affordance Heatmaps, and continuous robot actions under a unified flow-matching objective. Human videos supervise the three future-World streams, while robot trajectories additionally provide action supervision.
AI.result: On RoboCasa, CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D, and real-world manipulation, AffordanceWAM achieves consistent gains over RGB-only and robot-data-only baselines. Under fixed robot supervision, RoboCasa performance improves monotonically as affordance-annotated human video scales.
AI.conclusion: Affordance serves as an effective interface for both vision-language-action learning and human-to-robot transfer, enabling transfer without human action labels or retargeting.

title: Replication Without Persistence in Hosted LLMs: Measurement Sensitivity in Action-Time Belief Evaluation
summary: Behavioural evaluations of hosted language models can vary because the evaluated service, the measurement instrument, or both differ across runs. We separate three validation questions: whether a prior finding recurs on fresh data under its historical configuration (replication), whether the endpoint changes when the evaluation-and-inference configuration is rebuilt under the same identifier (measurement sensitivity), and whether the finding persists across subsequently tested identifiers under one common instrument (persistence). We study these questions in Regent Chess, a sequential environment in which a hidden, mutable state is recorded exactly, allowing stated beliefs to be scored against ground truth at action time; positive endpoint values mean worse performance than a matched-uniform comparator. The previously reported Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite deficit recurs on fresh games under its historical configuration (+0.0530, 95% CI [+0.0329,+0.0714]). In a back-to-back same-day H/R comparison under the same public identifier, the model-minus-uniform endpoint is 0.0429 lower under the rebuilt configuration (95% CI for the H-minus-R contrast [+0.0182,+0.0667]); all six configuration components vary jointly, so no component is isolated. Under rebuilt R, the prospectively frozen, interleaved same-window 4K comparison reverses sign between Gemini 3.1 and Gemini 3.7, identifiers that differ in release and product tier; additional descriptive and exploratory cells show the same directional pattern. Any additional serving-period contribution remains unresolved (-0.0166, [-0.0483,+0.0157]). Replication, measurement sensitivity, and persistence can therefore yield different conclusions within one evaluation, motivating explicit indexing of hosted-model behavioural claims by tested identifier, serving period, measurement instrument, and inference configuration.

AI.tldr: Hosted-LM behavioural evaluations conflate three validation questions—replication, measurement sensitivity, and persistence—which are dissociated empirically in the Regent Chess environment: a prior deficit replicates (+0.0530), the endpoint shifts under a rebuilt configuration of the same identifier (H−R contrast +0.0182 to +0.0667, 0.0429 lower under rebuilt R), and the 4K comparison reverses sign between two identifiers.
AI.motivation: Behavioural evaluations of hosted language models can vary because the evaluated service, the measurement instrument, or both differ across runs, so a single "reproduction" claim cannot distinguish a genuine prior finding from an artefact of a changed endpoint. The paper argues that this ambiguity must be decomposed into distinct validation questions rather than collapsed into one.
AI.method: The authors use Regent Chess, a sequential environment with a hidden mutable state recorded exactly, enabling stated beliefs to be scored against ground truth at action time; positive endpoint values indicate worse performance than a matched-uniform comparator. They separate three questions: replication (prior finding on fresh data under its historical configuration), measurement sensitivity (endpoint change when the evaluation-and-inference configuration is rebuilt under the same identifier), and persistence (finding across subsequently tested identifiers under one common instrument). Design features include a back-to-back same-day H/R comparison under the same public identifier, a prospectively frozen interleaved same-window 4K comparison, and descriptive/exploratory cells.
AI.result: The previously reported Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite deficit recurs on fresh games under its historical configuration (+0.0530, 95% CI [+0.0329, +0.0714]). In the same-day H/R comparison under one public identifier, the model-minus-uniform endpoint is 0.0429 lower under the rebuilt configuration (95% CI for the H−R contrast [+0.0182, +0.0667]); all six configuration components vary jointly, so no component is isolated. Under rebuilt R, the prospectively frozen interleaved same-window 4K comparison reverses sign between Gemini 3.1 and Gemini 3.7, identifiers differing in release and product tier, with additional descriptive and exploratory cells showing the same directional pattern. Any additional serving-period contribution remains unresolved (−0.0166, [−0.0483, +0.0157]).
AI.conclusion: Replication, measurement sensitivity, and persistence can yield different conclusions within a single evaluation, so hosted-model behavioural claims should be explicitly indexed by tested identifier, serving period, measurement instrument, and inference configuration.

title: Active Spatial Inspection for Effective and Efficient Embodied Exploration
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures, journal
summary: Achieving high task success and efficiency remains a central pursuit in embodied exploration. Existing frameworks typically guide agent behavior through a spatially coarse and indirect assessment of suggestive cues and directions, yet such designs may struggle to judge cue sufficiency and the need for further inspection, leading to early termination or excessive continuation and ultimately reducing task success and efficiency. This work rethinks embodied exploration from a spatially explicit standpoint and introduces the spatial-inspection-guided ACtive Exploration (ACE) framework coupling evidence-grounded perception with exposure-informed movement and establishing a spatially resolved decision paradigm. Evidence-grounded perception strengthens inferential validity by integrating granular localization with focused verification, turning suggestive cues into precise decisive visual support. Exposure-informed movement promotes directional judgment through prospective prioritization and retrospective suppression, selecting promising directions for efficient spatial progress. ACE alleviates the tension between preventing early termination and avoiding unnecessary continuation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ACE achieves 18.0% higher navigation task success and 10.3% higher exploration efficiency for question answering than prior state-of-the-art baselines, advancing effective and efficient embodied exploration.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ACE, a spatial-inspection-guided active exploration framework that replaces coarse cue-based guidance with spatially explicit decision-making, improving navigation success and exploration efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing embodied exploration frameworks guide agents using spatially coarse and indirect suggestive cues and directions. Such designs often fail to judge cue sufficiency and whether further inspection is needed, causing early termination or excessive continuation, which lowers task success and efficiency.
AI.method: ACE couples evidence-grounded perception with exposure-informed movement under a spatially resolved decision paradigm. Evidence-grounded perception integrates granular localization with focused verification to convert suggestive cues into precise decisive visual support. Exposure-informed movement performs prospective prioritization and retrospective suppression to select promising directions for efficient spatial progress.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show ACE achieves 18.0% higher navigation task success and 10.3% higher exploration efficiency for question answering compared with prior state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: By establishing a spatially explicit exploration paradigm, ACE mitigates the tension between premature termination and unnecessary continuation, advancing effective and efficient embodied exploration.

title: The Wisdom of Artificial Deliberative Crowds
summary: The aggregation of many lay estimates often outperforms individual expert judgment, a phenomenon known as the wisdom of crowds. While this is usually attributed to the independence of estimates, an even stronger effect arises through deliberation: averaging the consensus estimates of small deliberating groups outperforms the classical wisdom of crowds, with individual judgments themselves also becoming more accurate after deliberation. Whether these improvements transfer to large language models deliberating amongst themselves is unknown. Here we adapt a three-stage deliberation paradigm previously used with human participants for use with large language models from three different families, and test it across four domains of increasing real-world stakes: visual numerical estimation (Study 1), peer review of machine-learning papers (Study 2), detection of hidden malicious behavior by an artificial intelligence agent (Study 3), and sports forecasting against a real prediction market (Study 4). Across domains, deliberation reduced collective error beyond passive aggregation of independent responses, and post-deliberation individual judgments retained this collective gain. Notably, the advantage required model diversity: groups composed of clones of a single model did not benefit from deliberating. These results establish machine deliberation as a general-purpose aggregation mechanism, and point to diversity as an active ingredient.

AI.tldr: Deliberation among diverse large language models reduces collective error beyond passive aggregation, replicating the "wisdom of crowds" effect but only when models are non-identical.
AI.motivation: Human deliberation within small groups outperforms classical wisdom-of-crowds aggregation by producing more accurate consensus and individual judgments. It was unknown whether such deliberative gains transfer to large language models deliberating among themselves, and what conditions drive them.
AI.method: The authors adapted a three-stage deliberation paradigm, originally designed for human participants, for LLMs drawn from three different model families. They evaluated it across four domains of increasing real-world stakes: visual numerical estimation, peer review of machine-learning papers, detection of hidden malicious behavior by an AI agent, and sports forecasting benchmarked against a real prediction market.
AI.result: Across all domains, deliberation reduced collective error beyond passive aggregation of independent responses, and post-deliberation individual judgments retained the collective gain. Crucially, the advantage depended on model diversity: groups consisting of clones of a single model showed no benefit from deliberation.
AI.conclusion: Machine deliberation constitutes a general-purpose aggregation mechanism, with model diversity acting as an active ingredient required for its benefit.

title: Behavior Trees for Robotic Systems: An Empirical Study on Practices and Experiences
comment: 54 pages, 13 figures, journal
summary: Over the last decade, behavior trees (BT) have become one of the dominant behavior models for coordinating missions of robotic systems. Yet empirical evidence on BT adoption in real-world contexts remains limited, especially regarding practitioners experiences and practices. Without practitioner-grounded evidence from both academic and industrial settings, the research community risks developing guidelines and tools that are plausible in principle but only partly aligned with real challenges. This scarcity of evidence leads to ad-hoc practices, impeding software reuse, maintenance, and evolution. This paper reports a mixed-methods study combining a technical action research investigation at an automotive company with a survey of 34 robotics practitioners. Our results indicate that BTs improve team communication and the understandability of robotic decision-making logic, reflecting BTs practical value beyond mission coordination. At the same time, practitioners face multiple non-trivial design and integration decisions, complicated by the lack of adequate guidelines and tool support. These decisions span architectural and language choices when implementing BTs and integrating them within ROS, for which we report observed patterns. Additionally, practitioners faced multi-factor granularity decisions and mixed experiences with current libraries. For the most used BT libraries, they reported implementation challenges and documentation gaps. Regarding planning algorithms, practitioners find deciding optimal BT node ordering challenging. Views on scalability remained inconclusive, and limitations in current libraries and practices hinder broader adoption. We conclude with cross-cutting observations and implications for both practitioners adopting BTs in robotic systems and researchers aiming to advance empirical understanding of BT adoption.

AI.tldr: A mixed-methods study (technical action research at an automotive company + survey of 34 robotics practitioners) examining how behavior trees (BTs) are actually adopted in practice, revealing practical benefits alongside significant design, integration, and tooling challenges.
AI.motivation: Behavior trees have become a dominant model for coordinating robotic missions, yet empirical evidence on their real-world adoption—particularly practitioners' experiences and practices—remains scarce. Without practitioner-grounded evidence from academic and industrial settings, the research community risks producing guidelines and tools that are plausible in principle but misaligned with real challenges, leading to ad-hoc practices that impede software reuse, maintenance, and evolution.
AI.method: A mixed-methods study combining a technical action research investigation at an automotive company with a survey of 34 robotics practitioners.
AI.result: BTs improve team communication and the understandability of robotic decision-making logic, showing value beyond mission coordination. However, practitioners face non-trivial design and integration decisions, worsened by inadequate guidelines and tool support. These span architectural and language choices for implementing BTs and integrating them within ROS (with reported patterns), multi-factor granularity decisions, and mixed experiences with current libraries. For the most-used BT libraries, practitioners reported implementation challenges and documentation gaps. For planning algorithms, deciding optimal BT node ordering was found challenging. Views on scalability remained inconclusive, and limitations in current libraries and practices hinder broader adoption.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers cross-cutting observations and implications for both practitioners adopting BTs in robotic systems and researchers aiming to advance empirical understanding of BT adoption, highlighting the need for better guidelines and tool support to overcome current barriers to broader adoption.

title: Agreement Overstates Evidence: Error Dependence in LLM Judge Consensus
summary: Consensus among LLM judges is often taken as strong evidence that a decision is correct. This assumes that judges make their errors independently. In practice, LLM judges are often trained and evaluated in similar ways, so they can make the same mistakes. We study how this dependency affects the reliability of consensus. We find substantial error correlation across both open-weight and frontier LLM judges. In our main bank of ten judges, the average pairwise correlation between judge errors is 0.21. As a result, the ten judges only provide roughly as much statistical information as 3.5 independent judges. The dependency is even stronger among the high-accuracy frontier judges we evaluate, including judges from different providers. In up to 28% of our comparisons, ignoring shared errors leads to the conclusion that one system is significantly better, while accounting for them does not. We also find that the pattern of errors matters. Errors shared by most judges and errors concentrated among a smaller group affect consensus differently and favor different voting methods. Measuring the overall amount of correlation alone is therefore insufficient. Our results suggest a simple approach: use a small set of trusted examples to estimate judge accuracy and identify shared mistakes. These shared errors should then be considered when analyzing the results, and the voting method should be chosen using trusted examples before it is applied to new data.

AI.tldr: LLM judge errors are substantially correlated (avg. pairwise 0.21), so ten judges carry only ~3.5 judges' worth of independent information; ignoring this shared-error structure flips significance conclusions in up to 28% of comparisons.
AI.motivation: Consensus among LLM judges is commonly treated as strong evidence of correctness, under the assumption that judges err independently. In reality, LLM judges are trained and evaluated similarly, so they may share the same mistakes, undermining the reliability of consensus-based decisions.
AI.method: The authors empirically measure error correlation across open-weight and frontier LLM judges (a main bank of ten judges), quantify the effective number of independent judges implied by the observed correlation, and compare significance conclusions with and without accounting for shared errors. They also analyze how the pattern of errors (errors shared by most judges vs. concentrated among a few) interacts with consensus and voting-method choice, and propose using a small set of trusted examples to estimate judge accuracy and identify shared mistakes.
AI.result: Substantial error correlation is found across judges; the average pairwise error correlation in the main bank of ten judges is 0.21, giving them the statistical information of only ~3.5 independent judges. Correlation is stronger among high-accuracy frontier judges, including those from different providers. In up to 28% of comparisons, ignoring shared errors yields the conclusion that one system is significantly better, while accounting for them does not. The pattern of errors also matters: broadly shared errors and more concentrated errors affect consensus differently and favor different voting methods, so the overall amount of correlation alone is insufficient.
AI.conclusion: LLM judge consensus should not be assumed to reflect independent evidence. A simple recommended approach is to use a small set of trusted examples to estimate judge accuracy and identify shared mistakes, account for these shared errors in the analysis, and select the voting method using trusted examples before applying it to new data.

title: VLPSA: Vision-Language-Poisson-Safe Actions for Full-Body Safety of Learned Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable increasingly general-purpose robotic manipulation, but such learned policies do not provide safety guarantees for collision avoidance---especially in environments outside of training distributions. This work presents Vision-Language-Poisson-Safe Actions (VLPSA), a safety filtering framework that provides full-body safety for VLA policies in cluttered and dynamic environments without retraining. VLPSA synthesizes Poisson Safety Functions (PSF) online from perception data, yielding a Control Barrier Function (CBF) that is enforced through a CBF-QP safety filter over the full body and any grasped object, treated as an extension of the final robot link. To enable real-time deployment while maintaining fine spatial resolution in critical task regions, VLPSA combines dual resolutions of this PSF using Boolean CBF compositions. We evaluate VLPSA on SafeLIBERO against safety-filtering baselines, where it achieves the highest collision avoidance rate among the evaluated methods, increasing collision avoidance from 23.1% for the base $π_{0.5}$ policy to 91.2% while surpassing its task success rate. We further deploy VLPSA on a Franka FR3 in cluttered scenes with dynamic obstacles and human interference, demonstrating real-time full-body safety during manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: VLPSA is a retraining-free safety filtering framework that provides full-body collision avoidance for VLA manipulation policies via online-synthesized Poisson Safety Functions enforced through a CBF-QP filter.
AI.motivation: Learned VLA policies enable general-purpose manipulation but offer no collision-avoidance guarantees, particularly in out-of-distribution environments. Existing safety must be added without retraining while preserving task performance.
AI.method: VLPSA synthesizes Poisson Safety Functions online from perception data to yield a Control Barrier Function. This is enforced via a CBF-QP safety filter over the full body and any grasped object (treated as an extension of the final robot link). Dual resolutions of the PSF are combined using Boolean CBF compositions to achieve real-time deployment while preserving fine spatial resolution in critical regions.
AI.result: On SafeLIBERO, VLPSA achieves the highest collision avoidance rate among evaluated baselines, raising avoidance from 23.1% (base π0.5 policy) to 91.2%, while exceeding the base task success rate. Real-time full-body safety is also demonstrated on a Franka FR3 in cluttered scenes with dynamic obstacles and human interference.
AI.conclusion: VLPSA delivers retraining-free, real-time full-body safety for VLA policies in cluttered and dynamic environments, improving collision avoidance without sacrificing task success.

title: IntLawNER: A Named Entity Recognition Dataset and Benchmark in International Law
summary: International law provides the normative framework through which states coordinate action, regulate armed conflict, and protect human rights, yet its texts remain without token-level named entity recognition (NER) resources. We introduce IntLawNER, a NER dataset and benchmark for codified sources of international law, covering 2,987 gold-annotated sentences and 8,094 entity spans from International Court of Justice (ICJ) decisions, UN Security Council resolutions, and European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) judgments, annotated with seven institution-specific entity types. We construct IntLawNER with a cost-effective hybrid algorithmic-agentic pipeline that reduces 468k source sentences to a compact annotation set through candidate retrieval, LLM-based vetting, and human review, with 89.6% of gold spans accepted unchanged from the silver layer. However, the silver-to-gold analysis reveals that human-machine aggregate agreement metrics can be misleading in domain-specific NER: Cohen's kappa=0.964 on boundary-matched spans masks a macro-F1 of 0.753 when missing entities, boundary errors, and label corrections are included. The benchmark shows that zero-shot span-based GLiNER collapses on entity types dependent on institutional function rather than surface form (0.243 micro-F1), while fine-tuned transformers struggle on rare labels. Carefully selected few-shot examples that demonstrate label contrasts improve every LLM over zero-shot prompting, with Claude Opus 4.6 reaching the best score of 0.873 micro-F1. We release IntLawNER as a benchmark and reusable resource for extracting references in international legal texts.

AI.tldr: IntLawNER is the first token-level NER dataset and benchmark for codified international law (2,987 gold sentences, 8,094 spans, 7 institution-specific types from ICJ, UNSC, ECtHR). Built via a hybrid algorithmic-agentic pipeline, it exposes pitfalls of aggregate agreement metrics and benchmarks zero-shot, fine-tuned, and few-shot LLM performance.
AI.motivation: International law supplies the normative framework for state coordination, armed-conflict regulation, and human rights protection, but lacks token-level NER resources. Existing domain NER work overlooks codified international legal sources, leaving reference extraction in these texts unsupported.
AI.method: Hybrid algorithmic-agentic pipeline: candidate retrieval reduces 468k source sentences to a compact annotation set, followed by LLM-based vetting and human review; annotation with seven institution-specific entity types. Silver-to-gold analysis compares Cohen's kappa on boundary-matched spans against macro-F1 including missing entities, boundary errors, and label corrections. Benchmarks include zero-shot span-based GLiNER, fine-tuned transformers, and zero-shot vs. contrastive few-shot LLM prompting.
AI.result: 89.6% of gold spans were accepted unchanged from the silver layer. Cohen's kappa=0.964 on boundary-matched spans masks macro-F1=0.753 once missing entities, boundary errors, and label corrections are included. Zero-shot GLiNER collapses on institution-function-dependent entity types (0.243 micro-F1); fine-tuned transformers struggle on rare labels; selected contrastive few-shot examples improve every LLM over zero-shot, with Claude Opus 4.6 reaching 0.873 micro-F1.
AI.conclusion: IntLawNER is released as a benchmark and reusable resource for extracting references in international legal texts. The work shows aggregate human-machine agreement metrics can mislead in domain-specific NER, and that contrastive few-shot exemplars are effective for LLM-based legal NER.

title: Tracker-Free Robotic Ultrasound Calibration with a Spherical-Marker Phantom and Threshold-Free Center Localization
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables
