summary: Robotic ultrasound (US) calibration is essential for accurately relating US images to the robot coordinate system, but accurate and automated calibration remains challenging because existing methods often require complex phantoms or external 3D trackers. In this work, we develop a tracker-free robotic US calibration framework using a spherical-marker phantom and a highly automated perception pipeline for sphere-center localization. The proposed threshold-free image-processing method localizes the spherical feature based on each US image's intensity distribution, eliminating hand-tuned intensity thresholds and improving robustness across imaging settings without per-system retuning. Multi-pose observations of the spherical fiducial are then used to estimate the US-to-EE transformation without external tracking or prior localization of the sphere center in the robot base frame. We validate the proposed framework on a robotic US platform through repeated sphere scans and further assess the calibrated system using geometrically distinct phantoms with known CAD models. Across 12 cross-validation folds, single-marker calibration achieved sphere-center accuracy and precision of $1.75\pm0.51$ mm and $0.85\pm0.11$ mm, respectively, compared with $1.72\pm0.51$ mm and $0.84\pm0.12$ mm for three-marker calibration. Across the three reconstruction sets, the single-marker calibration yielded pooled post-registration point-to-surface MAE$\pm$SD values of $0.41\pm0.35$ mm for the cone and $0.50\pm0.41$ mm for the triangular prism, closely matching the three-marker results of $0.40\pm0.35$ mm and $0.48\pm0.40$ mm, respectively.

AI.tldr: A tracker-free robotic ultrasound calibration framework using a spherical-marker phantom and a threshold-free, intensity-distribution-based sphere-center localization pipeline achieves single-marker calibration comparable to three-marker calibration, validated by repeat scans and CAD-based phantom reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Accurate, automated robotic US calibration is critical for mapping US images to the robot coordinate frame, yet existing methods often demand complex phantoms or external 3D trackers, limiting practicality and robustness across imaging settings and systems.
AI.method: Tracker-free calibration with a spherical-marker phantom and a highly automated perception pipeline for sphere-center localization. A threshold-free image-processing method localizes the spherical feature from each US image's intensity distribution, removing hand-tuned intensity thresholds and per-system retuning. Multi-pose observations of the spherical fiducial estimate the US-to-EE transformation without external tracking or prior sphere-center localization in the robot base frame. Validated via repeated sphere scans on a robotic US platform and geometrically distinct phantoms with known CAD models.
AI.result: Across 12 cross-validation folds: single-marker calibration yielded sphere-center accuracy 1.75±0.51 mm and precision 0.85±0.11 mm, versus 1.72±0.51 mm and 0.84±0.12 mm for three-marker calibration. Across three reconstruction sets, single-marker calibration gave pooled post-registration point-to-surface MAE±SD of 0.41±0.35 mm (cone) and 0.50±0.41 mm (triangular prism), closely matching three-marker results of 0.40±0.35 mm and 0.48±0.40 mm.
AI.conclusion: The proposed tracker-free, threshold-free robotic US calibration framework enables accurate and automated US-to-EE estimation with a single spherical marker, matching three-marker performance, and is robust across imaging settings without per-system retuning or external tracking.

title: EvidenT: Building Trustworthy Enterprise Assistants through Evidence Groundedness and Traceability
comment: Accepted in EMNLP Industry Track 2026
summary: Enterprise AI assistants must produce responses that are verifiable and traceable to source evidence. However, retrieval augmented generation (RAG) over heterogeneous enterprise data can suffer from citation drift, unsupported content, and weak source traceability. We present EvidenT (T = Trust + Transparency + Traceability), a lightweight pipeline that verifies extracted evidence against retrieved documents before answer generation, without model retraining. EvidenT combines structured passage extraction with deterministic lexical alignment to filter unsupported content, correct citation drift, and preserve source-span traceability. On approximately 500 real enterprise queries, EvidenT improves gold-source hit rate by an average of 29% over prompting baselines, produces no citations to nonretrieved urls, and achieves near-saturated answer-to-source lexical coverage.

AI.tldr: EvidenT is a lightweight, retraining-free pipeline that verifies extracted evidence against retrieved documents for lexical alignment before answer generation, improving citation accuracy and source traceability in enterprise RAG.
AI.motivation: RAG over heterogeneous enterprise data suffers from citation drift, unsupported content, and weak source traceability, so enterprise AI assistants fail to produce verifiable, traceable responses grounded in source evidence.
AI.method: EvidenT combines structured passage extraction with deterministic lexical alignment to verify evidence against retrieved documents prior to answer generation, filtering unsupported content, correcting citation drift, and preserving source-span traceability without any model retraining.
AI.result: On ~500 real enterprise queries, EvidenT lifts gold-source hit rate by an average of 29% over prompting baselines, yields no citations to non-retrieved URLs, and attains near-saturated answer-to-source lexical coverage.
AI.conclusion: Pre-generation, deterministic evidence verification is an effective, retraining-free approach for improving citation fidelity and traceability in enterprise RAG systems.

title: Layered e-skin for Shear Sensing
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to IEEE Sensors Journal
summary: This paper presents a stacked two-layer force-sensing resistor (FSR) array designed for robotic fingertips that combines high-resolution pressure mapping with shear-force estimation. A compliant lattice elastomer spacer converts shear loading into a measurable inter-layer displacement, producing relative center-of-pressure (CoP) shifts between layers. A physics-based moment balance links inter-layer CoP displacement to shear force, while an end-to-end CNN--GRU model captures nonlinear effects from load-dependent compression and contact redistribution. This model, with both layers as input, achieves coefficients of determination $R^2 = 0.914$ for $F_x$ and $R^2 = 0.944$ for $F_y$, consistently outperforming single-layer baselines for shear-force estimation. Robotic manipulation experiments show that, for contact-motion tracking, the deep layer tracks the translation and rotation imposed by the robot arm, whereas the superficial layer tracks the slip at the contact surface. Transient changes in the difference between the total pressure responses of the two layers provide the best slip-event detection performance among the tested cues. These results demonstrate that two-layer FSR arrays can provide three-axis force estimation, contact-motion tracking, and slip-event detection beyond conventional normal-force sensing.

AI.tldr: A stacked two-layer FSR array for robotic fingertips uses a compliant lattice elastomer spacer to convert shear into inter-layer CoP displacement, enabling three-axis force estimation, contact-motion tracking, and slip-event detection.
AI.motivation: Conventional force-sensing resistor arrays mainly provide normal-force sensing, limiting robotic fingertips that need shear and slip information for dexterous manipulation.
AI.method: Stacked two-layer FSR array with a compliant lattice elastomer spacer converting shear loading into inter-layer displacement (relative CoP shifts). A physics-based moment balance links inter-layer CoP displacement to shear force, complemented by an end-to-end CNN--GRU model that captures nonlinear load-dependent compression and contact redistribution using both layers as input.
AI.result: The CNN--GRU model achieves R^2 = 0.914 for F_x and R^2 = 0.944 for F_y, outperforming single-layer baselines. In robotic manipulation experiments, the deep layer tracks arm-imposed translation and rotation, while the superficial layer tracks contact-surface slip. Transient changes in the difference of total pressure responses between layers give the best slip-event detection among tested cues.
AI.conclusion: Two-layer FSR arrays extend beyond conventional normal-force sensing, providing three-axis force estimation, contact-motion tracking, and slip-event detection for robotic fingertips.

title: AutoGym: Blueprint-First Generation of Verifiable Agent Gyms
comment: Submitted to NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Who Verifies the Agents?
summary: Training agents with reinforcement learning requires a gym, comprising a task, an executable environment in which the task can be attempted, and a verifier that reliably distinguishes success from failure. Constructing such gyms remains manual, expensive, and static. Task sets saturate as models improve and are increasingly exposed to contamination. Synthetic generation offers scale, but single-pass synthesis produces tasks whose difficulty is largely cosmetic. Models comparable in capability solve them despite convoluted phrasing, and correctness must be adjudicated post-hoc by unreliable LLM judges. We present AutoGym, a framework that generates complete gyms (tasks, executable environments, and verifiers) from a minimal domain seed or prior model trajectories. AutoGym introduces three mechanisms. (1) Blueprint-first generation specifies the valid solution space, environment requirements, and verification criteria before the environment is materialized, making solvability a construction prerequisite rather than a property verified after the fact. (2) Explicit generation parameters control task topology, interaction depth, capability axes, question obfuscation, and distractor composition, enabling fine-grained difficulty steering. (3) Active curriculum synthesis uses performance-informed calibration to adjust the distribution over these parameters as model capabilities evolve. Across productivity and temporal-reasoning settings, AutoGym generates gyms spanning the capability spectrum, including instances that challenge frontier models.

AI.tldr: AutoGym is a framework that generates complete reinforcement-learning gyms—tasks, executable environments, and verifiers—from a minimal domain seed or prior model trajectories, using blueprint-first generation, controllable difficulty parameters, and active curriculum synthesis.
AI.motivation: Constructing RL gyms is manual, expensive, and static. Task sets saturate as models improve and are prone to contamination. Synthetic single-pass generation yields only cosmetically difficult tasks (solvable despite convoluted phrasing), and correctness relies on unreliable post-hoc LLM judges.
AI.method: AutoGym introduces three mechanisms: (1) Blueprint-first generation that specifies the valid solution space, environment requirements, and verification criteria before materializing the environment, making solvability a construction prerequisite; (2) Explicit generation parameters controlling task topology, interaction depth, capability axes, question obfuscation, and distractor composition for fine-grained difficulty steering; (3) Active curriculum synthesis using performance-informed calibration to adjust the parameter distribution as model capabilities evolve.
AI.result: Across productivity and temporal-reasoning settings, AutoGym generates gyms spanning the capability spectrum, including instances that challenge frontier models.
AI.conclusion: AutoGym enables scalable, difficulty-steerable, and verifiable gym generation for RL training, producing tasks that remain challenging even for frontier models.

title: Latent Policy Steering: An Efficient and Flexible Framework for Cross-Embodiment Transfer
summary:
The performance of learned robot visuomotor policies depends heavily on the size and quality of their training data, yet collecting high-quality demonstrations remains costly for robots in the real world. Although large-scale robot and human datasets are increasingly available, embodiment gaps and mismatched action spaces make them difficult to leverage directly. Cross-embodiment transfer, reusing experience from other embodiments to improve learning on a target embodiment, is therefore crucial for scaling robot learning beyond per-robot data collection.
  In this work, we find that efficient transfer can be achieved by learning from what is shared across embodiments, the visual dynamics of how the world responds to motion, and by effectively exploiting the scarce target-embodiment data at test time. The proposed framework, called Latent Policy Steering (LPS), implements an embodiment-agnostic pretraining phase, which trains an image-based World Model (WM) with optical flow across diverse embodiments. The resulting WM is finetuned on the target embodiment with robot actions. It then steers the base policy toward better actions by searching in the WM's latent space for plans that stay close to the finetuning data. LPS is a policy-agnostic framework: it can flexibly accommodate different policies without having to retrain them. In Robomimic and real-world evaluations, LPS improves the average performance of Diffusion Policy relatively by 16% and 62%, and Pi0.5 by 8% and 14%, with only 50 demonstrations on an unseen target embodiment.

AI.tldr: Latent Policy Steering (LPS) enables cross-embodiment transfer by pretraining an embodiment-agnostic World Model on optical flow, finetuning it with scarce target-robot actions, and steering any base policy via latent-space search, yielding up to 62% relative gains with only 50 demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Learned robot visuomotor policies require large, high-quality demonstration data, but real-world collection is costly. Existing large-scale robot and human datasets are hard to reuse directly due to embodiment gaps and mismatched action spaces. Cross-embodiment transfer is thus essential for scaling robot learning beyond per-robot data collection.
AI.method: LPS leverages what is shared across embodiments: visual dynamics of how the world responds to motion. It has three components: (1) an embodiment-agnostic pretraining phase training an image-based World Model (WM) with optical flow across diverse embodiments; (2) finetuning the WM on the target embodiment with robot actions; (3) at test time, steering the base policy toward better actions by searching in the WM's latent space for plans close to the finetuning data. LPS is policy-agnostic and accommodates different policies without retraining them.
AI.result: In Robomimic and real-world evaluations with only 50 demonstrations on an unseen target embodiment, LPS improves average performance of Diffusion Policy by 16% (Robomimic) and 62% (real-world), and Pi0.5 by 8% and 14%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Efficient cross-embodiment transfer is achievable by learning shared visual dynamics across embodiments and exploiting scarce target-embodiment data at test time through latent-space policy steering, substantially boosting policy performance under limited target data.

title: MAWILE: Multi-Axis Workbench for Inspecting LLM Evaluators
summary: Large language model (LLM) judges provide a flexible and scalable method for evaluating model and agent outputs, but their verdicts can be sensitive to incidental changes in the evaluated response, judge instructions, and scoring rubric. Existing systems examine important subsets of these failure modes, but auditing a configured judge requires testing both the judge instrument and the items it evaluates. We introduce MAWILE, a developer-facing workbench for auditing judge sensitivity across four surfaces: the judge prompt, judge rubric, target-system input, and target-system output. Given a user-supplied judge and representative evaluation items, MAWILE constructs and validates controlled perturbations, re-executes the judge, and localizes the resulting sensitivity. Each perturbation declares whether the verdict should remain invariant or change in a specified direction, allowing the same system to measure both robustness to irrelevant variations and sensitivity to meaningful changes. MAWILE audits binary, ordinal, and pairwise judges without requiring gold labels. The code for this tool is available at: github.com/megagonlabs/mawile-judge.

AI.tldr: MAWILE is a developer-facing workbench that audits the sensitivity of LLM judge verdicts across four perturbation surfaces—judge prompt, rubric, target-system input, and output—using controlled perturbations with declared invariance/direction expectations, without requiring gold labels.
AI.motivation: LLM judges offer a flexible, scalable way to evaluate model and agent outputs, but their verdicts are sensitive to incidental changes in the evaluated response, judge instructions, and scoring rubric. Existing systems only examine subsets of these failure modes; a proper audit must test both the judge instrument and the items it evaluates.
AI.method: Given a user-supplied judge and representative evaluation items, MAWILE constructs and validates controlled perturbations, re-executes the judge, and localizes the resulting sensitivity. It covers four surfaces: judge prompt, judge rubric, target-system input, and target-system output. Each perturbation declares whether the verdict should stay invariant or change in a specified direction, enabling the same system to measure robustness to irrelevant variations and sensitivity to meaningful changes.
AI.result: MAWILE audits binary, ordinal, and pairwise judges without requiring gold labels, and localizes sensitivity to specific perturbation surfaces. The tool is publicly released at github.com/megagonlabs/mawile-judge.
AI.conclusion: MAWILE provides a practical audit procedure for judge sensitivity, supporting both invariance and directional-change testing and extending judge auditing beyond single-surface or label-dependent approaches.

title: FRAMES: Failure Recovery And Monitoring of Embodied Skills for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
comment: Accepted for poster presentation at the IROS 2026 Workshop on Full-Shift Robot Co-Workers: Active Perception and Interaction for Human Environments
summary: Large language model (LLM) planners can decompose natural-language instructions and select reusable robot skills, but choosing the correct skill does not guarantee successful physical execution. This gap is especially important in humanoid loco-manipulation, where errors during approach, grasping, transport, or placement can invalidate the remainder of a long-horizon plan. We present FRAMES, a failure-aware supervisory framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid that operates above the CEER whole-body controller. A Planner Agent selects subtasks through parameterized mid-level skills, while a vision-language-model-based Monitor Agent evaluates each skill using temporal multi-view observations and structured robot and contact evidence. Detected failures stop the active skill and provide grounded feedback to a Recovery Agent. The framework further includes a Memory Module for reusing prior skill experience, and geometric grounding via depth and segmentation. We independently evaluate the monitoring module of the framework in MuJoCo using 100 trials comprising 50 failed and 50 successful executions across five tasks. The monitor detects 48 of 50 failures, correctly accepts 46 of 50 successful executions, and achieves 94.0% overall accuracy. These results provide initial evidence for the monitoring component, while end-to-end evaluation of the complete recovery loop remains ongoing.

AI.tldr: FRAMES is a failure-aware supervisory framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid layered above a whole-body controller. A Planner Agent picks parameterized skills, a VLM-based Monitor Agent verifies execution via multi-view temporal observations plus robot/contact evidence, and a Recovery Agent acts on grounded feedback, supported by a Memory Module and geometric grounding. In MuJoCo monitoring tests (100 trials, 5 tasks), it detects 48/50 failures, accepts 46/50 successes, reaching 94.0% accuracy; end-to-end recovery evaluation is still ongoing.
AI.motivation: LLM planners can decompose instructions and select reusable robot skills, but correct skill selection does not guarantee successful physical execution. This gap is critical in humanoid loco-manipulation, where errors in approach, grasping, transport, or placement can invalidate the rest of a long-horizon plan.
AI.method: FRAMES operates as a supervisory layer above the CEER whole-body controller on the Unitree G1. A Planner Agent selects subtasks via parameterized mid-level skills; a VLM-based Monitor Agent evaluates each skill using temporal multi-view observations and structured robot and contact evidence. Detected failures halt the active skill and feed grounded feedback to a Recovery Agent. Additional components include a Memory Module for reusing prior skill experience and geometric grounding via depth and segmentation.
AI.result: The monitoring module was independently evaluated in MuJoCo over 100 trials (50 failed, 50 successful executions) across five tasks. It detects 48 of 50 failures, correctly accepts 46 of 50 successful executions, and achieves 94.0% overall accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Results provide initial evidence for the monitoring component alone; end-to-end evaluation of the complete recovery loop remains ongoing.

title: GaitVista: Reliability-Aware AI Measurement toward Accessible Longitudinal Gait Assessment
summary: Tracking recovery of walking function requires detecting meaningful gait change across rehabilitation sessions, yet objective 3D measurement remains confined to specialized motion-capture laboratories. Small camera sets and body-worn inertial sensors broaden access, but reliability varies across joints and time, allowing sensing failures to masquerade as patient change. We present \textsc{GaitVista}, a reliability-aware measurement layer whose lightweight gate assigns joint- and frame-specific visual contributions using camera coverage, local visual quality, cross-modal disagreement, and root-motion continuity, and exposes them for inspection. Across seven clean and degraded sensing conditions on TotalCapture, \textsc{GaitVista} reduces average full-body and lower-body error by \textbf{27.7\%} and \textbf{27.8\%}, attains the lowest worst-condition error among fusion methods, and reduces the gap to a joint-frame oracle from $2.76$--$5.33$~cm for condition-blind baselines to $1.11$~cm. On MoVi with image-derived keypoints, it is the only deployable fusion method to improve over both unimodal streams, reducing marker-supported error by \textbf{6.4\%} relative to the strongest learned fusion baseline. On TotalCapture, it improves bilateral knee-flexion waveform accuracy by \textbf{18.9\%}. Raw inertial measurements from five TotalCapture participants show location- and time-varying magnetic disturbance, supporting the design's reliability premise. Both benchmarks contain neurologically healthy participants in controlled settings and retain participant-specific IMU calibration; we therefore report progress toward accessible gait assessment, not validated clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: GaitVista is a reliability-aware fusion layer for 3D gait measurement using few cameras plus wearable IMUs, using a lightweight gate to weight joint- and frame-specific visual contributions for more robust walking-function tracking.
AI.motivation: Tracking walking recovery needs objective detection of meaningful gait change across rehabilitation sessions, but 3D motion capture is confined to specialized labs. Sparse cameras and body-worn inertial sensors widen access, yet their reliability varies across joints and over time, so sensing failures can be mistaken for genuine patient change.
AI.method: GaitVista introduces a reliability-aware measurement layer with a lightweight gate that assigns joint- and frame-specific visual contributions based on camera coverage, local visual quality, cross-modal disagreement, and root-motion continuity, and makes these contributions inspectable.
AI.result: Across seven clean and degraded sensing conditions on TotalCapture, GaitVista cuts average full-body and lower-body error by 27.7% and 27.8%, achieves the lowest worst-condition error among fusion methods, and narrows the joint-frame oracle gap from 2.76-5.33 cm for condition-blind baselines to 1.11 cm. On MoVi with image-derived keypoints, it is the only deployable fusion method improving over both unimodal streams, reducing marker-supported error by 6.4% over the strongest learned fusion baseline. On TotalCapture it improves bilateral knee-flexion waveform accuracy by 18.9%. Raw IMU data from five participants show location- and time-varying magnetic disturbance, supporting the reliability premise.
AI.conclusion: GaitVista advances toward accessible gait assessment by making unreliable sensing contributions explicit and adaptive. Because both benchmarks use neurologically healthy participants in controlled settings and retain participant-specific IMU calibration, the authors frame this as progress rather than validated clinical deployment.

title: React When You Need To: Event-Triggered Asynchronous Inference for VLA Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models commonly predict action chunks, limiting their ability to react to environmental changes during execution. Existing asynchronous inference methods improve reactivity but typically rely on a fixed inference gap. In this paper, we propose an event-guided dynamic inference strategy that adapts the inference gap according to scene changes observed since the previous inference. Thereby, it simultaneously preserves motion consistency and prompt reactivity. Across static and dynamic real-world settings, our method consistently performs best, averaging 95% success and exceeding the strongest baseline by 55 percentage points. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance. The project page is available at https://react-when-you-need-to.github.io/.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an event-guided dynamic inference strategy for VLA models that adapts the inference gap based on observed scene changes, improving reactivity while preserving motion consistency and achieving 95% average success.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action models predict action chunks, which limits their ability to react to environmental changes during execution. Existing asynchronous inference methods improve reactivity but rely on a fixed inference gap, which is suboptimal.
AI.method: The authors introduce an event-guided dynamic inference strategy that adapts the inference gap according to scene changes observed since the previous inference, balancing motion consistency and prompt reactivity.
AI.result: Across static and dynamic real-world settings, the method consistently performs best, averaging 95% success and exceeding the strongest baseline by 55 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: The event-guided dynamic inference strategy effectively addresses the limitations of fixed inference gaps in asynchronous inference for VLA models, yielding substantial performance gains in real-world settings.

title: Splitting Documents at Lower Cost: Multi-Split Boundary Decisions for LLM-Based Page Stream Segmentation
comment: Accepted at the DocInsights Workshop at EMNLP 2026
summary: Scanned mail, uploaded PDFs, and consolidated attachments often arrive as page streams that must be split into individual documents before downstream classification, extraction, or routing. Zero-shot large language models can detect document boundaries without task-specific training, but standard Page Classification (PC) and Boundary Decision (BD) formulations resolve only one boundary per model call. We introduce Multi-Split Boundary Decision (MSBD), which predicts multiple boundaries within a page window in a single call, reducing the number of inference requests. We evaluate MSBD across multiple language models, document collections, input modalities, and window sizes. The results reveal a model- and corpus-dependent operating range in which MSBD preserves strong segmentation accuracy while substantially improving inference efficiency, followed by a sharp decline at larger windows. MSBD provided the strongest overall accuracy--efficiency trade-off, while large windows expose distinct over- and under-segmentation behavior across models. These findings show that multi-boundary prediction can make zero-shot page stream segmentation more efficient when the window size is selected for the target corpus.

AI.tldr: Multi-Split Boundary Decision (MSBD) predicts multiple document boundaries per LLM call for zero-shot page stream segmentation, improving inference efficiency while preserving accuracy within a model- and corpus-dependent window range.
AI.motivation: Page streams from scanned mail, uploaded PDFs, and consolidated attachments must be split into individual documents before classification, extraction, or routing. Zero-shot LLMs avoid task-specific training, but standard Page Classification (PC) and Boundary Decision (BD) formulations detect only one boundary per call, limiting efficiency.
AI.method: Introduce MSBD, which predicts multiple boundaries within a page window in a single model call. Evaluate across multiple language models, document collections, input modalities, and window sizes.
AI.result: A model- and corpus-dependent operating range exists where MSBD preserves strong segmentation accuracy and substantially improves inference efficiency, followed by a sharp decline at larger windows. MSBD achieves the strongest overall accuracy–efficiency trade-off; large windows reveal distinct over- and under-segmentation behavior across models.
AI.conclusion: Multi-boundary prediction makes zero-shot page stream segmentation more efficient when window size is selected appropriately for the target corpus.

title: REBOOT: From Failure to Recovery - A Dataset and Benchmark for Precision Assembly
comment: Project website: https://nanayawoa.github.io/REBOOT
summary: Robot learning policies fail in characteristic ways: they stall in uncertain states, drift during contact-rich alignment, and miss targets by millimetres in precision tasks. Yet training datasets consist largely of successful demonstrations, while real-world benchmarks often reduce performance to binary success. This limits both supervision for recovery and analysis of where failures occur. We introduce REBOOT (Recovery Episode Benchmark for Off-nominal Trajectories), the first robot manipulation benchmark designed around failure as a first-class signal. REBOOT contains 2,160 demonstrations across 18 precision assembly tasks, each decomposed into five shared phases: Align(pick), Engage(pick), Transport, Align(place), and Engage(place), enabling phase-level evaluation beyond terminal success. Failures are introduced across phases and paired with expert recovery trajectories that return the system to a valid continuation state. Tasks are annotated with rotational symmetry, engagement-clearance precision tier, and assembly direction through matched install-remove pairs. Failure episodes are labeled by phase and categorical failure mode, enabling attribution to kinematic stage and tolerance violation. Data includes synchronized RGB-D observations from four viewpoints and grounded natural-language descriptions of phase-level success and failure conditions. Half the dataset contains expert demonstrations; the other half contains recovery demonstrations sampled to reflect failures observed in imitation-learned policy rollouts. We benchmark action-chunked transformer, diffusion, and $π_0$-FAST policies using phase-level completion rates, revealing model-specific failure points hidden by binary evaluation. Dataset and code: https://nanayawoa.github.io/REBOOT

AI.tldr: REBOOT is the first robot manipulation benchmark treating failure as a first-class signal, with 2,160 demonstrations across 18 precision assembly tasks decomposed into five shared phases, paired failure/recovery trajectories, phase- and mode-level labels, synchronized RGB-D and grounded language annotations, enabling phase-level evaluation that exposes model-specific failure points hidden by binary success metrics.
AI.motivation: Robot learning policies fail characteristically (stalling in uncertain states, drifting during contact-rich alignment, missing targets by millimetres), yet training datasets are dominated by successful demonstrations and real-world benchmarks reduce performance to binary success. This limits both supervision for recovery learning and analysis of where failures occur, motivating a benchmark designed around failure as a first-class signal.
AI.method: REBOOT contains 2,160 demonstrations over 18 precision assembly tasks, each decomposed into five shared phases (Align(pick), Engage(pick), Transport, Align(place), Engage(place)). Failures are injected across phases and paired with expert recovery trajectories returning the system to a valid continuation state. Tasks are annotated with rotational symmetry, engagement-clearance precision tier, and assembly direction via matched install-remove pairs; failure episodes are labeled by phase and categorical failure mode. Data includes synchronized RGB-D from four viewpoints and grounded natural-language descriptions of phase-level success/failure conditions. Half the dataset is expert demonstrations; the other half is recovery demonstrations sampled to reflect failures observed in imitation-learned policy rollouts. Action-chunked transformer, diffusion, and π0-FAST policies are benchmarked using phase-level completion rates.
AI.result: Phase-level completion rates reveal model-specific failure points that binary evaluation obscures, showing that different policy architectures (action-chunked transformer, diffusion, π0-FAST) fail at distinct phases and modes across the precision assembly tasks.
AI.conclusion: REBOOT enables phase-attributed and failure-mode-attributed evaluation and provides recovery supervision beyond successful demonstrations, offering finer-grained diagnosis of robot manipulation policies than terminal binary success. Dataset and code are released at https://nanayawoa.github.io/REBOOT.

title: Text, Pixels, or Both? Evaluating Input Representations for Multimodal Document QA
comment: Accepted as a poster at the Context Beyond the Window (CBW) Workshop at COLM 2026 and the DocInsights Workshop at EMNLP 2026
summary: Every document QA system begins with a choice that is rarely studied on its own: whether to feed the model page images, extracted text, or both. We isolate this choice, holding the prompt, judge, and scoring pipeline fixed, across four commercial model endpoints, two corpora, and two context regimes (gold evidence pages and the full document). On documents that fit the image budget, page images lead on accuracy at every document length on both corpora, but this advantage carries a growing latency and cost premium: text latency stays roughly flat as documents lengthen while image latency rises steadily. Text and images also fail on different questions, with exactly one representation correct on 19--25% of items across the reported cells, so neither subsumes the other. Exploiting this complementarity, a lightweight TF-IDF router that reads only the question text gains 2.6 points over always-text while cutting median latency 30% relative to always-vision, on a document-disjoint held-out split.

AI.tldr: This paper isolates the representation choice in document QA—page images vs. extracted text vs. both—and finds that images are more accurate but slower and costlier, text is fast and flat-scaling, and the two fail on different questions. A TF-IDF router over the question alone exploits this complementarity to beat always-text accuracy while cutting latency versus always-vision.
AI.motivation: Document QA systems must implicitly decide whether to feed page images, extracted text, or both, yet this choice is rarely studied in isolation. Prior comparisons are confounded by differing prompts, judges, or scoring pipelines, leaving unclear which representation is preferable and under what conditions.
AI.method: The representation choice is isolated by holding the prompt, judge, and scoring pipeline fixed while varying only the input modality. Evaluation spans four commercial model endpoints, two corpora, and two context regimes (gold evidence pages and the full document). On top of this, a lightweight TF-IDF router that uses only the question text is trained to select between text and vision, evaluated on a document-disjoint held-out split.
AI.result: On documents fitting the image budget, page images lead on accuracy at every document length on both corpora, but with a growing latency and cost premium: text latency stays roughly flat as documents lengthen while image latency rises steadily. Text and images fail on different questions, with exactly one representation correct on 19–25% of items across reported cells, so neither subsumes the other. The TF-IDF router gains 2.6 points over always-text while cutting median latency 30% relative to always-vision.
AI.conclusion: Neither representation dominates: images offer higher accuracy, text offers superior and more stable efficiency, and their errors are complementary. A simple question-only router can capture much of this complementarity, improving accuracy over always-text while reducing latency relative to always-vision, motivating representation selection as a first-class design decision in document QA.

title: Characterizing Wildlife Response to Biomimetic and Conventional Underwater Vehicles
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 1 table
summary: Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) are a promising alternative to divers for scalable collection of natural ocean ecology data. However, these robots may disturb local fauna and cause drastic behavioral differences compared to other monitoring techniques, decreasing their value as scientific tools. A promising prospect is to make AUVs that are more biomimetic, with the hope that taking on the form and behavior of a non-predatory animal may reduce adverse responses. We present the first dataset comparing fish disturbance in response to a conventional thruster-driven AUV, a sea turtle inspired flipper-driven AUV, and a diver. Experiments were conducted at a biodiversity hotspot in a Caribbean reef, and images of the scene were analyzed using computer vision to localize and study fish behavior change. Both AUVs cause measurable changes in fish behavior. Although no between-robot differences remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons, point estimates generally favor the biomimetic AUV, motivating larger studies capable of resolving modest effects and further design changes to optimize for disturbance. We also observe larger responses during diver transects than during AUV transects, although this exploratory comparison is based on a small diver sample with several confounds. While conclusions must be taken as preliminary due to operational and experimental limitations, this study provides the community with a first known dataset and benchmarks to quantify the behavioral impacts of biomimetic robots for ecological monitoring in the wild.

AI.tldr: First dataset comparing fish disturbance responses to a conventional thruster-driven AUV, a sea-turtle-inspired flipper-driven AUV, and a diver on a Caribbean reef, using computer vision to quantify behavior change.
AI.motivation: AUVs could scale up natural ocean ecology data collection, but they may disturb local fauna and alter animal behavior relative to other monitoring methods, undermining their value as scientific tools. The hope is that biomimetic AUVs—mimicking the form and behavior of non-predatory animals—may reduce adverse responses, yet no comparative data existed in the wild.
AI.method: Experiments were conducted at a biodiversity hotspot on a Caribbean reef. Fish disturbance was compared across three treatments: a conventional thruster-driven AUV, a sea-turtle-inspired flipper-driven AUV, and a diver. Images of the scene were analyzed with computer vision to localize and assess changes in fish behavior.
AI.result: Both AUVs caused measurable changes in fish behavior. After correction for multiple comparisons, no between-robot differences remained significant, though point estimates generally favored the biomimetic AUV. Responses during diver transects were larger than during AUV transects, but this exploratory comparison rests on a small diver sample with several confounds.
AI.conclusion: Due to operational and experimental limitations, findings are preliminary. The study provides the community with the first known dataset and benchmarks to quantify the behavioral impacts of biomimetic robots for ecological monitoring in the wild, motivating larger studies to resolve modest effects and guide design changes optimizing for reduced disturbance.

title: Self-Organizing Agent Teams Learn to Reason Together
comment: Preprint
summary: Collective intelligence depends not only on what team members know, but also on how they organize their work. When the structure of a solution is unknown, useful roles and divisions of labor cannot be specified in advance; teams must learn from experience how to organize reasoning as it unfolds. Human teams routinely adapt this way, while existing AI agent teams rely on fixed protocols, explicit task decomposition, or routing. We introduce Self-Organizing Agent Teams (SAT), fixed teams of AI agents that learn reusable strategies from prior collaborations to organize roles, conversational phases, participation, and information flow. These strategies enable what we call collaborative computation: agents exchange, challenge, repair, and synthesize partial reasoning into solutions no member produced independently. In two independent settings, we learn teamwork strategies that transfer unchanged to unseen benchmarks, using only 15 mathematics and 25 graduate-level knowledge problems. Across five mathematics and physics benchmarks, self-organizing teams average 66.7% accuracy, versus 48.8% for their strongest member, 58.7% for compute-matched inference by that agent, and 59.0% for a perfect router over members' independent answers; on AIME 2026, they exceed this router by 13.4 points. Because gains vary across benchmarks, we ask when self-organizing collaboration helps. Across eight benchmarks, demonstrability (the organizational-psychology construct of whether a team can distinguish correct from incorrect reasoning) strongly tracks improvement over the strongest member (Spearman $ρ=0.90$, $p=0.005$): teams benefit most when correct reasoning can be recognized once it appears. More broadly, these results suggest that organization itself can become an agent capability: agent teams can learn how to reason together and produce solutions their members could not reach independently.

AI.tldr: SAT is a framework where fixed teams of AI agents learn reusable collaboration strategies from prior teamwork, enabling collaborative computation that outperforms their strongest members and even a perfect router, with gains predicted by "demonstrability."
AI.motivation: Collective intelligence depends on team organization, not just member knowledge. When solution structure is unknown, useful roles and divisions of labor cannot be pre-specified; human teams adapt through experience, but existing AI agent teams rely on fixed protocols, explicit task decomposition, or routing, which limits emergent organization.
AI.method: The authors introduce Self-Organizing Agent Teams (SAT): fixed teams of AI agents that learn reusable strategies from prior collaborations to organize roles, conversational phases, participation, and information flow. These strategies support "collaborative computation," where agents exchange, challenge, repair, and synthesize partial reasoning. Strategies are learned in two independent settings using only 15 mathematics and 25 graduate-level knowledge problems, then transferred unchanged to unseen benchmarks.
AI.result: Across five mathematics and physics benchmarks, self-organizing teams average 66.7% accuracy, versus 48.8% for the strongest member, 58.7% for compute-matched inference by that agent, and 59.0% for a perfect router over members' independent answers; on AIME 2026 they exceed this router by 13.4 points. Across eight benchmarks, demonstrability strongly tracks improvement over the strongest member (Spearman rho=0.90, p=0.005): teams benefit most when correct reasoning can be recognized once it appears.
AI.conclusion: Organization itself can become an agent capability: agent teams can learn how to reason together and produce solutions their members could not reach independently. Gains are not uniform but are predicted by demonstrability, indicating collaboration helps most when correctness is recognizable in reasoning.

title: VT-Bridge: Bridging Pretrained Foundation VLAs to VTLAs via Lightweight Residual Adaptation
summary: Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) models have demonstrated clear advantages over Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models in contact-rich manipulation. However, developing VTLA models is severely constrained by the massive amounts of vision-tactile data and computational resources required. To address this bottleneck, we propose VT-Bridge, a lightweight residual adaptation strategy that bridges pretrained foundation VLAs to VTLAs. Rather than training a VTLA model from scratch or modifying the original architecture of a pretrained VLA, VT-Bridge employs an identical lightweight residual-adapter architecture across VLA backbones and uses backbone-specific weights to refine actions at the robot execution frequency. This design substantially lowers the data and training barriers. Specifically, it requires up to 50 vision-tactile demonstrations per task to fine-tune a VLA backbone and train a 0.98M-parameter residual adapter. Experiments with three representative VLA backbones ($π_0$, $π_{0.5}$, and SmolVLA) across four contact-rich manipulation tasks further demonstrate its consistent effectiveness across VLA architectures. On average, VT-Bridge raises the task completion rate from 11.7% with task-level VLA fine-tuning alone to 62.9%. Together, these findings demonstrate the broad applicability, effectiveness, and accessibility of VT-Bridge for contact-rich manipulation. The project page is available at https://hoxnocha.github.io/vt-bridge-web/.

AI.tldr: VT-Bridge is a lightweight residual adaptation strategy that bridges pretrained foundation VLAs to VTLAs using a shared residual-adapter design with backbone-specific weights, requiring only ~50 vision-tactile demos per task and 0.98M adapter parameters.
AI.motivation: VTLA models outperform VLA models in contact-rich manipulation, but their development is bottlenecked by massive vision-tactile data and compute requirements.
AI.method: Instead of training from scratch or altering the pretrained VLA architecture, VT-Bridge applies an identical lightweight residual-adapter architecture across VLA backbones, with backbone-specific weights refining actions at robot execution frequency. A VLA backbone is fine-tuned and the 0.98M-parameter residual adapter trained using up to 50 vision-tactile demonstrations per task.
AI.result: Evaluated with three VLA backbones (π0, π0.5, SmolVLA) on four contact-rich tasks, VT-Bridge consistently improved performance across architectures, raising average task completion rate from 11.7% (task-level VLA fine-tuning alone) to 62.9%.
AI.conclusion: VT-Bridge demonstrates broad applicability, effectiveness, and accessibility for contact-rich manipulation, substantially lowering data and training barriers to obtaining VTLA capabilities.

title: Generative Embodied Multiple Behavior Control Systems for Human-like Agents
comment: Manuscript under review
summary: An enduring and richly elaborated dichotomy in cognitive neuroscience is that of human behavior control mechanisms, divided into habitual versus goal-directed. While existing human-like agent frameworks primarily focus on modeling goal- directed behavior, habitual behavior has been largely overlooked, though it plays a crucial role in human daily life. In this paper, we address this gap by studying multiple behavior control systems that jointly model goal-directed and habitual behaviors. We propose a human behavior control mechanism-inspired framework which the Habitual Controller retrieves cue-triggered behaviors from personal- ized habit memory, while the Goal-directed Controller employs a context-aware world model to predict action consequences and estimate their values. The Arbiter dynamically balances the influence of both systems according to individual differ- ences and momentary internal states. To reconstruct diverse human-level behavior instructions in 3D environments, we further develop a keyframe-guided 3D mo- tion generation module. Through extensive evaluation methods, human studies, and ablations studies, experimental results demonstrate that human-likeness per- formance is significantly improved by our approach. The efficacy of our approach indicates the benefits of leveraging habitual behavior and multiple behavior con- trol system coordination for believable embodied human-like agents.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a human-like agent framework that jointly models goal-directed and habitual behavior control, using a Habitual Controller with personalized habit memory, a Goal-directed Controller with a context-aware world model, and a dynamic Arbiter, plus a keyframe-guided 3D motion generation module, achieving significantly improved human-likeness in 3D environments.
AI.motivation: Cognitive neuroscience distinguishes human behavioral control into habitual and goal-directed mechanisms. Existing human-like agent frameworks mainly model goal-directed behavior while largely overlooking habitual behavior, despite its crucial role in daily human life. This leaves a gap in achieving believable embodied agents.
AI.method: The authors propose a behavior control framework inspired by human cognition, comprising: (1) a Habitual Controller that retrieves cue-triggered behaviors from personalized habit memory; (2) a Goal-directed Controller that uses a context-aware world model to predict action consequences and estimate their values; (3) an Arbiter that dynamically balances both systems based on individual differences and momentary internal states. Additionally, a keyframe-guided 3D motion generation module is developed to reconstruct diverse human-level behavior instructions in 3D environments.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations, human studies, and ablation studies show that human-likeness performance is significantly improved by the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging habitual behavior and coordinating multiple behavior control systems benefits the creation of believable embodied human-like agents.

title: Becoming a Fruit Ninja: Real-Time Probabilistic Kinodynamic Planning for Manipulator Projectile Interception
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation
summary: Projectile interception is a challenging dynamic manipulation problem. Intercepting a thrown object with a robot arm requires reaching a point on the object's path as the object passes through it. Slicing also fixes the blade's velocity and orientation at contact. The goal is therefore a subset of the states of the robot and arrival times that moves as the object falls, and the arm must reach it within its actuator limits in milliseconds. We present FRUITNINJA, an anytime sampling-based planner that grows a tree on the GPU in batches toward the interception manifold. Each edge is an exact cubic whose travel time is found by a parallel search against the arm's dynamics, so every edge satisfies the actuator limits. Plans are ranked by a risk-aware objective over the uncertainty in the object's position and the arm's arrival time. We evaluate on a Franka Research 3 against six baselines in a calibrated real-time simulator, where FRUITNINJA cuts 96.7% of tosses in the open and 68.3% among five obstacles, versus the best baseline's 68.3% and 35.0% respectively.

AI.tldr: FRUITNINJA is an anytime, GPU-accelerated sampling-based planner that grows a tree in batches toward the interception manifold for projectile interception, with each edge validated against actuator limits and plans ranked by a risk-aware objective; it achieves 96.7% interception in the open and 68.3% among obstacles, outperforming the best baseline.
AI.motivation: Projectile interception is a challenging dynamic manipulation task requiring the robot arm to reach a moving point on the object's path within milliseconds and within actuator limits; slicing further constrains blade velocity and orientation at contact, making the interception manifold a moving subset of robot states and arrival times.
AI.method: FRUITNINJA grows a tree on the GPU in batches toward the interception manifold. Each edge is an exact cubic whose travel time is found by a parallel search against the arm's dynamics, ensuring every edge satisfies actuator limits. Plans are ranked by a risk-aware objective accounting for uncertainty in object position and arm arrival time.
AI.result: Evaluated on a Franka Research 3 against six baselines in a calibrated real-time simulator, FRUITNINJA cuts 96.7% of tosses in the open and 68.3% among five obstacles, versus the best baseline's 68.3% and 35.0% respectively.
AI.conclusion: FRUITNINJA demonstrates that GPU-accelerated, anytime sampling-based planning with dynamics-feasible edges and risk-aware ranking substantially improves projectile interception success, particularly in obstacle-rich settings, on a real robot platform.

title: Toward Auditable and Calibrated AI for Dementia-Related Crash Severity Prediction: A Selective Deferral Framework to Support Human Review
comment: This is the author's preprint version of a paper accepted for presentation at HICSS 60 (Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences), 2027, Hawaii, USA. The final published version will appear in the official conference proceedings. Conference site: https://hicss.hawaii.edu/
summary: Public crash databases increasingly support automated safety analysis, but crash severity prediction remains difficult to translate into public-sector decision workflows when models are evaluated primarily as ordinary classifiers. This study reframes dementia-related crash severity modeling as a decision-aware triage problem in which a system must classify crashes into no-injury/property-damage-only (O), minor or moderate injury (BC), and fatal or severe injury (KA), while also controlling outcome leakage, reporting severe under-triage, calibrating confidence, and preserving every raw prediction for audit. Using 4,781 Texas crash records with structured fields and police narratives, we evaluate structured, narrative, fusion, calibrated fusion, BERT-family, and local large-language-model baselines under a stratified 70/15/15 split. In the reported split, leakage-controlled Gemma obtains the highest observed macro-F1 (0.545; 95% bootstrap CI [0.507, 0.583]). The best calibrated fusion model obtains macro-F1 of 0.522 and expected calibration error of 0.033. Selective deferral improves performance among cases retained for automatic classification. At 70% coverage, macro-F1 rises to 0.573 and severity cost falls to 0.577, while deferred cases are treated as candidates for a proposed human-review process and are not further evaluated in the present experiment. The study contributes a reproducible, leakage-controlled, and uncertainty-aware evaluation framework for crash AI systems, emphasizing auditability and selective deferral rather than accuracy alone.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes dementia-related crash severity prediction as a decision-aware triage problem (3-class: O, BC, KA) with leakage control, calibration, and selective deferral, rather than evaluating models as ordinary classifiers.
AI.motivation: Public crash databases increasingly support automated safety analysis, but crash severity prediction is hard to translate into public-sector decision workflows when models are judged mainly as ordinary classifiers. The authors aim to align evaluation with real decision needs: controlling outcome leakage, reporting severe under-triage, calibrating confidence, preserving raw predictions for audit, and enabling selective deferral to human review.
AI.method: Using 4,781 Texas crash records (structured fields plus police narratives) under a stratified 70/15/15 split, they evaluate structured-only, narrative-only, fusion, calibrated fusion, BERT-family, and local large-language-model baselines. The task is triage into O (no-injury/property-damage-only), BC (minor/moderate injury), and KA (fatal/severe injury), with leakage-controlled experimental design, calibration, and selective deferral at varying coverage.
AI.result: In the reported split, leakage-controlled Gemma achieves the highest observed macro-F1 (0.545; 95% bootstrap CI [0.507, 0.583]). The best calibrated fusion model reaches macro-F1 0.522 with expected calibration error 0.033. Selective deferral improves retained-case performance: at 70% coverage, macro-F1 rises to 0.573 and severity cost falls to 0.577; deferred cases are treated as candidates for a proposed human-review process and are not further evaluated here.
AI.conclusion: The study contributes a reproducible, leakage-controlled, uncertainty-aware evaluation framework for crash AI systems, emphasizing auditability and selective deferral rather than accuracy alone. It positions triage-oriented, decision-aware metrics as more useful for public-sector workflows than standard classifier evaluation.

title: From Documented Strengths to Force Limits: Material-Informed Robotic Insertion for Construction Assembly
summary: Insertion is a fundamental operation in robotic construction assembly, where variations in material properties and assembly conditions make it difficult to select contact forces that complete the task without exceeding the assembly's capacity. Although construction documents encode engineering knowledge about materials and their conditions, translating this knowledge into load limits for a specific assembly remains difficult. This paper presents SAGE (Source-grounded Assembly Gating and Execution), a system that converts documented material evidence into capacity estimates for robotic insertion. SAGE restricts a large language model (LLM) to extracting tensile and compressive strengths from retrieved passages and tables and records their sources. A response model then interpolates offline finite element (FE) solutions to convert these strengths and the assembly conditions into axial load capacity. For fits with positive clearance, the estimated capacity sets the policy's axial force limit; for interference fits, it is compared with measured support demand to determine admission. On the primary benchmark, SAGE reduces mean capacity error from 80.65\% for direct LLM estimates based on the same evidence to 10.74\%. Without refitting, the mean error remains 8.00\% on 16 additional geometries. Under the assigned support release model, SAGE correctly classifies 59 of 62 scored simulation runs, with only conservative errors. In recorded xArm6 demonstrations, SAGE takes material documents as input and completes physical insertion in 9 of 13 trials. These results show that assigning document interpretation to the LLM and force calculation to an explicit mechanical model produces accurate capacity estimates and traceable insertion decisions.

AI.tldr: SAGE converts documented material evidence into capacity estimates for robotic insertion by having an LLM extract strengths from sources while an explicit FE-based model computes axial load capacity and gates insertion policies.
AI.motivation: Robotic construction assembly is sensitive to material and condition variations, making contact force selection difficult. Construction documents encode relevant engineering knowledge, but translating that knowledge into assembly-specific load limits remains hard.
AI.method: SAGE restricts an LLM to extracting tensile and compressive strengths from retrieved passages and tables with source records. A response model interpolates offline finite element solutions to convert these strengths and assembly conditions into axial load capacity. For positive-clearance fits, the capacity sets the policy's axial force limit; for interference fits, it is compared against measured support demand for admission.
AI.result: Mean capacity error drops from 80.65% (direct LLM estimates) to 10.74% on the primary benchmark, remaining 8.00% on 16 additional geometries without refitting. Under the assigned support release model, SAGE correctly classifies 59 of 62 scored simulation runs, all errors conservative. In xArm6 demonstrations, physical insertion succeeds in 9 of 13 trials.
AI.conclusion: Assigning document interpretation to the LLM and force calculation to an explicit mechanical model yields accurate, traceable capacity estimates and insertion decisions.

title: A Survey on the Linear Representation Hypothesis
summary: The term "linear representation hypothesis" (LRH) has appeared across diverse subfields of artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and cognitive science. But previous works have not consistently treated the LRH as a falsifiable scientific hypothesis; we analyze these inconsistencies and examine their implications for how prior theoretical and methodological results should be interpreted. Based on this analysis, we argue that claims regarding linear representations become well-defined only through careful examination of the model, representation location, feature definition, and evaluation dataset. We therefore propose a more rigorous formalization of the LRH that makes these dependencies explicit and allows the hypothesis to be evaluated as a falsifiable scientific claim. Finally, we identify some non-trivial open problems that warrant further attention from the research community.

AI.tldr: This paper critically examines the "linear representation hypothesis" (LRH), arguing prior work has not treated it as a falsifiable scientific hypothesis, and proposes a rigorous formalization that makes key dependencies explicit.
AI.motivation: The LRH has been invoked across AI, neuroscience, and cognitive science, but prior works have inconsistently treated it, leading to ambiguous claims and unclear interpretation of theoretical and methodological results.
AI.method: The authors analyze these inconsistencies and their implications for interpreting prior results, then propose a more rigorous formalization of the LRH that makes dependencies on the model, representation location, feature definition, and evaluation dataset explicit, enabling falsifiable evaluation.
AI.result: The analysis shows that claims about linear representations become well-defined only when the model, representation location, feature definition, and evaluation dataset are carefully specified, and the proposed formalization makes these dependencies explicit.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues for treating the LRH as a falsifiable scientific hypothesis via a precise formalization, and identifies several non-trivial open problems warranting further research attention.

title: HIGenNTO: Scalable Humanoid Interaction Generation via Noise-Space Trajectory Optimization
summary: Humanoid robots can acquire complex skills by imitating kinematic humanoid motion references, yet reliable references for contact-rich interactions remain difficult to obtain: motion capture deteriorates under occlusion and close physical contact, while retargeting introduces additional contact and geometric inconsistencies. We present HIGenNTO, a framework that synthesizes humanoid-scene interaction motion references by optimizing the initial noise of a pretrained text-conditioned motion model under sparse spatiotemporal and scene constraints. The same formulation satisfies desired contacts, avoids collisions, and maintains stable support while retaining the prior's realism and temporal coherence, generating interaction motions from scratch and composing long-horizon behaviors stage-wise. Across robot-environment and robot-object tasks, HIGenNTO produces motions that can be executed by tracking policies in simulation and used to train depth-conditioned visuomotor policies operating solely from onboard sensing. We deploy these policies on a Unitree G1 across four contact-rich tasks. Finally, the task specifications themselves can be written by a coding agent, which proposes interaction tasks and compiles them into prompt, constraint, and scene programs, authoring three of our eight evaluated tasks and four further behaviors. Together, these results establish a scalable path from high-level task descriptions to physically executable humanoid interactions.

AI.tldr: HIGenNTO synthesizes humanoid-scene interaction motion references by optimizing the initial noise of a pretrained text-conditioned motion model under sparse spatiotemporal and scene constraints, enabling contact-rich behaviors that transfer to real robot visuomotor policies.
AI.motivation: Reliable kinematic references for contact-rich humanoid interactions are hard to obtain: motion capture degrades under occlusion and close physical contact, and retargeting introduces contact and geometric inconsistencies.
AI.method: The framework optimizes the initial noise of a pretrained text-conditioned motion model subject to sparse spatiotemporal and scene constraints, simultaneously satisfying desired contacts, avoiding collisions, and maintaining stable support while preserving prior realism and temporal coherence. It generates motions from scratch and composes long-horizon behaviors stage-wise; a coding agent can also author task specifications by compiling them into prompt, constraint, and scene programs.
AI.result: Across robot-environment and robot-object tasks, HIGenNTO produces motions executable by tracking policies in simulation and usable to train depth-conditioned visuomotor policies that operate solely from onboard sensing. Policies were deployed on a Unitree G1 across four contact-rich tasks; the coding agent authored three of eight evaluated tasks plus four further behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a scalable path from high-level task descriptions to physically executable humanoid interactions.

title: Building Trustworthy Mental Health Benchmarks on Bluesky: A Validation-Aware Weak-Supervision Framework
comment: This is the author's preprint version of a paper accepted for presentation at HICSS 60 (Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences), 2027, Hawaii, USA. The final published version will appear in the official conference proceedings. Conference site: https://hicss.hawaii.edu/
summary: Decentralized social media platforms create new opportunities and challenges for computational mental health research because data access, moderation, labeling, and deployment responsibilities are distributed across multiple technical and governance layers. This paper presents a validation-aware weak-supervision system for constructing and evaluating suicidal ideation (SI) and broader mental health (MH) disclosure benchmarks on Bluesky, a decentralized social media platform built on the AT Protocol. The system integrates public firehose collection, task-specific lexicon filtering, Llama-3-8B-assisted binary annotation, human-adjudicated validation subsets, and transformer-based model benchmarking. Using this pipeline, we construct two task-specific corpora containing 8,346 SI-labeled posts and 9,988 MH-labeled posts. The evaluation shows that model performance depends strongly on both task definition and validation protocol. BERT+LSTM achieves the highest SI stratified cross-validation F1-score, RoBERTa achieves the strongest SI holdout F1-score, and DistilRoBERTa achieves the best MH cross-validation F1-score. Human validation reveals different weak-label failure modes across tasks, with SI labels dominated by false negatives and MH labels dominated by false positives. These findings show that decentralized social media can support reproducible mental health benchmarking, but only when system design, label provenance, validation strategy, and deployment constraints are evaluated together.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a validation-aware weak-supervision pipeline for building and evaluating suicidal ideation (SI) and mental health (MH) disclosure benchmarks on Bluesky, showing that model performance depends on task definition and validation protocol.
AI.motivation: Decentralized social media platforms pose new opportunities and challenges for computational mental health research, since data access, moderation, labeling, and deployment responsibilities are distributed across multiple technical and governance layers.
AI.method: The system integrates public firehose collection, task-specific lexicon filtering, Llama-3-8B-assisted binary annotation, human-adjudicated validation subsets, and transformer-based model benchmarking.
AI.result: Two task-specific corpora were built with 8,346 SI-labeled posts and 9,988 MH-labeled posts. BERT+LSTM achieved the highest SI stratified cross-validation F1, RoBERTa the strongest SI holdout F1, and DistilRoBERTa the best MH cross-validation F1. Human validation showed SI labels dominated by false negatives and MH labels by false positives.
AI.conclusion: Decentralized social media can support reproducible mental health benchmarking, but only when system design, label provenance, validation strategy, and deployment constraints are evaluated together.

title: Simultaneous Forward and Inverse Human-in-the-Loop Optimization
comment: Accepted at the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
summary: Subjective user experience is important to human-robot interaction, but the outcomes users value, and how those preferences vary across individuals and contexts, are often unknown. While inverse learning approaches using human data can help identify user rewards, in many assistive settings the experimental costs of executing a control policy, measuring biomechanical or physiological outcomes, and collecting user feedback often limit the number of queries and optimization iterations. Here, we present Simultaneous Forward and Inverse Human-In-the-Loop Optimization (SFIHILO), which efficiently infers individual-specific reward functions from preferences over human outcomes and identifies a final control policy that maximizes the learned reward. SFIHILO bootstraps a forward model to predict user outcomes from control policies, uses this model for active querying to accelerate inverse reward learning, and then optimizes the final control policy without additional user trials. We score candidate policies by their expected reduction in uncertainty across both forward and inverse beliefs, targeting a regional preference boundary to robustly inform this simultaneous learning process. In simulation, we show that SFIHILO was effective across user heterogeneity, outcome dimensionalities, precision requirements, noise levels, and nonstationarity; compared with mutual information approaches, the proposed active querying strategy significantly improved sample efficiency in inverse learning while preserving forward model accuracy. This approach demonstrates the potential to infer latent human goals, enabling more transferable and effective human-robot interaction.

AI.tldr: SFIHILO simultaneously learns a forward outcome model and inverse reward model from human preferences, using uncertainty-reduction active querying and final policy optimization without extra user trials, showing improved sample efficiency in simulation.
AI.motivation: Subjective user experience matters in human-robot interaction, but the outcomes users value and how preferences vary across individuals and contexts are often unknown. Inverse learning from human data can identify user rewards, yet assistive settings impose high experimental costs for executing control policies, measuring biomechanical or physiological outcomes, and collecting feedback, limiting queries and optimization iterations.
AI.method: The paper presents Simultaneous Forward and Inverse Human-In-the-Loop Optimization (SFIHILO). It bootstraps a forward model to predict user outcomes from control policies, uses this model for active querying to accelerate inverse reward learning, and then optimizes the final control policy without additional user trials. Candidate policies are scored by expected uncertainty reduction across both forward and inverse beliefs, targeting a regional preference boundary to robustly inform simultaneous learning.
AI.result: In simulation, SFIHILO was effective across user heterogeneity, outcome dimensionalities, precision requirements, noise levels, and nonstationarity. Compared with mutual information approaches, the proposed active querying strategy significantly improved sample efficiency in inverse learning while preserving forward model accuracy.
AI.conclusion: SFIHILO demonstrates the potential to infer latent human goals, enabling more transferable and effective human-robot interaction.

title: Hapi: A Multivariable Land-Surface Transformer for Medium-Range Hydrological Forecasting at Continental Scale
summary: Accurate flood forecasts several days in advance are essential for flood control, water-resource management, and emergency response. Producing them at high resolution over a continental domain calls for local hydrological detail together with spatial context extending from river basins to synoptic weather systems. We developed Hapi, a U-Net Swin Transformer that uses fine three-dimensional patches and hierarchical shifted-window attention to forecast discharge, surface runoff, snow water equivalent, and soil wetness across the contiguous United States. The model produces 24--72-hour forecasts at $0.05^{\circ}$ resolution, with learned Laplacian task weights adjusting each variable's contribution to training. On 2024 test data using reconstructed weather and land-surface inputs from ERA5-Land, Hapi outperformed an operational physics-based model and a state-of-the-art AI model in flood detection. Independent validation against 3,881 U.S. Geological Survey gauges and a Hurricane Helene case study supported its advantage over the physics-based model in reproducing daily discharge. Controlled experiments showed that learned task weighting strengthens rare-flood detection, which is particularly sensitive to changes in precipitation inputs. Hapi produced a four-variable, 72-hour forecast across the contiguous United States with an average inference time of 0.11 seconds on a single A100 GPU.

AI.tldr: Hapi, a U-Net Swin Transformer, produces 24–72-hour, 0.05° flood forecasts across the contiguous United States, outperforming operational physics-based and state-of-the-art AI models.
AI.motivation: Accurate multi-day flood forecasts are essential for flood control, water-resource management, and emergency response, but continental-scale high-resolution forecasting requires both local hydrological detail and broad spatial context spanning river basins to synoptic weather systems.
AI.method: Hapi uses fine three-dimensional patches and hierarchical shifted-window attention. It forecasts discharge, surface runoff, snow water equivalent, and soil wetness, with learned Laplacian task weights adjusting each variable's training contribution. Evaluation used 2024 test data with reconstructed ERA5-Land weather and land-surface inputs, 3,881 USGS gauges, and a Hurricane Helene case study.
AI.result: Hapi outperformed an operational physics-based model and a state-of-the-art AI model in flood detection and surpassed the physics-based model in reproducing daily discharge. Learned task weighting improved rare-flood detection, which is highly sensitive to precipitation input changes. It delivered a four-variable, 72-hour continental forecast in 0.11 seconds average inference time on a single A100 GPU.
AI.conclusion: Hapi demonstrates that a U-Net Swin Transformer with learned task weighting enables accurate, high-resolution, continental-scale multi-day flood forecasting at very low computational cost.

title: Density-Driven Area Coverage for Nonholonomic Multi-Robot Systems with Safety Guarantee
summary: Density-Driven Optimal Control (D2OC) provides a principled approach to distributing multi-robot teams over non-uniform spatial distributions. Applying D2OC to nonholonomic robots, however, creates a gap between safety constraints imposed on a reference motion and the physical inputs that determine the actual robot motion. We address this issue by enforcing the safety constraint directly on the robot's physical inputs while preserving the density-driven coverage objective. The proposed framework combines D2OC with a control barrier function safety filter through a feedback-linearizing look-ahead point, allowing safety and actuator limits to be considered together during control. We further derive a safety margin that accounts for the look-ahead geometry, robot footprint, and motion during each control interval. Simulation results show that the proposed method maintains the required physical separation while achieving coverage performance comparable to a conventional reference-tracking approach, which can satisfy safety on the reference motion yet violate the corresponding physical clearance. Experiments on multiple nonholonomic robots in the Robotarium further demonstrate safe execution while driving the robots toward the desired spatial distribution. These results show that enforcing safety directly on the physical inputs can eliminate the mismatch between safety certification and physical robot motion in density-driven multi-robot coverage.

AI.tldr: D2OC for nonholonomic multi-robot coverage is combined with a control barrier function safety filter via a feedback-linearizing look-ahead point, enforcing safety directly on physical inputs while preserving the density-coverage objective.
AI.motivation: Density-Driven Optimal Control (D2OC) distributes multi-robot teams over non-uniform spatial distributions, but applying it to nonholonomic robots creates a gap: safety constraints are imposed on a reference motion, while the actual robot motion is determined by physical inputs. This mismatch means safety certification on the reference trajectory does not guarantee physical clearance.
AI.method: The framework combines D2OC with a control barrier function (CBF) safety filter through a feedback-linearizing look-ahead point, so that safety and actuator limits are considered together during control while the density-driven coverage objective is preserved. A safety margin is derived that accounts for the look-ahead geometry, robot footprint, and motion during each control interval.
AI.result: Simulations show the method maintains the required physical separation while achieving coverage performance comparable to a conventional reference-tracking approach, which can satisfy safety on the reference motion yet violate the corresponding physical clearance.
