Experiments on multiple nonholonomic robots in the Robotarium demonstrate safe execution while driving the robots toward the desired spatial distribution.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing safety directly on physical inputs eliminates the mismatch between safety certification and physical robot motion in density-driven multi-robot coverage.

title: Trustworthy Agentic AI: Failure Modes, Mitigation Strategies, and a Lifecycle Framework for Autonomous LLM Systems
summary: Agentic AI systems built on large language models can plan over multiple steps, use external tools, retain information in memory, and coordinate with other agents. These capabilities make them more useful than static language models, but they also introduce new security and operational risks. Untrusted content from websites, emails, documents, and databases can enter the same context as system instructions; persistent memory can carry compromised information across sessions; and access to external tools can turn an incorrect model response into a consequential real-world action. This article reviews the trustworthiness of agentic AI across five interconnected dimensions: safety and robustness, alignment and human oversight, transparency and auditability, privacy and data governance, and regulatory compliance. It organizes key failure modes, including indirect prompt injection, backdoor triggers, goal misgeneralization, memory contamination, and cross-session data leakage, into a unified taxonomy. It also examines major mitigation approaches, such as instruction hierarchies, context isolation, spotlighting, process-based supervision, constrained tool use, and privacy-preserving memory, while distinguishing techniques supported by empirical evidence from those that remain largely conceptual. Building on this analysis, we introduce the Trustworthy Agent Development Lifecycle (TADL), a six-phase framework covering specification, design, training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring. For each phase, TADL identifies relevant trust activities, expected evidence, and risk-based decision gates. Although TADL has not yet been empirically validated, it provides a structured foundation for developing and evaluating more secure and accountable agentic systems. The article concludes by identifying gaps in current benchmarks and outlining priorities for future research.

AI.tldr: This article reviews the trustworthiness of LLM-based agentic AI across five dimensions, organizes failure modes (e.g., indirect prompt injection, memory contamination) into a taxonomy, examines mitigation approaches, and proposes the six-phase Trustworthy Agent Development Lifecycle (TADL).
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems, while more capable than static LLMs due to multi-step planning, tool use, memory, and multi-agent coordination, introduce novel security and operational risks: untrusted content entering the instruction context, persistent memory carrying compromised information across sessions, and tool access converting model errors into real-world actions. A structured review of trustworthiness is needed.
AI.method: The paper conducts a review organized along five interconnected trustworthiness dimensions: safety and robustness, alignment and human oversight, transparency and auditability, privacy and data governance, and regulatory compliance. It builds a unified taxonomy of failure modes and surveys mitigation techniques, distinguishing empirically supported methods from conceptual ones, then derives the TADL framework from this analysis.
AI.result: A unified taxonomy of key failure modes (indirect prompt injection, backdoor triggers, goal misgeneralization, memory contamination, cross-session data leakage) and an examination of mitigations including instruction hierarchies, context isolation, spotlighting, process-based supervision, constrained tool use, and privacy-preserving memory, with a clear separation of evidence-backed versus conceptual techniques.
AI.conclusion: The proposed TADL—a six-phase framework spanning specification, design, training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring, with trust activities, expected evidence, and risk-based decision gates per phase—offers a structured foundation for building accountable agentic systems, though it lacks empirical validation. The article closes by identifying benchmark gaps and future research priorities.

title: AquaWorld: Structure-Consistent Underwater World Generation for Robot Simulation
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures
summary: Underwater robot simulation requires diverse environments in which terrain, scene composition, tasks, and currents remain mutually consistent. We present AquaWorld, a world-generation framework that preserves these relationships through shared terrain structure. A language-conditioned plan generates 3D terrain and shared structural references that guide asset placement, task definition, and inflow specification under stochastic variation. The framework incorporates over 10,000 underwater-compatible assets, predicts reusable terrain-conditioned mean-flow fields through a CFD-supervised residual model, and supports conventional underwater vehicles and bio-inspired robotic fish. On 24 paired terrains, structure-consistent randomization produces substantially better cross-factor consistency than independent randomization. In a matched-budget policy-training comparison, structurally coherent randomization achieves a validation success rate 21% higher than independent randomization. In separate physical experiments, a simulation-trained visual navigation policy succeeds in 95% of physical tank trials without updating its perception or control modules. Overall, AquaWorld provides a practical way to generate varied underwater environments while retaining the structural relationships needed for flow simulation and robot learning.

AI.tldr: AquaWorld is a world-generation framework for underwater robot simulation that keeps terrain, scene composition, tasks, and currents mutually consistent via shared terrain structure, improving cross-factor consistency and policy training.
AI.motivation: Underwater robot simulation needs diverse environments, but terrain, scene composition, tasks, and currents must remain mutually consistent. Independent randomization breaks these relationships, harming flow simulation and robot learning.
AI.method: A language-conditioned plan generates 3D terrain and shared structural references that guide asset placement, task definition, and inflow specification under stochastic variation. The framework includes over 10,000 underwater-compatible assets, a CFD-supervised residual model predicting reusable terrain-conditioned mean-flow fields, and support for conventional underwater vehicles and bio-inspired robotic fish.
AI.result: On 24 paired terrains, structure-consistent randomization yields substantially better cross-factor consistency than independent randomization. In a matched-budget policy-training comparison, structurally coherent randomization achieves a 21% higher validation success rate. A simulation-trained visual navigation policy succeeds in 95% of physical tank trials without updating perception or control modules.
AI.conclusion: AquaWorld provides a practical way to generate varied underwater environments while retaining the structural relationships needed for flow simulation and robot learning.

title: ProcessLight: Process Supervision for Large Language Model Based Traffic Signal Control
comment: This paper has been accepted by The 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026)
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been introduced into traffic signal control (TSC) as decision agents due to their strengths in human-readable reasoning generation. Yet, existing LLM TSC methods optimize only from final outcomes and fail to distinguish valid from flawed reasoning steps, causing useful or misleading steps to be jointly updated and thus impairing the model's learning of effective reasoning. To bridge this gap, we propose an LLM-based framework ProcessLight to decompose signal decisions into verifiable semantic steps. Building on ProcessLight, we further develop Step-wise Traffic Process Policy Optimization (STeP-PO), a novel reinforcement learning framework that optimizes structured reasoning processes through step-level credit assignment. Specifically, STeP-PO uses step quality scores to evaluate local reasoning quality and step importance to measure each step's influence on the final action, and then assigns step-level advantages over a semantic step tree structure. The resulting step-level advantages are propagated to reasoning tokens, enabling fine-grained policy optimization beyond outcome-only rewards. Extensive experiments over multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/wenzhaoabc/processlight.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ProcessLight and STeP-PO, an LLM-based framework and RL method that decompose traffic signal decisions into verifiable semantic steps and optimize them via step-level credit assignment, outperforming outcome-only approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based traffic signal control (TSC) methods optimize only from final outcomes, failing to distinguish valid from flawed reasoning steps. This causes useful and misleading steps to be jointly updated, impairing the model's learning of effective reasoning.
AI.method: The authors propose ProcessLight, an LLM-based framework that decomposes signal decisions into verifiable semantic steps. Building on it, they develop Step-wise Traffic Process Policy Optimization (STeP-PO), an RL framework that performs step-level credit assignment. STeP-PO uses step quality scores to assess local reasoning quality and step importance to measure each step's influence on the final action, assigning step-level advantages over a semantic step tree structure, which are then propagated to reasoning tokens for fine-grained policy optimization beyond outcome-only rewards.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ProcessLight and STeP-PO enable fine-grained, step-level optimization of LLM reasoning for traffic signal control, overcoming the limitations of outcome-only reward optimization.

title: SHAFT: A Slack-Compensating, Helical-Buckling-Attenuating Flexible-Shaft Transmission for Lightweight Multi-DoF Manipulation
comment: 9 pages, 14 figures, submitted as proceedings of IROS2026
summary: Lightweight and slim manipulators enable safe operation in human living environments. Proximal actuation using remote transmission mechanisms, such as wire-driven or Bowden cables, effectively reduces inertia and arm size by relocating motors near the base and transmitting torque to distal joints. Existing approaches either increase mass through additional components, such as pulleys for direction changes, or suffer from reduced transmission efficiency due to friction losses. Flexible shaft transmission avoids both mass increase and excessive friction losses, but faces increasing angular transmission error due to helical buckling caused by slack generated at joint bending. To address this problem, we propose SHAFT: a Slack-compensating, Helical-buckling-Attenuating Flexible- shaft Transmission mechanism. This mechanism compensates for slack through a proximal tensioner, improving the angular transmission error and efficiency of flexible shaft transmission without increasing the moving mass of the arm section. In a transmission path containing four 90-degree bends, the proposed mechanism demonstrated approximately 30% higher efficiency and approximately 65% lower angular transmission error compared to a flexible shaft transmission without a tensioner. Using this mechanism, we fabricated a 6-Degree-of-Freedom (DoF) arm with a 1-DoF gripper manipulator consisting of a rotary module housing motors with a tensioner, and a 280 g weight for the arm module. The proposed manipulator represents a novel remote actuation system for achieving lightweight construction with high efficiency, contributing to the acceleration of safe robot deployment in human environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SHAFT, a slack-compensating, helical-buckling-attenuating flexible-shaft transmission mechanism that improves efficiency and reduces angular transmission error in remotely actuated lightweight manipulators.
AI.motivation: Lightweight and slim manipulators are needed for safe operation in human living environments. Proximal actuation with remote transmission (wire-driven or Bowden cables) reduces inertia and arm size by relocating motors near the base. However, existing approaches either gain mass through extra components like pulleys for direction changes, or lose transmission efficiency to friction. Flexible shaft transmission avoids both issues but suffers from increasing angular transmission error caused by helical buckling from slack at joint bending.
AI.method: The authors propose SHAFT: a Slack-compensating, Helical-buckling-Attenuating Flexible-shaft Transmission mechanism. It compensates for slack via a proximal tensioner, improving angular transmission error and efficiency without increasing the moving mass of the arm section. They validated it on a transmission path with four 90-degree bends and built a 6-DoF arm with a 1-DoF gripper manipulator, comprising a rotary module housing motors with a tensioner and a 280 g arm module.
AI.result: In a path with four 90-degree bends, the mechanism achieved approximately 30% higher efficiency and approximately 65% lower angular transmission error compared to a flexible shaft transmission without a tensioner.
AI.conclusion: SHAFT provides a novel remote actuation system enabling lightweight construction with high efficiency, contributing to accelerating safe robot deployment in human environments.

title: CTSpinoPelvic1K: spine, pelvis, ribs and femora in one coordinate frame, annotated for lumbosacral transitional anatomy
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Dataset (802 annotated CT records, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22139642; code at https://github.com/OpenSpineConsortium/CTSpinoPelvic1K. Submitted to Medical Physics as a Medical Physics Dataset Article
summary:
Purpose: A vertebra at the lumbosacral junction is named by counting caudally from C2 on whole-spine imaging, but a lumbar case is planned on lumbar-only imaging (T12 to S1), without C2. Abdominopelvic CT holds that span plus the lowest ribs and pelvis. Where a lumbosacral transitional vertebra (LSTV) alters the count, the local anatomy is ambiguous: four rib-free vertebrae may be an L1 with a lumbar rib or an L5 assimilated to the sacrum, and six may be a sixth lumbar vertebra, a T12 with aplastic ribs, or a lumbarized S1. CTSpinoPelvic1K asks whether local morphology resolves it without the count. CTSpine1K's vertebrae and CTPelvic1K's pelvis covered these patients but were never joined; this release joins them on one series and adds the bones neither had. It provides 802 CT records with per-level ribs and femora, levels anchored on the lowest rib-bearing vertebra and S1, and classes for L6, T13, a separate S1 and lumbar ribs, so anomalies are recorded as such.
  Acquisition and Validation Methods: Records pair CTSpine1K and CTPelvic1K labels on each patient's bone-richest series under a VerSe-native scheme. Validation covered geometric invariants (802/802 pass), rib-vertebra incidence across 5,749 ribs (0.035% offset), and spinopelvic measures matching published values.
  Data Format and Usage Notes: NIfTI image/label pairs with patient-grouped LSTV-stratified five-fold splits and a loader; archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22139642.
  Potential Applications: Classifying a vertebra from local features; updating cadaveric morphometry; spinopelvic assessment; opportunistic screening; and, absent a public preoperative lumbar cohort, surgical planning research (377 records prone). Limitations: thoracic ground truth is field-of-view limited; postural angles supine; no held-out test set; ribs are triaged-review pseudolabels; Castellvi grades two-reader consensus on 33 records.

AI.tldr: CTSpinoPelvic1K is a released dataset of 802 CT records that joins CTSpine1K and CTPelvic1K labels on each patient's bone-richest series and adds ribs and femora, anchoring levels on the lowest rib-bearing vertebra and S1 so lumbosacral transitional vertebra anomalies (L6, T13, separate S1, lumbar ribs) are recorded as such, enabling vertebra identification from local morphology without whole-spine counting.
AI.motivation: A lumbosacral vertebra is normally named by counting caudally from C2 on whole-spine imaging, but lumbar cases are planned on lumbar-only imaging (T12–S1) without C2. Abdominopelvic CT spans that region plus the lowest ribs and pelvis, yet when a lumbosacral transitional vertebra (LSTV) alters the count, local anatomy becomes ambiguous—four rib-free vertebrae may be an L1 with a lumbar rib or an L5 assimilated to the sacrum, and six may be a sixth lumbar vertebra, a T12 with aplastic ribs, or a lumbarized S1. The paper asks whether local morphology can resolve this ambiguity without the count. CTSpine1K's vertebrae and CTPelvic1K's pelvis covered these patients but were never joined.
AI.method: The release joins CTSpine1K and CTPelvic1K labels on each patient's bone-richest series under a VerSe-native scheme, adding the bones neither had. It provides 802 CT records with per-level ribs and femora, levels anchored on the lowest rib-bearing vertebra and S1, and classes for L6, T13, a separate S1, and lumbar ribs. Validation covered geometric invariants (802/802 pass), rib-vertebra incidence across 5,749 ribs (0.035% offset), and spinopelvic measures matching published values. Data are NIfTI image/label pairs with patient-grouped LSTV-stratified five-fold splits and a loader.
AI.result: The dataset passes geometric invariants in 802/802 records, shows a 0.035% offset in rib-vertebra incidence across 5,749 ribs, and yields spinopelvic measures matching published values. It is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22139642 with patient-grouped, LSTV-stratified five-fold splits and a loader.
AI.conclusion: CTSpinoPelvic1K enables classifying a vertebra from local features, updating cadaveric morphometry, spinopelvic assessment, opportunistic screening, and—absent a public preoperative lumbar cohort—surgical planning research (377 records prone). Limitations: thoracic ground truth is field-of-view limited; postural angles are supine; there is no held-out test set; ribs are triaged-review pseudolabels; and Castellvi grades are a two-reader consensus on only 33 records.

title: A Direct Rigid Transmission 2-DoF Wrist Extension for Tendon-Driven Hand
comment: Accepted at "IROS 2026 Sensors and Actuators for Dexterous Manipulation Workshop"
summary: Dexterous manipulation in confined spaces requires local control of hand orientation. Without a wrist, a dexterous hand must obtain this local orientation through coordinated motion of the robot arm, often involving several joints and a more complex end-effector path. We present CRAFT-Wrist, a concentric 2-DoF wrist extension that mounts between a robot arm and the CRAFT Hand without modifying the hand. Two XC430-T240BB-T servos drive sideways and front-back rotation through short rigid transmissions. Our initial hardware prototype actuates both axes under load, achieving a demonstrated workspace of $\pm20^{\circ}$ in radial--ulnar deviation (left--right) and a front-back range of $+80^{\circ}$ in flexion and $-18^{\circ}$ in extension. We characterize the resulting finger-motor loading across several wrist postures and demonstrate how the wrist supplies local orientation in grasping, nail hammering, and blackboard wiping. Demonstrations and assembly instructions are available at https://craft-wrist.github.io/.

AI.tldr: CRAFT-Wrist is a concentric 2-DoF wrist extension mounted between a robot arm and the CRAFT Hand, providing local hand orientation without modifying the hand, and is demonstrated in grasping and tool-use tasks.
AI.motivation: Dexterous manipulation in confined spaces requires local control of hand orientation. Without a wrist, a dexterous hand must achieve this local orientation via coordinated motion of several robot arm joints, resulting in more complex end-effector paths.
AI.method: A concentric 2-DoF wrist extension is mounted between a robot arm and the CRAFT Hand without modifying the hand. Two XC430-T240BB-T servos drive sideways and front-back rotation through short rigid transmissions. The authors characterize finger-motor loading across several wrist postures.
AI.result: The hardware prototype actuates both axes under load, achieving a workspace of ±20° in radial–ulnar deviation (left–right) and a front-back range of +80° in flexion and −18° in extension. The wrist supplies local orientation in grasping, nail hammering, and blackboard wiping.
AI.conclusion: The CRAFT-Wrist provides a compact, add-on 2-DoF solution for local hand orientation, potentially simplifying arm coordination and enabling dexterous manipulation in confined spaces. Demonstrations and assembly instructions are publicly available.

title: DVA-Neurons: Design and Verification of Adaptive LIF Neurons: From Single-Neuron Dynamics to Multi-Neuron Spiking Networks
summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a promising path toward ultra-low-power artificial intelligence inference by emulating the event-driven computation of biological neurons. However, two challenges limit their practical deployment. First, fixed-parameter Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons lack the adaptation mechanisms observed in biology, where neurons modulate their excitability based on firing history. Second, scaling from single neurons to multi-neuron networks introduces challenges in synaptic weight distribution and inter-neuron spike routing that are absent in isolated designs. This paper addresses both issues through the extension, verification, and physical implementation of adaptive LIF neurons at three architectural scales. This work contributes: a 2nd-order neuron with two-stage synaptic filtering for richer temporal dynamics; a fully-connected 6-neuron spiking network with configurable weights (100 to 5) demonstrating weight-based inter-neuron communication; and a direct verification methodology enabling per-cycle observation of all internal states. All designs were synthesized targeting Selected Area Electron Diffraction (SAED) 14 nm Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor (CMOS) technology at 1 GHz and verified with Cocotb-based Python testbenches under pulsed current stimuli (amplitude 80, ISI=3). The results show that adaptation effectively modulates firing: 31% suppression in the 2nd-order neuron (25 vs.\ 36 spikes) and 31% reduction in postsynaptic firing in the network (18 vs.\ 26 spikes). Physically, the 2nd-order neuron costs 1.77x more area and 1.52x more power than the 1st-order baseline, while the 6-neuron network demonstrates near-linear scaling (5.7x area, 5.3x power). Seven verification bugs spanning testbench connectivity, fixed-point overflow, and Verilog expression-width semantics are documented.

AI.tldr: This paper extends, verifies, and physically implements adaptive LIF spiking neurons at three architectural scales in 14 nm CMOS, showing ~31% firing suppression from adaptation and near-linear network scaling.
AI.motivation: Fixed-parameter LIF neurons lack biological adaptation mechanisms that modulate excitability based on firing history, and scaling from single neurons to multi-neuron networks introduces synaptic weight distribution and inter-neuron spike routing challenges absent in isolated designs.
AI.method: The work develops a 2nd-order neuron with two-stage synaptic filtering, a fully-connected 6-neuron spiking network with configurable weights (100 to 5), and a per-cycle direct verification methodology. All designs were synthesized in SAED 14 nm CMOS at 1 GHz and verified with Cocotb-based Python testbenches under pulsed current stimuli (amplitude 80, ISI=3).
AI.result: Adaptation suppresses firing by 31% in the 2nd-order neuron (25 vs. 36 spikes) and 31% in postsynaptic network firing (18 vs. 26 spikes). The 2nd-order neuron costs 1.77x more area and 1.52x more power than the 1st-order baseline, while the 6-neuron network scales near-linearly (5.7x area, 5.3x power). Seven verification bugs were documented across testbench connectivity, fixed-point overflow, and Verilog expression-width semantics.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive LIF neurons provide effective firing modulation and scale near-linearly to multi-neuron spiking networks in nanoscale CMOS, with a documented verification methodology; however, adaptation incurs area and power overhead that must be traded off in ultra-low-power SNN deployment.

title: StateMem: Single-State Residual Memory with Adaptive Inference for Vision-Language-Action Policies
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, conference
summary: Memory-dependent robotic manipulation often requires later actions to use information from earlier interactions. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) policies primarily rely on current observations, limiting historical information retention. Memory-augmented VLAs, such as MemoryVLA, address this limitation with external memory banks but require explicit storage and retrieval. To address these limitations, we propose StateMem, a single-state residual memory framework for VLA policies that uses prediction error to update a persistent memory token through low-rank residuals and to adaptively route cached prefixes. A training-free controller adjusts the routing threshold online, while fast correction compensates for stale prefix features during cache reuse. We evaluate StateMem on LIBERO, RoboMemArena, and real-world manipulation tasks. On LIBERO, StateMem achieves an average success rate of 97.6% and reduces the average VLM prefix refresh rate by 20.25% relative to full refresh. In the Occlusion category of RoboMemArena, StateMem achieves the best performance among single-VLA methods, reaching 21.8% Task Success Rate (TSR) and 44.3% Cumulative Success Rate (CSR). Across six real-world manipulation tasks, it achieves +21% in average success rate.

AI.tldr: StateMem is a single-state residual memory framework for vision-language-action policies that uses prediction error to update a persistent memory token via low-rank residuals and adaptively route cached prefixes, improving memory-dependent manipulation without external memory banks.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA policies rely mainly on current observations, limiting retention of historical information. Memory-augmented VLAs (e.g., MemoryVLA) address this with external memory banks but require explicit storage and retrieval, which is inefficient.
AI.method: StateMem maintains a persistent memory token updated by prediction error through low-rank residuals, and adaptively routes cached prefixes. A training-free controller adjusts the routing threshold online, and fast correction compensates for stale prefix features during cache reuse.
AI.result: On LIBERO, StateMem achieves 97.6% average success rate and reduces average VLM prefix refresh rate by 20.25% vs. full refresh. On RoboMemArena's Occlusion category it reaches 21.8% TSR and 44.3% CSR, best among single-VLA methods. Across six real-world tasks it gains +21% average success rate.
AI.conclusion: StateMem provides an efficient single-state residual memory mechanism that enhances historical information retention in VLA policies while reducing computation, outperforming prior single-VLA approaches and improving real-world manipulation.

title: From Research Frontier to Laboratory Bench: Design of a Four-Tier Experimental Teaching System for Multimodal Medical Image Intelligent Diagnosis
summary: Undergraduate programmes in intelligent medical engineering are expanding, yet laboratory curricula lag behind the multimodal, long-tailed, and distributionally shifting realities of clinical AI. This design paper presents an advanced experimental teaching system that translates an ongoing multimodal deep learning research project on endometrial carcinoma into a structured undergraduate lab sequence. We identify three educational gaps (modality, authenticity, and deployment) and derive four pedagogical principles from constructive alignment, experiential learning, the research teaching nexus, and the CDIO framework. The curriculum comprises four progressive tiers plus an engineering layer, with 32 laboratory units over 64 contact hours, delivered via a custom virtual clinical workstation using de-identified multi-institutional data. Each tier maps to a specific technical bottleneck, prerequisite coursework, and criterion-referenced deliverables. Data governance, safety, and assessment protocols are specified. Learning outcome data will be collected across two implementation cycles.

AI.tldr: A design paper proposing an advanced undergraduate laboratory curriculum for intelligent medical engineering, translating an ongoing multimodal deep learning research project on endometrial carcinoma into a four-tier lab sequence plus an engineering layer (32 units, 64 contact hours) delivered through a custom virtual clinical workstation.
AI.motivation: Undergraduate intelligent medical engineering programmes are expanding, but laboratory curricula lag behind the multimodal, long-tailed, and distributionally shifting realities of clinical AI. The work addresses three educational gaps: modality, authenticity, and deployment.
AI.method: Four pedagogical principles (constructive alignment, experiential learning, the research teaching nexus, and the CDIO framework) are used to derive the curriculum. It comprises four progressive tiers plus an engineering layer, with each tier mapped to a specific technical bottleneck, prerequisite coursework, and criterion-referenced deliverables. Delivery uses a custom virtual clinical workstation with de-identified multi-institutional data, alongside specified data governance, safety, and assessment protocols.
AI.result: The curriculum design is presented as a 32-unit, 64-contact-hour sequence with tiered technical bottlenecks and deliverables; learning outcome data collection is planned across two implementation cycles, so no empirical results are yet reported.
AI.conclusion: The proposed system offers a structured way to align undergraduate clinical AI laboratory teaching with authentic, multimodal, and deployment-oriented research practice, with outcome evaluation to follow over two implementation cycles.

title: Decentralized Multi-Robot Exploration with Probabilistic Peer Intent and Multi-hop Plan Propagation
summary: Efficient coordination under limited communication remains a key challenge in decentralized multi-robot exploration. While centralized approaches benefit from global information sharing, they are often impractical in large-scale or communication-constrained environments. Existing Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based approaches, such as Decentralized Monte Carlo Exploration (DMCE), enable decentralized planning by taking peer intent into account. This peer intent is obtained by communicating sequences of planned waypoints with robots within direct communication range. In this work, we extend this idea by introducing Probabilistic Peer Intent (PPI), which converts peer trajectories into a continuous spatial representation of predicted intent and incorporates it into local MCTS action evaluation. We additionally study the effects of sharing peer intent beyond direct communication range by propagating plans over multiple hops. Experiments across multiple simulated environments and team sizes show that PPI and Multi-hop propagation can each improve decentralized exploration, with their relative benefits depending on environment structure and team size. We also demonstrate the real-world deployment of our method on three robots operating in different environment types.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Probabilistic Peer Intent (PPI) and multi-hop plan propagation to improve decentralized multi-robot exploration within an MCTS framework, showing environment- and team-size-dependent gains plus real-world deployment on three robots.
AI.motivation: Decentralized multi-robot exploration under limited communication is challenging; centralized methods rely on global information and are impractical at scale. Existing MCTS-based decentralized planners such as DMCE use peer intent but only through waypoint sequences shared with robots in direct communication range, limiting coordination quality and reach.
AI.method: The work extends DMCE by proposing PPI, which converts communicated peer trajectories into a continuous spatial representation of predicted intent and integrates it into local MCTS action evaluation. It also studies sharing peer intent beyond direct range by propagating plans over multiple hops.
AI.result: Across multiple simulated environments and team sizes, both PPI and multi-hop propagation improve decentralized exploration, with relative benefits depending on environment structure and team size. Real-world deployment is demonstrated on three robots in different environment types.
AI.conclusion: Probabilistic intent representation and multi-hop plan sharing are effective, complementary enhancements to decentralized MCTS exploration, with effectiveness conditioned on environment and team characteristics; the approach transfers to physical multi-robot systems.

title: ISA-Bench: A Benchmark for Computational Reasoning Across Instruction Set Architectures
summary: Large language model code generation benchmarks primarily evaluate well-resourced languages like Python and Java, where models benefit from abundant training data. They provide limited evidence about reasoning in unfamiliar computational models: deriving arithmetic from a single subtract instruction, coordinating parallel programs across communicating nodes, or wiring logic gates into circuits. We present ISA-Bench, a benchmark of programming games with constrained instruction sets. For each game we provide a full execution stack (parser, VM, and verifier), enabling automated evaluation with structured feedback for iterative refinement. Reasoning models achieve higher average solve rates than code-specialized and general-purpose models, but unfamiliar syntax remains a major source of failure. Models solve more tasks with iterative feedback, though the gains vary substantially across architectures. We introduce a reasoning--execution gap (REG) analysis that reveals a recurring disconnect between identifying a plausible computational strategy and expressing it as a correct program in the target ISA. Code is open-sourced.

AI.tldr: ISA-Bench is a new benchmark of programming games with constrained instruction sets, offering a full execution stack (parser, VM, verifier) for automated evaluation and iterative refinement. Reasoning models outperform code-specialized and general-purpose models, but unfamiliar syntax causes frequent failures; a reasoning–execution gap (REG) analysis exposes the disconnect between choosing a strategy and expressing it correctly in the target ISA.
AI.motivation: Existing code generation benchmarks mainly cover well-resourced languages such as Python and Java, where models benefit from abundant training data. They therefore offer limited evidence about reasoning in unfamiliar computational models—for example, deriving arithmetic from a single subtract instruction, coordinating parallel programs across communicating nodes, or wiring logic gates into circuits. The paper aims to fill this gap by evaluating models on constrained instruction sets that demand genuine computational reasoning rather than memorized language patterns.
AI.method: The authors present ISA-Bench, a benchmark of programming games built around constrained instruction sets. For each game, they provide a complete execution stack comprising a parser, a VM, and a verifier, which enables automated evaluation with structured feedback for iterative refinement. They evaluate reasoning models, code-specialized models, and general-purpose models, and introduce a reasoning–execution gap (REG) analysis to diagnose when models identify a plausible computational strategy but fail to translate it into a correct program in the target ISA.
AI.result: Reasoning models achieve higher average solve rates than code-specialized and general-purpose models. However, unfamiliar syntax remains a major source of failure. Models improve their solve rates when given iterative feedback, but the magnitude of these gains varies substantially across architectures. The REG analysis reveals a recurring disconnect between strategy identification and correct program expression in the target ISA.
AI.conclusion: ISA-Bench shifts code generation evaluation toward unfamiliar, constrained computational models and shows that strong reasoning ability does not automatically translate into correct low-level program expression. The recurring reasoning–execution gap highlights syntax and ISA-expression as distinct bottlenecks, motivating feedback-driven evaluation and targeted improvements. The code is open-sourced.

title: BEACON: Belief-Enabled Adaptive CONtrol for Imitation Learning under Uncertainty
summary: Robot manipulation tasks often involve hidden state information that cannot be directly observed and must be inferred through sequential physical interactions. In such partially observable settings, conditioning an imitation learning policy directly on the recent raw observation history leads to poor performance. This is due to state aliasing, wherein identical observations may arise from different hidden states, and the policy receives conflicting action labels for the same input. To enable history-aware disambiguation capability, we propose conditioning a diffusion policy on a structured representation of the hidden states using Bayesian belief that exposes both the current most likely state estimate and the remaining uncertainty. This representation replaces raw history with a structured, compact input, enabling the policy to implicitly modulate between exploratory and exploitative behaviors based on belief uncertainty, without explicit mode switching or reward shaping. We evaluate across two domains with qualitatively different belief representations: a continuous belief for cornstalk gripper alignment via tactile sensing, and a discrete categorical distribution for latched door opening. In both domains, the belief-conditioned policy substantially outperforms the observation-only baseline and approaches privileged ground-truth performance, with ablations illustrating that the policy adapts its exploration behavior depending on the belief uncertainty at inference time.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes conditioning a diffusion imitation-learning policy on a Bayesian belief representation of hidden states (most-likely estimate plus residual uncertainty) instead of raw observation history, enabling history-aware disambiguation and implicit exploration/exploitation modulation.
AI.motivation: In partially observable robot manipulation, hidden states must be inferred through sequential physical interaction. Conditioning a policy directly on recent raw observation history suffers from state aliasing: identical observations can originate from different hidden states, so the policy receives conflicting action labels for the same input, degrading imitation learning performance.
AI.method: The authors condition a diffusion policy on a structured Bayesian belief representation of the hidden states, which exposes both the current most-likely state estimate and the remaining uncertainty. This belief replaces raw history as a compact, structured input, allowing the policy to implicitly modulate between exploratory and exploitative behavior according to belief uncertainty, without explicit mode switching or reward shaping.
AI.result: Evaluated on two domains with qualitatively different belief representations: a continuous belief for cornstalk gripper alignment via tactile sensing, and a discrete categorical distribution for latched door opening. In both, the belief-conditioned policy substantially outperforms the observation-only baseline and approaches privileged ground-truth performance. Ablations show the policy adapts its exploration behavior based on belief uncertainty at inference time.
AI.conclusion: Structured Bayesian belief conditioning provides an effective, compact alternative to raw history for imitation learning under partial observability, resolving state aliasing and yielding near-privileged performance with uncertainty-driven, implicit exploration.

title: When Should a VLM Look? Paying Only for Visual Calls That Were Needed and Used
comment: 30 pages, 7 figures, 14 tables. Preprint under review
summary: Vision-language agents that crop and zoom are trained with rewards that credit a successful tool call, yet a successful call does not show that the model needed to look or used the pixels it received. On our cold-start checkpoint only 10% to 12% of visual calls were both needed and used, and released agents make spurious calls 36% to 87% of the time on individual benchmarks. Outcome rewards, judge rewards, and branch probes each observe one side of this failure, and about two thirds of what an outcome reward pays goes to calls that were neither needed nor used. CounterCredit asks both questions of every image-returning call at its realized pre-call state, using the policy's own gold-answer score. A decision value compares the realized visual branch with answering immediately; an evidence value compares the returned crop with random same-size patches substituted into the same call. A call verified on both earns cashback and every other executed call pays rent; the price is bounded so that every correct trajectory outranks every wrong one, and a dual-channel GRPO advantage keeps the price in its own units. From the same cold start, prompt pool, and budget, CounterCredit reaches 89.5% on V*, 80.2% on HR-Bench-4K, and 76.4% on HR-Bench-8K, 6.3 to 9.4 points above outcome-only GRPO at 1.78 against 1.84 calls per question, and lowers the spurious-call rate to 31% to 36%, the lowest among the agents evaluated. The same recipe lifts a Qwen3-VL-8B base from 75.4 to 80.8 on average.

AI.tldr: CounterCredit verifies each image-returning tool call for both necessity and use, paying it only if the crop's pixels causally matter, and improves vision-language agents' accuracy while cutting spurious calls.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language agents are trained with rewards that credit a successful tool call, but success doesn't prove the model needed to look or actually used the returned pixels. On the authors' cold-start checkpoint only 10%–12% of visual calls were both needed and used, and released agents make spurious calls 36%–87% of the time. Existing rewards (outcome rewards, judge rewards, branch probes) each capture only one side of this failure, with about two-thirds of outcome-reward credit going to calls that were neither needed nor used.
AI.method: CounterCredit interrogates every image-returning call at its realized pre-call state using the policy's own gold-answer score. A decision value compares the realized visual branch against answering immediately; an evidence value compares the returned crop against random same-size patches substituted into the same call. A call verified on both earns cashback, while every other executed call pays rent. The price is bounded so that every correct trajectory outranks every wrong one, and a dual-channel GRPO advantage keeps the price in its own units.
AI.result: From the same cold start, prompt pool, and budget, CounterCredit reaches 89.5% on V*, 80.2% on HR-Bench-4K, and 76.4% on HR-Bench-8K, 6.3–9.4 points above outcome-only GRPO, at 1.78 versus 1.84 calls per question. It lowers the spurious-call rate to 31%–36%, the lowest among evaluated agents. The recipe also lifts a Qwen3-VL-8B base from 75.4 to 80.8 on average.
AI.conclusion: CounterCredit provides fine-grained, causal credit assignment for visual tool calls, rewarding calls that are both necessary and actually used, and yields higher accuracy and fewer spurious calls than outcome-only GRPO across high-resolution benchmarks and model scales.

title: Rapidly-Iterating Grid-Based Near-Optimal Kinodynamic Motion Planning
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics
summary: This paper develops the Rapidly-iterating kinoDynamic Grid (RDG) algorithm, an asymptotically near-optimal kinodynamic motion planning algorithm that produces high quality solutions through rapid iteration. The algorithm leverages a state space grid decomposition to perform node selection, dynamics propagation, and graph revision in constant time complexity with respect to the number of nodes in the trajectory tree. Through a covering ball sequence induction proof, the algorithm is shown to be asymptotically near-optimal and probabilistically complete. Different subsystems of the algorithm are evaluated against common nearest-neighbor search-based methods at generating exploration bias. The RDG algorithm is evaluated through simulated trials in complex, kinodynamic motion planning problem environments up to 10 DOF relative to similar sparse, kinodynamic planning algorithms with optimality guarantees, SST and DIRT. The RDG algorithm outperforms both SST and DIRT in mean final solution quality by up to 104% and 40% respectively. Additionally, RDG maintained a 100% success rate, even on a 10-DOF test case where both SST and DIRT did not.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RDG, an asymptotically near-optimal kinodynamic motion planning algorithm using state space grid decomposition for constant-time node selection, dynamics propagation, and graph revision, outperforming SST and DIRT in solution quality.
AI.motivation: Kinodynamic motion planning with optimality guarantees typically relies on sparse trajectory trees and nearest-neighbor search, which can be computationally expensive and limit solution quality, especially in high-dimensional spaces. There is a need for an algorithm that produces high-quality solutions efficiently through rapid iteration.
AI.method: RDG leverages a state space grid decomposition to perform node selection, dynamics propagation, and graph revision in constant time complexity with respect to the number of nodes in the trajectory tree. It is proven asymptotically near-optimal and probabilistically complete via a covering ball sequence induction proof. Subsystems are evaluated against nearest-neighbor search-based methods for exploration bias generation.
AI.result: In simulated trials on complex kinodynamic problems up to 10 DOF, RDG outperformed SST and DIRT in mean final solution quality by up to 104% and 40% respectively. RDG maintained a 100% success rate, including on a 10-DOF test case where both SST and DIRT failed.
AI.conclusion: RDG provides an effective asymptotically near-optimal kinodynamic motion planning approach with constant-time operations via grid decomposition, achieving superior solution quality and reliability compared to SST and DIRT.

title: Beyond Linear Context: Graph-Guided Evidence Navigation for Long-Novel Reasoning with a Local 9B Language Model
comment: 10 pages, 11 figures, 2 tables. Code, graph data and an interactive demo: https://github.com/fuxiaoji/novel-graph-lab
summary: Long-context models read a novel the way a person reads a printout: one token after another, in narrative order, with the whole history competing for a fixed budget of attention. A detective does not work that way. They sort what happened when, and they keep a map of who relates to whom, so a clue from chapter one can meet a question asked at the end of the book. We test whether a frozen knowledge graph can give a small local model that same freedom. Thirty detective novels and 234 multiple-choice questions are answered by one fixed qwen3.5:9b reader under nine conditions: five graph routes, a recent-window baseline, whole-book compression, ordinary vector retrieval, and a question-only control. The strongest graph route reaches 53.85% (126/234) against 46.15% for the recent window, 51.28% for compression, 51.71% for vector retrieval and 40.17% for question-only. On the subset that no model can answer without the book, the graph route reaches 42.86%. None of the fifteen graph-baseline contrasts survives Holm correction, so we present the result as exploratory evidence about a design. Two structural findings survive scrutiny better than the headline number: annotated evidence concentrates in the topological core of these graphs (2.35x enrichment, pooled), and the two graph-building pipelines differ so much in annotation coverage (16% versus 73% of clue paragraphs) that pooled accuracy alone would hide which bottleneck is being measured.

AI.tldr: A frozen knowledge graph is tested as an alternative to sequential long-context reading for a small local model on 30 detective novels and 234 multiple-choice questions; the best graph route reaches 53.85% versus 46.15% for a recent-window baseline, but no contrast survives Holm correction, so results are presented as exploratory design evidence.
AI.motivation: Long-context models process text in narrative order with a fixed attention budget, whereas detectives reason by sorting events in time and mapping relations, letting early clues meet late questions. The paper asks whether a frozen knowledge graph can grant a small local model that same non-sequential, relational freedom.
AI.method: Thirty detective novels and 234 multiple-choice questions are answered by one fixed qwen3.5:9b reader under nine conditions: five graph routes, a recent-window baseline, whole-book compression, ordinary vector retrieval, and a question-only control. Fifteen graph-versus-baseline contrasts are evaluated with Holm correction, plus analyses of where annotated evidence sits in graph topology and of differences between two graph-building pipelines.
AI.result: The strongest graph route reaches 53.85% (126/234), against 46.15% for the recent window, 51.28% for compression, 51.71% for vector retrieval, and 40.17% for question-only; on the subset unanswerable without the book, the graph route reaches 42.86%. None of the fifteen graph-baseline contrasts survives Holm correction. Two structural findings hold up better: annotated evidence concentrates in the topological core of the graphs (2.35x enrichment, pooled), and the two graph-building pipelines differ sharply in annotation coverage (16% versus 73% of clue paragraphs), so pooled accuracy alone would obscure which bottleneck is being measured.
AI.conclusion: The graph route shows a numerical edge over all baselines, but the lack of statistical significance after correction means the result is exploratory evidence about a design rather than a confirmed gain. The more robust contributions are structural: evidence concentrates in graph cores, and pipeline coverage differences must be reported separately, since pooled accuracy hides the measured bottleneck.

title: Distributed Infrastructure Sensors and Cues for Robotic Fire-Fighting and Safety System on a Lunar Base
comment: 12 pages, 14 figures,Earth and Space Conference 2026 2
summary: There are renewed efforts to build a lunar base and house a team of astronauts on the Moon for extended periods. However, important challenges remain, such as a rapid-response fire-hazard management system. In the event of a fire or toxic leak inside an early crewed lunar habitat, a single pressurized cylinder must be handled within minutes. However, suited astronauts and radio-delayed support from Earth cannot guarantee such response times. We describe a prototype fire-fighting and emergency response safety technology that embeds intelligence in the habitat itself: using thin ceramic QR codes affixed every few meters, each carries a local floor map, safe sensor limits, and step-by-step hazard responses. A low-power rover decodes a plate in a matter of seconds, polls the adjoining temperature-gas sensor cluster, and acts immediately, eliminating the need for a global map . In a representative layout, the interior is divided into roughly one code per two square meters. Simulations show that rapid-response firefighting both simplifies the task and avoids costly resource use and indeterminate outcomes. Because knowledge is spread across passive plates, damage is localized, procedures can be updated by replacing a single code, and processor demands remain minimal. title: AgentRouter: Heterogeneous Model Routing for Cost-Optimal Multi-Step Agentic Workflows
comment: Accepted at the AgenticUQ Workshop, ICML 2026. Camera-ready version
summary: Enterprise agentic systems that route every trajectory step to a frontier model waste 60-80% of their inference budget on subtasks that smaller models handle equally well. Existing routing solutions optimize single-turn query assignment but ignore a property unique to agentic workflows: subtask complexity varies widely within a single trajectory. A planning step may require frontier-class reasoning while a subsequent formatting step needs only a 7B model. We formalize step-level model routing as a sequential assignment problem over agent trajectories and propose AgentRouter, a lightweight classifier (12M parameters, <5ms overhead per step on an A100 GPU) that maps each trajectory step to one of four model tiers using five features extractable at routing time. Trained on 50,000 annotated agent trajectory steps spanning planning, coding, research, and data analysis tasks, AgentRouter achieves 72% cost reduction relative to frontier-only baselines, retaining 97.3% of frontier-only quality (less than 3% degradation in end-to-end task completion); per-step routing accuracy reaches 91% on minimal-complexity steps and 85% on efficient-tier steps, with 76-82% on the harder mid-range and frontier tiers. On the same benchmarks, RouteLLM and FrugalGPT (applied per-step) achieve only 31% and 44% cost reduction respectively, because their single-turn training signal misses trajectory-level quality dependencies.

AI.tldr: AgentRouter is a lightweight 12M-parameter classifier that performs step-level model routing over agent trajectories, cutting inference cost by 72% while retaining 97.3% of frontier-only quality.
AI.motivation: Enterprise agentic systems route every trajectory step to a frontier model, wasting 60-80% of the inference budget on subtasks that smaller models handle equally well. Existing routing methods optimize single-turn query assignment and ignore a property unique to agentic workflows: subtask complexity varies widely within a single trajectory (e.g., planning needs frontier reasoning while formatting needs only a 7B model).
AI.method: The paper formalizes step-level model routing as a sequential assignment problem over agent trajectories and proposes AgentRouter, a lightweight classifier (12M parameters, <5ms overhead per step on an A100 GPU) that maps each trajectory step to one of four model tiers using five features extractable at routing time. It is trained on 50,000 annotated agent trajectory steps spanning planning, coding, research, and data analysis tasks.
AI.result: AgentRouter achieves 72% cost reduction relative to frontier-only baselines while retaining 97.3% of frontier-only quality (less than 3% degradation in end-to-end task completion). Per-step routing accuracy reaches 91% on minimal-complexity steps and 85% on efficient-tier steps, with 76-82% on the harder mid-range and frontier tiers. RouteLLM and FrugalGPT, applied per-step, achieve only 31% and 44% cost reduction respectively, as their single-turn training signal misses trajectory-level quality dependencies.
AI.conclusion: Step-level routing that accounts for intra-trajectory complexity variation substantially outperforms single-turn routing baselines, enabling large inference-cost savings with minimal quality loss in agentic workflows.

title: Task-Oriented Co-Design and Optimization of Geared Actuators for Robotic Applications
summary: Different tasks performed by legged robots impose distinct torque and speed requirements on actuators. Existing robotic actuators are generally optimized at the component level for metrics such as torque or power density, without explicit task guidance. System-level optimization across components such as motors, gearboxes, and sensors is challenging because of the high computational cost and coupling among mechanical, electrical, and electromagnetic behaviors. Consequently, improvements in individual components may not translate into better robot performance in a specific task. To this end, we present a systematic optimization framework for task-oriented co-design of actuator hardware and control. First, surrogate models are employed to accelerate motor evaluation and support global exploration of the coupled design space. Then, a hierarchical mixed-variable optimization strategy is adopted, combining discrete enumeration with continuous search over dimensions and real-valued indices. These indices are rounded to select admissible values for the remaining discrete choices before each evaluation. Within this search, rated output torque density and task performance are jointly optimized, with Bezier-parameterized joint torque profiles determined for each hardware candidate. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed framework is validated through actuator fabrication and experiments on a two-degree-of-freedom jumping leg. Based on its measured mass, the fabricated prototype achieves a nominal rated output torque density of 35.7 N m/kg, approximately 60% higher than that of a widely used commercial geared joint actuator, while being 18.6% lighter. Under matched bench conditions, it achieves 12.0% greater jump height at twice-rated torque. Together, these results demonstrate a systematic route from task requirements to actuator design and control.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic task-oriented co-design framework for legged-robot actuators that jointly optimizes hardware and control, validated on a 2-DoF jumping leg achieving 35.7 N·m/kg torque density and 12.0% higher jump height.
AI.motivation: Legged robots have task-specific torque and speed requirements, but existing actuators are optimized at the component level (e.g., torque or power density) without explicit task guidance. System-level co-optimization of motors, gearboxes, and sensors is difficult due to high computational cost and tight coupling among mechanical, electrical, and electromagnetic behaviors, so component-level gains often fail to improve task-specific robot performance.
AI.method: The framework first uses surrogate models to accelerate motor evaluation and enable global exploration of the coupled design space. A hierarchical mixed-variable optimization strategy combines discrete enumeration with continuous search over dimensions and real-valued indices; indices are rounded to select admissible discrete values before each evaluation. Rated output torque density and task performance are jointly optimized, with Bezier-parameterized joint torque profiles determined for each hardware candidate.
AI.result: Validated via actuator fabrication and experiments on a two-degree-of-freedom jumping leg. The prototype achieves a nominal rated output torque density of 35.7 N·m/kg, ~60% higher than a widely used commercial geared joint actuator while being 18.6% lighter. Under matched bench conditions, it delivers 12.0% greater jump height at twice-rated torque.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate a systematic route from task requirements to actuator design and control, showing that task-oriented co-design of actuator hardware and control can outperform component-level optimization for specific robotic tasks.

title: A Compact Stance-Indexed Anterior-Posterior COP Representation for Parkinson's Disease Classification from Plantar VGRF
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures; supplementary material is included in the same PDF
summary: Parkinson's disease alters gait and bilateral coordination, but machine-learning performance also depends on how continuous gait signals are represented. This study investigates whether preserving anterior-posterior center-of-pressure (AP-COP) information at fixed locations across normalized stance provides a compact and informative representation of plantar-force gait signals. Bilateral vertical ground reaction force recordings from 165 participants in the Gait in Parkinson's Disease Database were evaluated using repeated fully nested participant-level cross-validation. We propose AP-COP10, comprising AP-COP position and bilateral asymmetry across five stance windows. AP-COP10 achieved an AUC of 0.894 and outperformed three harmonized literature-derived COP representations under the same evaluation pipeline. The complementary 25 non-AP-COP descriptors alone achieved an AUC of 0.856, while the complete 35-feature representation achieved 0.908. Removing AP-COP10 from the complete representation produced a statistically supported loss in discrimination, whereas adding the complementary descriptors to AP-COP10 yielded only a small, unsupported improvement. Feature competition indicated that the most informative stance-indexed descriptors were concentrated in early and early-mid stance, while source-study holdout and sensor-perturbation analyses supported the robustness of the representation. These findings indicate that stance-indexed AP-COP retains discriminative information that is not readily recovered by broader engineered gait descriptors, supporting compact and interpretable representations for machine-learning analysis of pathological gait.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AP-COP10, a compact stance-indexed representation of anterior-posterior center-of-pressure and bilateral asymmetry across five stance windows, which discriminates Parkinson's disease gait with AUC 0.894 and outperforms literature-derived COP representations.
AI.motivation: Parkinson's disease alters gait and bilateral coordination, but machine-learning performance also depends on how continuous gait signals are represented. The authors ask whether preserving AP-COP information at fixed locations across normalized stance yields a compact and informative representation of plantar-force gait signals.
AI.method: Bilateral vertical ground reaction force recordings from 165 participants in the Gait in Parkinson's Disease Database were evaluated using repeated fully nested participant-level cross-validation. AP-COP10 encodes AP-COP position and bilateral asymmetry across five stance windows, and was compared against three harmonized literature-derived COP representations, complementary non-AP-COP descriptors, and the complete 35-feature set, with feature-competition, source-study holdout, and sensor-perturbation analyses.
AI.result: AP-COP10 achieved an AUC of 0.894, outperforming the three harmonized literature-derived COP representations under the same pipeline. The 25 complementary non-AP-COP descriptors alone reached 0.856, and the complete 35-feature representation reached 0.908. Removing AP-COP10 caused a statistically supported loss in discrimination, whereas adding complementary descriptors to AP-COP10 yielded only a small, unsupported improvement. Informative stance-indexed descriptors concentrated in early and early-mid stance, and robustness was supported by holdout and perturbation analyses.
AI.conclusion: Stance-indexed AP-COP retains discriminative information not readily recovered by broader engineered gait descriptors, supporting compact and interpretable representations for machine-learning analysis of pathological gait.

title: Expert-Play Contouring Control: Faster-than-Demonstration Planning from Slow Expert and Fast Play
summary: Expert demonstrations often specify what a robot should do, but not how fast it can do it. Imitation Learning (IL) inherits demonstration timing, while directly accelerating the learned motion can fail when faster execution changes the robot-object dynamics. We study faster-than-demonstration execution as a dynamics-aware control problem and introduce Expert-Play Contouring Control (EPCC), which combines slow expert demonstrations with fast, non-expert play. Expert demonstrations train a latent trajectory generator whose predictions are reparameterized into a time-independent contour of successful task progression, while play trains a world model (WM) of fast-action outcomes. At deployment, our proposed planner uses the WM to optimize actions that makes maximize progress along the expert-derived contour while penalizing deviation from the intended task evolution. Averaged across three visuomotor manipulation tasks, EPCC achieves a $2.0\times$ the throughput of the IL baseline, including $2.2\times$ that of the throughput of the strongest acceleration baseline on a task with interaction-sensitive object dynamics. Our analysis shows that the gains concentrate where faster execution changes robot-object evolution. Together, our results highlight a simple yet effective principle: demonstrations provide task intent, while play data provides the dynamic coverage needed to execute that intent faster.

AI.tldr: EPCC combines slow expert demonstrations with fast non-expert play to enable faster-than-demonstration execution, achieving 2.0x throughput over imitation learning baselines.
AI.motivation: Expert demonstrations specify task intent but not execution speed. Imitation Learning inherits demonstration timing, and naive acceleration fails when faster execution alters robot-object dynamics.
AI.method: EPCC (Expert-Play Contouring Control) treats faster-than-demonstration execution as a dynamics-aware control problem. Expert demos train a latent trajectory generator reparameterized into a time-independent contour of task progression; play data trains a world model of fast-action outcomes; a planner uses the WM to maximize progress along the contour while penalizing deviation.
AI.result: Across three visuomotor manipulation tasks, EPCC achieves 2.0x the throughput of the IL baseline, including 2.2x the strongest acceleration baseline on a task with interaction-sensitive object dynamics. Gains concentrate where faster execution changes robot-object evolution.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrations provide task intent, while play data provides the dynamic coverage needed to execute that intent faster.

title: R-GEAN: Regimen-Guided Edit Action Network for Within-Admission Medication Change Prediction
summary: The medications prescribed to a patient often change during a hospital admission as clinicians start, stop, or continue therapies. We study whether models can predict which medication classes are added or removed between 24 hours after admission and discharge. Metrics that compare the complete discharge regimen can reward models for copying medications that remain unchanged, even when they identify no actual changes. We therefore introduce a leakage-controlled benchmark that predicts net ATC3 additions and removals using only prior completed admissions and information available within the first 24 hours of the current admission. Addition candidates are classes not active at 24 hours, whereas removal candidates are classes active at that time. We also introduce R-GEAN, an asymmetric candidate-scoring network with independent addition and removal predictors. Across 240,480 admissions from 82,286 patients, R-GEAN achieves the highest predefined summary of addition, removal, changed-regimen, and action-pattern performance, termed the edit composite (0.464), compared with 0.435 for the strongest primary comparator. Reimplemented RETAIN, GAMENet, and MICRON baselines obtain 0.428, 0.420, and 0.288, respectively. R-GEAN's advantage is concentrated in correctly identifying medication classes no longer active at discharge, while rare additions and admissions with multiple medication changes remain difficult. Rankings based on micro-F1 over the reconstructed discharge regimen and the edit composite correlate weakly across the evaluated models (Spearman r = 0.20). The continuation baseline achieves the highest complete-regimen score despite predicting no additions or removals. These results show that complete-regimen and edit-level evaluation measure different aspects of medication prediction. The benchmark evaluates observed prescribing changes, not treatment appropriateness

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a leakage-controlled benchmark for predicting net medication changes (ATC3 additions/removals) using only prior admissions and the first 24 hours of the current admission, and introduces R-GEAN, an asymmetric candidate-scoring network that outperforms reimplemented baselines on an edit-level composite metric.
AI.motivation: Medication regimens frequently change during admission, but conventional evaluation of complete discharge regimens can reward models for simply copying unchanged medications. This leakage inflates performance even when no actual additions or removals are identified, so existing metrics do not properly assess a model's ability to predict prescribing changes.
AI.method: The authors introduce a leakage-controlled benchmark predicting net ATC3 additions and removals using only prior completed admissions plus information available within the first 24 hours of the current admission. Addition candidates are classes not active at 24 hours; removal candidates are classes active at that time. They also propose R-GEAN, an asymmetric candidate-scoring network with independent addition and removal predictors. Evaluation covers 240,480 admissions from 82,286 patients and compares against reimplemented RETAIN, GAMENet, and MICRON baselines.
AI.result: R-GEAN achieves the highest edit composite (0.464) versus 0.435 for the strongest primary comparator; reimplemented RETAIN, GAMENet, and MICRON obtain 0.428, 0.420, and 0.288, respectively. Its advantage is concentrated in correctly identifying classes no longer active at discharge, while rare additions and admissions with multiple changes remain difficult. Micro-F1 over the reconstructed discharge regimen correlates weakly with the edit composite across models (Spearman r = 0.20), and the continuation baseline achieves the highest complete-regimen score despite predicting no additions or removals.
AI.conclusion: Complete-regimen and edit-level evaluation measure different aspects of medication prediction, so leakage-controlled, change-focused benchmarks are needed. The benchmark evaluates observed prescribing changes rather than treatment appropriateness.

title: ARCGym: Benchmarking Deep Reinforcement Learning in Autonomous Robotic Colonoscopy
summary: Simulations for learning-based autonomous colonoscopic navigation focus mainly on fully actuated capsule robots, failing to capture the contact-rich navigation of long and flexible clinical colonoscopes. We present the Autonomous Robotic Colonoscopy Gym (ARCGym), an open-source reinforcement learning environment and benchmark for image-based navigation in clinically derived deformable colon anatomies. ARCGym supports multiple types of colonoscope robots, spanning capsule robots and flexible endoscopes, with this work focusing on flexible endoscopes including magnetic-driven tip actuation and clinically used proximally translational actuation. This work includes five CT-reconstructed colons representing typical clinical scenarios, a set of clinically meaningful navigation subtasks, and unified success metrics. We introduce a reward combining depth-based lumen alignment with a lumen-visibility score to improve learning under occlusions. Experiments across tasks, robots, and anatomies show that autonomous navigation remains challenging for both magnetic-driven and proximal-insertion flexible robots, with proximal-insertion actuation remaining an open problem.

AI.tldr: ARCGym is an open-source reinforcement learning environment and benchmark for image-based autonomous navigation of flexible colonoscopes in clinically derived deformable colon anatomies, featuring five CT-reconstructed colons, clinically meaningful subtasks, unified metrics, and a depth-based lumen-alignment reward. Experiments show autonomous navigation remains challenging for both magnetic-driven and proximal-insertion flexible robots.
AI.motivation: Existing simulations for learning-based autonomous colonoscopic navigation focus mainly on fully actuated capsule robots and fail to capture the contact-rich navigation of long, flexible clinical colonoscopes, leaving a gap in realistic benchmarks for flexible endoscope autonomy.
AI.method: The authors present ARCGym, an open-source RL environment and benchmark for image-based navigation in clinically derived deformable colon anatomies. It supports multiple colonoscope robot types (capsule robots and flexible endoscopes), with this work focusing on flexible endoscopes including magnetic-driven tip actuation and clinically used proximally translational actuation. The benchmark includes five CT-reconstructed colons representing typical clinical scenarios, clinically meaningful navigation subtasks, and unified success metrics. A reward is introduced combining depth-based lumen alignment with a lumen-visibility score to improve learning under occlusions.
AI.result: Experiments across tasks, robots, and anatomies demonstrate that autonomous navigation remains challenging for both magnetic-driven and proximal-insertion flexible robots, with proximal-insertion actuation remaining an open problem.
AI.conclusion: ARCGym provides a clinically grounded, open-source benchmark for flexible colonoscope navigation, establishing a challenging baseline and highlighting proximal-insertion actuation as an unresolved research problem.

title: OptiSkill: A Hierarchical and Evolving SkillBank for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling
comment: Accepted by EMNLP 2026 Main Conference
summary: Automated operations research (OR) modeling requires LLMs to translate natural-language decision problems into correct mathematical programs. Existing methods can improve individual formulations, but they often solve problems in isolation, retaining little reusable experience and repeating similar formulation errors. Prior memory-based approaches store examples, thoughts, or insights as references, while OR modeling requires reusable formulation skills that transfer across problem narratives and guide concrete modeling decisions. We propose OptiSkill, a skill-augmented framework that builds a hierarchical and evolving SkillBank for LLM-based OR modeling. SkillBank stores solver-verified experience as reusable skills, with Global Strategies for problem-level formulation skeletons and Step Experiences for local error-prevention rules. It is further refined through stable batch-level test-time evolution, where candidate skills are incorporated only after validation. Experiments on eight OR modeling benchmarks show that OptiSkill improves formulation accuracy across LLM backbones, outperforms strong agentic baselines, and gains further by expanding SkillBank coverage and reliability. Code and data are available at https://github.com/rachhhhing/OptiSkill

AI.tldr: OptiSkill is a skill-augmented framework that builds a hierarchical, evolving SkillBank for LLM-based automated operations research (OR) modeling, storing solver-verified reusable skills to improve formulation accuracy across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Automated OR modeling requires LLMs to translate natural-language decision problems into correct mathematical programs. Existing methods improve individual formulations but solve problems in isolation, retaining little reusable experience and repeating formulation errors. Prior memory-based approaches store examples, thoughts, or insights as references, whereas OR modeling demands reusable formulation skills that transfer across problem narratives and guide concrete modeling decisions.
AI.method: The authors propose OptiSkill, a skill-augmented framework that constructs a hierarchical and evolving SkillBank. The SkillBank stores solver-verified experience as reusable skills, organized into Global Strategies (problem-level formulation skeletons) and Step Experiences (local error-prevention rules). The SkillBank is refined via stable batch-level test-time evolution, where candidate skills are incorporated only after validation.
AI.result: Experiments on eight OR modeling benchmarks show that OptiSkill improves formulation accuracy across LLM backbones, outperforms strong agentic baselines, and gains further from expanding SkillBank coverage and reliability.
AI.conclusion: Reusable, solver-verified formulation skills organized hierarchically with validated test-time evolution enhance LLM-based OR modeling, and the approach benefits from broader, more reliable skill coverage. Code and data are available at https://github.com/rachhhhing/OptiSkill.

title: Kinematic Interface for the Wild: Modular Bimanual Loco-Manipulation Capture from 360$^{\circ}$ Cameras Alone
comment: 10 pages, 9 figures
summary: A wrist-mounted camera for UMI-style data collection must do two jobs: record the manipulation and localize in the scene. Most handheld devices localize online from workspace-facing views crowded by hands and objects, or add dedicated tracking hardware. Room-scale bimanual capture therefore still tends to instrument the operator or the scene for accurate localization. We present KIWI (Kinematic Interface for the Wild), a capture kit whose only electronics are off-the-shelf cameras. Our core system splits the two jobs across the two lenses of a 360-degree camera. The rear lens faces the room and builds a shared metric map that registers both hands, and an optional head camera, in one frame without workspace co-visibility; the front lens records the manipulation, and offline IMU fusion bridges front-lens tracking loss. Through our quick-release plate, the camera module attaches to chopstick grippers, parallel-jaw grippers, hand-wrist mounts, or robot flanges. Across six bimanual recordings, combining the rear and front lenses failed to localize only 0.1% of query frames, whereas front-only bimanual feature alignment failed on 24.8% of frames and lost one recording entirely; against evaluation fiducials, localization error stayed within 4.5 mm. KIWI's recovered poses were sufficiently consistent for the four wrist streams alone to reconstruct the scene as a 3D Gaussian splat.

AI.tldr: KIWI is a wrist-mounted, off-the-shelf-camera capture kit for room-scale bimanual data collection that uses a 360-degree camera's rear lens for room-side localization and its front lens (plus offline IMU fusion) for manipulation recording, achieving near-complete frame coverage and millimetre-level accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing UMI-style wrist-mounted devices couple manipulation recording with localization but typically localize online from workspace-facing views cluttered by hands and objects, or require dedicated tracking hardware. As a result, room-scale bimanual capture still tends to instrument the operator or the scene to achieve accurate localization, which is cumbersome and limits practicality.
AI.method: KIWI (Kinematic Interface for the Wild) uses only off-the-shelf cameras as electronics and splits the two jobs across the two lenses of a 360-degree camera.
