The rear lens faces the room and builds a shared metric map that registers both hands, and an optional head camera, into one frame without requiring workspace co-visibility; the front lens records the manipulation, with offline IMU fusion bridging front-lens tracking loss. A quick-release plate lets the camera module attach to chopstick grippers, parallel-jaw grippers, hand-wrist mounts, or robot flanges.
AI.result: Across six bimanual recordings, combining rear and front lenses failed to localize only 0.1% of query frames, whereas front-only bimanual feature alignment failed on 24.8% of frames and lost one recording entirely. Against evaluation fiducials, localization error stayed within 4.5 mm. The recovered poses were consistent enough that the four wrist streams alone could reconstruct the scene as a 3D Gaussian splat.
AI.conclusion: By decoupling room-side localization from workspace-facing manipulation recording using a single 360-degree camera, KIWI enables accurate, room-scale bimanual capture with minimal, off-the-shelf hardware and no instrumentation of the operator or scene, with recovered poses precise enough for downstream 3D scene reconstruction.

title: PINNForge: Execution-Grounded Evolutionary Design of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for PDE Solving via Large Language Models
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) require coordinated choices over network representation, sampling, loss construction, and optimization, while effective configurations often vary substantially across partial differential equations (PDEs). Existing automated PINN design methods can search candidate configurations, but information revealed during actual training is still used mainly for evaluation rather than to improve subsequent design, leading to repeated trial-and-error and inefficient use of training budget. We propose PINNsForge, an LLM-driven evolutionary framework for execution-feedback-based automated PINN design. PINNsForge generates diverse candidate configurations from PDE-related prior knowledge, evaluates them through actual training, and feeds high-performing designs together with accumulated execution evidence back to the LLM. Guided by observed optimization behavior, the LLM then refines, recombines, and explores coupled PINN design components, forming a continual cycle of generation, execution, feedback, and evolution. Unlike one-shot search or evaluation-only feedback, PINNsForge progressively converts training experience into improved design decisions for the target PDE. Across 25 PDE benchmarks, PINNsForge achieves the lowest mean MSE on 24 tasks compared with RoPINN, PINNsFormer, and PINNsAgent. Ablation studies further confirm the importance of the PDE knowledge base, execution feedback, and evolutionary search: removing these components increases the mean MSE to 3.74$\times$, 12.10$\times$, and 10.10$\times$ that of the full PINNsForge, respectively.

AI.tldr: PINNsForge is an LLM-driven evolutionary framework that uses execution feedback to automate PINN design, achieving the lowest mean MSE on 24 of 25 PDE benchmarks with ablations confirming the value of its knowledge base, feedback, and evolutionary search.
AI.motivation: PINNs require coordinated choices over network representation, sampling, loss construction, and optimization, yet effective configurations vary substantially across PDEs. Existing automated design methods can search configurations but use training-time information mainly for evaluation rather than to improve subsequent design, causing repeated trial-and-error and inefficient use of training budget.
AI.method: PINNsForge generates diverse candidate configurations from PDE-related prior knowledge, evaluates them through actual training, and feeds high-performing designs plus accumulated execution evidence back to the LLM. Guided by observed optimization behavior, the LLM refines, recombines, and explores coupled PINN design components, forming a continual generation-execution-feedback-evolution cycle that converts training experience into improved design decisions.
AI.result: Across 25 PDE benchmarks, PINNsForge achieves the lowest mean MSE on 24 tasks compared with RoPINN, PINNsFormer, and PINNsAgent. Ablations show that removing the PDE knowledge base, execution feedback, and evolutionary search increases mean MSE to 3.74x, 12.10x, and 10.10x that of the full method, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Feedback-driven, evolutionary LLM-based design that treats execution evidence as guidance—not just evaluation—substantially outperforms one-shot search and evaluation-only feedback for automated PINN configuration.

title: Commonsense-Grounded Path Planning from Abstract Instructions
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027
summary: We present \emph{commonsense ranked search} (CoRS), a novel path planner that turns an abstract instruction into a route that follows commonsense. While existing methods respect the considerations written down in advance, a robot working among people must follow those left unstated too, as with a wet floor that a worker avoids without being told. CoRS leverages large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) as commonsense knowledge to reason about these latent considerations in its planning. Given an abstract instruction (\emph{e.g.}, ``move carefully'') and visual observations of each region in the environment, CoRS derives a consideration for each region, as in ``this wet floor is slippery and worth a detour.'' It then compares the considerations between regions to see which of the two the robot should avoid more, as in ``the crowd is worse than the wet floor.'' These judgments sort the regions into a commonsense ranking, whose costs drive a conventional search that always returns a valid route. We build a benchmark for planning under latent considerations, with three environments, 1350 problems, and five instructions at three levels of abstraction. Experiments show that CoRS discovers the unstated considerations and goes around the ones worth a detour while crossing the rest, a behavior that recent LLM-based planners do not achieve.

AI.tldr: CoRS is a path planner that uses LLMs and VLMs to infer and rank unstated commonsense considerations in an environment, converting these rankings into costs for a conventional search that yields valid routes under latent constraints.
AI.motivation: Existing planners only respect explicitly specified considerations. However, robots operating among people must also account for implicit, commonsense factors (e.g., avoiding a wet floor without being told), which prior methods fail to handle.
AI.method: Given an abstract instruction and visual observations of each region, CoRS derives a per-region consideration via LLMs/VLMs. It then compares considerations between regions to determine relative avoidance, producing a commonsense ranking of regions. These rankings supply costs that drive a conventional search which always returns a valid route.
AI.result: A benchmark for planning under latent considerations was built with three environments, 1350 problems, and five instructions across three abstraction levels. Experiments show CoRS identifies unstated considerations, detours around regions worth avoiding, and crosses the rest—behavior recent LLM-based planners do not achieve.
AI.conclusion: CoRS successfully plans under latent commonsense considerations by leveraging LLM/VLM knowledge and pairwise region comparisons, outperforming existing LLM-based planners while guaranteeing valid routes.

title: Spatial-Interactor: Learning Spatial Reasoning through Interaction with the Observable Physical World
summary: Spatial reasoning is essential for vision-language models (VLMs) to understand and act in the physical world. Reasoning in dynamic environments requires VLMs to perceive local state transitions caused by object motion and viewpoint changes and integrate them over long trajectories to maintain an updated spatial state, yet existing VLMs remain limited in both capabilities. Current spatial training primarily focuses on static questions about object attributes and spatial relations, providing limited direct supervision for state transitions; in contrast, interaction trajectories naturally connect a preceding observation, an action, and a subsequent observation, offering direct supervision for local state transitions, while complete trajectories reveal dependencies among consecutive transitions. We therefore introduce Spatial-Interactor, a framework that trains VLMs to model physical-world state transitions through interaction, organizing this learning process into a three-level curriculum covering L1 passive world-state transitions, L2 active self-state transitions, and L3 long-horizon interaction trajectories. Accordingly, we construct the Learning from Spatial Interaction dataset (LSI-108K) from simulated and real interaction trajectories, with tasks aligned with the objective of each level. Our two-stage training strategy applies Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to L1 and L2 for local transition modeling, and On-Policy Distillation (OPD) then uses privileged self-distillation: a teacher branch given segment-level transition descriptions supervises the student's on-policy CoT, helping the student learn to integrate consecutive transitions over L3 long trajectories. Experiments across multiple VLMs and spatial benchmarks show consistent gains in local transition modeling and long-horizon integration.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Spatial-Interactor, a framework that trains VLMs to model physical-world state transitions via interaction, using a three-level curriculum (L1 passive world-state transitions, L2 active self-state transitions, L3 long-horizon trajectories) supported by the LSI-108K dataset and a two-stage SFT + On-Policy Distillation training strategy, achieving consistent gains in local transition modeling and long-horizon integration.
AI.motivation: Spatial reasoning is essential for VLMs to understand and act in the physical world, but reasoning in dynamic environments requires perceiving local state transitions from object motion and viewpoint changes and integrating them over long trajectories. Existing VLMs are limited in both capabilities, because current spatial training focuses mainly on static questions about object attributes and spatial relations, offering little direct supervision for state transitions.
AI.method: The authors propose Spatial-Interactor, which trains VLMs to model state transitions through interaction, organized into a three-level curriculum: L1 passive world-state transitions, L2 active self-state transitions, and L3 long-horizon interaction trajectories. They build the Learning from Spatial Interaction dataset (LSI-108K) from simulated and real interaction trajectories with level-aligned tasks. A two-stage training strategy applies SFT to L1 and L2 for local transition modeling, followed by On-Policy Distillation (OPD) using privileged self-distillation, where a teacher branch with segment-level transition descriptions supervises the student's on-policy CoT over L3 long trajectories.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple VLMs and spatial benchmarks show consistent gains in both local transition modeling and long-horizon integration.
AI.conclusion: Interaction trajectories provide direct supervision for local state transitions, and complete trajectories reveal dependencies among consecutive transitions. By structuring spatial learning into a three-level curriculum with SFT plus On-Policy Distillation, Spatial-Interactor effectively improves VLMs' ability to model local transitions and integrate them over long horizons for dynamic spatial reasoning.

title: Whole-Body UMI: Transferring UMI Manipulation Skills to Humanoid Whole-Body Manipulation via Real-Time Motion Generation
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Project website: https://wholebody-umi.github.io/
summary: Collecting whole-body demonstrations for humanoid manipulation mostly relies on teleoperation, which is costly and hard to scale up. The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) provides a scalable data collection paradigm, but end-effector trajectories alone underdetermine humanoid whole-body coordination, which is insufficient for whole-body demonstration collection. Therefore, we introduce Whole-Body UMI (WB-UMI), a task-agnostic, real-time and end-effector conditioned motion generator that decouples whole-body coordination learning from task semantics learning through a shared end-effector interface. A diffusion policy learns from native UMI demonstrations, while WB-UMI learns independently from retargeted motion capture, requiring no body trackers or paired image--whole-body demonstrations during task-specific data collection. In real deployment, an asynchronous hierarchy integrates the diffusion policy, motion generator, and a whole-body controller with latency compensation and measured-state feedback. Real-robot experiments on G1 support real-time closed-loop transfer across four tasks, achieving 90% success in drawer closing, 80% in shelf pick-and-place, 30% in ball toss, and 40% in Loco-PnP, which shows the effectiveness of this hierarchy in transferring native UMI skills to humanoid whole-body manipulation.

AI.tldr: WB-UMI is a task-agnostic, real-time, end-effector-conditioned whole-body motion generator that extends the UMI paradigm to humanoid manipulation by decoupling whole-body coordination learning from task semantics learning via a shared end-effector interface, enabling scalable whole-body demonstration collection without body trackers.
AI.motivation: Collecting whole-body humanoid manipulation demonstrations relies heavily on costly, hard-to-scale teleoperation. While UMI offers a scalable data collection paradigm, its end-effector trajectories alone underdetermine humanoid whole-body coordination, making it insufficient for whole-body demonstration collection. A method is needed to bridge scalable end-effector data with whole-body motion without requiring paired image–whole-body demonstrations or body trackers.
AI.method: WB-UMI decouples whole-body coordination learning from task semantics learning through a shared end-effector interface. A diffusion policy learns from native UMI demonstrations, while WB-UMI independently learns from retargeted motion capture, requiring no body trackers or paired image–whole-body demonstrations during task-specific collection. For real deployment, an asynchronous hierarchy integrates the diffusion policy, the motion generator, and a whole-body controller with latency compensation and measured-state feedback, enabling real-time closed-loop control.
AI.result: Real-robot experiments on the G1 humanoid achieve real-time closed-loop transfer across four tasks: 90% success in drawer closing, 80% in shelf pick-and-place, 30% in ball toss, and 40% in Loco-PnP.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchy effectively transfers native UMI skills to humanoid whole-body manipulation, demonstrating that decoupling whole-body coordination from task semantics via a shared end-effector interface is a viable and scalable approach.

title: Enforcing Narrative Reliability and Epistemic Pacing in LLM-Driven Detective Games via Structured Knowledge Trees
comment: 10 pages
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) enable open-ended dialogue in interactive games, but their non-deterministic outputs make it difficult to preserve authorial control, factual consistency, and the intended sequence of information disclosure. These challenges are particularly significant in detective games, where premature revelation or fabricated details can undermine the logic of player progression. We present a Structured Knowledge Tree architecture coupled with a tri-agent LLM pipeline for controlling dialogue in an open-ended interrogation game. The system separates knowledge retrieval, dialogue generation, and response verification to ensure that the virtual suspect reveals only information permitted by the current narrative state. We evaluate the approach through The Interrogation of Adrian Gale, a playable detective-game testbed, and a formal user study examining hallucination reduction, adherence to authored disclosure sequences, and perceived logical progression. Our results demonstrate that the structured architecture reduces critical hallucinations by 64.78% and entirely prevents premature narrative disclosure. While the strict mechanical constraints introduced usability trade-offs regarding forced conversational reveals, the system successfully enforces rigorous epistemic pacing and provides players with a clear, subjective sense of progression toward solving the case.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Structured Knowledge Tree architecture with a tri-agent LLM pipeline to control dialogue in an open-ended detective interrogation game, reducing critical hallucinations by 64.78% and eliminating premature narrative disclosure.
AI.motivation: LLMs enable open-ended dialogue in interactive games, but their non-deterministic outputs make it hard to preserve authorial control, factual consistency, and the intended sequence of information disclosure. This is especially problematic in detective games, where premature revelation or fabricated details can undermine the logic of player progression.
AI.method: The authors design a Structured Knowledge Tree architecture combined with a tri-agent LLM pipeline, separating knowledge retrieval, dialogue generation, and response verification so that a virtual suspect reveals only information permitted by the current narrative state. They evaluate it via The Interrogation of Adrian Gale, a playable detective-game testbed, and a formal user study.
AI.result: The structured architecture reduces critical hallucinations by 64.78% and entirely prevents premature narrative disclosure. Strict mechanical constraints introduced usability trade-offs regarding forced conversational reveals, but the system enforces rigorous epistemic pacing and gives players a clear, subjective sense of progression toward solving the case.
AI.conclusion: Structuring LLM-based dialogue through separated retrieval, generation, and verification roles can enforce authorial control and epistemic pacing in open-ended detective games, at the cost of some conversational flexibility.

title: ForceRFT: Refining VLA Actions through Force-Guided Residual Reinforcement Learning
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: Force-conditioned vision-language-action (VLA) policies can respond to contact, but when trained solely on demonstrations, their recovery behavior may be limited by demonstration coverage, and they do not learn from deployment outcomes. Human corrective imitation provides additional recovery examples, but its objective matches local action targets without explicitly optimizing task return. We present ForceRFT, a force-guided residual reinforcement learning framework that learns contact-dependent corrections from human supervision and autonomous task outcomes. A frozen, demonstration-trained SmolVLA-based prior generates force-conditioned action chunks, while a lightweight residual actor refines individual end-effector pose commands using wrist feedback acquired during chunk execution. The decision-time wrist wrench, its temporal change, and the selected base motion condition both residual correction and value estimation. Human corrections supervise the residual actor, while verified autonomous transitions train the twin critics and support value-guided updates to the same actor. Bootstrapping is restricted to autonomous segments, preventing TD credit from crossing human-intervention boundaries. Real-robot experiments on plug insertion, ring-on-peg assembly, and whiteboard wiping show higher autonomous success rates than the evaluated demonstration-trained and residual-imitation baselines. Comparisons with residual imitation support value-guided residual optimization, while plug-insertion ablations indicate the benefit of direct execution-time wrist feedback.

AI.tldr: ForceRFT is a force-guided residual reinforcement learning framework for contact-rich VLA policies that combines human corrective imitation with autonomous value-based learning, using execution-time wrist force feedback to refine actions and improve real-robot success.
AI.motivation: Force-conditioned VLA policies trained only on demonstrations have recovery behavior limited by demonstration coverage and cannot learn from deployment outcomes. Human corrective imitation adds recovery examples but optimizes local action targets without explicitly optimizing task return.
AI.method: A frozen demonstration-trained SmolVLA-based prior generates force-conditioned action chunks; a lightweight residual actor refines per-EE pose commands using wrist wrench feedback during chunk execution. Decision-time wrench, its temporal change, and the selected base motion condition both the residual correction and value estimation. Human corrections supervise the residual actor, while verified autonomous transitions train twin critics for value-guided actor updates, with bootstrapping restricted to autonomous segments to avoid TD credit crossing intervention boundaries.
AI.result: Real-robot experiments on plug insertion, ring-on-peg assembly, and whiteboard wiping show higher autonomous success rates than demonstration-trained and residual-imitation baselines. Comparisons with residual imitation support value-guided residual optimization, and plug-insertion ablations show direct execution-time wrist feedback is beneficial.
AI.conclusion: Combining force-conditioned priors, residual correction from execution-time wrist feedback, human corrective supervision, and return-optimizing value learning yields more robust contact-rich VLA policies than imitation-only or demonstration-only approaches.

title: LazyAgent: Demand-Driven Materialization and Physical Optimization of Agentic Programs
summary: Current agent runtimes that plan before acting generally execute a step once it becomes ready. We present LazyAgent, a unified execution framework for agent-authored programs organized around a live, goal-derived demanded set. LazyAgent refreshes a backward closure from requested outputs as execution state changes and materializes a ready node only when the active goal requires it. This replaces repeated local judgments with one linear-time graph analysis followed by constant-time membership tests, allowing programs to remain broad while execution stays request-specific. On programs that describe more than the current request needs, LazyAgent consistently outperforms the strongest goal-stopping eager baseline by refusing unrelated work before it starts. Adding one unrelated product raises the eager bill by 22.5% and LazyAgent's by 0.0%. LazyAgent saves 42.0% of measured CPU on production scientific workflows and 51.7% of container time on a live release gate spanning four repositories. We also prove and verify exact equivalence when the request reaches the whole graph, leaving no unrelated work to avoid. Beyond permission, goal-relative output projection saves up to approximately 90% of a shared step on two third-party test suites while the identical eager control saves 0.0%; the advantage disappears when the omitted output has no other consumer or the request needs it. Ordering, reuse, and pruning can also save cost, but do not replace permission. Finally, we show that current public benchmarks are eager-shaped and contain almost no unrequested work. A pre-registered planning intervention did not broaden them. These findings motivate benchmarks built from standing programs and sequences.

AI.tldr: LazyAgent is a unified execution framework for agent-authored programs that uses a live, goal-derived demanded set: a backward closure from requested outputs is refreshed as state changes, and nodes materialize only when the active goal requires them. This replaces repeated local eager judgments with one linear-time graph analysis plus constant-time membership tests, avoiding unrelated work while proving exact whole-graph equivalence.
AI.motivation: Agent runtimes that plan before acting typically execute a step as soon as it becomes ready. When programs describe more than the current request needs, this eager style performs unrelated work. The paper targets goal-relative execution: keeping programs broad while execution stays request-specific, and questioning existing benchmarks that are eager-shaped and contain almost no unrequested work.
AI.method: LazyAgent organizes agent-authored programs around a live, goal-derived demanded set. It refreshes a backward closure from requested outputs as execution state changes, materializing a ready node only when the active goal requires it. This substitutes repeated local judgments with one linear-time graph analysis followed by constant-time membership tests. The approach is evaluated against the strongest goal-stopping eager baseline, on production scientific workflows, a live release gate spanning four repositories, and two third-party test suites, with proof and verification of exact equivalence when the request reaches the whole graph. A pre-registered planning intervention tested whether public benchmarks can be broadened.
AI.result: On programs describing more than the current request needs, LazyAgent consistently outperforms the strongest goal-stopping eager baseline by refusing unrelated work before it starts. Adding one unrelated product raises the eager bill by 22.5% and LazyAgent's by 0.0%. LazyAgent saves 42.0% of measured CPU on production scientific workflows and 51.7% of container time on a live release gate spanning four repositories. Exact equivalence holds when the request reaches the whole graph, leaving no unrelated work to avoid. Goal-relative output projection saves up to approximately 90% of a shared step on two third-party test suites while the identical eager control saves 0.0%; the advantage disappears when the omitted output has no other consumer or the request needs it. Ordering, reuse, and pruning can also save cost but do not replace permission. Current public benchmarks are eager-shaped and contain almost no unrequested work, and a pre-registered planning intervention did not broaden them.
AI.conclusion: Permission—deciding what work is permitted relative to the active goal—is the primary source of savings, and ordering, reuse, and pruning do not substitute for it. LazyAgent preserves program breadth while making execution request-specific, with exact whole-graph equivalence as a correctness guarantee. Because existing public benchmarks are eager-shaped with little unrequested work, the findings motivate benchmarks built from standing programs and sequences to properly expose goal-relative execution benefits.

title: Physical-Touch Observability from Wrist Wrench in Granular Scooping
summary: Mining and earthmoving are important real-world deployment settings for embodied intelligence. Autonomous transport and driving systems have improved substantially, but loading and scooping still often depend on skilled human operators, exposing personnel and equipment to operational risk. For robotic scooping, pre-contact RGB-D sensing reveals surface geometry but not the resistance, compaction, tool engagement, or load transfer that emerge during interaction. We test whether the current scoop's six-axis wrist force/torque (F/T), or wrist wrench, contains information about final collected volume, and whether that information depends on the correctly paired action-terrain interaction. We call this property physical-touch observability. Using 6,700 real-robot scoops across 67 terrains, we evaluate correctly paired current-scoop F/T against pre-contact prediction and correspondence-breaking controls under terrain-held-out testing. At the retrospective 60% sequence boundary, correctly paired F/T reduces mean absolute error by 14.2% relative to Action-only and by 21.9% relative to cross-terrain mismatched F/T. Engineered signal summaries reproduce the result across model architectures. Together, these findings position wrist wrench not merely as a low-level feedback signal, but as a task-level perceptual modality through which embodied robots can infer hidden physical states during interaction, providing a foundation for response-aware autonomy in mining and other contact-rich tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether six-axis wrist force/torque (wrist wrench) sensed during robotic scooping carries information about final collected volume, a property they term "physical-touch observability." Across 6,700 real-robot scoops on 67 terrains, correctly paired current-scoop F/T beats pre-contact prediction and correspondence-breaking controls, reducing mean absolute error by 14.2% versus Action-only and 21.9% versus cross-terrain mismatched F/T, positioning wrist wrench as a task-level perceptual modality for contact-rich autonomy.
AI.motivation: Autonomous transport and driving have advanced, but loading and scooping in mining and earthmoving still rely on skilled human operators, exposing people and equipment to operational risk. Pre-contact RGB-D sensing reveals only surface geometry, not the resistance, compaction, tool engagement, or load transfer that emerge during interaction, so a means of inferring hidden physical states during contact is needed.
AI.method: They define "physical-touch observability" as whether the current scoop's six-axis wrist force/torque contains information about final collected volume, and whether that information depends on correctly paired action-terrain interaction. Using 6,700 real-robot scoops across 67 terrains, they evaluate correctly paired current-scoop F/T against pre-contact prediction and correspondence-breaking controls under terrain-held-out testing, and test whether engineered signal summaries reproduce the effect across model architectures.
AI.result: At the retrospective 60% sequence boundary, correctly paired F/T reduces mean absolute error by 14.2% relative to Action-only and by 21.9% relative to cross-terrain mismatched F/T. Engineered signal summaries reproduce the result across model architectures.
AI.conclusion: Wrist wrench is not merely a low-level feedback signal but a task-level perceptual modality through which embodied robots can infer hidden physical states during interaction, providing a foundation for response-aware autonomy in mining and other contact-rich tasks.

title: FireWorldBench: Benchmarking Complex Physical World Intelligence through Coupled-Field Fire Dynamics
summary: Understanding the physical world requires more than object recognition, scene description, and short-term visual prediction, as real-world physical systems involve multiple continuous fields, latent causal mechanisms, partial observations, and intervention-sensitive dynamics. We propose FireWorldBench, a benchmark for evaluating complex physical world intelligence in multimodal large language models and agents through coupled-field fire dynamics. Fire provides a canonical stress-test environment, where multiple interacting physical fields jointly shape observable states and temporal dynamics. FireWorldBench is organized along two complementary axes, a physical capability axis and a fire scenario task axis, jointly covering physical-state understanding, temporal dynamics, causal mechanisms, and intervention reasoning. The benchmark comprises 520 fire-world entries, including 494 controlled simulation worlds and 26 real-world-aligned event groups, spanning 47 scene archetypes across 7 environment families. These entries combine structured textual observations, multiple 2D physical-field visualizations, and 3D event-level scene modeling, yielding 9,074 text-image interleaved question-answer pairs across choice-based and open-ended report-generation formats. FireWorldBench evaluates whether models can infer latent physical states, explain underlying mechanisms, forecast coupled-field evolution, and assess intervention consequences from multimodal partial observations, providing a challenging testbed for complex physical world intelligence.

AI.tldr: FireWorldBench is a new benchmark for evaluating complex physical-world intelligence in multimodal LLMs and agents using coupled-field fire dynamics, with 9,074 text-image QA pairs across understanding, dynamics, causality, and intervention axes.
AI.motivation: Real-world physical systems involve multiple continuous fields, latent causal mechanisms, partial observations, and intervention-sensitive dynamics—capabilities that go beyond object recognition, scene description, and short-term visual prediction. Existing evaluations do not adequately test this complex physical intelligence, so a dedicated stress-test environment is needed.
AI.method: The authors introduce FireWorldBench, organized along two complementary axes: a physical capability axis and a fire scenario task axis. It covers physical-state understanding, temporal dynamics, causal mechanisms, and intervention reasoning. The benchmark contains 520 fire-world entries—494 controlled simulation worlds and 26 real-world-aligned event groups—spanning 47 scene archetypes across 7 environment families. Entries combine structured textual observations, multiple 2D physical-field visualizations, and 3D event-level scene modeling, yielding 9,074 text-image interleaved QA pairs in choice-based and open-ended report-generation formats.
AI.result: FireWorldBench provides a challenging testbed comprising 520 entries and 9,074 interleaved text-image QA pairs, spanning 47 scene archetypes and 7 environment families, designed to probe latent physical-state inference, mechanism explanation, coupled-field forecasting, and intervention-consequence assessment under multimodal partial observations.
AI.conclusion: FireWorldBench evaluates whether multimodal models can infer latent physical states, explain underlying mechanisms, forecast coupled-field evolution, and assess intervention consequences from partial multimodal observations, offering a rigorous testbed for advancing complex physical-world intelligence.

title: SmoLSTM: A Compact Vision-Language-Action Model with Recurrent Memory that Persists
comment: Submitted to ICRA 2027
summary: Vision-language-action models often predict actions from only the current observation, which can leave tasks involving object occlusion or visually identical objects ambiguous without episode history. The usual countermeasure, widening the observation window, turns the horizon into a hyperparameter and lets per-step cost grow with it. We instead capture the episode in a recurrent state. SmoLSTM couples a frozen 256M-parameter SmolVLM backbone to a matrix-memory LSTM control layer in which observation tokens and action queries are unified in a single causal stream that is never reset throughout the entire episode. Recurrent-state storage is therefore O(1) in episode length. A flow-matching action head predicts chunks of 10 end-effector pose deltas and gripper commands at each control step. Our single policy, trained jointly on 7,461 demonstrations across 140 tasks and evaluated on held-out initial states, performs best, reaching 85.1% subgoal coverage and 77.5% full-task success on LIBERO-Mem with 0.04B trainable parameters, surpassing both the benchmark's own object-centric baseline and recent memory-based approaches. Resetting the recurrent state at every control step reduces full-task success to 7.0%, showing that the trained policy relies on context carried between decisions. The same model achieves 79.6% average success on standard LIBERO.

AI.tldr: SmoLSTM couples a frozen SmolVLM backbone with a matrix-memory LSTM control layer that carries a persistent recurrent state across an entire episode, achieving strong memory-dependent task performance at O(1) state cost.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action models typically predict actions from only the current observation, making tasks with object occlusion or visually identical objects ambiguous. The standard fix—widening the observation window—introduces a horizon hyperparameter and increases per-step cost. The paper instead aims to capture episode history in a fixed-size recurrent state.
AI.method: SmoLSTM couples a frozen 256M-parameter SmolVLM backbone to a matrix-memory LSTM control layer, unifying observation tokens and action queries into a single causal stream never reset during the episode, giving O(1) recurrent-state storage. A flow-matching action head predicts chunks of 10 end-effector pose deltas and gripper commands per control step. The policy is trained jointly on 7,461 demonstrations over 140 tasks.
AI.result: Evaluated on held-out initial states, the single policy reaches 85.1% subgoal coverage and 77.5% full-task success on LIBERO-Mem with 0.04B trainable parameters, surpassing the benchmark's object-centric baseline and recent memory-based approaches. Resetting the recurrent state each control step drops full-task success to 7.0%, and the same model achieves 79.6% average success on standard LIBERO.
AI.conclusion: Encoding episode history in a persistent recurrent state offers an efficient, hyperparameter-free alternative to observation-window widening, and the large performance drop under per-step state resets confirms the policy relies on context carried between decisions.

title: Tutoring Large Language Models to be Domain-adaptive, Precise and Safe
comment: This is a preprint of a PhD thesis submitted to IIT KGP. The final, official version of record is available through the university's institutional repository
summary: This thesis proposes a framework for "responsible intelligence" to address AI's critical challenges in safety, ethics, and cultural sensitivity. It advances three core areas: First, it improves domain adaptation in specialized fields using active learning and graph-based knowledge to reduce hallucinations. Second, it enhances ethical rigor via a novel decoding-time alignment mechanism that proactively blocks harmful text generation in real-time. Finally, it ensures cultural and multilingual safety through language-specific steering that respects diverse linguistic and social norms. Ultimately, this work provides a blueprint for building next-generation AI that is contextually knowledgeable, ethically sound, and culturally adaptable.

AI.tldr: This thesis proposes a "responsible intelligence" framework with three components: active learning plus graph-based knowledge for domain adaptation, a decoding-time alignment mechanism for real-time ethical safety, and language-specific steering for culturally aware multilingual safety.
AI.motivation: AI faces critical challenges in safety, ethics, and cultural sensitivity, requiring a principled framework for building responsible systems.
AI.method: Three approaches: (1) active learning and graph-based knowledge for domain adaptation to reduce hallucinations; (2) a novel decoding-time alignment mechanism that proactively blocks harmful text generation in real time; (3) language-specific steering respecting diverse linguistic and social norms.
AI.result: Improved domain adaptation in specialized fields with reduced hallucinations; enhanced ethical rigor via real-time blocking of harmful generation; ensured cultural and multilingual safety through language-specific steering.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a blueprint for next-generation AI that is contextually knowledgeable, ethically sound, and culturally adaptable.

title: PileBelief: Persistent Physical State for Interaction-Driven World Modeling
summary: World models allow robots to anticipate action consequences before execution. This capability is especially valuable in excavation, where each scoop reshapes the terrain and affects subsequent actions. Local observations, however, cannot fully reveal the underlying support and material conditions. We present PileBelief, an interaction-driven persistent world model for partially observed excavation that retains physical evidence beyond the visible surface. It combines an observation-conditioned physical prior with world-addressed deformation memory and physical-response memory. Action-aligned reads and gated residual corrections refine terrain-change and outcome predictions. With deployment weights fixed, completed interactions update measured belief, while hypothetical actions advance a separate imagined state. Compared with a current-observation-only baseline, PileBelief reduces five-step joint prediction error by 10.8% and offline action-selection regret by 65.5%. Experiments on Newton/MPM and real excavation datasets further demonstrate improved terrain-change and bucket-volume prediction. Our method enables multi-step prediction and candidate-action ranking from local observations, even when the underlying soil state is unknown. These results identify persistent physical belief as a useful representation for world models of environments that robots continually reshape.

AI.tldr: PileBelief is an interaction-driven persistent world model for partially observed excavation that maintains physical evidence beyond the visible surface via observation-conditioned priors and world-addressed deformation and physical-response memories, improving multi-step prediction and action ranking.
AI.motivation: Excavation is a domain where each scoop reshapes the terrain and influences later actions, so anticipating action consequences is valuable; however, local observations cannot reveal underlying support and material conditions, and current-observation-only models lack persistent physical evidence.
AI.method: The model combines an observation-conditioned physical prior with world-addressed deformation memory and physical-response memory. Action-aligned reads and gated residual corrections refine terrain-change and outcome predictions. With deployment weights fixed, completed interactions update a measured belief, while hypothetical actions advance a separate imagined state.
AI.result: Compared with a current-observation-only baseline, PileBelief reduces five-step joint prediction error by 10.8% and offline action-selection regret by 65.5%. Experiments on Newton/MPM and real excavation datasets further show improved terrain-change and bucket-volume prediction.
AI.conclusion: PileBelief enables multi-step prediction and candidate-action ranking from local observations even when the underlying soil state is unknown, identifying persistent physical belief as a useful representation for world models of environments robots continually reshape.

title: Event Signature Transfer: Model-Agnostic Forecast Scenario Construction from Historical Events
summary: Forecasters often know an event is imminent but not the shape, size, or timing of its effect. We introduce Event Signature Transfer (EST), a training-free, model-agnostic operator that turns a completed past event into an explicit forecast scenario. EST removes a source event's own trend and seasonality, then scales and retimes the remaining event signature onto a native forecast, preserving the forecast's linked structure and reducing to it exactly at zero strength. Because it reads only output quantiles, EST applies to any quantile forecaster, with no training, no model internals, at transfer time. Across twelve real episodes and ten synthetic scenarios on Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5 and Toto-2.0, manually configured EST reduces real-episode WQL by 21.7-90\% in-sample. On Chronos-2, it leads eleven of twelve matched comparisons against covariate conditioning, activation editing and raw replay. The operator builds a scenario; it does not estimate its likelihood.

AI.tldr: Event Signature Transfer (EST) is a training-free, model-agnostic operator that converts a completed past event into an explicit forecast scenario by stripping its trend and seasonality and rescaling/retiming the residual signature onto a native forecast, yielding large WQL gains across Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5 and Toto-2.0.
AI.motivation: Forecasters frequently know an event is imminent but lack knowledge of the shape, size, or timing of its effect, and existing forecasters cannot readily inject such scenario knowledge without retraining or accessing model internals.
AI.method: EST removes a source event's own trend and seasonality, then scales and retimes the remaining event signature onto a native forecast, preserving the forecast's linked structure and reducing exactly to that forecast at zero strength. It reads only output quantiles, so it applies to any quantile forecaster with no training and no model internals at transfer time.
AI.result: Across twelve real episodes and ten synthetic scenarios on Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5 and Toto-2.0, manually configured EST reduces real-episode WQL by 21.7-90% in-sample. On Chronos-2 it leads eleven of twelve matched comparisons against covariate conditioning, activation editing and raw replay.
AI.conclusion: EST provides a practical way to encode event knowledge as an explicit forecast scenario without retraining; however, it only constructs the scenario and does not estimate its likelihood.

title: A Reconfigurable Dual-Opposition Architecture for Single-Hand Assembly and Manipulation
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables
summary: In-hand assembly is constrained by the need to maintain grasps on two separate parts while controlling their relative motion within a single hand. To enable both in-hand assembly and manipulation, we present a reconfigurable dual-opposition architecture. Specifically, to support simultaneous grasping of two parts and coordinated in-hand manipulation, four independently actuated fingers are organized into two virtual finger (VF) oppositions, with their relative configuration controlled by a reconfigurable palm. To describe hand motion and simultaneous two-object grasping configurations, a kinematic model of the fingers and palm and an object-size-conditioned workspace formulation are built. To further evaluate motion performance and assembly capability, finger-joint motion and palm tracking are characterized, and in-hand assembly is demonstrated through tasks involving grasping, alignment, fastening, and pressing. Ablation experiments further demonstrate the importance of finger abduction/adduction and palm reconfiguration for successful in-hand assembly. In simulation, the proposed hand achieves a mean continuous sphere rotation success rate of 98.6% over diameters of 40-230 mm, compared with 73.8% for the LEAP Hand. After policy fine-tuning with external disturbances, the proposed hand achieves 92.8% success under disturbances from multiple directions, compared with 45.2% for the LEAP Hand. Hardware demonstrations further show in-hand rotation of objects of different sizes using policies trained in simulation. Together, these results show that the proposed architecture supports both assembly of two separately held parts and coordinated manipulation of a single object within one hand.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a reconfigurable dual-opposition hand architecture enabling simultaneous grasping of two separate parts and coordinated in-hand manipulation, achieving high simulation success rates and demonstrating in-hand assembly tasks.
AI.motivation: In-hand assembly is challenging because it requires maintaining grasps on two separate parts while controlling their relative motion within a single hand. Existing hands typically support either in-hand manipulation or assembly, not both.
AI.method: A reconfigurable dual-opposition architecture is proposed: four independently actuated fingers are organized into two virtual finger (VF) oppositions, with relative configuration controlled by a reconfigurable palm. A kinematic model of fingers and palm along with an object-size-conditioned workspace formulation is built. Finger-joint motion and palm tracking are characterized, and assembly tasks (grasping, alignment, fastening, pressing) plus ablation experiments are conducted.
AI.result: The hand achieves 98.6% mean continuous sphere rotation success rate over 40-230 mm diameters in simulation, versus 73.8% for the LEAP Hand. After policy fine-tuning with external disturbances, it achieves 92.8% success under multi-directional disturbances versus 45.2% for LEAP Hand. Hardware demonstrations show in-hand rotation of objects of different sizes using simulation-trained policies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed reconfigurable dual-opposition architecture supports both assembly of two separately held parts and coordinated manipulation of a single object within one hand, with ablation confirming the importance of finger abduction/adduction and palm reconfiguration.

title: From Inference Engine to Inference Control Plane: Connecting vLLM, llm-d, and the Evolution of Efficient Distributed LLM Serving
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Systems synthesis and research agenda on vLLM, llm-d, distributed inference control, KV-state management, routing, disaggregation, heterogeneous accelerators, reliability, and agentic/multimodal serving. No new experimental measurements are claimed; empirical and organization-reported results are attributed to the cited sources
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference is evolving from an engine-local optimization problem into a distributed control problem involving reusable state, phase placement, heterogeneous accelerators, networking, autoscaling, reliability, and service-level objectives. This paper connects that transition across peer-reviewed systems research, open-source implementations, and documented production studies. It treats vLLM and llm-d as complementary layers: model-serving engines optimize execution through mechanisms such as PagedAttention, continuous batching, kernels, quantization, and parallelism, while an inference control plane can optimize where, when, and under what policy execution occurs across a fleet. The contribution is synthesis rather than a new benchmark; all reported performance and deployment results remain attributed to their original sources. The combined evidence suggests that the scarce resource in modern inference is shifting from raw FLOPs alone toward managed state, placement, network movement, reliability, and decision quality. We propose an Inference Execution Planner that selects feasible execution plans rather than only endpoints, including aggregated versus disaggregated topology, KV source and transfer action, hardware variant, routing/admission policy, and slower scaling decisions. We also provide a source-local benchmark atlas, a bottleneck-migration taxonomy, practical deployment guidance, an evaluation framework based on SLO-goodput, and research questions for agentic, multimodal, heterogeneous, and resilient inference.

AI.tldr: This synthesis paper frames LLM inference as a distributed control problem rather than a local engine optimization, surveying peer-reviewed systems, open-source (vLLM, llm-d), and production evidence to propose an Inference Execution Planner and accompanying frameworks.
AI.motivation: LLM inference has shifted from engine-local optimization to a distributed control problem spanning reusable state, phase placement, heterogeneous accelerators, networking, autoscaling, reliability, and SLOs. Existing work is fragmented across paper, code, and production sources, and the field lacks a unified framing connecting these layers.
AI.method: A synthesis (not a new benchmark) connecting peer-reviewed systems research, open-source implementations, and documented production studies. The authors treat vLLM and llm-d as complementary layers: serving engines (PagedAttention, continuous batching, kernels, quantization, parallelism) optimize execution, while a control plane optimizes where, when, and under what policy execution occurs across a fleet. They propose an Inference Execution Planner selecting feasible plans (aggregated vs disaggregated topology, KV source/transfer action, hardware variant, routing/admission policy, scaling decisions), plus a source-local benchmark atlas, bottleneck-migration taxonomy, deployment guidance, an SLO-goodput evaluation framework, and open research questions.
AI.result: All reported performance and deployment results remain attributed to their original sources (source-local); no new benchmark is introduced. The synthesized evidence suggests the scarce resource in modern inference is shifting from raw FLOPs alone toward managed state, placement, network movement, reliability, and decision quality.
AI.conclusion: Modern LLM inference should be treated as a distributed control problem, and optimization should target managed state, placement, network movement, reliability, and decision quality rather than FLOPs alone. The Inference Execution Planner, benchmark atlas, bottleneck-migration taxonomy, SLO-goodput evaluation framework, and research questions chart a path toward agentic, multimodal, heterogeneous, and resilient inference.

title: Barrier Certificate Synthesis for Non-Polynomial Robotic Dynamics via Polynomial Lifting
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Safe operation of robotic systems requires trajectories to remain within a prescribed safe set under admissible control inputs. Barrier certificates provide such guarantees by certifying a controlled-invariant region within that set. Sum-of-squares optimization offers a systematic way to synthesize such certificates, but its direct application requires polynomial dynamics, excluding common robotic nonlinearities, including trigonometric terms. We address this limitation using exact polynomial lifting, which replaces non-polynomial dynamics with polynomial-augmented dynamics subject to lifting-induced algebraic constraints, preserving nonlinear geometry without approximation. We formulate lifted-domain joint barrier synthesis that computes a certificate with a state-feedback control witness and develop a sampled-data safety filter for zero-order-hold implementation. To assess whether the benefits of lifting persist across synthesis frameworks, we also adapt a sample-guided successive-barrier method to the lifted representation. On coordinated-turn and planar multirotor models, exact lifting improves certified coverage in both methods: at matched sample sizes, lifted successive-barrier synthesis achieves higher coverage with fewer barriers and lower computational cost, while lifted joint barrier synthesis provides higher coverage and lower computational cost than the finest tested piecewise resolution. In closed-loop experiments, the safety filter maintains feasibility and safety across all evaluated trajectories, reduces spatial conservativeness, and requires less intervention for both models.

AI.tldr: The paper uses exact polynomial lifting to enable sum-of-squares barrier certificate synthesis for robotic systems with non-polynomial (e.g., trigonometric) dynamics, and develops a sampled-data safety filter for zero-order-hold implementation, demonstrating improved certified coverage and lower conservativeness.
AI.motivation: Barrier certificates guarantee that trajectories stay within a prescribed safe set under admissible control. Sum-of-squares optimization can systematically synthesize such certificates, but its direct use requires polynomial dynamics, which excludes common robotic nonlinearities such as trigonometric terms. The paper aims to overcome this limitation without approximating the nonlinear geometry.
AI.method: The authors apply exact polynomial lifting, replacing non-polynomial dynamics with polynomial-augmented dynamics subject to lifting-induced algebraic constraints, preserving nonlinear geometry exactly. They formulate a lifted-domain joint barrier synthesis that computes a certificate together with a state-feedback control witness, and develop a sampled-data safety filter for zero-order-hold implementation. They also adapt a sample-guided successive-barrier method to the lifted representation to test whether lifting benefits persist across synthesis frameworks.
AI.result: On coordinated-turn and planar multirotor models, exact lifting improves certified coverage in both methods. At matched sample sizes, lifted successive-barrier synthesis achieves higher coverage with fewer barriers and lower computational cost, while lifted joint barrier synthesis provides higher coverage and lower computational cost than the finest tested piecewise resolution. In closed-loop experiments, the safety filter maintains feasibility and safety across all evaluated trajectories, reduces spatial conservativeness, and requires less intervention for both models.
AI.conclusion: Exact polynomial lifting makes sum-of-squares barrier synthesis applicable to non-polynomial robotic dynamics, improving certified coverage, reducing conservativeness and computational cost, and yielding a practical sampled-data safety filter that maintains safety and feasibility in closed loop.

title: CraftBench-UE: Deterministic Evaluation for Coding Agents in Unreal Engine
summary: Building gameplay features in a game engine requires more than code, as code that compiles and runs does not necessarily implement the requested gameplay. We introduce CraftBenchUE, an evaluation harness that runs agents in an isolated Unreal Engine environment, reconstructs their saved submissions in fresh projects, and applies deterministic build, asset, and runtime checks without an LLM judge. Based on the harness, we built a benchmark consisting of 70 tasks spanning C++ source, Blueprint assets, and editor scripting. We evaluate seven models under two editor-tool configurations, with a file-and-shell baseline on C++ tasks. We further pair tasks that specify the same gameplay and use the same runtime tests, but require C++ and Blueprint as the deliverables. Across the 10 paired tasks, C++ completion rates exceed Blueprint by 30.0 and 42.9 percentage points in the two tool configurations. Among on-time Blueprint submissions in this paired set that pass asset checks, 42.2% and 50.0% fail explicit runtime assertions. These submissions satisfy asset requirements but fail the required gameplay tests. We will release the harness, task benchmark, and our trajectory findings with the report.

AI.tldr: CraftBenchUE is an LLM-judge-free evaluation harness that runs agents in isolated Unreal Engine environments, rebuilds saved submissions in fresh projects, and applies deterministic build, asset, and runtime checks. A 70-task benchmark (C++ source, Blueprint assets, editor scripting) shows C++ deliverable completion exceeds Blueprint by 30.0/42.9 points across two tool configurations, and many asset-check-passing Blueprint submissions still fail explicit runtime gameplay assertions.
AI.motivation: Building gameplay features in a game engine requires more than compiling and running code; code that builds does not necessarily implement the requested gameplay. Existing evaluation of agents on engine-level tasks is limited by the absence of automated, deterministic verification that a submission actually realizes the intended gameplay in a real engine project.
AI.method: CraftBenchUE: an evaluation harness that executes agents in an isolated Unreal Engine environment, reconstructs their saved submissions in fresh projects, and applies deterministic build, asset, and runtime checks without an LLM judge. A 70-task benchmark spanning C++ source, Blueprint assets, and editor scripting. Seven models are evaluated under two editor-tool configurations, with a file-and-shell baseline on C++ tasks. Additionally, 10 paired tasks specify identical gameplay and use identical runtime tests but require C++ versus Blueprint deliverables.
AI.result: C++ completion rates exceed Blueprint by 30.0 and 42.9 percentage points in the two tool configurations across the 10 paired tasks. Among on-time Blueprint submissions in the paired set that pass asset checks, 42.2% and 50.0% fail explicit runtime assertions—satisfying asset requirements while failing the required gameplay tests.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic engine-grounded checks without an LLM judge reveal that asset validity does not imply gameplay correctness, and that deliverable modality (C++ vs. Blueprint) strongly affects completion. The harness, task benchmark, and trajectory findings will be released with the report.

title: Stable and Efficient Real-World Online VLA Post-Training via Asynchronous Replay-Anchored Policy Improvement
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures
summary: Online post-training of vision-language-action (VLA) models requires efficient use of robot interaction and reliable policy improvement from continually collected experience. We propose asynchronous Replay-Anchored Policy improvement (RAPolicy), a framework that performs rollout and learning concurrently while grounding both critic and actor updates in replayed behavior. The critic learns chunk-level values from recorded actions and constructs Bellman targets without predicting next actions, reducing computation and dependence on action-value estimates outside replay coverage. The one-step flow actor reuses the initial noise stored during rollout and learns through advantage-weighted conditional likelihood, directly supervising the action mapping used for execution. We evaluate RAPolicy across four single-task settings and one joint five-task setting in the real world, with online training budgets of only 1--2 hours. Starting from policies fine-tuned on just 10 demonstrations per task, RAPolicy rapidly adapts to new single tasks and achieves an average 86.3% success rate. In the joint multi-task setting, RAPolicy improves overall success rate from 52% to 88% while preserving performance on already reliable tasks and improving weaker capabilities. Overall, RAPolicy substantially outperforms the baselines in aggregate task success while requiring fewer human interventions, demonstrating stable policy improvement and high online training efficiency. Project page: https://flyfaerss.github.io/RAPolicy.

AI.tldr: RAPolicy is an asynchronous online post-training framework for VLA models that anchors critic and actor updates in replayed behavior, enabling efficient real-world policy improvement with short online training budgets.
AI.motivation: Online post-training of VLA models needs efficient use of robot interaction and reliable policy improvement from continually collected experience, which existing approaches struggle to achieve.
AI.method: Performs rollout and learning concurrently. The critic learns chunk-level values from recorded actions and builds Bellman targets without next-action prediction, reducing computation and reliance on out-of-replay action-value estimates. The one-step flow actor reuses the initial rollout noise and learns via advantage-weighted conditional likelihood, directly supervising the executed action mapping.
AI.result: Evaluated on four single-task and one joint five-task real-world settings with 1-2 hour online budgets, starting from policies fine-tuned on 10 demos per task. Achieves 86.3% average success on single tasks; in joint multi-task, success rises from 52% to 88%, preserving reliable tasks and improving weaker capabilities. Outperforms baselines in aggregate success with fewer human interventions.
AI.conclusion: RAPolicy demonstrates stable policy improvement and high online training efficiency, offering an effective route to rapid real-world adaptation of VLA models.

title: Do Not Trust the Benchmark: Limitations of General LLM Rankings and a Case for Task-Specific Evaluation
summary: Benchmark scores increasingly influence the development, marketing, and selection of large language models (LLMs). Yet an overall score is interpretable only in relation to the system tested, the questions included, and the conditions of evaluation. This perspective examines five connected limitations of general LLM rankings: differences between evaluated and publicly available systems; commercial incentives and dependencies in external evaluation; benchmark saturation, defective tests, and data contamination; models exploiting scoring procedures; and the limited relevance of general scores to users' tasks. Documented cases illustrate why these problems require different responses. I argue for evaluation procedures that disclose the tested configuration, validate questions and successful task completion, report performance alongside cost and execution time, and make the scope of generalization explicit. I then discuss \textbf{Isotanta}, a crowdsourced benchmarking platform, as a practical example of contributed questions and repeated evaluation. A larger question pool may improve task coverage, while repeated sampling can improve the stability of estimates on that pool; neither guarantees validity or personalization. The paper distinguishes the platform's current shared ranking from proposed task-specific and user-provided evaluations. Its central argument is that model selection requires evidence about performance on the intended work, not simply a high position on a general leaderboard.

AI.tldr: General LLM leaderboard rankings are interpretable only relative to the tested system, question set, and evaluation conditions; the paper identifies five limitations of such rankings and argues for evaluation procedures that disclose configuration, validate questions and task completion, report cost and execution time, and state the scope of generalization, using the crowdsourced platform Isotanta as a practical example of contributed questions and repeated evaluation.
AI.motivation: Benchmark scores increasingly shape LLM development, marketing, and selection, yet an overall score is only interpretable in relation to the system tested, the questions included, and the evaluation conditions. This creates a risk that users select models based on leaderboard position rather than evidence of performance on their intended work.
AI.method: A perspective/argumentative analysis of five connected limitations of general LLM rankings: (1) differences between evaluated and publicly available systems, (2) commercial incentives and dependencies in external evaluation, (3) benchmark saturation, defective tests, and data contamination, (4) models exploiting scoring procedures, and (5) limited relevance of general scores to users' tasks. Documented cases are used to show these problems require different responses. The paper then discusses Isotanta, a crowdsourced benchmarking platform, as a practical example of contributed questions and repeated evaluation.
AI.result: The five limitations are shown to be distinct problems requiring distinct responses, illustrated through documented cases. Isotanta demonstrates that a larger contributed question pool may improve task coverage and that repeated sampling can improve the stability of estimates on that pool; however, neither guarantees validity or personalization. The paper distinguishes the platform's current shared ranking from proposed task-specific and user-provided evaluations.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues for evaluation procedures that disclose the tested configuration, validate questions and successful task completion, report performance alongside cost and execution time, and make the scope of generalization explicit. Its central argument is that model selection requires evidence about performance on the intended work, not simply a high position on a general leaderboard.

title: H-VLA: Hierarchical Vision-Language-Action Model with Key-Action Reasoning and Motion Planning in a Unified Action Space
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for robotic manipulation, but many existing methods still rely on direct mappings from language and visual observations to dense actions. This formulation can weaken the semantic reasoning capability inherited from pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs), which are mainly optimized for visual-linguistic understanding rather than low-level control, and becomes fragile under spatial variations, including changes in object positions, scene layouts, robot embodiments, and camera viewpoints. To address these limitations, we propose H-VLA, a hierarchical VLA framework that decouples high-level key-action reasoning from low-level motion generation. H-VLA combines a Key-Action Model for predicting a key-action as the next manipulation subgoal, a Motion Planning Model for generating dense future actions conditioned on the predicted key-action, and a Unified Camera-Centric Action Space for consistent representation across datasets, embodiments, and viewpoints. We further adopt a two-stage training strategy that emphasizes key-action reasoning during pre-training and dense motion generation during fine-tuning. Experiments show that H-VLA achieves strong performance on SimplerEnv, reaching 91% on Google Robot visual matching, 84% on Google Robot variant aggregation, and 81% on WidowX visual matching. On Agilex real-robot tasks, H-VLA improves over the strongest baseline by 10, 47, and 16 percentage points under in-distribution, out-of-distribution position, and out-of-distribution scene/object settings, respectively.

AI.tldr: H-VLA is a hierarchical Vision-Language-Action framework that decouples high-level key-action reasoning from low-level dense motion generation, using a unified camera-centric action space and two-stage training to improve robustness and manipulation performance.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA methods rely on direct mappings from language and visual observations to dense actions, which weakens the semantic reasoning inherited from pre-trained VLMs (optimized for visual-linguistic understanding, not low-level control) and makes them fragile under spatial variations such as object positions, scene layouts, robot embodiments, and camera viewpoints.
AI.method: H-VLA is a hierarchical VLA framework with three components: a Key-Action Model that predicts a key-action as the next manipulation subgoal; a Motion Planning Model that generates dense future actions conditioned on the predicted key-action; and a Unified Camera-Centric Action Space for consistent representation across datasets, embodiments, and viewpoints. A two-stage training strategy emphasizes key-action reasoning during pre-training and dense motion generation during fine-tuning.
AI.result: On SimplerEnv, H-VLA reaches 91% on Google Robot visual matching, 84% on Google Robot variant aggregation, and 81% on WidowX visual matching. On Agilex real-robot tasks, it outperforms the strongest baseline by 10, 47, and 16 percentage points under in-distribution, out-of-distribution position, and out-of-distribution scene/object settings, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling high-level key-action reasoning from low-level motion generation, combined with a unified camera-centric action space and two-stage training, yields a more robust and semantically grounded VLA model that generalizes better across spatial and embodiment variations.

title: Expansion Counts under Standard A* Tie-Breaking Strategies on the Final Plateau
summary: In the A* search algorithm, the tie-breaking strategies for nodes with the same $f$-value determines which states A* expands on the final $f$-layer. For nine standard tie-breaking strategies, we show that under a consistent heuristic, every pair has positive-cost instances favoring each strategy over the other by an arbitrarily large additive expansion gap. A parameterized unit-cost grid example also gives unbounded expansion-count ratios between low-$h$ with FIFO and LIFO. In unit-cost search with $h > 0$ at non-goals, exact heuristic values near the goal lead to complementary extremal results: low-$h$ minimizes the number of remaining expansions from a common configuration within the perfect region, while high-$h$ maximizes the total number of expansions when every final-plateau state with $h=1$ is a goal predecessor. Finally, with the evaluation function $f_α = g + αh$, when $h>0$ at non-goals, every heuristic weight $0 \leq α<1$ eliminates tie-breaking sensitivity, and all tie-breaking strategies expand the same set of states.

AI.tldr: Under consistent heuristics, no single tie-breaking strategy dominates: every pair of nine standard strategies has positive-cost instances where either one wins by an arbitrarily large additive expansion gap. Weighted evaluation with 0 ≤ α < 1 removes all such tie-breaking sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Tie-breaking among nodes with equal f-value determines which states A* expands on the final f-layer, yet the relative strength of standard tie-breaking strategies is not well understood. The paper aims to characterize how tie-breaking affects A* expansion counts and whether any strategy is universally superior.
AI.method: The authors analyze nine standard tie-breaking strategies under consistent heuristics, constructing positive-cost instances that yield arbitrarily large additive expansion gaps for every pair of strategies. They also build a parameterized unit-cost grid example to produce unbounded expansion-count ratios between low-h with FIFO and LIFO. They study unit-cost search with h > 0 at non-goals, examining exact heuristic values near the goal (the "perfect region"), and analyze the weighted evaluation function f_α = g + αh for 0 ≤ α < 1.
AI.result: Every pair of the nine tie-breaking strategies has positive-cost instances favoring each over the other by an arbitrarily large additive expansion gap. In the unit-cost grid example, low-h with FIFO versus LIFO gives unbounded expansion-count ratios. For unit-cost search with h > 0 at non-goals, low-h minimizes remaining expansions from a common configuration within the perfect region, while high-h maximizes total expansions when every final-plateau state with h = 1 is a goal predecessor. For f_α = g + αh with h > 0 at non-goals, every weight 0 ≤ α < 1 eliminates tie-breaking sensitivity, and all strategies expand the same set of states.
AI.conclusion: Tie-breaking strategies cannot be ranked by a universal criterion, since any pair can exhibit arbitrarily large performance gaps depending on the instance. The choice of tie-breaking thus matters substantially in unit-cost, consistent-heuristic settings. However, using a weighted evaluation f_α = g + αh with 0 ≤ α < 1 eliminates tie-breaking sensitivity entirely, expanding identical state sets across strategies.

title: "Dear LLaVA, Please Drive": A Depth-Aware Vision-Language Agent for Closed-Loop Robotic Control
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) provide a compelling foundation for reasoning-driven mobile navigation, offering rich contextual understanding and strong generalization from large-scale pretraining. Most existing navigation frameworks rely on imitation learning and therefore require substantial labeled trajectory data, limiting their scalability and robustness. In this work, we propose a parameter-efficient approach to fine-tune a pretrained VLM for autonomous navigation using an Imperative Learning paradigm. By optimizing against differentiable geometric cost fields rather than labeled trajectories, our model learns to generate collision-free paths exclusively from stereoscopic depth observations. We introduce a unified end-to-end navigation pipeline for natural-language-driven robotic control. This system leverages a shared VLM backbone with task-specific Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules, effectively bridging the gap from semantic target selection to low-level trajectory planning. Our approach achieves competitive Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) in unseen environments while updating less than 1% of the model's total parameters. Qualitative real-world experiments validate sim-to-real generalization and stable path planning without fine-tuning on real-world data. These results highlight a practical approach for deploying VLM-based agents on mobile robots, enabling high-level semantic navigation without the prohibitive requirement for large-scale, labeled trajectory data.

AI.tldr: A parameter-efficient Imperative Learning approach fine-tunes a pretrained VLM for mobile navigation by optimizing against differentiable geometric cost fields from stereo depth, using shared backbone with task-specific LoRA modules.
AI.motivation: Most VLM-based navigation frameworks rely on imitation learning, requiring substantial labeled trajectory data, which limits scalability and robustness.
AI.method: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of a pretrained VLM via Imperative Learning, optimizing against differentiable geometric cost fields instead of labeled trajectories. Model learns collision-free paths from stereoscopic depth. A unified end-to-end pipeline uses a shared VLM backbone with task-specific LoRA modules, bridging semantic target selection to low-level trajectory planning.
AI.result: Competitive SPL in unseen environments while updating less than 1% of total parameters. Qualitative real-world experiments confirm sim-to-real generalization and stable path planning without real-world fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Offers a practical approach for deploying VLM-based agents on mobile robots, enabling high-level semantic navigation without large-scale labeled trajectory data.

title: TicTacBench: Benchmarking Timing Closure Capabilities of Coding Agents
comment: Accepted at ICCD26
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to the emergence of coding agents capable of performing complex engineering tasks, including register-transfer level (RTL) design and optimization. Existing RTL benchmarks mainly evaluate functional correctness and performance, power, and area (PPA) of the generated RTL designs, leaving agents' ability for \emph{timing closure} under-evaluated. We propose TicTacBench, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate coding agents' capabilities for RTL-level timing closure under post-place-and-route (post-PnR) evaluation. TicTacBench contains 30 diverse tasks, each provided with a suboptimal RTL design, realistic timing constraints, functional equivalence verification, and timing reports. With over 300 runs of coding agents driven by 8 frontier LLMs, we find that even the best agent can only close 53.3\% of tasks with 7.18\% area-delay product (ADP) degradation and 8.83\% energy-delay-squared product (EDDP) improvement on average. We identify common failure categories that explain why agents fail to close timing. Then we propose TicTacSkill, a new method that guides agents to follow standard timing-closure procedures and improves the Timing Closure Rate by 9\%. These results suggest that while coding agents have made significant progress in RTL design, their timing-closure capability still has substantial room for improvement.

AI.tldr: TicTacBench benchmarks coding agents on RTL timing closure under post-PnR evaluation; top agents close only 53.3% of tasks, and the proposed TicTacSkill improves closure rate by 9%.
AI.motivation: Existing RTL benchmarks focus on functional correctness and PPA, leaving agents' timing-closure ability largely unevaluated.
AI.method: Introduces TicTacBench, 30 tasks each with a suboptimal RTL design, realistic timing constraints, functional equivalence verification, and timing reports; evaluates over 300 runs of coding agents driven by 8 frontier LLMs. Proposes TicTacSkill, guiding agents through standard timing-closure procedures.
AI.result: The best agent closes only 53.3% of tasks, with 7.18% ADP degradation and 8.83% EDDP improvement on average. Common failure categories are identified. TicTacSkill improves the Timing Closure Rate by 9%.
AI.conclusion: Coding agents show significant progress in RTL design, but their timing-closure capability still has substantial room for improvement.
