title: Embodied Snap: Octopus-Inspired Distributed Reach-and-Attach with a Speed-Limited Soft Arm
comment: Submitted to ICRA 2027
summary: Reach-and-attach of soft robotic arms with passive suction requires accurate targeting and sufficient contact speed, yet geared actuators can impose a speed limit that improved trajectory tracking alone cannot overcome. This paper proposes an embodied snap controller that separates slow servo-driven preloading from rapid elastic release, enabling a compliant arm to move beyond its direct tendon-driven speed limit. Octopus biology motivates the controller's section-wise organizational prior, rather than reproduction of the octopus nervous system. A learned policy shared across three sections selects preloads, aim, tendon slack, and release timing, determining where, how, and when to load and release the body. The policy is optimized offline using a hardware-validated recurrent model within experimentally supported bounds. Across five optimization seeds and 400 unseen simulated targets, attachment success is $(73\pm4)\%$ at a $5\text{ cm}$ lateral tolerance, and the shared policy reaches the matched centralized controller's mean final reward after a median $17\%$ of the common evaluation budget. Hardware characterization achieves tip speeds of 1.56-1.64 m/s, at least $108\%$ above direct tendon-driven release. In 18 open-loop hardware trials across six placements, 17 exceed the 1 m/s snap threshold and nine retrieve the object, with successful retrieval at five placements. These results demonstrate a practical division of responsibility in the control problem: learned control prepares the body, and passive body mechanics execute the rapid movement needed for dynamic reach-and-attach.

AI.tldr: A learned "embodied snap controller" separates slow servo-driven preloading from rapid elastic release, letting a compliant soft arm exceed its direct tendon-driven speed limit for reach-and-attach tasks. Validated in simulation (73±4% attachment success) and hardware (tip speeds 1.56-1.64 m/s, 9/18 retrievals).
AI.motivation: Soft robotic arms with passive suction need accurate targeting and sufficient contact speed for reach-and-attach, but geared actuators impose a speed limit that better trajectory tracking alone cannot overcome. The work aims to move beyond the direct tendon-driven speed ceiling.
AI.method: An embodied snap controller decouples slow servo-driven preloading from rapid elastic release. Octopus biology motivates a section-wise organizational prior. A learned policy shared across three sections selects preloads, aim, tendon slack, and release timing (where, how, and when to load and release). The policy is optimized offline using a hardware-validated recurrent model within experimentally supported bounds.
AI.result: Across five optimization seeds and 400 unseen simulated targets, attachment success is (73±4)% at a 5 cm lateral tolerance; the shared policy reaches the matched centralized controller's mean final reward after a median 17% of the common evaluation budget. Hardware tip speeds reach 1.56-1.64 m/s, at least 108% above direct tendon-driven release. In 18 open-loop hardware trials across six placements, 17 exceed the 1 m/s snap threshold and nine retrieve the object, with success at five placements.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate a practical division of responsibility: learned control prepares the body, while passive body mechanics execute the rapid movement needed for dynamic reach-and-attach.

title: Leaky-integrator reconstruction: taming error accumulation in recursive differenced time-series forecasting
summary: We introduce leaky-integrator reconstruction, a training-free method that cures the error accumulation of recursive differenced forecasting. Our first contribution is diagnostic: predicting one-step changes and integrating them by cumulative summation, the standard remedy for non-stationarity, is a discrete integrator with a pole on the unit circle, and we show this makes recursive rollout of a nonlinear model diverge, its 336-step error reaching several times that of a well-behaved forecaster (normalised MAE 1.6-3.8 versus about 0.8) across every neural architecture tested. Our second, central contribution is the fix: move the pole inside the unit circle with a leaky integrator H(z) = 1/(1 - gamma z^-1), gamma < 1, which provably bounds the accumulated error variance. Applied at reconstruction time with a single fixed gamma=0.9 (no retraining, a two-line change to any deployed one-step or foundation-model forecaster), it shrinks error at every horizon, the mean gain over seven diverging architectures and twenty datasets growing from ~3% at H=24 to 23% at H=96, 37% at H=192 and 51% (43-74% across those architectures) at H=336 (78% with an oracle pole). Crucially, it is provably inert where no pathology exists (stable or joint predictors already at the irreducible rate), making it a safe, general default.

AI.tldr: The paper diagnoses recursive differenced forecasting's error accumulation as a pole on the unit circle of a discrete integrator and proposes leaky-integrator reconstruction (gamma<1), a training-free fix that provably bounds error variance and improves long-horizon accuracy.
AI.motivation: Recursive differenced forecasting is the standard remedy for non-stationarity in time series, but it suffers from error accumulation during multi-step rollout. The authors seek to explain why such recursive rollouts diverge and to provide a general, safe correction.
AI.method: Diagnostic analysis treats cumulative-summation integration of one-step differences as a discrete integrator H(z)=1/(1-z^-1) with a pole on the unit circle, causing divergence of nonlinear recursive rollout. The fix replaces it with a leaky integrator H(z)=1/(1-gamma z^-1), gamma<1, applied at reconstruction time with a fixed gamma=0.9, requiring no retraining and only a minor code change to deployed one-step or foundation-model forecasters.
AI.result: Standard recursive differenced forecasting yields normalised MAE 1.6-3.8 versus about 0.8 for a well-behaved forecaster at 336 steps across all neural architectures tested. Leaky-integrator reconstruction reduces error at every horizon: ~3% at H=24, 23% at H=96, 37% at H=192, and 51% at H=336 (43-74% across architectures; 78% with an oracle pole), averaged over seven diverging architectures and twenty datasets. It is provably inert where no pathology exists (stable or joint predictors already at the irreducible rate).
AI.conclusion: The unit-circle pole diagnosis explains recursive differenced forecasting divergence, and leaky-integrator reconstruction is a safe, general default that bounds error variance and improves long-horizon accuracy without retraining.

title: MIRA-PRM: Mission-Informed Reusable Roadmap Planning for Mobile Gas-Sensing Inspection
comment: 17 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to Measurement Science and Technology
summary: Mobile gas-sensing inspection requires a mobile platform to reliably reach ordered sampling poses. We present MIRA-PRM, a mission-informed probabilistic roadmap that combines geometry-, mission-flow-, and inspection-conditioned sampling with locally adaptive connectivity and evidence-gated refinement. Eight development campaigns comprising 142,448 planner runs evaluated mission scaling, repeated-query adaptation, finite node budgets, target distributions, local map repair, ablation, cross-family comparison, and parameter sensitivity. MIRA-PRM maintained 100% seed-level success as ordered targets increased from two to eight, and achieved 97.67% seed-level success under a 40-node ceiling, compared with 67.17% for PRM and 86.50% for PRM*. Local repair reduced event time by 79.9-81.9% and node additions by 90.8-94.3% relative to rebuilding. On a separate frozen holdout of 12 maps, 48 ordered missions, and three seeds per map-mission unit, MIRA-PRM produced 96/144 validated successes, versus 82/144 for PRM, 89/144 for PRM*, and 70/144 for LE-HG-PRM. On paired common-success runs, MIRA-PRM reduced wall time by 16.89% relative to PRM* and 81.01% relative to LE-HG-PRM, but was 52.23% slower than PRM; paths were 0.54-1.86% longer. All validated paths passed independent full-segment checks and clearance non-inferiority. The results support a reliability-oriented trade-off in structured simulations and motivate external-map and physical mobile-sensing validation.

AI.tldr: MIRA-PRM is a mission-informed probabilistic roadmap with geometry-, mission-flow-, and inspection-conditioned sampling plus locally adaptive connectivity and evidence-gated refinement. Across 142,448 planner runs and a frozen holdout, it achieved higher success rates (100% up to eight ordered targets; 96/144 vs. 82/144 for PRM and 89/144 for PRM* on holdout) while maintaining validated path quality.
AI.motivation: Mobile gas-sensing inspection requires a mobile platform to reliably reach a sequence of ordered sampling poses, so planning must prioritize mission reliability rather than only short paths. Conventional roadmap planners (PRM, PRM*) degrade under finite node budgets, growing target counts, and local map changes, motivating a mission-aware planner.
AI.method: MIRA-PRM combines geometry-, mission-flow-, and inspection-conditioned sampling with locally adaptive connectivity and evidence-gated refinement. It was evaluated via eight development campaigns (142,448 planner runs) covering mission scaling, repeated-query adaptation, finite node budgets, target distributions, local map repair, ablation, cross-family comparison, and parameter sensitivity, plus a frozen holdout of 12 maps, 48 ordered missions, and three seeds per map-mission unit.
AI.result: MIRA-PRM kept 100% seed-level success as ordered targets grew from two to eight, and reached 97.67% under a 40-node ceiling versus 67.17% (PRM) and 86.50% (PRM*). Local repair cut event time by 79.9-81.9% and node additions by 90.8-94.3% versus rebuilding. On the holdout it achieved 96/144 validated successes, versus 82/144 (PRM), 89/144 (PRM*), and 70/144 (LE-HG-PRM). On paired common-success runs it reduced wall time by 16.89% versus PRM* and 81.01% versus LE-HG-PRM, though it was 52.23% slower than PRM, with paths 0.54-1.86% longer. All validated paths passed full-segment and clearance non-inferiority checks.
AI.conclusion: The findings support a reliability-oriented trade-off in structured simulations, with MIRA-PRM favoring mission success and repair efficiency over raw path optimality or speed relative to PRM. External-map and physical mobile-sensing validation remain necessary to confirm generalization.

title: AgentBetta: Verification-Driven Adaptive Configuration of an AI Nano-Agent through Selective Expansion and Verified Contraction
summary: Large language model agents are typically deployed with predefined configurations, although the required model capability, context, tools, permissions, memory, and computational resources can vary substantially across tasks. This study develops and evaluates AgentBetta, an adaptive AI Nano-Agent framework that represents these factors as an executable configuration and updates them through verification-driven diagnosis, selective expansion, and verification-based counterfactual contraction. The evaluation distinguishes controlled mechanism validation from external agent comparisons. On the AB-ConfigBench benchmark, AgentBetta achieved 91.38% verified success while reducing median context allocation from 64,000 to 8,000 context characters and median tool exposure from five tools to zero compared with the fully provisioned configuration. The configuration-deficiency diagnosis achieved a macro-F1 score of 0.819 with precision of 1.000 across the evaluated dimensions, and selective expansion avoided unnecessary changes to unrelated configuration dimensions. Post-success contraction preserved verification outcomes in 56.41% of evaluated one-dimension contraction probes, indicating that some successful configurations contained removable capability under the tested conditions. External evaluations indicate that adaptive configuration can improve the balance between verified task completion and capability exposure; however, the results vary across benchmarks and agent families. In particular, the cross-family replication did not reproduce the primary-backbone accuracy ordering, and specialized systems remained advantageous for certain task domains. These results support interpreting AgentBetta as a configuration-adaptation mechanism that regulates capability allocation and inference expenditure rather than as a universal replacement for specialized agent architectures.

AI.tldr: AgentBetta is an adaptive "Nano-Agent" framework that treats model capability, context, tools, permissions, memory, and compute as an executable configuration updated via verification-driven diagnosis, selective expansion, and counterfactual contraction. On AB-ConfigBench it reaches 91.38% verified success while cutting median context from 64,000 to 8,000 characters and median tool exposure from five tools to zero; external results show benefits vary by benchmark and agent family, framing it as a capability-allocation mechanism rather than a universal replacement for specialized agents.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are usually deployed with fixed, predefined configurations even though required model capability, context, tools, permissions, memory, and compute vary substantially across tasks, leading to over-provisioning (unnecessary capability exposure and inference expenditure) or under-provisioning (task failure). The paper seeks a configuration-adaptation mechanism that right-sizes these factors per task.
AI.method: AgentBetta represents the six factors as an executable configuration and iteratively updates it through three mechanisms: (1) verification-driven diagnosis of configuration deficiencies, (2) selective expansion along the deficient dimensions avoiding changes to unrelated dimensions, and (3) verification-based counterfactual contraction after success. Evaluation separates controlled mechanism validation (AB-ConfigBench, including one-dimension contraction probes) from external agent comparisons, plus a cross-family replication.
AI.result: On AB-ConfigBench: 91.38% verified success, with median context allocation reduced from 64,000 to 8,000 context characters and median tool exposure from five tools to zero versus the fully provisioned configuration. Deficiency diagnosis achieved macro-F1 0.819 with precision 1.000 across evaluated dimensions; selective expansion avoided unnecessary changes to unrelated dimensions. Post-success contraction preserved verification outcomes in 56.41% of one-dimension contraction probes. External evaluations showed adaptive configuration can improve the balance between verified completion and capability exposure, but results varied across benchmarks and agent families; cross-family replication did not reproduce the primary-backbone accuracy ordering, and specialized systems retained advantages in certain domains.
AI.conclusion: AgentBetta should be interpreted as a configuration-adaptation mechanism that regulates capability allocation and inference expenditure, not as a universal replacement for specialized agent architectures. Its diagnosis is high-precision, contraction is only partially effective, and external gains are benchmark- and family-dependent.

title: Prescribed-Time Contracting-Boundary Control of a Tendon-Driven Flexible Arm
summary: This study develops a prescribed-time performance-shaping control method for curvature tracking of a single-segment flexible arm actuated by three antagonistic tendon pairs. A Cartesian curvature representation is introduced to avoid the undefined bending direction at the straight configuration and to establish an explicit six-tendon kinematic mapping. A cubic performance boundary contracts smoothly from an initially admissible error bound to a nonzero terminal accuracy bound within a prescribed time. Based on this boundary, a dual transformation combining static symmetric error scaling and time-varying behavior shaping maps the tracking error into a fixed unit box. The resulting controller guarantees boundary invariance, prescribed-time entry into the terminal accuracy region, and subsequent asymptotic convergence. Numerical evaluations with Python and OpenCR--MuJoCo, together with a supervised reduced-order experiment on a two-section, four-channel platform, provide complementary validation. Across six experimental trials, no violation of the prescribed boundary is observed, and the proposed controller reduces the mean terminal curvature RMSE by 32.5% relative to a matched baseline, with comparable terminal-band entry times. These results support the feasibility of the proposed approach in the reduced-order experimental setting.

AI.tldr: A prescribed-time performance-shaping controller enables curvature tracking of a three-antagonistic-tendon-pair flexible arm, guaranteeing boundary invariance and prescribed-time convergence, with 32.5% lower terminal curvature RMSE than a baseline.
AI.motivation: Curvature tracking of flexible tendon-driven arms is challenging: the bending direction is undefined at the straight configuration, and tendon kinematics with antagonistic pairs must be explicitly mapped. In addition, tracking performance needs guaranteed transient and terminal accuracy within a user-specified time.
AI.method: A Cartesian curvature representation avoids undefined bending direction at the straight configuration and yields an explicit six-tendon kinematic mapping. A cubic performance boundary contracts from an admissible initial error bound to a nonzero terminal accuracy bound in prescribed time; a dual transformation combines static symmetric error scaling with time-varying behavior shaping to map the error into a fixed unit box. The controller enforces boundary invariance, prescribed-time entry into the terminal accuracy region, and asymptotic convergence.
AI.result: Validation combines Python and OpenCR--MuJoCo numerical evaluations with a supervised reduced-order experiment on a two-section, four-channel platform. Across six trials, the prescribed boundary is never violated, and mean terminal curvature RMSE drops 32.5% versus a matched baseline with comparable terminal-band entry times.
AI.conclusion: The proposed prescribed-time performance-shaping control is feasible in the reduced-order experimental setting, delivering guaranteed boundary invariance and improved terminal curvature accuracy for the flexible arm.

title: Are Human-Aligned Models Models of Humans? A Turing-Test Gap in Preference Alignment
summary: Human-feedback alignment has made language models useful assistants and is commonly described as aligning them with humans. However, the responses people prefer from an AI need not be the responses they themselves would give. We distinguish alignment with human preferences from alignment with human behavior, and show that alignment with human preferences can make model behavior less human-like even when both preferences and responses come entirely from humans. We call this the Turing-test gap. We show that preference alignment preserves the human response distribution only under a restrictive condition, and find no consistent evidence that real human preferences satisfy it. Empirically, the loss of human-response likelihood increases with the strength of preference weighting, regardless of its direction, and the gap also appears under standard DPO. These results establish human-likeness as an explicit dimension of alignment rather than something assumed to follow from preference alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper distinguishes alignment with human preferences from alignment with human behavior, identifying a "Turing-test gap" where preference alignment can reduce how human-like a model's responses are, even when both preferences and responses come from humans. Preference alignment preserves the human response distribution only under a restrictive condition that real human preferences do not consistently satisfy, and the loss of human-response likelihood grows with preference weighting strength (appearing even under standard DPO). The authors conclude human-likeness should be treated as an explicit dimension of alignment.
AI.motivation: Human-feedback alignment is commonly framed as aligning language models with humans, but the responses people prefer are not necessarily the responses they would themselves give. The paper aims to correct this conflation by separating preference alignment from behavioral alignment and showing that optimizing for the former can systematically degrade the latter.
AI.method: The authors formally distinguish alignment with human preferences from alignment with human behavior and characterize the condition under which preference alignment preserves the human response distribution. They test empirically whether real human preferences satisfy this condition, and measure how human-response likelihood changes as preference weighting strength varies in both directions, including under standard DPO.
AI.result: Preference alignment preserves the human response distribution only under a restrictive condition, and no consistent evidence indicates that real human preferences meet it. Empirically, loss of human-response likelihood increases with the strength of preference weighting regardless of direction, and the gap also appears under standard DPO.
AI.conclusion: Human-likeness should be regarded as an explicit, independently optimized dimension of alignment rather than an assumed byproduct of preference alignment; preference alignment and behavioral human-likeness can diverge even when both derive solely from human data.

title: Transferring the Intelligence of VLMs to Robotic Control
comment: For more detail, https://robodawn.top/
summary: Humans can seamlessly adapt to both physical and digital worlds, suggesting that while a digital-to-real gap exists in embodiment, environment and task, human intelligence itself may transfer across this gap. This naturally raises a fundamental question: can the intelligence of vision-language models (VLMs) similarly generalize from the digital world to the physical world for robotic control? We investigate this question through RoboDawn, a human-intuitive interface that exposes robotic control to an agentic VLM through a compact set of discrete translation, rotation, and gripper commands. Using this interface, the VLM controls a robot in a closed loop: it observes the current visual state, reasons about the next action, executes it, and adapts subsequent decisions to the resulting state. Furthermore, we introduce an in-context learning (ICL) scheme that uses a few demonstrations to ground the VLM in both interface usage and task-solving strategies. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 C2R and RoboDojo demonstrate that RoboDawn achieves strong performance without task-specific robot training. In the zero-shot setting, RoboDawn outperforms several strong policies trained on benchmarkspecific robot data, while a single in-context demonstration further yields substantial performance gains and establishes state-of-the-art (SOTA) results. On RoboTwin 2.0 C2R, the success rate increases from 53.2% zero-shot to 73.6% one-shot, exceeding the solid baseline π0.5 (46.0%). Similar gains are observed on RoboDojo, where success rate improves from 35.67% zero-shot to 47.17% one-shot. The same framework also transfers to real-world robots, performing block-in-basket and block stacking on Franka.

AI.tldr: RoboDawn lets an agentic VLM control a robot via a compact discrete action interface with in-context demonstrations, achieving strong transfer from digital to physical worlds and SOTA results without robot-specific training.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether VLM intelligence, like human intelligence, can transfer from the digital world to the physical world for robotic control despite the digital-to-real gap in embodiment, environment, and task.
AI.method: RoboDawn: a human-intuitive interface exposing robotic control to an agentic VLM through a compact set of discrete translation, rotation, and gripper commands. The VLM runs in a closed loop—observing visual state, reasoning about the next action, executing it, and adapting to the resulting state. An in-context learning (ICL) scheme uses a few demonstrations to ground the VLM in interface usage and task-solving strategies.
AI.result: On RoboTwin 2.0 C2R and RoboDojo, RoboDawn achieves strong performance without task-specific robot training. Zero-shot, it outperforms several strong policies trained on benchmark-specific robot data. On RoboTwin 2.0 C2R, success rate rises from 53.2% zero-shot to 73.6% one-shot, exceeding the π0.5 baseline (46.0%). On RoboDojo, success rate improves from 35.67% zero-shot to 47.17% one-shot. The framework also transfers to real-world Franka robots for block-in-basket and block stacking.
AI.conclusion: VLM intelligence can transfer from the digital world to physical robotic control, and a simple discrete interface plus ICL enables SOTA performance without robot-specific training, generalizing from simulation to real robots.

title: PhysAI-Bench: A Benchmark for LLM-Based Agentic Decision-Making in Autonomous UAV-Centric Physical AI
summary: Recent advances in Physical AI have accelerated the use of foundation models in autonomous systems such as unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), which must perceive, reason, plan, and act in dynamic environments. Existing benchmarks assess physical perception, intuitive physics, embodied navigation, and collaborative reasoning, but rarely evaluate the agentic decision-making required for reliable autonomy. We introduce \textit{PhysAI-Bench}, a benchmark for evaluating this capability. It contains 10,178 standardized decision instances automatically extracted from conversational traces of autonomous UAV missions. Each instance preserves mission context, temporal dependencies, physical constraints, Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool calls, Agent-to-Agent (A2A) interactions, sensor observations, and AI-native 6G network conditions, including latency, packet loss, throughput, edge load, and network slicing. We expose only information preceding each decision, preventing future-event leakage and approximating online decision-making. We evaluate 29 foundation models using a two-stage protocol. We select model-specific configurations from 12 combinations of zero-, three-, and five-shot prompting and four temperatures, tested in three runs on a 35-instance, human-verified development set. We then freeze each selected configuration and evaluate it in three runs on a fixed, episode-disjoint set of 500 instances. GPT-5.3 achieves the highest accuracy (52.00%), followed by GPT-5.2 (49.40%) and Grok~4.5 (49.07%). Few-shot prompting generally improves performance, while temperature has limited influence. The results demonstrate that reliable agentic decision-making in Physical AI remains an open challenge. The dataset is available at https://github.com/maferrag/physai-bench

AI.tldr: PhysAI-Bench is a new benchmark of 10,178 decision instances extracted from autonomous UAV mission traces, evaluating agentic decision-making in Physical AI across 29 foundation models. Top accuracy is only 52.00% (GPT-5.3), showing reliable autonomy remains unsolved.
AI.motivation: Foundation models are increasingly used in autonomous systems like UAVs that must perceive, reason, plan, and act in dynamic environments, yet existing benchmarks cover physical perception, intuitive physics, embodied navigation, and collaborative reasoning but rarely assess the agentic decision-making needed for reliable autonomy.
AI.method: The authors built PhysAI-Bench with 10,178 standardized decision instances automatically extracted from conversational traces of autonomous UAV missions. Each instance retains mission context, temporal dependencies, physical constraints, MCP tool calls, A2A interactions, sensor observations, and AI-native 6G network conditions (latency, packet loss, throughput, edge load, network slicing). Only information preceding each decision is exposed to prevent future-event leakage and approximate online decision-making. Evaluation uses a two-stage protocol: model-specific configs selected from 12 combinations of zero-, three-, and five-shot prompting and four temperatures over three runs on a 35-instance human-verified development set, then frozen and tested over three runs on a fixed, episode-disjoint set of 500 instances.
AI.result: Across 29 foundation models, GPT-5.3 achieves the highest accuracy (52.00%), followed by GPT-5.2 (49.40%) and Grok 4.5 (49.07%). Few-shot prompting generally improves performance, while temperature has limited influence.
AI.conclusion: Reliable agentic decision-making in Physical AI remains an open challenge, as even the best model barely exceeds half accuracy. The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/maferrag/physai-bench.

title: An Empirical Study and Open Testbed for Federated Fine-Tuning of Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Adapting a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model to a new robot, environment, or task requires demonstrations that are collected locally and often discarded. Federated learning is a promising approach to exploiting such distributed demonstrations by learning a shared policy. However, whether it can adapt large pretrained VLAs remains an open question, and a lack of reproducible benchmarks for pretrained VLAs and reusable training frameworks makes existing results difficult to compare. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study of federated fine-tuning of three modern pretrained VLA policies on the 40 simulated tasks of the LIBERO manipulation benchmark, and on six real-world tasks in two real-robot experiments, with demonstrations collected across two and three sites, respectively. Our study analyzes the key choices in this setting, spanning multiple federated parameter scopes, three aggregation algorithms, and evaluation under distribution shift. Based on the study, we derive a series of lessons, including the dominance of the federated scope over the choice of aggregation algorithm and the difficulty of matching centralized fine-tuning on physical robots, where cross-site heterogeneity is stronger than simulation captures. We also highlight opportunities for federated VLA learning, such as the ability to match centralized fine-tuning on heterogeneous data, to remain at least as robust as centralized fine-tuning under distribution shift, and to personalize, with each client federating part of the policy and keeping the rest local, which helps where the policy's pretraining is weak but leaves no usable global model. We open-source \decentvla{}, the model- and runtime-agnostic testbed behind the study, to facilitate future research and fair comparisons in federated VLA learning.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic study of federated fine-tuning of modern pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, evaluated on LIBERO simulation tasks and real-robot experiments across multiple sites, and releases an open-source testbed to standardize future research.
AI.motivation: Adapting pretrained VLAs to new robots, environments, or tasks requires locally collected demonstrations that are typically discarded. Federated learning can exploit such distributed data by learning a shared policy, but whether it can adapt large pretrained VLAs is unclear, and the lack of reproducible benchmarks and reusable training frameworks impedes comparison of existing results.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic study of federated fine-tuning of three modern pretrained VLA policies. Evaluation spans the 40 simulated tasks of the LIBERO manipulation benchmark and six real-world tasks in two real-robot experiments, with demonstrations collected across two and three sites, respectively. The study analyzes key design choices, including multiple federated parameter scopes, three aggregation algorithms, and evaluation under distribution shift.
AI.result: The study derives several lessons: the federated scope dominates the choice of aggregation algorithm; matching centralized fine-tuning on physical robots is difficult due to cross-site heterogeneity stronger than simulation captures. Opportunities are highlighted, including matching centralized fine-tuning on heterogeneous data, remaining at least as robust as centralized fine-tuning under distribution shift, and personalizing by having each client federate part of the policy while keeping the rest local—helpful where pretraining is weak but leaving no usable global model.
AI.conclusion: Federated fine-tuning of pretrained VLAs is feasible and offers notable benefits, but design choices such as federated scope and cross-site heterogeneity on real robots are critical. The authors open-source the model- and runtime-agnostic testbed behind the study to facilitate future research and fair comparisons in federated VLA learning.

title: ScholarStack: Layered Research Asset Orchestration and Cross-Task Reuse for Scientific Agents
summary: Scientific agents support a range of literature-based research tasks, such as retrieval, question answering, evidence-grounded generation, and claim assessment. Most existing systems, however, are organized around individual tasks: the same papers are repeatedly retrieved, segmented, and interpreted, and the understanding built in one task is difficult to reuse in the next. We present ScholarStack, a layered research asset framework that compiles a paper collection into reusable, versioned, and provenance-preserving assets at three complementary levels: source-grounded paper-level statements, domain-level organization, and evidence-grounded cross-paper syntheses. A common access interface returns task-specific views at the evidence granularity each task requires, preserving study conditions, source traceability, and verification status. We instantiate the framework on four task families spanning ten task settings, comparing agents that use the compiled assets with task-specific baselines under matched base models. Quality gains concentrate on tasks that require cross-paper evidence, such as multi-paper question answering and literature review generation, and query-time token cost falls on every task where it is measured, with assets compiled once and reused across tasks. These results suggest that layered research assets can serve as shared infrastructure for scientific agents, shifting literature-based assistance from isolated document processing toward cumulative, evidence-grounded workflows.

AI.tldr: ScholarStack is a layered research asset framework that compiles paper collections into reusable, versioned, provenance-preserving assets across three levels (paper-level statements, domain-level organization, cross-paper syntheses), enabling task-specific views at required evidence granularity; it improves quality on cross-paper tasks and reduces query-time token cost.
AI.motivation: Most existing scientific agent systems are organized around individual tasks, causing repeated retrieval, segmentation, and interpretation of the same papers, and making the understanding built in one task hard to reuse in the next. This motivates shared, cumulative infrastructure rather than isolated document processing.
AI.method: ScholarStack compiles a paper collection into reusable, versioned, and provenance-preserving assets at three complementary levels: source-grounded paper-level statements, domain-level organization, and evidence-grounded cross-paper syntheses. A common access interface returns task-specific views at the evidence granularity each task requires, preserving study conditions, source traceability, and verification status. The framework is instantiated on four task families spanning ten task settings, comparing agents using compiled assets against task-specific baselines under matched base models.
AI.result: Quality gains concentrate on tasks requiring cross-paper evidence, such as multi-paper question answering and literature review generation. Query-time token cost falls on every task where it is measured, as assets are compiled once and reused across tasks.
AI.conclusion: Layered research assets can serve as shared infrastructure for scientific agents, shifting literature-based assistance from isolated document processing toward cumulative, evidence-grounded workflows.

title: A Horizon-slicing Approach to Minimum Obstacle Displacement Planning for Robot Navigation
comment: Accepted for publication in Intelligent Service Robotics
summary: In this paper, we investigate the Minimum Obstacle Displacement Planning problem from a robot motion planning perspective. The problem involves determining a feasible path to a goal location by displacing movable obstacles when no collision-free path initially exists. We show that this problem is computationally challenging and, in particular, NP-hard when obstacles are modeled as polygons in the plane. Besides an exact formulation of the minimum obstacle displacement problem generalizing other problems in the literature, and the associated optimal solution, this paper proposes an approximate solution that is less intensive from a computational standpoint, and differs from the optimal solution by a fraction of the optimal cost, being able to trade-off between path length and amount of obstacle displacements.

AI.tldr: This paper studies Minimum Obstacle Displacement Planning: finding a feasible path to a goal by displacing movable obstacles when no collision-free path exists. It proves NP-hardness for polygonal obstacles, gives an exact optimal formulation, and proposes a computationally lighter approximation with a bounded cost gap that can trade off path length against displacement amount.
AI.motivation: Robot motion planning typically assumes a collision-free path exists or that the robot must avoid static obstacles. However, many real scenarios require the robot to move (displace) movable obstacles to reach the goal when no collision-free path initially exists, motivating a formulation that accounts for both path length and the amount of obstacle displacement.
AI.method: The problem is formalized for polygonal obstacles in the plane as a minimum obstacle displacement problem that generalizes prior formulations in the literature, with an exact optimal solution. In addition, an approximate solution is developed that is less computationally intensive and differs from the optimal cost by a bounded fraction, allowing a trade-off between path length and total obstacle displacement.
AI.result: The Minimum Obstacle Displacement Planning problem is shown to be computationally challenging and NP-hard when obstacles are polygonal in the plane. An exact formulation and associated optimal solution are provided, and an approximate solution is proposed that reduces computational burden while maintaining a bounded relative cost gap and enabling trade-offs between path length and displacement amount.
AI.conclusion: Minimum Obstacle Displacement Planning is NP-hard for polygonal obstacles, necessitating exact and approximate approaches. The exact formulation captures the optimum and generalizes related problems, while the approximation offers scalability with a provable cost bound and controllable balance between path length and obstacle displacement.

title: On Probabilistic Inference Through Parametric Tensor Decomposition in Base Tensor Networks
comment: Accepted at: The 17th International Conference on Scalable Uncertainty Management (SUM 2026)
summary: Probabilistic inference is generally only tractable in low-treewidth graphical models, limiting its effective applicability in high-treewidth settings. Many existing methods improve efficiency by exploiting specific parametric structure, such as symmetries. However, they typically require such structure to be explicitly present, limiting their applicability to a broader range of graphical models. To address this limitation, we propose a framework where tractable inference is controlled by latent parametric structure exploitation, rather than requiring it to be explicitly present a priori. Our approach first reparameterises a graphical model as a specific tensor network representation, which we call a base tensor network. This representation yields two key properties that allow inference tractability to be controlled by parametric structure: 1) First, the complexity of inference is mainly determined by the parametric structure of a single tensor, called the base tensor. We characterise several tractable classes of base tensors for which the entire base tensor network can be contracted efficiently. 2) Second, decomposing the base tensor yields again a collection of base tensor networks. This allows inference to be naturally reduced to decomposing the base tensor into tractable components with sufficient parametric structure. We call this procedure parametric tensor decomposition. By exploiting parametric structure within the base tensor, our framework enables a novel view on inference beyond settings where such structure is explicitly present.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for tractable probabilistic inference in high-treewidth graphical models by exploiting latent parametric structure via a tensor network reparameterisation, rather than requiring such structure to be explicitly present.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic inference is generally tractable only in low-treewidth graphical models, which limits applicability in high-treewidth settings. Existing methods that improve efficiency by exploiting parametric structure (e.g., symmetries) require such structure to be explicitly present, restricting their applicability to a broader range of graphical models.
AI.method: The approach first reparameterises a graphical model as a tensor network called a base tensor network, yielding two key properties: (1) inference complexity is mainly determined by the parametric structure of a single tensor, the base tensor, and several tractable classes of base tensors are characterised for which the entire network contracts efficiently; (2) decomposing the base tensor yields a collection of base tensor networks, reducing inference to decomposing the base tensor into tractable components with sufficient parametric structure, a procedure termed parametric tensor decomposition.
AI.result: The framework enables inference tractability to be controlled by parametric structure within the base tensor, allowing a novel view on inference beyond settings where such structure is explicitly present.
AI.conclusion: By exploiting latent parametric structure through base tensor networks and parametric tensor decomposition, the framework extends tractable inference to a broader range of graphical models than methods requiring explicit parametric structure.

title: Connectivity-Aware Exploration of Robotic Grasp Spaces
summary: Robotic grasping is typically formulated as the problem of identifying successful actions from a space of candidate grasp poses. However, the organization of successful actions within this space has received less attention. We study the multiscale structure of viable robotic grasps in $SE(3)$ and investigate whether this structure can be exploited for more efficient exploration. Using a large-scale grasp dataset, we show that successful grasp sets exhibit heterogeneous and reproducible connectivity structure across objects. We then introduce a connectivity-aware sampling strategy that incrementally explores the currently observed grasp space by prioritizing potential bridges between components, structural frontiers, boundary extensions, and geometric novelty. In controlled reconstruction experiments, the method recovers the connectivity structure of successful grasp sets substantially more efficiently than random sampling and farthest-point sampling. We further evaluate whether connectivity acquired under hidden grasp viability can improve subsequent grasp discovery, and whether structural experience from previously explored objects can be retrieved and transferred to unseen objects. These results suggest that the spatial organization of viable actions provides information relevant to grasp-space exploration beyond the viability of individual candidate actions. More broadly, they motivate structure-aware exploration as a means of exploiting the geometry of viable action spaces in robotic manipulation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the multiscale connectivity structure of viable grasps in SE(3) and proposes a connectivity-aware sampling strategy that exploits this structure to explore grasp space more efficiently than random or farthest-point sampling, with evidence for transfer across objects.
AI.motivation: Robotic grasping is usually framed as identifying successful actions among candidate grasp poses, but the organization of successful actions within the grasp space is underexplored. The authors hypothesize that the spatial structure of viable grasps carries information useful for efficient exploration, beyond the viability of individual candidates.
AI.method: Using a large-scale grasp dataset, they analyze the multiscale structure of viable grasp sets in SE(3), showing heterogeneous yet reproducible connectivity across objects. They then introduce a connectivity-aware sampling strategy that incrementally explores the observed grasp space by prioritizing potential bridges between components, structural frontiers, boundary extensions, and geometric novelty.
AI.result: In controlled reconstruction experiments, the connectivity-aware sampling strategy recovers the connectivity structure of successful grasp sets substantially more efficiently than random sampling and farthest-point sampling. Additional experiments assess whether connectivity acquired under hidden grasp viability improves later grasp discovery, and whether structural experience transfers from previously explored objects to unseen objects.
AI.conclusion: The spatial organization of viable actions provides information relevant to grasp-space exploration beyond individual action viability. This motivates structure-aware exploration for exploiting the geometry of viable action spaces in robotic manipulation.

title: Total Cost of Agency: Exact Attribution of Memory Injection Cost in Multi-Agent LLM Workflows
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Code, data, and evaluation harness in github: https://github.com/vsingh45/tca-compiler
summary: Every node in a multi-agent large language model (LLM) workflow retrieves context from memory and injects it into its prompt, where those injected tokens are billed as input tokens at the same per-token price as the system prompt and the user query. Production observability tools report total token cost but do not separate the tokens a node generates from the tokens it is handed, so this component of the bill is invisible to the teams paying it. We introduce the Total Cost of Agency (TCA), a decomposition of multi-agent workflow cost into base prompt, inference, memory injection, miss penalty and context-accumulation components, and an exact attribution method: a two-pass, non-billable token count that measures injected tokens directly rather than estimating them from word-count proxies. On a 200-task enterprise benchmark executed against real model APIs, memory injection accounts for 13.6 percent of the variable cost a compile-time optimizer can act on, about 12 percent of the full billed cost, and its share rises from a structural zero at workflow depth one to 27.6 percent at depth six. Injected tokens grow linearly with depth over the measured range (R^2 = 0.9974, depths two through six); a quadratic fit yields a negative leading coefficient, so the data do not exhibit convex growth at these depths. We show the component is controllable at fixed model tier: reducing the retrieval window capacity from 32 to 2 entries lowers injected tokens by 28.7 percent with an accuracy change within seed-level variation. We report in full that our graph-rewriting transforms are approximately cost-neutral in isolation, that two of the five decomposition terms are zero by construction in this harness, and that total workflow cost is dominated by model tier assignment, which we hold fixed and treat as prior work. Prompt caching is not evaluated; all figures are for the uncached case.

AI.tldr: The paper defines the Total Cost of Agency (TCA), decomposing multi-agent LLM workflow cost into base prompt, inference, memory injection, miss penalty, and context-accumulation terms, and provides an exact two-pass attribution method for injected tokens. On a 200-task enterprise benchmark, memory injection reaches 27.6% of cost at depth six and can be cut 28.7% via retrieval-window reduction with no significant accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Production observability tools report only total token cost, conflating tokens a node generates with tokens it is handed via memory injection. Since injected tokens are billed as input tokens at the same price as system prompts and user queries, this cost component remains invisible to the teams paying it, preventing targeted optimization.
AI.method: The authors propose TCA, a cost decomposition into base prompt, inference, memory injection, miss penalty, and context-accumulation components, paired with an exact attribution method: a two-pass, non-billable token count that measures injected tokens directly instead of estimating from word-count proxies. Validation uses a 200-task enterprise benchmark run against real model APIs, plus a controlled retrieval-window ablation (32 vs. 2 entries) at fixed model tier.
AI.result: Memory injection accounts for 13.6% of variable cost actionable by a compile-time optimizer and roughly 12% of full billed cost, rising from a structural zero at depth one to 27.6% at depth six. Injected tokens grow linearly with depth over depths two through six (R^2 = 0.9974); a quadratic fit gives a negative leading coefficient, indicating no convex growth in this range. Cutting retrieval window capacity from 32 to 2 entries reduces injected tokens by 28.7% with accuracy change within seed-level variation. The graph-rewriting transforms are approximately cost-neutral in isolation, two of five decomposition terms are zero by construction in this harness, and total cost is dominated by model tier assignment (held fixed). Prompt caching is not evaluated.
AI.conclusion: Memory injection is a measurable, non-trivial, and controllable cost component in multi-agent LLM workflows, invisible under current observability, reducible through retrieval-window tuning at fixed model tier without degrading accuracy. The paper positions model tier assignment as prior work and leaves prompt caching to future evaluation.

title: Fast and Robust Temporal Logic Planning via ADMM-based Trajectory Optimization
summary: We present a fast numerical method for safe continuous-time motion planning under Temporal Logic (TL) specifications. The method generates smooth continuous trajectories that remain collision-free while robustly satisfying temporal and logical task requirements. A central component of our method is the formulation of nonconvex safety and logic constraints as unions of convex sets where associated discrete decisions are encoded in a joint feasibility graph. This graph representation allows Euclidean projection onto the feasible set and proximal robustness maximization to be reformulated as shortest- and widest-path problems, respectively. Building on this structure, we develop a nonconvex splitting method based on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM), which decouples smooth spatio-temporal trajectory optimization from nonsmooth discrete constraint handling within the optimization. The resulting algorithm exhibits reliable convergence across benchmarks and scales to large-scale motion-planning problems, providing a 4.7x average speedup over the state of the art on discrete and continuous-time logic problems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a fast ADMM-based numerical method for continuous-time motion planning under temporal logic specifications, encoding nonconvex safety and logic constraints in a feasibility graph to enable Euclidean projection and robustness maximization as shortest- and widest-path problems.
AI.motivation: Continuous-time motion planning under temporal logic specifications requires smooth, collision-free trajectories that robustly satisfy temporal and logical requirements, but the associated safety and logic constraints are nonconvex, making optimization difficult and slow. Existing methods struggle with the nonsmooth discrete decisions and scale poorly to large problems.
AI.method: Nonconvex safety and logic constraints are formulated as unions of convex sets, with associated discrete decisions encoded in a joint feasibility graph. This representation reformulates Euclidean projection onto the feasible set and proximal robustness maximization as shortest- and widest-path problems. A nonconvex splitting method based on ADMM is then developed, decoupling smooth spatio-temporal trajectory optimization from nonsmooth discrete constraint handling.
AI.result: Numerical results confirm a 4.7x average speedup over the state of the art on discrete and continuous-time logic problems, with reliable convergence across benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The method generates smooth continuous trajectories that remain collision-free while robustly satisfying temporal and logical task requirements, and scales to large-scale motion-planning problems.

title: WorkWorlds: An Infrastructure for Evaluating AI Agents on Workplace Tasks
comment: 4 figures
summary: Many knowledge-work benchmarks are constructed around individual tasks, with the context needed for each task selected together with or after the task has been specified. This design measures performance on workplace-like tasks in an environment assembled for the task. When task specification guides which context is selected, the evaluation can encode task information into the environment and pre-complete part of the information-localization work that workplace performance normally requires. We introduce WorkWorlds, an evaluation infrastructure that separates organizational state from task specification. A world first fixes a revision, date, and employee seat and materializes the organizational state that employee can access; tasks are introduced only afterward. We implement WorkWorlds in a primary synthetic pharmaceutical company with 8 measured tasks across 6 employee seats, and construct additional organizational worlds. Across 192 matched evaluations, moving from task-curated context to the full role-visible workplace reduced evidence access from 90.4% to 74.5% and criterion pass from 79.4% to 68.2%, while pass conditional on evidence access remained nearly unchanged; most of the measured difference occurred before the agent reached sufficient evidence.

AI.tldr: WorkWorlds is an evaluation infrastructure that separates organizational state from task specification: it first fixes a revision, date, and employee seat and materializes the accessible organizational state, introducing tasks only afterward. Across 192 matched evaluations in a synthetic pharmaceutical company, moving from task-curated context to the full role-visible workplace reduced evidence access from 90.4% to 74.5% and criterion pass from 79.4% to 68.2%, while pass conditional on evidence access stayed nearly unchanged.
AI.motivation: Many knowledge-work benchmarks are built around individual tasks, with context selected together with or after task specification. This design measures performance in an environment assembled for the task rather than a workplace-like setting. When task specification guides context selection, the evaluation can encode task information into the environment and pre-complete part of the information-localization work that workplace performance normally requires.
AI.method: WorkWorlds separates organizational state from task specification. A world first fixes a revision, date, and employee seat and materializes the organizational state that employee can access; tasks are introduced only afterward. The authors implement WorkWorlds in a primary synthetic pharmaceutical company with 8 measured tasks across 6 employee seats, and construct additional organizational worlds, yielding 192 matched evaluations.
AI.result: Across 192 matched evaluations, moving from task-curated context to the full role-visible workplace reduced evidence access from 90.4% to 74.5% and criterion pass from 79.4% to 68.2%, while pass conditional on evidence access remained nearly unchanged. Most of the measured difference occurred before the agent reached sufficient evidence.
AI.conclusion: Task-curated context in knowledge-work benchmarks inflates measured performance by encoding task information into the environment and pre-completing information-localization work. Separating organizational state from task specification, as WorkWorlds does, yields a stricter evaluation in which most performance loss occurs during evidence localization rather than in downstream task execution.

title: Anatomy of a Closed-Loop Collapse: A Causal Case Study of a Compressed VLA Policy
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Accepted as a poster at the IROS 2026 Workshop on Building Scalable Infrastructure for Robot Learning: From Data Scaling to Real-World Deployment (ScaleInfra), Pittsburgh, PA, USA. Supplementary records: https://github.com/Xanadum/closed-loop-collapse
summary: Compressed manipulation policies can pass offline evaluation while failing in closed-loop execution; this dissociation is established in prior work and is not our claim. We contribute a causal anatomy of one naturally occurring case. An 8-layer distillation of Octo-Base retains 86% of parameters, passes every offline check we applied (0.996 and 1.000 teacher-ratios on the family's own validation metrics), and collapses in closed loop: 0/72 vs. the teacher's 40/72 on a simulated WidowX pick-and-place task. The collapse is structured, not diffuse: early task stages degrade gradually (the student moves the object at 90% of the teacher's rate and grasps at 55%), while transport-to-target fails categorically, at 0% in every training variant. Paired action-trace forensics isolate the signature: a negative, late-heavy $z$ residual, roughly 10x its post-repair magnitude, and persistent across the base distillation and both continuation branches. Four standard therapies fail under matched controls: continued training and in-domain offline data leave success at zero, even though the latter measurably improves marginal action statistics; command-level compensation recovers nothing at any offset, although the same perturbations degrade healthy policies; clamping the symptom in the command channel preserves grasping, yet success stays at floor. A minimal-pair intervention that substitutes half of the training stream with deployment-distribution teacher rollouts, with every other setting held fixed, restores parity with the teacher (18/36 vs. 17/36 held-out), eliminates that signature, and recovers a teacher-like perturbation-response profile. We claim existence, not universality. Operationally, offline gates, including a family's own validation metrics, are insufficient acceptance tests for compressed policies; a few dozen closed-loop trials sufficed to find what they missed.

AI.tldr: An 8-layer distillation of Octo-Base passes all offline checks but collapses in closed-loop execution (0/72 vs. teacher's 40/72); the failure is highly structured, traced to a specific late-heavy negative z-residual, and only fixed by mixing deployment-distribution teacher rollouts into training.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the dissociation between offline evaluation and closed-loop success for compressed manipulation policies. Rather than claiming this dissociation as new, the authors aim to provide a causal anatomy of one naturally occurring failure case, motivated by the practical need for better acceptance testing of compressed policies.
AI.method: The authors studied an 8-layer distillation of Octo-Base retaining 86% of parameters. They performed offline validation on the family's own metrics, closed-loop simulated WidowX pick-and-place evaluation (72 trials), paired action-trace forensics to identify failure signatures, matched-control tests of four standard therapies (continued training, in-domain offline data, command-level compensation, symptom clamping), and a minimal-pair intervention replacing half the training stream with deployment-distribution teacher rollouts.
AI.result: The distilled policy passed all offline checks (0.996 and 1.000 teacher-ratios) but scored 0/72 in closed loop versus 40/72 for the teacher. Failure was structured: early stages degraded gradually (90% object-move rate, 55% grasp rate), while transport-to-target failed categorically at 0% across all training variants. The signature was a negative, late-heavy z residual roughly 10x its post-repair magnitude, persistent across distillation and both continuation branches. All four standard therapies failed under matched controls. The minimal-pair intervention restored parity (18/36 vs. 17/36 held-out), eliminated the signature, and recovered a teacher-like perturbation-response profile.
AI.conclusion: The paper claims existence, not universality, of this failure mode. Operationally, offline gates—including a policy family's own validation metrics—are insufficient acceptance tests for compressed policies; a few dozen closed-loop trials were enough to reveal what offline evaluation missed.

title: Pretraining of Medical Visual Encoders Toward Multi-modal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) commonly reuse visual encoders pretrained with CLIP, although the features of these ViTs are ultimately consumed by autoregressive LLMs. We refer to this mismatch as the semantic-interface gap and introduce MedMLIP, a framework that pretrains the visual encoder through report generation with a frozen LLM, while employing Local Relational Distillation (LRD) to preserve relationships among visual patches to avoid visual collapse. We pretrain MedMLIP on IU-Xray and Open-PMC-300K and evaluate the resulting encoders on VQA-RAD and SLAKE. Only the ViT is transferred, while the guiding LLM and projector are replaced, allowing us to assess cross-LLM transferability. Our cross-LLM transfer experiments demonstrate the value of pretraining visual encoders for their autoregressive LLM interface while trying to preserve more fine-grained visual information. Code and the pretrained model are available at https://github.com/SkyCol/MedMLIP

AI.tldr: MedMLIP pretrains a visual encoder via report generation with a frozen LLM, using Local Relational Distillation to prevent visual collapse, and demonstrates cross-LLM transferability of the resulting ViT.
AI.motivation: MLLMs typically reuse CLIP-pretrained visual encoders, but these ViT features are consumed by autoregressive LLMs, creating a semantic-interface gap between the encoder's pretraining objective and its downstream use.
AI.method: MedMLIP pretrains the visual encoder through report generation guided by a frozen LLM, and applies Local Relational Distillation (LRD) to preserve relationships among visual patches and avoid visual collapse. Pretraining uses IU-Xray and Open-PMC-300K; only the ViT is transferred while the guiding LLM and projector are replaced.
AI.result: Evaluation on VQA-RAD and SLAKE via cross-LLM transfer experiments shows the value of pretraining visual encoders for their autoregressive LLM interface while preserving fine-grained visual information.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining visual encoders tailored to the autoregressive LLM interface, with relational distillation to retain patch-level detail, improves transferability across different LLMs and downstream medical VQA tasks.

title: On the Control of Mobile Ad-Hoc Agent Deployments in Partially Observed Space
comment: Paper accept at Algowin2026
summary: We study the online deployment of mobile ad hoc networks in unknown orthogonal environments, formalized as the Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art Gallery Problem. We give a full proof that CADENCE algorithms achieve full coverage while maintaining a connected visibility graph using at most $n/2 + h - 2$ agents in orthogonal worlds with $n$ corners and $h$ holes. We further evaluate deployment-order heuristics that reduce agent count and deployment time in practice.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes online deployment of mobile ad hoc networks in unknown orthogonal environments as the Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art Gallery Problem and proves that CADENCE algorithms achieve full coverage with a connected visibility graph using at most n/2 + h - 2 agents.
AI.motivation: Deploying mobile ad hoc networks in unknown environments requires guaranteeing both coverage and connectivity without prior knowledge of the environment, which the standard Art Gallery formulation does not directly address.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art Gallery Problem as a formalization and provide a full proof that CADENCE algorithms maintain full coverage and a connected visibility graph. They also evaluate deployment-order heuristics.
AI.result: CADENCE achieves full coverage with a connected visibility graph using at most n/2 + h - 2 agents in orthogonal worlds with n corners and h holes; deployment-order heuristics reduce agent count and deployment time in practice.
AI.conclusion: CADENCE provides proven worst-case guarantees for online deployment in unknown orthogonal environments, and practical heuristics can further improve efficiency.

title: Explainable Recommendations at Scale: LLM Rationales for YouTube Music Artist Discovery
summary: Modern music streaming platforms face a persistent tradeoff: exploiting familiar content versus driving the exploration of novel items. While users frequently desire discovery, they hesitate to select unknown artists over proven favorites. Providing transparent, natural language rationales that explain why an unexplored item is recommended lowers this barrier. However, while Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at this nuanced explainability, their real-time deployment is severely bottlenecked by prohibitive inference costs and computational overhead. In this paper, we present an industry case study of a decoupled recommendation architecture that successfully scales exploration without compromising latency. Our system isolates LLM inference asynchronously offline, pre-computing personalized candidate pools of undiscovered artists alongside tailored rationales. Large-scale online A/B experiments validate our design. We demonstrate that combining LLM-backed recommendations with these explanatory rationales significantly reduces the trust barrier for new content, yielding statistically significant improvements in both user exploration and overall engagement on the discovery surfaces.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an industry case study of a decoupled recommendation architecture that scales music discovery by moving LLM inference offline, pre-computing personalized pools of undiscovered artists with natural-language rationales, and validates it via large-scale online A/B experiments showing significant gains in exploration and engagement.
AI.motivation: Streaming platforms face a persistent tradeoff between exploiting familiar content and encouraging exploration of novel items. Users often desire discovery but hesitate to select unknown artists over proven favorites. Transparent, natural-language rationales explaining why an unexplored item is recommended can lower this trust barrier, and LLMs excel at generating such nuanced explanations—but their real-time deployment is severely bottlenecked by prohibitive inference costs and computational overhead.
AI.method: The authors design a decoupled recommendation architecture in which LLM inference is isolated asynchronously offline. The system pre-computes personalized candidate pools of undiscovered artists together with tailored natural-language rationales, so that LLM computation is removed from the online critical path while preserving personalized explainability.
AI.result: Large-scale online A/B experiments validate the design. Combining LLM-backed recommendations with explanatory rationales significantly reduces the trust barrier for new content, yielding statistically significant improvements in both user exploration and overall engagement on the discovery surfaces.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling LLM inference offline enables scalable, low-latency delivery of explainable discovery recommendations in production streaming systems. The approach resolves the tension between LLM-powered explainability and real-time latency constraints, demonstrating measurable gains in exploration and engagement.

title: Splat-CBF: Safe Next-Best-View Control in 3D Gaussian-Splat Maps
summary: Where to look and how to move? A robot navigating an unmapped environment must do both at once, and the two goals pull against each other. The regions most worth observing are the ones the map knows least about, and those are exactly where the robot cannot trust its collision margins. We resolve this tension by introducing Splat-CBF, an active perception control barrier function that steers the camera toward the next best view while collision avoidance is enforced as a hard constraint. Safety is enforced by a risk-aware control barrier function that turns the Average Value-at-Risk of the Gaussian field into a single smooth hard constraint. Perception is enforced by a second barrier that rewards camera orientations with high expected Fisher information gain near the robot's planned path. The two meet in a quadratic program where safety is hard and perception is soft, with a slack penalty that adapts to how often perception has already been relaxed and how close the robot is to an uncertain region. We verify the method in indoor simulations, a Isaac Kinova manipulator and in experiments on an Ackermann-drive robot. Our results assert that robot navigates faster, gathers more information, and runs faster online than safety-only and perception-only baselines, giving up informative motion only when safety requires it.

AI.tldr: Splat-CBF couples a risk-aware safety barrier with a Fisher-information perception barrier in a single quadratic program, enabling a robot to explore unmapped, uncertain environments while collision avoidance stays a hard constraint.
AI.motivation: A robot navigating an unmapped environment must decide where to look and how to move simultaneously, but these goals conflict: the regions most worth observing are those the map knows least about, which are precisely where collision margins are least trustworthy. The paper aims to resolve this perception-safety tension.
AI.method: Splat-CBF (active perception control barrier function) steers the camera toward the next best view while enforcing collision avoidance as a hard constraint. Safety is handled by a risk-aware CBF that converts the Average Value-at-Risk of the Gaussian field into a single smooth hard constraint. Perception is handled by a second barrier rewarding camera orientations with high expected Fisher information gain near the planned path. Both are combined in a quadratic program with safety hard and perception soft, using a slack penalty that adapts to the frequency of prior perception relaxations and the robot's proximity to uncertain regions.
AI.result: Validation spans indoor simulations, an Isaac Kinova manipulator, and experiments on an Ackermann-drive robot. Compared with safety-only and perception-only baselines, the method yields faster navigation, greater information gathering, and faster online runtime, sacrificing informative motion only when safety requires it.
AI.conclusion: Combining a hard risk-aware safety constraint with a soft, adaptively penalized perception objective in one quadratic program lets the robot trade off exploration and safety gracefully, achieving both better navigation and richer information gain than single-objective baselines.

title: Increasing Skill Level Recruits Deeper Attention Layers in a Frozen Chess Transformer
comment: 19 pages, 12 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/David-31415/maia-depth-migration. Built with chessformer-lens library: https://github.com/chessformer-lens/chessformer_lens
summary: Chess involves complex reasoning in a deterministic environment, which makes it a useful setting for studying the mechanisms of computation inside transformers. The Maia-3 chess transformer takes Elo, a measure of competitive chess skill, as an input to the pre-trained network, so we can vary the skill the network is conditioned on with no change to its weights. Here we investigate how turning this skill dial affects self-attention. Ablating every attention head at every Elo from 700 to 2500, we find 1) increasing skill pushes the causal center of mass of the computation deeper, monotonically, for every chess piece and move type we measured; 2) the depth migration is much greater for specific tactics, especially knight forks, than for other move types; 3) the migration consists of deeper heads getting recruited for more specialized computations while one shared shallow head keeps a roughly constant contribution. These results may shed light on how conditioning inputs redistribute computation in larger transformers.

AI.tldr: Analyzing attention-head ablations across Elo 700-2500 in the Maia-3 chess transformer, this work shows that higher skill conditioning shifts the causal center of mass deeper, most strongly for specific tactics like knight forks, via recruitment of deeper specialized heads while a shared shallow head stays constant.
AI.motivation: Chess provides a deterministic yet complex reasoning environment for probing transformer internals. Maia-3 accepts Elo as a conditioning input at fixed weights, allowing the authors to study how a conditioning signal redistributes computation—an open question for understanding mechanisms in larger transformers.
AI.method: The authors ablate every attention head at each Elo level from 700 to 2500 in Maia-3, measuring the causal center of mass of the computation per chess piece and move type to characterize how skill conditioning affects the depth distribution of self-attention.
AI.result: Three findings: (1) increasing skill monotonically pushes the causal center of mass deeper for every measured piece and move type; (2) depth migration is markedly larger for specific tactics, especially knight forks, than for other move types; (3) migration arises from deeper heads being recruited for specialized computations while one shared shallow head maintains a roughly constant contribution.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning inputs such as Elo can systematically redistribute computation across depth, with tactic-specific specialization. These results offer insight into how conditioning signals may reorganize computation in larger transformers.

title: DiagGen: Agentic Generation of Deformable Assets with Sim-based Diagnostics for Robotic Simulation
summary: While simulation-ready deformable assets are essential for in-silico robotic manipulation tasks, existing generation frameworks typically assess physical plausibility after generation, leaving an object's simulated response unused as feedback for repairing upstream errors. We present DiagGen, an agentic framework that turns a single in-the-wild image into a simulation-ready deformable asset through a generate--simulate--diagnose--refine loop. DiagGen constructs part-aware geometry and material parameters, then uses a VLM (vision-language model)-based agent to select semantically informative regions, probe them in a physics simulator, observe material responses, and route evidence-backed repair cues to the responsible generation stage. Experiments on 40 assets show that diagnostics provides useful repair cues and can moderately improve the quality of generated deformable assets. Finally, we show that unlike assets generated from visual foundation models which may not be simulatable, DiagGen-generated deformables can be directly dropped into a high-fidelity physical simulator for the planning and simulation of contact-rich pick-and-place tasks. The project's website is https://diaggen.github.io/.

AI.tldr: DiagGen is an agentic generate–simulate–diagnose–refine framework that converts a single in-the-wild image into a simulation-ready deformable asset by using a VLM-based agent to probe semantically informative regions in a physics simulator and route repair cues back to the responsible generation stage.
AI.motivation: Simulation-ready deformable assets are essential for in-silico robotic manipulation, but existing generation frameworks assess physical plausibility only after generation. The simulated response of an object is never used as feedback to repair upstream errors, limiting asset quality and simulatability.
AI.method: DiagGen runs a generate–simulate–diagnose–refine loop. It constructs part-aware geometry and material parameters from an in-the-wild image, then a VLM-based agent selects semantically informative regions, probes them in a physics simulator, observes material responses, and routes evidence-backed repair cues to the responsible generation stage.
AI.result: Experiments on 40 assets show diagnostics provide useful repair cues and moderately improve the quality of generated deformable assets. Unlike assets from visual foundation models that may not be simulatable, DiagGen-generated deformables can be directly dropped into a high-fidelity physical simulator for planning and simulation of contact-rich pick-and-place tasks.
AI.conclusion: DiagGen demonstrates that closing the loop between generation and simulation—via diagnostic probing and targeted repair—yields more physically plausible, directly simulatable deformable assets for robotic manipulation.

title: Echo State Network (ESN) for Signal Recovery in RF-Impaired IBFD MIMO Systems
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures. This work has been accepted by IEEE Milcom 2026
summary: In-band full-duplex (IBFD) multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems enable simultaneous transmission and reception on the same frequency band, improving spectral efficiency for next-generation wireless networks. However, IBFD-MIMO systems are susceptible to self-interference (SI), which may overpower signals of interest (SOI). In this scenario, blind source separation (BSS) algorithms can be adopted to remove SI and perform joint sensing and communication (JSAC), but BSS algorithms mostly assume an idealized linear and quasi-stationary signal model, which does not hold under realistic radio frequency (RF) impairments, such as I/Q imbalance, carrier frequency offset (CFO), phase noise, and power amplifier nonlinearity. This paper proposes a two-stage echo state network (ESN)-based scheme that is superior to BSS under these realistic conditions. A frozen ESN is trained offline to characterize the static SI path, while an adaptive ESN, updated online via recursive least squares, tracks the time-varying SOI path using sparse pilot symbols. We evaluate the proposed scheme's SOI recovery performance and acquisition speed with different block sizes, comparing it against other recurrent neural networks (RNN), such as long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU).
