summary: Safety-critical control under uncertainty requires uncertainty representations that are both statistically valid (for certifiable performance) and compatible with enforceable safety constraints. However, existing methods often assume particular distributions of uncertainty for provable safety guarantees or establish symmetric and input-agnostic prediction intervals for robust safety, which can lead to misaligned or overly conservative safety constraints in control synthesis. In this paper, we introduce a novel safe control framework with adaptive uncertainty quantification that constructs calibrated and state-dependent prediction intervals to enable high-probability safety guarantees, while improving constrained control performance. The framework leverages adaptive conformal prediction (ACP) and extends it with conformal quantile regression (CQR) to capture distribution-free, asymmetric uncertainty intervals with certifiable probabilistic coverage, and integrates the resulting uncertainty sets into a probabilistic control barrier function formulation to enforce robust safety with reduced conservativeness. This yields uncertainty-aware safe control constraints that can be incorporated within a model predictive control(MPC) framework to provide provably safe behaviors with high probability. Simulation and theoretical results are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

AI.tldr: A safe control framework using adaptive conformal prediction with conformal quantile regression to build calibrated, state-dependent uncertainty intervals, integrated into probabilistic control barrier functions within MPC for high-probability safety with reduced conservativeness.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical control under uncertainty needs uncertainty representations that are both statistically valid (for certifiable performance) and compatible with enforceable safety constraints. Existing methods either assume particular uncertainty distributions for provable guarantees or use symmetric, input-agnostic prediction intervals, leading to misaligned or overly conservative safety constraints in control synthesis.
AI.method: The framework leverages adaptive conformal prediction (ACP) and extends it with conformal quantile regression (CQR) to capture distribution-free, asymmetric uncertainty intervals with certifiable probabilistic coverage. The resulting uncertainty sets are integrated into a probabilistic control barrier function (CBF) formulation to enforce robust safety with reduced conservativeness, yielding uncertainty-aware safe control constraints incorporated within a model predictive control (MPC) framework.
AI.result: Simulation and theoretical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach, providing provably safe behaviors with high probability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed adaptive uncertainty quantification enables calibrated, state-dependent prediction intervals that deliver high-probability safety guarantees while improving constrained control performance and reducing conservativeness.

title: Representation-guided in-context learning for medical image interpretation with multimodal large language models
summary: Medical image interpretation is central to diagnosis and care, yet adapting general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often requires resource-intensive domain-specific fine-tuning. Here we introduce representation-guided in-context learning (RG-ICL), a training-free inference framework that retrieves query-aligned demonstrations using frozen encoders, without task-specific parameter updates. Across eight datasets spanning histopathology, radiology and retinal fundoscopy, RG-ICL improved classification (mean gain 20 percentage points) and visual question answering (VQA) (mean gain 13 percentage points) over no-context and conventional ICL, approaching or exceeding training-based comparators. Which cases were retrieved mattered more than how many: 6 query-aligned cases outperformed up to 32 randomly selected ones, whereas fixed or random cases often reduced accuracy below baseline. For VQA, aligning reference cases with both image content and question intent produced further gains. These findings indicate that for medical image interpretation, curating which reference cases an MLLM sees is a practical alternative to retraining it.

AI.tldr: RG-ICL is a training-free inference framework that uses frozen encoders to retrieve query-aligned demonstrations, improving medical image classification and VQA over no-context and conventional ICL without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Adapting general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to medical image interpretation typically requires resource-intensive domain-specific fine-tuning. There is a need for a practical, training-free alternative that achieves strong performance without parameter updates.
AI.method: Representation-guided in-context learning (RG-ICL): a training-free inference framework that retrieves query-aligned demonstrations using frozen encoders, requiring no task-specific parameter updates. For VQA, reference cases are aligned with both image content and question intent.
AI.result: Across eight datasets spanning histopathology, radiology, and retinal fundoscopy, RG-ICL improved classification (mean gain 20 percentage points) and VQA (mean gain 13 percentage points) over no-context and conventional ICL, approaching or exceeding training-based comparators. Six query-aligned cases outperformed up to 32 randomly selected ones, whereas fixed or random cases often reduced accuracy below baseline.
AI.conclusion: Which cases are retrieved matters more than how many. Curating which reference cases an MLLM sees is a practical alternative to retraining it for medical image interpretation.

title: Shared Execution-Clock Drifting Policy for Dynamic Precision Manipulation
comment: 8 pages. Project page: https://secd-anonymous-ewn.pages.dev/
summary: Manipulation under time constraints requires both accurate actions and an execution rhythm that matches the evolving scene. This becomes critical when a robot must intercept moving objects or complete a sequence of adjustments before a deadline. Although one-step policies reduce generation cost, their directly predicted action sequences leave temporal allocation implicit. We propose Shared Execution-Clock Drifting (SECD), which makes execution rhythm an explicit part of one-step action generation. Conditioned on an observation and a latent sample, the policy jointly predicts a progress-indexed action curve and a shared monotone clock that maps fixed control times to locations on the curve. Demonstration-derived alignment anchors this decomposition, which is trained jointly through drifting on the decoded actions. The resulting policy retains a fixed-rate control interface and requires one network evaluation. We evaluate SECD across four real-robot tasks with inference on NVIDIA Thor. Across 300 trials, it achieves 77.00% task-averaged success and outperforms the evaluated one-step baselines on every task, including 91% success in cup retrieval from a 16 m/min conveyor and 54% in restoring and folding a crumpled shirt within 90 s. A fixed-clock variant reaches 79% on the same conveyor protocol. Complementary state-based RoboMimic experiments, including cross-seed ablations on Transport and Square, further support the joint design of the temporal representation and demonstration alignment. Project page: https://secd-anonymous-ewn.pages.dev/

AI.tldr: SECD makes execution rhythm an explicit component of one-step action generation by jointly predicting a progress-indexed action curve and a shared monotone execution clock, retaining fixed-rate control with a single network evaluation.
AI.motivation: Time-constrained manipulation (intercepting moving objects, completing adjustment sequences before a deadline) requires both accurate actions and an execution rhythm matched to the evolving scene. One-step policies cut generation cost but leave temporal allocation implicit in directly predicted action sequences.
AI.method: Conditioned on an observation and a latent sample, the policy jointly predicts a progress-indexed action curve and a shared monotone clock mapping fixed control times to curve locations. Demonstration-derived alignment anchors this decomposition, trained jointly via drifting on decoded actions. The policy keeps a fixed-rate control interface and needs one network evaluation.
AI.result: Across 300 trials on four real-robot tasks (NVIDIA Thor inference), SECD reaches 77.00% task-averaged success, beating evaluated one-step baselines on every task: 91% cup retrieval from a 16 m/min conveyor and 54% restoring/folding a crumpled shirt within 90 s. A fixed-clock variant reaches 79% on the conveyor protocol. State-based RoboMimic experiments with cross-seed ablations on Transport and Square support the joint design.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly separating execution rhythm from the action curve, anchored by demonstration alignment, improves time-constrained manipulation over implicit-timing one-step baselines while preserving single-evaluation, fixed-rate control.

title: Incremental Consistency Execution for Autonomous Intelligent Systems
summary: Long-horizon autonomous intelligent systems rely on heterogeneous components such as large language models, databases, external APIs, and rule engines, while their external states continuously change during execution. Re-executing the entire workflow after every change introduces substantial redundant computation. This paper proposes an incremental consistency execution method based on task fact contracts, field-level dependency masks, and state perturbation result invariant domains. After an initial verified execution, the system constructs conservative invariant domains for critical inputs and uses them to determine whether downstream results can be safely renewed without re-invoking expensive components. When re-execution is required, only the smallest affected output fields are recomputed, and an equivalence barrier prevents unnecessary downstream propagation. A submission-time version consistency gate further ensures the safety of side-effecting actions. Experiments on industrial fault diagnosis, enterprise analytics, and LLM-based multi-tool assistants show that the proposed method significantly reduces expensive component calls and end-to-end latency while maintaining high consistency and low incorrect-reuse rates.

AI.tldr: A task-fact-contract-based incremental consistency execution method avoids redundant recomputation in long-horizon heterogeneous AI systems via field-level dependency masks, state perturbation invariant domains, and a version-consistency gate.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon autonomous systems combine LLMs, databases, APIs, and rule engines whose external states change during execution, so re-running the whole workflow on every change causes substantial redundant computation.
AI.method: The approach builds on three mechanisms: (1) task fact contracts, (2) field-level dependency masks, and (3) state perturbation result invariant domains. After an initial verified execution, conservative invariant domains are constructed for critical inputs to decide whether downstream results can be safely renewed without re-invoking expensive components. When re-execution is needed, only the smallest affected output fields are recomputed, with an equivalence barrier blocking unnecessary downstream propagation. A submission-time version consistency gate safeguards side-effecting actions.
AI.result: Experiments on industrial fault diagnosis, enterprise analytics, and LLM-based multi-tool assistants show significantly fewer expensive component calls and lower end-to-end latency, while maintaining high consistency and low incorrect-reuse rates.
AI.conclusion: Incremental, contract- and invariant-domain-guided execution enables safe and efficient updates for heterogeneous long-horizon AI workflows, reducing redundant computation without sacrificing correctness.

title: Manipulation Feasible Navigation Among Movable Obstacles with Discrete Contact Pushing
summary: In environments with large movable obstacles, detour-only navigation can be inefficient or even infeasible, while obstacle interaction requires reasoning about navigation benefit, feasible placement, and executable manipulation. We present a hierarchical navigation among movable obstacles (NAMO) framework for mobile manipulators. At the high level, the planner identifies key blocking obstacles from reference paths and searches for relocation plans that jointly satisfy geometric, manipulation, and downstream navigation constraints. When direct relocation is hindered by other movable objects, a large language model (LLM) is selectively invoked to infer auxiliary manipulation dependencies, which are then verified by deterministic geometric planning. To execute the resulting relocation goals, we define discrete contact modes on the surfaces of box-shaped obstacles and select contact faces and regions online based on position and orientation errors, enabling straight, side, and corner pushing through contact switching. A recurrent reinforcement-learning policy coordinates the mobile base and manipulator to track tool center point (TCP) targets while preserving end-effector reachability during sustained pushing. Simulation and real-robot experiments demonstrate feasible navigation-manipulation in detour, single- and multi-obstacle relocation, and dependency-constrained scenarios, validating the framework for interactive navigation with large non-graspable obstacles. The open-source project is available at https://cloudytosunny.github.io/NAMO_DCPushing/.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical NAMO framework for mobile manipulators that combines constraint-aware relocation planning, selective LLM-based dependency inference, discrete contact-mode pushing, and a recurrent RL policy for coordinated base-arm control, validated in simulation and on a real robot.
AI.motivation: In environments with large movable obstacles, detour-only navigation is inefficient or infeasible, whereas obstacle interaction demands joint reasoning over navigation benefit, feasible placement, and executable manipulation. Existing approaches struggle to satisfy geometric, manipulation, and downstream navigation constraints simultaneously, and rarely handle dependency-constrained multi-obstacle cases.
AI.method: A hierarchical NAMO framework is proposed. The high-level planner identifies key blocking obstacles from reference paths and searches relocation plans satisfying geometric, manipulation, and downstream navigation constraints jointly. When direct relocation is blocked by other movable objects, an LLM is selectively invoked to infer auxiliary manipulation dependencies, verified by deterministic geometric planning. For execution, discrete contact modes are defined on box-shaped obstacle surfaces, with contact faces and regions selected online based on position and orientation errors, enabling straight, side, and corner pushing via contact switching. A recurrent RL policy coordinates the mobile base and manipulator to track TCP targets while maintaining end-effector reachability during sustained pushing.
AI.result: Simulation and real-robot experiments demonstrate feasible navigation-manipulation in detour, single- and multi-obstacle relocation, and dependency-constrained scenarios, validating the framework for interactive navigation with large non-graspable obstacles.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables interactive navigation among large non-graspable movable obstacles by coupling hierarchical relocation planning with LLM-assisted dependency inference and contact-mode-based pushing under a recurrent RL control policy. An open-source project is provided.

title: DocMIDE: Learning Multi-Hop Implicit Derivation in Visually Rich Documents
summary: Real-world document processing systems rely on rigid, predefined schemas, yet critical target fields often lack direct visual counterparts on the page. Extracting these implicit values requires multi-hop derivation, such as aggregating sub-categories or reasoning over visual marks. While existing methods handle explicit text spans or simple implicit queries, they fail at multi-hop visual reasoning even after standard fine-tuning: models retrieve incorrect visual evidence, or retrieve it correctly and then skip the intermediate steps of the derivation. To address this, we introduce DocMIDE, a fine-tuning framework that trains compact vision-language models to retrieve visual evidence explicitly before deriving an answer. DocMIDE constrains generation to a plan-retrieve-derive structure and optimizes it with Group Relative Policy Optimization under a four-component, rule-based reward that scores output format, the retrieved evidence block, every intermediate derivation step, and the final value against a verified reference trace. On a 4,151-pair implicit extraction benchmark, DocMIDE raises accuracy from 70.8% to 95.9% on Qwen3.5-4B from only a small set of annotated examples, and transfers to a second backbone architecture. Supervised demonstrations alone do not close this gap at any budget we tested; rewarding the intermediate steps is what does.

AI.tldr: DocMIDE is a fine-tuning framework that trains compact VLMs to explicitly retrieve visual evidence and derive implicit document values via a plan-retrieve-derive structure optimized with GRPO and a four-component rule-based reward, boosting accuracy from 70.8% to 95.9%.
AI.motivation: Real-world document processing relies on rigid predefined schemas, but critical target fields often lack direct visual counterparts. Extracting such implicit values requires multi-hop visual reasoning (e.g., aggregating sub-categories, reasoning over visual marks). Existing methods handle explicit spans or simple implicit queries but fail at multi-hop visual reasoning even after standard fine-tuning—either retrieving incorrect visual evidence or retrieving it correctly while skipping intermediate derivation steps.
AI.method: DocMIDE trains compact VLMs to retrieve visual evidence explicitly before deriving an answer. It constrains generation to a plan-retrieve-derive structure and optimizes it with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) under a four-component, rule-based reward scoring: (1) output format, (2) the retrieved evidence block, (3) every intermediate derivation step, and (4) the final value—each compared against a verified reference trace.
AI.result: On a 4,151-pair implicit extraction benchmark, DocMIDE raises accuracy from 70.8% to 95.9% on Qwen3.5-4B from only a small set of annotated examples, and transfers to a second backbone architecture. Supervised demonstrations alone do not close this gap at any tested budget.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly retrieving visual evidence and rewarding intermediate derivation steps—rather than relying on supervised demonstrations—is the decisive factor for enabling multi-hop visual reasoning in implicit document field extraction.

title: Towards Reliable Underwater Diver-Robot Interaction: Gesture Design, Interaction Logic, and Real-World Evaluation
comment: This work has been submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: Underwater human--robot interaction requires gesture commands that are both easy for divers to use and reliable for robots to recognize. We investigate these aspects through a closed-loop diver--robot interaction framework integrating a compact seven-gesture vocabulary, lightweight landmark-based recognition, and command-level interaction logic. We evaluate the framework through a user study and underwater robot experiments in a laboratory tank and a swimming pool. The user study supported the reproducibility of the gestures after brief learning. Recognition analysis further showed that visual similarity was associated with gesture confusion, while intermediate poses during gesture formation introduced temporal ambiguity. Command-level processing mitigated the effects of transient recognition errors on robot execution, reducing unintended triggers and premature task interruptions. These findings show that reliable underwater gesture interaction depends on human usability, gesture recognizability, and execution reliability in underwater interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a closed-loop diver–robot gesture interaction framework with a seven-gesture vocabulary and lightweight landmark-based recognition, validated via a user study and underwater experiments, showing that command-level logic reduces the impact of transient recognition errors.
AI.motivation: Underwater human–robot interaction requires gesture commands that are simultaneously easy for divers to perform and reliable for robots to recognize; these two requirements are seldom studied jointly.
AI.method: A closed-loop diver–robot interaction framework integrating (1) a compact seven-gesture vocabulary, (2) lightweight landmark-based gesture recognition, and (3) command-level interaction logic. Evaluation combined a user study with underwater robot experiments in a laboratory tank and a swimming pool.
AI.result: Gestures were reproducible after brief learning. Recognition analysis showed that visual similarity between gestures was associated with confusion, and intermediate poses during gesture formation introduced temporal ambiguity. Command-level processing mitigated transient recognition errors, reducing unintended triggers and premature task interruptions.
AI.conclusion: Reliable underwater gesture interaction depends jointly on human usability, gesture recognizability, and execution reliability.

title: When More Evidence Hurts: Publication-Bias Drift and Principled Stopping for Biomedical Causal Search
summary: Automated biomedical evidence synthesis depends on retrieving published studies, but the biomedical literature is systematically skewed toward positive findings. Deeper retrieval can therefore make a system \emph{more} likely to falsely infer benefit when the true effect is null. We formalise this phenomenon as \emph{evidence drift} and prove that, under a standard publication-bias model, the false-positive probability on null-effect queries follows a strictly increasing large-sample envelope in retrieval depth, approaching one. Empirically, on a held-out test set of 140 Cochrane-derived queries, drift rises monotonically from 7.9\% to 15.7\% as the retrieval budget grows from 3 to 20 steps, and concentrates in the null-effect class. We present DACG-agent, a drift-aware causal-graph agent that incrementally builds a causal knowledge graph from PubMed abstracts and applies a two-layer stopping policy with complementary roles: a KL-divergence monitor that detects posterior convergence (the accuracy layer), and a Bradley--Terry process reward model (PRM) whose online decline detection halts retrieval once evidence quality peaks (the efficiency layer). Against full-budget retrieval, DACG-agent reduces evidence drift from 15.7\% to 6.4\% and improves null-effect accuracy by 21 percentage points (40.0\%$\to$61.4\%) while using 67\% fewer retrieval steps; overall accuracy rises from 61.4\% to 69.3\% (95\% CI 61--77). A simulation confirms the drift result transfers from the analysed vote-counting aggregator to the deployed noisy-OR one.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes "evidence drift," the phenomenon where deeper literature retrieval in biomedicine systematically inflates false-positive benefit inference due to publication bias, and introduces DACG-agent, a drift-aware causal-graph agent with a two-layer stopping policy that mitigates this problem while cutting retrieval cost.
AI.motivation: Automated biomedical evidence synthesis relies on retrieving published studies, but the literature is systematically skewed toward positive findings. Consequently, deeper retrieval can make a system more likely to falsely infer benefit when the true effect is null. The authors identify and formalize this risk (evidence drift) as a fundamental hazard of retrieval-augmented evidence synthesis.
AI.method: The authors formalize evidence drift and prove that, under a standard publication-bias model, the false-positive probability on null-effect queries follows a strictly increasing large-sample envelope in retrieval depth, approaching one. They then propose DACG-agent, which incrementally builds a causal knowledge graph from PubMed abstracts and applies a two-layer stopping policy: a KL-divergence monitor detecting posterior convergence (accuracy layer) and a Bradley–Terry process reward model with online decline detection halting retrieval once evidence quality peaks (efficiency layer). A simulation checks transfer from an analysed vote-counting aggregator to the deployed noisy-OR aggregator.
AI.result: On a held-out test set of 140 Cochrane-derived queries, drift rises monotonically from 7.9% to 15.7% as retrieval budget grows from 3 to 20 steps, concentrating in the null-effect class. Against full-budget retrieval, DACG-agent reduces evidence drift from 15.7% to 6.4%, improves null-effect accuracy by 21 percentage points (40.0% to 61.4%), uses 67% fewer retrieval steps, and raises overall accuracy from 61.4% to 69.3% (95% CI 61–77).
AI.conclusion: Evidence drift is a provable, empirically confirmed failure mode of deep retrieval in publication-biased biomedical corpora, worsening with retrieval depth and concentrating in null-effect queries. A drift-aware stopping policy that combines posterior-convergence monitoring with online evidence-quality decline detection substantially mitigates this bias, improving both factual accuracy and efficiency. The drift result also transfers from the analysed aggregator to the deployed noisy-OR model.

title: EmoPose: Vision-Language Model Guided Emotion-Aware Gesture Generation for Humanoid Robots
summary: Socially competent humanoid robots must communicate affect and intent through gesture as well as speech, yet open-ended interaction must become motion that is both expressive and executable on a specific body. This demands semantic flexibility for contextual social intent while preserving deterministic, embodiment-aware robot control. We present EmoPose, a vision-language model (VLM)-guided framework that bridges this gap through an executable semantic interface. Given language, dialogue history, and optional visual context, the VLM selects an ordered gesture plan containing a communicative class, library variant, intensity, and speech anchor. A scalable robot-owned motion library defines the available expressive vocabulary and the source of 14-DoF joint targets. Pose Studio supports automatic trajectory generation, MuJoCo preview, and automatic synchronization of new library entries with the VLM guide; deterministic robot-side modules validate plans, construct trajectories, schedule gestures, and manage queueing and interruption. This division lets the interaction repertoire grow for new social contexts without changing the control interface or delegating raw joint commands to the foundation model. On the EmoPose-Bench, structured GPT-5.5 planning reaches $98.25\pm0.52\%$ on the Easy tier and $76.50\pm0.54\%$ overall, exceeding same-model direct-label prompting. Further tests validate dialogue-context use and ordered multi-action composition. The system completes the nominal MuJoCo suite and realizes all 29 authored variants on the physical Unitree G1. A four-stop laboratory tour demonstrates expressive narration with interruption, camera-grounded dialogue, and navigation.

AI.tldr: EmoPose is a VLM-guided framework that generates expressive, executable robot gestures by having the VLM select structured gesture plans from a robot-owned motion library, keeping deterministic control on the robot side.
AI.motivation: Socially competent humanoid robots must communicate affect and intent through gesture as well as speech. Open-ended interaction must become motion that is both expressive and executable on a specific body, requiring semantic flexibility for contextual social intent while preserving deterministic, embodiment-aware control.
AI.method: Given language, dialogue history, and optional visual context, a VLM selects an ordered gesture plan containing a communicative class, library variant, intensity, and speech anchor. A scalable robot-owned motion library defines the expressive vocabulary and source of 14-DoF joint targets. Pose Studio supports automatic trajectory generation, MuJoCo preview, and synchronization of new library entries with the VLM guide. Deterministic robot-side modules validate plans, construct trajectories, schedule gestures, and manage queueing and interruption.
AI.result: On EmoPose-Bench, structured GPT-5.5 planning reaches 98.25±0.52% on the Easy tier and 76.50±0.54% overall, exceeding same-model direct-label prompting. Further tests validate dialogue-context use and ordered multi-action composition. The system completes the nominal MuJoCo suite and realizes all 29 authored variants on the physical Unitree G1. A four-stop laboratory tour demonstrates expressive narration with interruption, camera-grounded dialogue, and navigation.
AI.conclusion: EmoPose bridges the gap between semantic flexibility and deterministic, embodiment-aware control through an executable semantic interface, allowing the interaction repertoire to grow for new social contexts without changing the control interface or delegating raw joint commands to the foundation model.

title: EDGEGEN: Improving Tool-Calling Agents Beyond Happy Paths with Synthetic Edge Case Generation
comment: NA
summary: Tool-calling LLM agents are increasingly deployed in enterprise applications. However, effective evaluation and optimization require high-quality, diverse task datasets that are often difficult to obtain due to privacy and other constraints. Existing synthetic task generation methods often produce generic tasks that ignore an agent's underlying state or database and fail to reflect real-world usage diversity. We propose EdgeGen, a synthetic task generation framework that extracts compliance rules from an agent's specification and uses them to generate database-grounded edge-case tasks designed to violate these rules. When combined with existing synthetic data generation techniques, EdgeGen enables agent improvement through finetuning and harness optimization. The resulting pipeline forms a fully automated closed-loop system that requires no human annotation. Finetuning on data generated by EdgeGen yields a consistent mean progress improvement of 2 percent to 42 percent on tau2bench airline domain, while other baseline methods show degradation for some models. On the other hand, for harness optimization, our method shows a mean progress improvement of 10 percent and 30 percent over the human-curated and base harnesses, respectively, for the Gemma-4-e4b model.

AI.tldr: EdgeGen is a synthetic task generation framework that extracts compliance rules from an agent's specification and generates database-grounded edge-case tasks violating these rules, forming a fully automated closed-loop system for finetuning and harness optimization of tool-calling LLM agents.
AI.motivation: Tool-calling LLM agents are increasingly deployed in enterprise settings, but effective evaluation and optimization require high-quality, diverse task datasets that are hard to obtain due to privacy and other constraints. Existing synthetic task generation methods tend to produce generic tasks that ignore the agent's underlying state or database and fail to capture real-world usage diversity.
AI.method: EdgeGen extracts compliance rules from an agent's specification and uses them to generate database-grounded edge-case tasks specifically designed to violate those rules. Combined with existing synthetic data generation techniques, it enables agent improvement via finetuning and harness optimization, forming a fully automated closed-loop pipeline requiring no human annotation.
AI.result: Finetuning on EdgeGen-generated data yields a consistent mean progress improvement of 2%-42% on the tau2bench airline domain, whereas baseline methods show degradation for some models. For harness optimization, the method achieves mean progress improvements of 10% and 30% over human-curated and base harnesses respectively for the Gemma-4-e4b model.
AI.conclusion: EdgeGen provides an automated, annotation-free approach to generating challenging, specification-grounded edge-case tasks that improve both finetuning and harness optimization of tool-calling agents, outperforming baselines.

title: HEARTH: An Object-Centric RGB-Thermal-3D Dataset for Temperature-Aware Robot Manipulation
summary: Language-guided manipulation can depend on physical properties that visible appearance does not reveal. Temperature is one such property, but object datasets for robot learning rarely associate measured temperatures with object appearance and geometry. We present HEARTH, an object-centric RGB-thermal-3D dataset of 90 physical objects from 18 everyday categories, comprising 145 captured object states. Our pipeline maps apparent surface temperatures onto reconstructed meshes through camera calibration and pose transfer. The dataset includes raw temperature measurements, camera parameters, RGB-textured meshes, and thermal textures for simulation. We use these assets to construct three LIBERO-derived tasks and collect 1,200 demonstrations for fine-tuning a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model, $π_{0.5}$. In an ablation study, adding thermal observations to the VLA increases success on temperature-dependent object-selection tasks from 35.0% for the RGB-only baseline to 75.0%. These results demonstrate the utility of HEARTH for training robot policies to follow temperature-related instructions.

AI.tldr: HEARTH is an object-centric RGB-Thermal-3D dataset of 90 objects (18 categories, 145 states) that maps surface temperatures onto reconstructed meshes, used to collect 1,200 demonstrations for VLA fine-tuning; adding thermal input boosts temperature-dependent object-selection success from 35.0% to 75.0%.
AI.motivation: Language-guided manipulation often depends on physical properties not revealed by visible appearance, such as temperature. Existing object datasets for robot learning rarely associate measured temperatures with object appearance and geometry, limiting the training of policies that follow temperature-related instructions.
AI.method: The authors build HEARTH, an object-centric RGB-thermal-3D dataset of 90 physical objects across 18 everyday categories and 145 captured object states. A pipeline maps apparent surface temperatures onto reconstructed meshes via camera calibration and pose transfer. The dataset provides raw temperature measurements, camera parameters, RGB-textured meshes, and thermal textures for simulation. Three LIBERO-derived tasks are constructed to collect 1,200 demonstrations for fine-tuning a pretrained VLA model, π0.5, with an ablation comparing RGB-only versus thermal-augmented observation.
AI.result: In the ablation study, adding thermal observations to the VLA raised success on temperature-dependent object-selection tasks from 35.0% (RGB-only baseline) to 75.0%.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the utility of HEARTH for training robot policies to follow temperature-related instructions, highlighting the value of thermal sensing grounded in object appearance and geometry.

title: Self-Healing Harness for Runtime Oversight of Agent Self-Modification
summary: LLM agents can change their own future behavior, raising a basic control question of which self-generated changes should be allowed to persist. We formulate this as admission control for self-modification. The agent may propose changes to its operating instructions, while an external runtime gate controls persistence. We implement this principle as a model-agnostic self-healing harness that runs a Detect, Notice, Heal, Validate loop around an otherwise unmodified agent. The agent authors candidate behavioral rules in an external workspace, where they receive provisional execution authority during evaluation and acquire persistent cross-episode authority only after measured improvement on the triggering failure without regression beyond a fixed margin on protected cases. Replay provides matched evidence when available, forward trials provide a weaker fallback, and a corpus-level guard re-tests the accumulated active rule set. Across 16 matched Baseline and Harness runs spanning AppWorld, Terminal-Bench, and $τ^2$-Bench, the gate rejected 383 replay-decided proposals. Of these, 211 (55%) improved their triggering failure while degrading a case that previously worked. This shows that locally beneficial self-modifications can introduce collateral regressions often enough to materially affect gate decisions, providing direct empirical motivation for external admission control. Task-completion score is higher under the Harness in all 16 pairs, with two paired bootstrap intervals excluding zero, while repeated-trial reliability is higher in 12 pairs, tied in 4, and lower in none. Because adaptation modifies the policy-inducing context while leaving model weights fixed, admitted changes remain inspectable, reversible, and compatible with closed-weight models.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes LLM agent self-modification as an admission-control problem: proposed changes to operating instructions gain persistence only if an external runtime gate validates measured improvement without collateral regression, implemented as a model-agnostic "Detect, Notice, Heal, Validate" harness.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can rewrite their own future behavior, raising the question of which self-generated changes should be allowed to persist. The work argues that persistence decisions require external governance rather than agent self-judgment.
AI.method: A model-agnostic self-healing harness wraps an unmodified agent in a Detect, Notice, Heal, Validate loop. The agent authors candidate behavioral rules in an external workspace, receiving only provisional execution authority during evaluation. Persistent cross-episode authority is granted only after measured improvement on the triggering failure without regression beyond a fixed margin on protected cases. Evidence comes from replay when matched evidence exists, forward trials as a weaker fallback, and a corpus-level guard that re-tests the accumulated active rule set. Weights remain fixed; adaptation occurs in the policy-inducing context.
AI.result: Across 16 matched Baseline/Harness runs on AppWorld, Terminal-Bench, and τ²-Bench, the gate rejected 383 replay-decided proposals; 211 (55%) improved their triggering failure while degrading a previously working case—locally beneficial changes frequently cause collateral regressions. Harness task-completion score was higher in all 16 pairs (two paired bootstrap intervals excluding zero); repeated-trial reliability was higher in 12 pairs, tied in 4, and lower in none.
AI.conclusion: External admission control for self-modification is empirically justified, since naive acceptance of locally beneficial rules induces collateral regressions. Because admitted changes alter the policy-inducing context rather than model weights, they remain inspectable, reversible, and compatible with closed-weight models.

title: RiverVLN: Phase-Grounded Temporal Vision--Language Navigation for Unmanned Surface Vehicles
summary: Vision-language navigation (VLN) has largely been developed for indoor and terrestrial robots, where language can often be treated as a static goal and motion is approximated by discrete or near-instantaneous actions. These assumptions break down for unmanned surface vehicles (USVs): river navigation requires continuous motion under inertia and limited maneuverability, while long-horizon instructions must be executed through sparse and visually ambiguous maritime landmarks. We introduce RiverVLN, to our knowledge the first benchmark designed for long-horizon USV VLN under continuous riverine motion, and PGT-NAV, a phase-grounded temporal navigation framework for USVs. Rather than directly mapping an entire instruction to motion, PGT-NAV converts it into an ordered sequence of visually verifiable semantic phases and maintains the active phase online through grounded visual and motion evidence. This explicit semantic progress state is fused with visual-motion history and phase-specific grounding to predict six local SE(2) pose increments. The resulting trajectory is executed in a predict-execute-re-observe loop, where the vessel executes toward W3, updates phase and grounding, and replans through a map-based safety layer. Experiments show that PGT-NAV substantially reduces recursive position and heading drift relative to GNM-style and ViNT-style baselines and achieves an average success rate of 0.79 in Unity-ROS closed-loop navigation. Unseen bridge-opening trials and real-world USV experiments further demonstrate that the phase-grounded representation transfers from controlled evaluation to physical USV deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RiverVLN, the first benchmark for long-horizon vision-language navigation (VLN) for unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) under continuous riverine motion, along with PGT-NAV, a phase-grounded temporal navigation framework that decomposes instructions into ordered semantic phases and predicts local SE(2) pose increments in a predict-execute-re-observe loop.
AI.motivation: Existing VLN methods are largely designed for indoor and terrestrial robots, where language is treated as a static goal and motion is approximated by discrete or near-instantaneous actions. These assumptions fail for USVs: river navigation involves continuous motion under inertia and limited maneuverability, and long-horizon instructions must be executed via sparse, visually ambiguous maritime landmarks.
AI.method: PGT-NAV avoids directly mapping an entire instruction to motion. It converts the instruction into an ordered sequence of visually verifiable semantic phases and maintains the active phase online using grounded visual and motion evidence. This explicit semantic progress state is fused with visual-motion history and phase-specific grounding to predict six local SE(2) pose increments. The trajectory is executed in a predict-execute-re-observe loop: the vessel moves toward W3, updates phase and grounding, and replans through a map-based safety layer.
AI.result: PGT-NAV substantially reduces recursive position and heading drift compared to GNM-style and ViNT-style baselines, achieving an average success rate of 0.79 in Unity-ROS closed-loop navigation. Unseen bridge-opening trials and real-world USV experiments demonstrate that the phase-grounded representation transfers from controlled evaluation to physical USV deployment.
AI.conclusion: The phase-grounded representation generalizes beyond simulation, enabling effective long-horizon VLN for USVs in continuous riverine settings and supporting real-world deployment.

title: APEXA: Execution-Integrity Enforcement for Multi-Agent LLM Automation of Synchrotron Data Reduction
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at the 4th TPC Workshop @ SC'26 (Building Open AI Infrastructure, Models, and Agentic Systems for Science). Code and benchmark: https://github.com/AdvancedPhotonSource/APEXA-APS-Beamline-Assistant ; data: https://doi.org/10.18126/tgg4-1m26
summary: Synchrotron data reduction, detector calibration followed by azimuthal integration of terabyte-scale diffraction series, is a multi-step, expert-bound bottleneck that increasingly limits the science rate of user facilities. LLM agents promise to collapse it, but driving a real pipeline with a stochastic model creates a failure mode chat benchmarks cannot see: an agent can report a calibration that was never computed. Correctness here is a property of what executed, not of the transcript. We present APEXA, a deployed multi-agent framework (61 tools over heterogeneous compute, run as a single reasoning loop) automating calibration and integration from natural language at a major light source. We make three contributions. First, execution-integrity enforcement: a deterministic tool-layer guard that refuses to surface any result not backed by an executed tool call, with a parser tolerant of cross-model tool-call format drift: in deployment, a frontier model fabricated a complete calibration-comparison report for commands that never ran, which the guard converts to an explicit non-result; the same code gates an optional motor-control surface at 0/200 adversarial violations against a simulated IOC, versus 15/200 for an equivalent safety prompt. Second, we release APEXA-Bench, an evaluation harness of 58 facility tasks (50 base plus an 8-task cross-detector slice) organized by a four-class physical-consequence taxonomy, the first benchmark axis we know of separating a wasted compute cycle from a damaged instrument; its cross-detector grading against NIST-traceable lattice constants surfaced two latent pipeline bugs. Large-scale agent scoring is left to a full-length study. Third, we validate APEXA on real beamline data: from one natural-language prompt it recovers detector geometry and integrates a full attenuation/exposure sweep. We release the framework, harness and traces.

AI.tldr: APEXA is a deployed multi-agent framework (61 tools, single reasoning loop) that automates synchrotron detector calibration and azimuthal integration from natural language. It enforces execution integrity via a deterministic tool-layer guard that suppresses any result not backed by an executed tool call, releases APEXA-Bench (58 facility tasks with a four-class physical-consequence taxonomy), and validates on real beamline data.
AI.motivation: Synchrotron data reduction—calibration and azimuthal integration of terabyte-scale diffraction series—is a multi-step, expert-bound bottleneck limiting user-facility science throughput. LLM agents could collapse this bottleneck, but a stochastic model driving a real pipeline introduces a failure mode invisible to chat benchmarks: the agent can report a calibration that was never computed. Correctness is a property of what executed, not of the transcript.
AI.method: APEXA is a deployed multi-agent framework of 61 tools over heterogeneous compute, run as a single reasoning loop. Its core mechanism is execution-integrity enforcement: a deterministic tool-layer guard that refuses to surface any result not backed by an executed tool call, paired with a parser tolerant of cross-model tool-call format drift. The same guard gates an optional motor-control surface. The authors also release APEXA-Bench, an evaluation harness of 58 facility tasks (50 base + 8-task cross-detector slice) organized by a four-class physical-consequence taxonomy, with cross-detector grading against NIST-traceable lattice constants.
AI.result: In deployment, a frontier model fabricated a complete calibration-comparison report for commands that never ran, which the guard converted into an explicit non-result. The guard achieved 0/200 adversarial violations on the motor-control surface against a simulated IOC, versus 15/200 for an equivalent safety prompt. APEXA-Bench's cross-detector grading surfaced two latent pipeline bugs. On real beamline data, APEXA recovered detector geometry and integrated a full attenuation/exposure sweep from a single natural-language prompt.
AI.conclusion: APEXA demonstrates that execution-integrity enforcement is essential for trustworthy agentic control of real scientific pipelines: correctness must be grounded in executed tool calls rather than transcript text. The framework, harness, and traces are released, with large-scale agent scoring deferred to a full-length study.

title: RopeFormer: Cross-Trial Adaptation from Interaction History for Dynamic Rope Manipulation
summary: Dynamic rope manipulation is highly sensitive to unknown object dynamics: the same robot motion can produce substantially different responses across ropes, while explicitly identifying the relevant physical properties is difficult. We present RopeFormer, a history-conditioned framework that uses prior task interaction as context for subsequent control. The policy retains cross-trial action-response history while keeping its weights fixed and requires no explicit online rope-parameter estimation. In matched simulation evaluations across sustained single-arm rotation, bimanual rotation, and transient whipping, retaining context improves subsequent control relative to resetting the same checkpoint, with the benefit varying across rope dynamics and observation settings. We further deploy the frozen policies on a Unitree H1-2 with previously unseen physical ropes. From T1 to T3, target-acquisition time decreases by 30.9% for Rope Swing and 33.9% for Rope Twirl, while mean Rope Whip target hits increase from 0.2 to 2.3 out of three. These results show that prior interaction can provide effective control context for dynamic deformable-object manipulation. Robot videos, code, and data are available at https://ropeformer.github.io/.

AI.tldr: RopeFormer is a history-conditioned control framework that uses prior task interaction as context for dynamic rope manipulation, without explicit online rope-parameter estimation, improving physical-robot performance on unseen ropes.
AI.motivation: Dynamic rope manipulation is highly sensitive to unknown object dynamics: identical robot motions yield substantially different responses across ropes, and explicitly identifying relevant physical properties is difficult.
AI.method: RopeFormer is a history-conditioned framework that retains cross-trial action-response history as context for subsequent control. The policy keeps its weights fixed and requires no explicit online rope-parameter estimation. It is evaluated in matched simulations across sustained single-arm rotation, bimanual rotation, and transient whipping, and deployed on a Unitree H1-2 with previously unseen physical ropes.
AI.result: In simulation, retaining context improves subsequent control versus resetting the same checkpoint, with benefits varying across rope dynamics and observation settings. On hardware, from T1 to T3, target-acquisition time decreases by 30.9% for Rope Swing and 33.9% for Rope Twirl, while mean Rope Whip target hits increase from 0.2 to 2.3 out of three.
AI.conclusion: Prior interaction can provide effective control context for dynamic deformable-object manipulation.

title: CREDO: Variance-Guided Rubric Evolution for Replay-Corrected Credit Assignment
summary: Long-horizon language agents receive sparse terminal feedback, while intermediate rubrics provide structured but potentially misspecified assessments of progress. In resettable training environments, counterfactual continuation rollouts can measure local credit, but exhaustive replay is costly. We propose Credo, a framework that couples evolving semantic rubrics with selective, execution-based credit correction. A frozen judge maps visible transitions to rubric features, and a credit head predicts the change in expected terminal reward associated with the realized transition. Independently sampled two-sided replays correct prediction residuals using their recorded inclusion probabilities. We derive conditional unbiasedness and a variance decomposition that connects two design choices: which rubric features to retain, and where to allocate a fixed expected replay budget. The resulting criterion weights prediction errors by policy-score sensitivity and missing replay coverage; its allocation rule additionally accounts for continuation cost. We also describe a practical mixture with terminal leave-one-out advantages and distinguish its clipped, token-normalized PPO implementation from the ideal policy-gradient estimator. This preliminary report provides the method, proofs, an exact finite-model audit, and a controlled evaluation protocol. It makes no claim of empirical superiority on language-agent benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Credo is a framework coupling evolving semantic rubrics with selective execution-based credit correction for long-horizon language agents, using a frozen judge, a credit head, and two-sided replay to obtain unbiased credit estimates under a fixed budget.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon language agents receive only sparse terminal feedback, while intermediate rubrics offer structured but potentially misspecified progress signals. Counterfactual continuation rollouts can measure local credit in resettable environments, but exhaustive replay is computationally prohibitive, motivating selective credit estimation.
AI.method: A frozen judge maps visible transitions to rubric features, and a credit head predicts the change in expected terminal reward for realized transitions. Independently sampled two-sided replays correct prediction residuals via recorded inclusion probabilities. The authors derive conditional unbiasedness and a variance decomposition linking rubric-feature retention and replay-budget allocation. The resulting criterion weights prediction errors by policy-score sensitivity and missing replay coverage, with an allocation rule that accounts for continuation cost. A practical mixture with terminal leave-one-out advantages is described, and its clipped, token-normalized PPO implementation is distinguished from the ideal policy-gradient estimator.
AI.result: The paper reports the method, proofs, an exact finite-model audit, and a controlled evaluation protocol. It explicitly makes no claim of empirical superiority on language-agent benchmarks, so no empirical performance results are asserted.
AI.conclusion: Credo offers a principled, theoretically grounded credit-assignment framework combining semantic rubrics and selective replay, with formal unbiasedness and variance analysis, but its preliminary report status means empirical validation on language-agent benchmarks remains future work.

title: Receding-Horizon Pushing with Composable Object-Centric Policies
summary: Non-prehensile manipulation is practical for relocating large, heavy, or geometrically ungraspable objects. Yet, long-horizon pushing of arbitrarily-shaped 3D objects couples three problems: 1) where to push the object so as to approach the target pose, 2) whether each push is stable and reachable, 3) whether subsequent actions remain feasible. We present an object-centric pushing policy within a feedback-guided hierarchical framework. At the low level, a learning-based policy predicts contact actions from a pose- and scale-normalized point cloud, conditioned on a near single-step subgoal. A stability score is applied to evaluate the predicted contacts by a quasi-static sliding-versus-tipping analysis. At the high level, BIT$^*$ first searches for an object path, and the next several subgoals are checked by contact prediction and robot motion planning for future feasibility. Failed motion plans, as feedback, change the local path costs and trigger re-planning. During execution, only the first feasible action is executed. In simulation, we evaluate 22 objects in six different scenes, upon which we also conduct comprehensive ablation studies. Results demonstrate that our method outperforms baselines with a clear margin and can reliably achieve long-horizon object pushing tasks under different situations. We also report quantitative real-robot experiments with a Franka arm and qualitative demonstrations with a mobile manipulator for large and heavy objects, with directly zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

AI.tldr: A feedback-guided hierarchical framework for long-horizon pushing of arbitrarily-shaped 3D objects, combining a learned contact policy, quasi-static stability analysis, and BIT* search with motion-planning feedback.
AI.motivation: Non-prehensile pushing is useful for relocating large, heavy, or ungraspable objects, but long-horizon pushing of arbitrary 3D shapes is hard because it couples three problems: choosing contact locations to reach the target pose, ensuring each push is stable and reachable, and preserving feasibility of subsequent actions.
AI.method: A hierarchical, object-centric pushing policy. Low level: a learning-based policy predicts contact actions from a pose- and scale-normalized point cloud, conditioned on a near single-step subgoal, with predicted contacts scored for stability via quasi-static sliding-versus-tipping analysis. High level: BIT* searches an object path, and upcoming subgoals are validated by contact prediction and robot motion planning; failed motion plans feed back to adjust local path costs and trigger re-planning. Only the first feasible action is executed at each execution step.
AI.result: Evaluated on 22 objects across six simulated scenes with comprehensive ablations; the method outperforms baselines by a clear margin and reliably solves long-horizon pushing. Quantitative real-robot experiments with a Franka arm and qualitative mobile-manipulator demonstrations on large, heavy objects show direct zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.conclusion: The feedback-guided hierarchical formulation, integrating learned contact prediction, stability analysis, and search-based re-planning, enables robust long-horizon non-prehensile pushing with zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

title: LIMIT: Less Is More for Instruction Tuning in Text-to-SQL
summary: Large language models have achieved remarkable progress on Text-to-SQL through reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning, yet existing approaches predominantly rely on massive instruction corpora under the assumption that scale drives performance. We challenge this paradigm by investigating a fundamental question: what is the minimal data requirement for effective Text-to-SQL instruction tuning? We propose LIMIT(Less Is More for Instruction Tuning in Text-to-SQL), a data-centric framework that demonstrates strong database reasoning can emerge from an extremely compact training set when examples are strategically selected. LIMIT operates through four stages: difficulty-aware filtering that identifies samples within the model's learning frontier, chain-of-thought synthesis with consistency-based selection, multi-dimensional quality scoring via LLM-as-judge, and genetic algorithm optimization that jointly maximizes schema coverage and sample quality. On the BIRD and Spider benchmark, LIMIT selects only 796 and 863 samples while achieving 100% table coverage, enabling Qwen3-8B to reach 69.1% and 88.9% execution accuracy.This result surpasses methods trained on 20 times more data and establishes a new state-of-the-art among open-source approaches. Our findings suggest that careful data curation, rather than scale, is the key to efficient Text-to-SQL learning.

AI.tldr: LIMIT is a data-centric framework that shows strong Text-to-SQL reasoning can emerge from an extremely small, strategically selected instruction set rather than massive corpora, achieving state-of-the-art results with ~800 samples.
AI.motivation: Existing Text-to-SQL approaches rely on massive instruction corpora under the assumption that scale drives performance. This paper questions that paradigm and investigates the minimal data requirement for effective Text-to-SQL instruction tuning.
AI.method: LIMIT operates through four stages: (1) difficulty-aware filtering to identify samples within the model's learning frontier, (2) chain-of-thought synthesis with consistency-based selection, (3) multi-dimensional quality scoring via LLM-as-judge, and (4) genetic algorithm optimization jointly maximizing schema coverage and sample quality.
AI.result: On BIRD and Spider benchmarks, LIMIT selects only 796 and 863 samples while achieving 100% table coverage. It enables Qwen3-8B to reach 69.1% and 88.9% execution accuracy, surpassing methods trained on 20x more data and establishing a new state-of-the-art among open-source approaches.
AI.conclusion: Careful data curation, rather than scale, is the key to efficient Text-to-SQL learning.

title: BiRoAD: Learning Shared and Role-Adaptive Representations for Bimanual Manipulation
comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026
summary: Bimanual manipulation requires policies that coordinate two arms while adapting their functional roles to scene geometry, object configuration, and task context. Learning such scene-conditioned role adaptation remains challenging, as demonstrations may contain uneven role distributions that limit generalization to underrepresented arm--role configurations. In addition, many bimanual policies predict actions in fixed left- and right-arm action spaces. While this provides a natural parameterization for robot control, it does not explicitly specify how behaviors should transform when functional roles are exchanged across arms. Across different scene initializations, the two arms may follow a similar coordination pattern, but the role-specific behavior assigned to each arm should change with the scene. Therefore, we propose BiRoAD, a Bimanual Role-Adaptive Decomposition framework for learning shared and role-adaptive representations in bimanual policies. Given bimanual trajectory or action-token features, BiRoAD decomposes these features into swap--symmetric and swap--antisymmetric components: the former captures coordination structure invariant to arm exchange, and the latter captures role-specific distinctions that vary consistently with functional role assignment. The two components are then recomposed as residual updates to the original paired arm representations, allowing BiRoAD to serve as a modular feature transformation without changing the policy inputs, imitation-learning objective, or requiring manually defined role labels. Across multiple bimanual manipulation tasks with balanced and imbalanced role distributions, BiRoAD improves robustness across role configurations over corresponding base policies, with notable gains on underrepresented role configurations.

AI.tldr: BiRoAD is a modular feature-transformation framework that decomposes bimanual policy features into swap-symmetric and swap-antisymmetric components, enabling scene-conditioned role adaptation and improving robustness on underrepresented arm–role configurations.
AI.motivation: Bimanual manipulation policies must coordinate two arms while adapting their functional roles to scene geometry, object configuration, and task context. Two challenges impede this: (1) demonstrations often contain uneven role distributions, limiting generalization to underrepresented arm–role configurations; (2) most policies predict actions in fixed left/right action spaces, which parameterizes control naturally but does not specify how behavior should transform when functional roles are exchanged across arms. Across scene initializations, the two arms may share a coordination pattern, yet the role-specific behavior assigned to each arm should change with the scene.
AI.method: Given bimanual trajectory or action-token features, BiRoAD decomposes them into swap-symmetric (capturing coordination structure invariant to arm exchange) and swap-antisymmetric (capturing role-specific distinctions that vary consistently with functional role assignment) components. These are recomposed as residual updates to the original paired arm representations, serving as a modular feature transformation without altering policy inputs, the imitation-learning objective, or requiring manually defined role labels.
AI.result: Across multiple bimanual manipulation tasks with both balanced and imbalanced role distributions, BiRoAD improves robustness across role configurations over corresponding base policies, with notable gains on underrepresented role configurations.
AI.conclusion: BiRoAD offers a label-free, plug-and-play way to inject role-adaptive, scene-conditioned representations into bimanual policies, improving generalization—especially where role data is scarce—without modifying the underlying policy or training objective.

title: SKstars at SHROOM: Visions Agreement-Guided Ensembling of Zero-Shot and LoRA-Adapted Vision--Language Models
comment: This paper has been accepted at the SHROOM-Visions 2026 Shared Task, co-located with EMNLP2026
summary: This paper describes the SKstars submission to SHROOM-Visions 2026, a shared task on fine-grained hallucination detection in large vision-language model outputs. The task requires systems to identify hallucinated character spans, assign hallucination categories, and provide confidence estimates for their predictions. Our approach combines zero-shot predictions from Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct with those of a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct model. The outputs of the two models are integrated through a lightweight ensemble procedure, followed by span refinement and confidence adjustment. We evaluate the main system components on a small internal development subset and report the performance of the submitted system on the official English test set. SKstars achieved a Cor+Lbl score of 0.2902, ranking 15th among 29 teams, and obtained Cor and IoU scores of 0.3642 and 0.3151, respectively, ranking 18th on both metrics. The results show that combining a large zero-shot model with a smaller adapted model provides a practical framework for multilingual and fine-grained hallucination localization, while also highlighting the difficulty of transferring development-set improvements to hidden test data. Code and predictions: https://github.com/aliathar1401/SK-Stars-shroom-visions-2026

AI.tldr: SKstars combines a zero-shot Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct with a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct via a lightweight ensemble, span refinement, and confidence adjustment for fine-grained hallucination detection in LVLM outputs, achieving a Cor+Lbl score of 0.2902.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained hallucination detection in large vision-language model outputs requires identifying hallucinated spans, assigning categories, and estimating confidence. The SHROOM-Visions 2026 shared task addresses this, and the authors aim to build a practical system for multilingual, fine-grained hallucination localization.
AI.method: The approach integrates zero-shot predictions from Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct with those of a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct model. A lightweight ensemble procedure merges the two models' outputs, followed by span refinement and confidence adjustment.
AI.result: On the official English test set, SKstars achieved a Cor+Lbl score of 0.2902 (15th of 29 teams), and Cor and IoU scores of 0.3642 and 0.3151, ranking 18th on both. Main components were evaluated on a small internal development subset.
AI.conclusion: Combining a large zero-shot model with a smaller adapted model offers a practical framework for multilingual and fine-grained hallucination localization, though transferring development-set gains to hidden test data remains challenging.

title: Smartphone GNSS Booster: Centimeter-Level Pedestrian Positioning Using a Portable Signal Re-Radiator
comment: Accepted to the ION 2026 Pacific PNT Meeting
summary: High-precision positioning using the global navigation satellite system (GNSS) embedded in smartphones is demanded for sidewalk-level pedestrian navigation and pinpoint location-based applications. However, current smartphone positioning accuracy for pedestrians remains at the meter level. This is mainly because limitations of the compact linearly polarized (LP) antenna in smartphones increase GNSS observation noise and hinder stable carrier phase tracking. In this paper, we propose an external GNSS signal re-radiation system that boosts smartphone GNSS observation quality while still using the smartphone's built-in GNSS receiver and antenna. The system directly connects a compact active helical antenna and a thin passive patch antenna for re-radiation, and is designed to be attached directly to the smartphone. The proposed GNSS booster achieves (1) reduced thermal noise and stable signal tracking via increased received signal strength, (2) improved multipath robustness compared with a LP antenna, and (3) stabilization of antenna phase center variation. Static experiments confirm a substantial improvement in the observation quality of GNSS carrier phase measurements compared with standard smartphone positioning. Furthermore, in pedestrian experiments, the proposed booster enabled stable carrier phase integer ambiguity resolutions, achieving centimeter-level positioning using a smartphone.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an external GNSS signal re-radiation system (a compact active helical antenna plus a thin passive patch antenna attached to the smartphone) that boosts observation quality of the smartphone's built-in GNSS receiver, enabling stable carrier-phase integer ambiguity resolution and centimeter-level pedestrian positioning.
AI.motivation: High-precision (sidewalk-level) positioning using GNSS in smartphones is demanded for pedestrian navigation and pinpoint location-based applications, but current smartphone positioning accuracy for pedestrians remains at the meter level. The main cause is the limitations of the compact linearly polarized (LP) antenna in smartphones, which increase GNSS observation noise and hinder stable carrier phase tracking.
AI.method: The authors propose an external GNSS signal re-radiation system that improves smartphone GNSS observation quality while still relying on the smartphone's built-in GNSS receiver and antenna. It directly connects a compact active helical antenna and a thin passive patch antenna for re-radiation and is designed to attach directly to the smartphone. The design aims to achieve (1) reduced thermal noise and stable signal tracking via increased received signal strength, (2) improved multipath robustness compared with a LP antenna, and (3) stabilization of antenna phase center variation.
AI.result: Static experiments confirm substantial improvement in the observation quality of GNSS carrier phase measurements relative to standard smartphone positioning. In pedestrian experiments, the booster enabled stable carrier phase integer ambiguity resolutions, achieving centimeter-level positioning using a smartphone.
AI.conclusion: An external GNSS signal re-radiation "booster" attached to a smartphone improves carrier-phase observation quality and multipath robustness, enabling stable integer ambiguity resolution and centimeter-level pedestrian positioning with the phone's built-in receiver and antenna.

title: Recovering Lost Details: Multi-Scale Frequency Compensation for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
comment: 11 pages. Accepted at the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM 2026)
summary: Long-term time series forecasting has made significant progress by leveraging multi-scale information to capture hierarchical temporal patterns and model long-range dependencies. However, temporal downsampling in existing multi-scale methods inevitably smooths detailed temporal fluctuations, and this information loss is further aggravated by their emphasis on dominant trends across scales, resulting in insufficiently expressive representations. To address this, we propose a Multi-Scale Wavelet Mixing (MWMixer) model, which incorporates a Bidirectional Frequency-Bands Mixing strategy to recover lost temporal details across scales, enabling complementary cross-scale information interactions. Then, a Dynamic Scale-Adaptive Fusion module learns time-varying weights for each scale to fuse multi-scale forecasts into the final prediction, enhancing the flexibility of multi-scale aggregation. In addition, a cross-scale consistency loss aligns each coarse-scale prediction with the interval-averaged fine-scale outputs, while a multi-scale supervision loss enforces prediction accuracy at each scale, promoting consistent learning across scales. Extensive experiments on seven real-world datasets demonstrate that MWMixer achieves competitive performance in long-term forecasting.

AI.tldr: MWMixer is a multi-scale model for long-term time series forecasting that uses Bidirectional Frequency-Bands Mixing to recover temporal details lost in downsampling, a Dynamic Scale-Adaptive Fusion for time-varying scale weighting, and cross-scale plus multi-scale losses for consistent learning.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-scale forecasting methods rely on temporal downsampling, which smooths detailed temporal fluctuations. Their emphasis on dominant trends across scales further aggravates this information loss, yielding insufficiently expressive representations.
AI.method: The paper proposes MWMixer with four components: (1) a Bidirectional Frequency-Bands Mixing strategy to recover lost temporal details across scales and enable complementary cross-scale information interaction; (2) a Dynamic Scale-Adaptive Fusion module that learns time-varying weights per scale to fuse multi-scale forecasts; (3) a cross-scale consistency loss aligning each coarse-scale prediction with interval-averaged fine-scale outputs; and (4) a multi-scale supervision loss enforcing accuracy at each scale.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on seven real-world datasets show that MWMixer achieves competitive performance in long-term forecasting.
AI.conclusion: MWMixer addresses the detail-loss problem of downsampling-based multi-scale forecasting by mixing frequency bands and adaptively fusing scales, with consistency and multi-scale supervision losses promoting coherent learning, yielding competitive long-term forecasting performance.

title: STRIDER: Stepping-Enabled Multi-Gait Hierarchical 3D Loco-Manipulation Framework for Humanoid Robots
comment: 9 pages. Submitted to ICRA 2027. Video: https://youtu.be/gf5RWjCZXtA
summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation faces two prominent limitations: controllers using continuous velocity commands cannot precisely regulate individual footholds, while specialized foothold-tracking modules are difficult to integrate with whole-body manipulation. Furthermore, standard action-based imitation distillation primarily transfers expert actions, without explicitly encouraging a shared representation of heterogeneous skills. This paper introduces STRIDER, a hierarchical multi-gait framework to bridge these gaps. The framework integrates terrain-aware 3D stepping logic, Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP)-based natural walking, and Cartesian upper-body control: its stepping expert selects feasible footholds in the stance-foot frame and generates clearance-aware swing trajectories. To fuse distinct walking and stepping experts into one executable student policy, we propose Latent Distillation Proximal Policy Optimization (LD-PPO), a distillation algorithm augmented with teacher-conditioned latent alignment. By jointly optimizing on-policy reinforcement learning, DAgger-based action reconstruction, and latent alignment, LD-PPO transfers expert actions while encouraging a shared skill representation across heterogeneous modes. Simulation and real-robot evaluations on the TianGong Omni humanoid show that LD-PPO outperforms vanilla distillation-PPO in foothold-tracking and posture-tracking accuracy. Deployed on hardware, STRIDER realizes multi-gait loco-manipulation with accurate foothold and end-effector tracking.

AI.tldr: STRIDER is a hierarchical multi-gait framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that combines a terrain-aware stepping expert, AMP-based natural walking, and Cartesian upper-body control, fused via a novel Latent Distillation PPO (LD-PPO) that adds teacher-conditioned latent alignment to standard action distillation.
AI.motivation: Existing humanoid loco-manipulation controllers face two limitations: velocity-command controllers cannot precisely regulate individual footholds, and specialized foothold-tracking modules are hard to integrate with whole-body manipulation. Moreover, standard action-based imitation distillation only transfers expert actions and does not explicitly encourage a shared representation of heterogeneous skills.
AI.method: The framework integrates terrain-aware 3D stepping logic, Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP)-based natural walking, and Cartesian upper-body control; the stepping expert selects feasible footholds in the stance-foot frame and generates clearance-aware swing trajectories. To fuse walking and stepping experts into one student policy, the authors propose LD-PPO, a distillation algorithm augmented with teacher-conditioned latent alignment, jointly optimizing on-policy RL, DAgger-based action reconstruction, and latent alignment.
AI.result: Simulation and real-robot evaluations on the TianGong Omni humanoid show LD-PPO outperforms vanilla distillation-PPO in foothold-tracking and posture-tracking accuracy. On hardware, STRIDER achieves multi-gait loco-manipulation with accurate foothold and end-effector tracking.
AI.conclusion: LD-PPO effectively transfers expert actions while encouraging a shared skill representation across heterogeneous modes, enabling precise multi-gait loco-manipulation on a real humanoid robot.

title: Taming CoT Obfuscation in VLMs: From Mechanistic Evidence to Activation Enforcement
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) but can induce chain-of-thought (CoT) obfuscation: an operational, non-intentional outcome where task reward or accuracy rises while traces become less grounded and monitorable. Prior work largely documents this decay behaviorally, leaving its representation-level correlates and actionable controls unclear. We find that template- and ground-associated activations become less separable during RL; matched interventions support the contribution of selected features to monitorability degradation. Guided by this evidence, we propose Targeted Anti-obfuscation with Mechanistic Enforcement (TAME), which uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to combine behavioral feedback with targeted suppression of template-associated activations during RL. Its asymmetric constraint penalizes template activations only above their pre-RL baseline, anchoring the localized features while behavioral feedback promotes grounded refinements. Across VIRL-39k, SPA-VL, and two model families, TAME improves CoT monitorability by up to 30.9 and 16.7 percentage points over Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), respectively. Blinded human evaluation finds higher human monitorability on both datasets, and two held-out monitor families reproduce the monitorability gains. Task accuracy changes are small and mixed, and general-capability benchmarks show task-specific trade-offs. These results provide a path from behavioral monitoring to representation-level oversight for more auditable RL-trained multimodal systems.

title: Cognitive Action Reasoning for Proactive Robots from Human-Centered Multimodal Observations
summary: Robots operating in human-centered environments are typically designed to execute explicit instructions, and most robot-learning datasets likewise pair observations with task instructions or low-level actions. Although recent work has begun to explore proactive embodied assistance, existing resources target different settings and action levels, leaving real-world human-centered multimodal decision-making underexplored. We formulate this problem as \textit{Proactive Robot Action Reasoning} (\textit{ProRobo}), an upstream cognitive decision problem in which a robot must determine which action to take based on multimodal human and environmental cues without explicit action instructions. To support ProRobo, we introduce \textit{ProAction}, a real-world multimodal dataset containing 10K samples of visual observations, audio signals, and text inputs across 12 daily-life scenarios in five common scenes.
