To construct cognitively grounded high-level action supervision, we develop a two-stage human-in-the-loop pipeline that combines appraisal-guided candidate generation with Affective Theory-of-Mind-guided human refinement, explicitly incorporating contextual judgment about human states, urgency, feasibility, and potential risk into action annotation. Based on this supervision, we benchmark representative Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and introduce \textit{MMC2Act}, a reference model that implicitly learns the mapping from multimodal observations to cognitively grounded high-level actions. Experiments across modality settings, subject-disjoint generalization, cross-dataset transfer, and human evaluation show that general-purpose MLLMs struggle with proactively reasoning high-level actions from multimodal cues, whereas training on \textit{ProAction} substantially improves performance.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates Proactive Robot Action Reasoning (ProRobo), introduces the ProAction real-world multimodal dataset (10K samples, visual/audio/text, 12 scenarios, 5 scenes) with cognitively grounded high-level action supervision, and proposes MMC2Act, a reference model that outperforms general-purpose MLLMs on this task.
AI.motivation: Robots in human-centered environments typically follow explicit instructions, and existing robot-learning datasets pair observations with task instructions or low-level actions. Prior proactive embodied assistance resources target different settings and action levels, leaving real-world human-centered multimodal decision-making underexplored.
AI.method: The authors formulate ProRobo, where a robot determines which action to take from multimodal human and environmental cues without explicit action instructions. They introduce ProAction, a dataset of 10K samples spanning visual observations, audio signals, and text inputs across 12 daily-life scenarios in five scenes. Supervision is built via a two-stage human-in-the-loop pipeline combining appraisal-guided candidate generation with Affective Theory-of-Mind-guided human refinement, encoding context about human states, urgency, feasibility, and potential risk. They benchmark representative MLLMs and introduce MMC2Act, a reference model that implicitly learns the mapping from multimodal observations to cognitively grounded high-level actions.
AI.result: Experiments across modality settings, subject-disjoint generalization, cross-dataset transfer, and human evaluation show that general-purpose MLLMs struggle to proactively reason high-level actions from multimodal cues, whereas training on ProAction substantially improves performance.
AI.conclusion: Real-world human-centered multimodal decision-making for proactive robot assistance is underexplored; the proposed ProRobo formulation, ProAction dataset, and MMC2Act model provide a foundation, demonstrating that task-specific training markedly enhances proactive high-level action reasoning compared with general-purpose MLLMs.

title: Unsupervised Brain Anomaly Detection as a Bayesian Inverse Problem with Diffusion Prior
summary: Unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) aims to localize abnormal regions in medical scans without pixel-level annotations. A typical strategy seeks to reconstruct a pseudo-healthy image that preserves subject-specific anatomy. Recently, diffusion models have been proposed to perform UAD. However, these methods rely on heuristic noise schedules or synthetic corruptions to balance subject-specificity and anomaly removal. In this work, we propose an alternative formulation of UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem under a diffusion prior. First, we introduce a latent spatial anomaly mask that models pixel-wise consistency between a test image and its latent corresponding pseudo-healthy image. Then, we propose an approximation of the unknown generation process that links healthy anatomy, anomalies, and the observed image, enabling a well-defined likelihood within the Bayesian framework. Building on recent advances in diffusion-based inverse problem methods, we jointly infer the pseudo-healthy image and the anomaly mask via annealed posterior sampling. We evaluate our approach on FDG PET (ADNI) and FLAIR MRI (BraTS 2021), demonstrating improved anomaly localization performance compared to other diffusion-based approaches and validating the contribution of our introduced model. Our code is available at https://github.com/HuguesRoy/UAD_DAPS.

AI.tldr: This paper reformulates unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) in medical imaging as a Bayesian inverse problem under a diffusion prior, jointly inferring a pseudo-healthy image and a latent spatial anomaly mask via annealed posterior sampling.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based UAD methods rely on heuristic noise schedules or synthetic corruptions to balance subject-specificity and anomaly removal, lacking a principled formulation.
AI.method: Introduces a latent spatial anomaly mask modeling pixel-wise consistency between the test image and its pseudo-healthy counterpart; proposes an approximation of the unknown generation process linking healthy anatomy, anomalies, and the observed image to define a likelihood; jointly infers the pseudo-healthy image and anomaly mask through annealed posterior sampling.
AI.result: Evaluated on FDG PET (ADNI) and FLAIR MRI (BraTS 2021), demonstrating improved anomaly localization performance over other diffusion-based approaches and validating the introduced model's contribution.
AI.conclusion: Framing UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem with a diffusion prior enables principled joint inference of pseudo-healthy images and anomaly masks, outperforming heuristic diffusion-based alternatives.

title: Design and Control of a Cable-Driven Switchable Actuator with Torque/Tension Dual Modes for Exoskeletons
summary: Existing wearable exoskeleton architectures are typically constrained by a single mechanical output modality, providing either joint torque around an anatomical joint or linear traction along a limb-training-oriented direction, which limits adaptability to diverse training scenarios. This letter presents a cable-driven switchable actuator (CDSA) that can rapidly switch between torque and tension modes while centralizing all sensing and actuation components at the proximal drive unit. A Coupled Movable Pulley Mechanism (CMPM) provides tension amplification at the distal end-effector, while a bidirectional Cable-Driven Ratchet Mechanism (CDRM) enables mode switching and preload regulation. To eliminate the need for distal instrumentation, multi-source proximal sensors are integrated with a data-driven fusion model to estimate distal output forces. An adaptive dual-mode force control strategy based on iterative learning control (ILC) is further developed. Platform experiments demonstrate transmission efficiencies of $(92.4 \pm 2.0)\%$ and $(96.5 \pm 3.3)\%$ in the torque and tension modes, respectively, along with a tension amplification ratio of $2.77 \pm 0.10$ under tension mode. Tracking tests on simulated knee-joint gait trajectories and short-stroke tension profiles yield stable control, with RMSEs of $(4.52 \pm 0.51)\%$ and $(3.15 \pm 0.19)\%$ of the uncontrolled peak value, respectively. Finally, seated human-coupled experiments validate the system's controllable force generation in both joint-torque and linear-traction application modes.

AI.tldr: This letter proposes a cable-driven switchable actuator (CDSA) that can rapidly switch between torque and tension modes, centralizing all sensing/actuation proximally, enabling adaptive dual-mode force control validated on a platform and in seated human-coupled experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing wearable exoskeleton architectures are typically constrained by a single mechanical output modality, providing either joint torque around an anatomical joint or linear traction along a limb-training-oriented direction, which limits adaptability to diverse training scenarios. A single-modality actuator cannot accommodate varied training needs, motivating a reconfigurable output actuator.
AI.method: The proposed CDSA switches rapidly between torque and tension modes with all sensing and actuation centralized at the proximal drive unit. A Coupled Movable Pulley Mechanism (CMPM) provides distal tension amplification, and a bidirectional Cable-Driven Ratchet Mechanism (CDRM) enables mode switching and preload regulation. Distal instrumentation is eliminated via multi-source proximal sensors integrated with a data-driven fusion model to estimate distal output forces. An adaptive dual-mode force control strategy based on iterative learning control (ILC) is developed.
AI.result: Platform experiments show transmission efficiencies of (92.4 ± 2.0)% (torque) and (96.5 ± 3.3)% (tension), and a tension amplification ratio of 2.77 ± 0.10 in tension mode. Tracking simulated knee-joint gait trajectories and short-stroke tension profiles yields stable control with RMSEs of (4.52 ± 0.51)% and (3.15 ± 0.19)% of the uncontrolled peak value, respectively. Seated human-coupled experiments validate controllable force generation in both joint-torque and linear-traction modes.
AI.conclusion: The CDSA successfully achieves rapid dual-mode switching with high transmission efficiency, effective tension amplification, and stable ILC-based dual-mode force control. Proximal-only sensing with data-driven fusion eliminates distal instrumentation, and human-coupled validation confirms the system's controllable force generation in both joint-torque and linear-traction application modes.

title: How Many Pixels Is a Digit Worth? Place-Aware Coordinate Entropy for GUI Agent Confidence Estimation
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference)
summary: GUI agents predict click coordinates as digit-token sequences, but standard text-LLM confidence estimation methods rank correct clicks from wrong ones only weakly. GUI-specific alternatives use K samples or new supervision, but still leave room for improvement. We trace part of this to place-value asymmetry: bounding-box correctness often makes higher-place digits more important than lower-place digits, so uniform aggregation weakens the signal that determines correctness. The fix is to weight each digit's Shannon entropy by its place value. We call this Place-Aware Coordinate Entropy (PACE). Across fixed-scale agents on ScreenSpot-Pro and ScreenSpot-v2, PACE wins both AUROC and selective accuracy on all primary comparisons in a single forward pass, matching or outperforming K-sample baselines at a fraction of the cost. PACE provides a per-click confidence estimate that turns coordinate-token internals into a practical confidence signal for GUI agent deployment.

AI.tldr: PACE (Place-Aware Coordinate Entropy) weights each coordinate digit's Shannon entropy by its place value, yielding a per-click confidence estimate that improves AUROC and selective accuracy for GUI agents in a single forward pass.
AI.motivation: GUI agents predict click coordinates as digit-token sequences, but standard text-LLM confidence estimation only weakly separates correct from incorrect clicks. Existing GUI-specific alternatives rely on K samples or new supervision and remain suboptimal. Part of the issue is place-value asymmetry: bounding-box correctness often makes higher-place digits more important than lower-place ones, so uniform aggregation of digit uncertainties dilutes the signal that determines correctness.
AI.method: The authors propose Place-Aware Coordinate Entropy (PACE), which weights each digit's Shannon entropy by its place value before aggregating into a per-click confidence estimate. It operates in a single forward pass without extra samples or supervision.
AI.result: Across fixed-scale agents on ScreenSpot-Pro and ScreenSpot-v2, PACE achieves higher AUROC and selective accuracy than baselines on all primary comparisons, matching or outperforming K-sample baselines at a fraction of the cost.
AI.conclusion: PACE converts coordinate-token internals into a practical per-click confidence signal for GUI agent deployment, offering a cheap, single-pass alternative to sampling-based confidence estimation.

title: FeasibleFlow: One-Step Joint Transport of Configuration Feasibility and Trajectories for End-to-End Driving
summary: End-to-end autonomous driving maps current observations directly to future trajectories, yet those trajectories must remain valid as the scene evolves. Future state modeling aims to address this temporal mismatch, but general representations often contain information unrelated to ego planning and affect trajectory generation only through auxiliary supervision, static conditioning, or proposal evaluation. We propose FeasibleFlow, a one-step end-to-end generative framework that jointly transports a configuration-space feasibility field and multimodal ego trajectories. Our Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow uses the pathwise Jacobian-vector product in the MeanFlow identity to incorporate field evolution into trajectory transport. Because safety feedback is sparser than progress feedback, we further introduce the Anchor-relative ranker (ARR) and Pareto-ReinFlow to balance safety and progress in candidate selection and generation, respectively. Experiments on the NAVSIM benchmark demonstrate the strong performance of FeasibleFlow and validate both the joint transport of feasibility and trajectories and the proposed safety-first mechanisms.

AI.tldr: FeasibleFlow is a one-step end-to-end generative framework for autonomous driving that jointly transports a configuration-space feasibility field and multimodal ego trajectories, improving temporal validity via Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow, and balancing safety and progress with Anchor-relative ranker and Pareto-ReinFlow.
AI.motivation: End-to-end autonomous driving maps current observations directly to future trajectories, but these trajectories must stay valid as the scene evolves. Existing future state modeling suffers from a temporal mismatch, and general representations often carry planning-irrelevant information and influence trajectory generation only through auxiliary supervision, static conditioning, or proposal evaluation.
AI.method: FeasibleFlow jointly transports a configuration-space feasibility field and multimodal ego trajectories in a one-step generative framework. Its Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow leverages the pathwise Jacobian-vector product in the MeanFlow identity to incorporate field evolution into trajectory transport. To address sparser safety feedback relative to progress feedback, the Anchor-relative ranker (ARR) and Pareto-ReinFlow are introduced for candidate selection and generation respectively.
AI.result: Experiments on the NAVSIM benchmark demonstrate strong performance of FeasibleFlow and validate both the joint transport of feasibility and trajectories and the proposed safety-first mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: FeasibleFlow effectively couples feasibility-field evolution with trajectory transport, and the proposed safety-first mechanisms (ARR and Pareto-ReinFlow) successfully balance safety and progress, as confirmed by NAVSIM benchmark results.

title: When and How Should an Agent Clarify? CIGAsk: Teaching LLMs to Clarify via Counterfactual Information Gain
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Findings)
summary: Instruction-tuned LLMs faced with underspecified queries often commit to a single interpretation rather than ask for clarification, producing confidently wrong answers. In our experiments, prompting alone is insufficient: models either ask for clarification on every query or ask vague questions that fail to recover the missing information. Addressing this failure requires learning two coupled skills: when to ask rather than answer and how to ask a question that recovers the disambiguating information. Existing recipes either address only one of these skills or require a separately trained critic. We propose CIGAsk, an RL recipe that teaches both skills through two complementary reward signals within a multi-turn GRPO loop. Counterfactual Information Gain (CIG) compares the gold-answer log-likelihood under a frozen reference model with and without the user response, providing per-turn credit that guides how to ask. The Asymmetric Ambiguity Bonus assigns a signed reward at the terminal token based on the gold ambiguity label, guiding when to ask. Across three clarification benchmarks spanning table, passage, and open-domain QA, CIGAsk-7B outperforms the strongest external baseline despite using a smaller backbone. It also transfers across datasets without per-dataset tuning while preserving single-turn QA performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

AI.tldr: CIGAsk is an RL recipe that teaches LLMs both when to ask clarifying questions and how to ask them, using two complementary rewards in a multi-turn GRPO loop, outperforming larger baselines across clarification benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Instruction-tuned LLMs facing underspecified queries tend to commit to a single interpretation, producing confidently wrong answers. Prompting alone fails: models either ask for clarification on every query or ask vague questions that fail to recover missing information. Solving this requires learning two coupled skills—when to ask versus answer, and how to ask a question that recovers disambiguating information. Existing approaches address only one skill or require a separately trained critic.
AI.method: CIGAsk is a reinforcement learning recipe using a multi-turn GRPO loop with two complementary reward signals. Counterfactual Information Gain (CIG) compares the gold-answer log-likelihood under a frozen reference model with and without the user response, yielding per-turn credit that guides how to ask. The Asymmetric Ambiguity Bonus assigns a signed terminal reward based on the gold ambiguity label, guiding when to ask.
AI.result: Across three clarification benchmarks covering table, passage, and open-domain QA, CIGAsk-7B outperforms the strongest external baseline despite using a smaller backbone. It transfers across datasets without per-dataset tuning while preserving single-turn QA performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Integrating per-turn credit (CIG) with a terminal ambiguity signal (Asymmetric Ambiguity Bonus) in a GRPO loop jointly learns when and how to ask clarifying questions, yielding a smaller model that generalizes across datasets and preserves single-turn QA ability.

title: Elevator-VIGS: Separating Elevator Motion from Robot Motion in Visual-Inertial Gaussian Splatting SLAM
summary: We present Elevator-VIGS, a visual-inertial 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM system that keeps tracking and mapping through elevator rides. Inside a moving elevator, the two sensors are in conflict. The camera sees only the robot's motion relative to the elevator, while the IMU senses that motion plus the elevator's motion relative to the world. This conflict is challenging for existing visual-inertial estimators. If vision dominates, the estimator tracks only the robot's motion within the elevator and misses the elevator's rise, and if the conflict remains, the estimator diverges. We observe that the conflict comes from forcing both observations into a single coordinate frame. We instead estimate the robot's pose in the elevator's coordinate frame, and the elevator's motion relative to the world as a per-keyframe transport state, the elevator's rise and vertical velocity, within dense visual-inertial bundle adjustment. Elevator-VIGS detects rides zero-shot with a vision-language model and a depth network, and constrains the transport state at the departure and the arrival. We record real-world and simulated elevator sequences. On these sequences, Elevator-VIGS achieves state-of-the-art tracking and rendering performance. On four elevator-free public benchmarks it keeps the state-of-the-art performance of VIGS-SLAM. Project page: https://ruizhou-cn.github.io/elevator-vigs/.

AI.tldr: Elevator-VIGS is a visual-inertial 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM system that maintains tracking and mapping during elevator rides by resolving the camera-IMU frame conflict via a per-keyframe transport state within dense visual-inertial bundle adjustment.
AI.motivation: Inside a moving elevator, camera and IMU observations conflict: the camera perceives only the robot's motion relative to the elevator, while the IMU senses that motion plus the elevator's motion relative to the world. Existing visual-inertial estimators fail—if vision dominates, the elevator's rise is missed; if the conflict persists, the estimator diverges. The paper identifies this conflict as stemming from forcing both observations into a single coordinate frame.
AI.method: The authors estimate the robot's pose in the elevator's coordinate frame and model the elevator's motion relative to the world as a per-keyframe transport state (elevator's rise and vertical velocity) within dense visual-inertial bundle adjustment. Elevator-VIGS detects rides zero-shot using a vision-language model and a depth network, and constrains the transport state at departure and arrival.
AI.result: On recorded real-world and simulated elevator sequences, Elevator-VIGS achieves state-of-the-art tracking and rendering performance. On four elevator-free public benchmarks, it retains the state-of-the-art performance of VIGS-SLAM.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling the robot's in-elevator pose from the elevator's world-frame motion as a transport state within bundle adjustment resolves the visual-inertial conflict, enabling robust SLAM through elevator rides without sacrificing performance in elevator-free scenarios.

title: Brain-Token Learning: Microstate-Based Tokenization and Multi-Scale Interaction for Long-Horizon EEG Sequence Modeling
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive window into dynamic brain activity, yet modeling long-horizon EEG sequences remains challenging due to their high temporal complexity, substantial variability across subjects, and the lack of biologically meaningful sequence representations. Existing tokenization strategies, such as fixed-window and patch-based representations, discretize EEG signals according to artificial temporal boundaries, which may disrupt intrinsic brain-state dynamics. In this work, we propose Brain-Token Learning, a neuroscience-inspired framework that introduces Brain Tokenization for long-horizon EEG sequence modeling. Instead of partitioning EEG signals into predefined temporal segments, Brain Tokenization represents EEG as sequences of recurrent microstate-derived brain tokens, where each token corresponds to a quasi-stable large-scale brain state with variable temporal duration. Based on these biologically grounded tokens, we further develop a multi-scale token interaction module consisting of Latent State Aggregation and State Transition Modeling to jointly capture global brain-state context and local microstate transitions. We evaluate Brain-Token on five heterogeneous EEG datasets, including the newly collected long-horizon NeuroLong dataset and four affective or clinical EEG datasets (SEED, DEAP, MDD, and NSSI). Extensive experiments demonstrate that Brain-Token consistently outperforms conventional CNN/LSTM architectures, Transformer-based models, and domain adaptation methods across diverse EEG scenarios. Further analysis verifies the effectiveness of microstate-based tokenization and multi-scale interaction for learning robust and interpretable EEG representations. These results establish Brain-Token as a biologically grounded tokenization paradigm for long-horizon EEG sequence modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Brain-Token Learning, a neuroscience-inspired framework that tokenizes long-horizon EEG as sequences of recurrent microstate-derived brain tokens (variable-duration quasi-stable brain states), coupled with a multi-scale token interaction module (Latent State Aggregation and State Transition Modeling), achieving consistent gains over CNN/LSTM, Transformer, and domain adaptation baselines on five EEG datasets.
AI.motivation: Modeling long-horizon EEG is difficult due to high temporal complexity, substantial inter-subject variability, and the absence of biologically meaningful sequence representations. Existing tokenization strategies (fixed-window and patch-based) discretize EEG along artificial temporal boundaries, which can disrupt intrinsic brain-state dynamics.
AI.method: Brain Tokenization replaces predefined temporal segmentation with sequences of recurrent microstate-derived brain tokens, each corresponding to a quasi-stable large-scale brain state of variable duration. On top of these biologically grounded tokens, a multi-scale token interaction module is built, comprising Latent State Aggregation (global brain-state context) and State Transition Modeling (local microstate transitions).
AI.result: Evaluated on five heterogeneous EEG datasets—the newly collected long-horizon NeuroLong dataset plus four affective/clinical datasets (SEED, DEAP, MDD, NSSI)—Brain-Token consistently outperforms conventional CNN/LSTM architectures, Transformer-based models, and domain adaptation methods. Ablations/analyses confirm the contribution of microstate-based tokenization and multi-scale interaction to robust, interpretable EEG representations.
AI.conclusion: Brain-Token establishes a biologically grounded tokenization paradigm for long-horizon EEG sequence modeling, with empirical evidence supporting its effectiveness and interpretability across diverse EEG scenarios.

title: Imagine then Verify: Affordance-Targeted Active Perception for Task-Oriented Grasping in Cluttered Scenes
summary: Task-oriented grasping (TOG) requires robots to grasp functional parts of objects (e.g., the handle of a mug for pouring), yet these affordance regions are frequently occluded in cluttered scenes. Active perception via next-best-view (NBV) planning can resolve such occlusions by moving the camera for more informative observations. However, existing NBV methods typically optimize viewpoints for grasping the target object as a whole without distinguishing which part is task-relevant. A naive adaptation, fully scanning the target object before predicting the affordance, wastes most of the viewpoint budget on task-irrelevant surfaces (e.g., the mug body for pouring). To address this, we propose ATAP, an Affordance-Targeted Active Perception framework that shifts viewpoint planning from exhaustive target scanning to targeted affordance verification. ATAP hypothesizes the occluded target geometry via a generative shape prior and predicts the affordance distribution over the imagined complete surface. In cluttered scenes, severe occlusion can make the location of the hidden affordance ambiguous, leaving multiple locations plausible given the partial observation. ATAP therefore introduces an uncertainty-aware viewpoint planner that jointly optimizes expected entropy reduction over these competing hypotheses and expected affordance verification gain from real observations. This process iterates until the affordance is sufficiently verified for grasp execution. Experiments in simulation and real-world cluttered scenes show that ATAP substantially improves the functional grasp success rate over fixed-view TOG baselines, and outperforms reconstruction-based active perception with over 57% fewer NBV steps.

AI.tldr: ATAP is an affordance-targeted active perception framework for task-oriented grasping in clutter that shifts next-best-view planning from exhaustive object scanning to targeted affordance verification via generative shape priors and uncertainty-aware viewpoint planning.
AI.motivation: Task-oriented grasping requires grasping functional parts (e.g., a mug handle), but these affordance regions are often occluded in cluttered scenes. Existing NBV methods optimize viewpoints for the target object as a whole and ignore which part is task-relevant, so naive affordance-based adaptation wastes the viewpoint budget scanning task-irrelevant surfaces like the mug body.
AI.method: ATAP hypothesizes the occluded target geometry with a generative shape prior and predicts the affordance distribution over the imagined complete surface. It introduces an uncertainty-aware viewpoint planner that jointly optimizes expected entropy reduction over competing affordance-location hypotheses and expected affordance verification gain from real observations, iterating until the affordance is sufficiently verified for grasp execution.
AI.result: In simulation and real-world cluttered scenes, ATAP substantially improves the functional grasp success rate over fixed-view TOG baselines and outperforms reconstruction-based active perception with over 57% fewer NBV steps.
AI.conclusion: Targeting viewpoint planning at affordance verification rather than exhaustive object reconstruction makes active perception for task-oriented grasping significantly more efficient and effective in cluttered environments.

title: LADDER: Graph-Guided Diffusion Language Models for Efficient Multi-Hop Reasoning
summary: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) has remarkably enhanced large language models on complex reasoning by leveraging structured entity topologies. However, existing frameworks heavily rely on standard autoregressive language models where the nature of inherent sequential generation severely hinders overall inference efficiency. Inspired by Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) that offer massive parallelism via continuous refine-in-parallel decoding, we aim to accelerate GraphRAG in the discrete space. However, it remains non-trivial for two challenges. First, partially denoised drafts are highly dynamic and uncertain, making dynamic graph grounding non-trivial. Second, raw denoising states are inherently noisy and unstable, making synchronous graph retrieval and multi-hop aggregation computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present LADDER, a novel framework that bridges diffusion language modeling with GraphRAG through graph-guided parallel decoding. Specifically, (i) we propose an event-driven self-clocking retrieval, inspired by our key insight that 88% of target entities emerge early in the partially denoised state, leading final commitment by an average of 5.7-9.6 steps. This mechanism dynamically triggers graph retrieval only when the set of graph-linkable entities expands, yielding an asynchronous self-clocking policy that bypasses learned gates or heuristic thresholds. (ii) An incomplete-query graph propagation module is designed to process the newly emerging entity queries using a specialized graph foundation model, continuously aggregating multi-hop evidence to sharpen parallel predictions and accelerate overall decoding convergence. Extensive experiments on three challenging multi-hop QA benchmarks show that LADDER raises average exact match from 39.6% to 45.2% while achieving a 4.1x latency reduction.

AI.tldr: LADDER bridges diffusion language models with GraphRAG via graph-guided parallel decoding, using event-driven self-clocking retrieval and incomplete-query graph propagation to improve accuracy and cut latency.
AI.motivation: Existing GraphRAG frameworks rely on autoregressive language models whose inherently sequential generation limits inference efficiency. Diffusion Language Models offer massive parallelism through continuous refine-in-parallel decoding, but applying them to GraphRAG in discrete space is non-trivial due to two challenges: (1) partially denoised drafts are highly dynamic and uncertain, complicating dynamic graph grounding; (2) raw denoising states are noisy and unstable, making synchronous graph retrieval and multi-hop aggregation computationally prohibitive.
AI.method: LADDER (i) proposes an event-driven self-clocking retrieval mechanism, based on the insight that 88% of target entities emerge early in the partially denoised state, advancing final commitment by 5.7-9.6 steps on average. This dynamically triggers graph retrieval only when the set of graph-linkable entities expands, forming an asynchronous self-clocking policy that avoids learned gates or heuristic thresholds. (ii) It designs an incomplete-query graph propagation module that handles newly emerging entity queries using a specialized graph foundation model, continuously aggregating multi-hop evidence to sharpen parallel predictions and accelerate decoding convergence.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three challenging multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that LADDER raises average exact match from 39.6% to 45.2% while achieving a 4.1x latency reduction.
AI.conclusion: LADDER successfully integrates diffusion language modeling with GraphRAG through graph-guided parallel decoding, simultaneously improving reasoning accuracy and inference efficiency.

title: PINGU: Extending Air-Bearing Spacecraft Emulators with Open-Source Actuators and Learned Control for Contact-Rich Proximity Operations
summary: Low-cost planar air-bearing testbeds have matured into a standard proxy for free-flying spacecraft GNC, but they remain largely thruster-only and are rarely equipped for contact-rich, inertia-coupled manipulation. Building on the open-source ATMOS testbed, we contribute a reaction wheel and two force/torque-sensed robotic arms (LEVION) with interchangeable end-effectors, integrated as first-class control actuators through a unified ROS 2 abstraction layer. On top of the software stack we build a reinforcement-learning training environment and digital twin, and a controller that exploits these added degrees of freedom, letting classical optimal controllers and learned policies be swapped on the same hardware without modification. We validate the integrated system, PINGU, across four benchmark tasks: point-to-pose navigation (classical LQR vs. sim-to-real PPO), dynamic disturbance rejection under arm-induced center-of-mass shifts, reaction-wheel momentum stabilization, and force-controlled docking. The results show that these additions extend an ATMOS-class emulator into the contact-rich regime and bridge classical optimal control and reinforcement learning on one reproducible platform.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the open-source ATMOS planar air-bearing testbed into PINGU by adding a reaction wheel and two force/torque-sensed robotic arms (LEVION) with interchangeable end-effectors, unified through a ROS 2 abstraction layer, and validates the platform across four benchmark tasks spanning classical optimal control and sim-to-real reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Low-cost planar air-bearing testbeds are a standard proxy for free-flying spacecraft GNC but remain largely thruster-only and are rarely equipped for contact-rich, inertia-coupled manipulation. There is a need to extend such emulators beyond thruster-only operation and to bridge classical optimal control with reinforcement learning on a single reproducible platform.
AI.method: Building on the open-source ATMOS testbed, the authors add a reaction wheel and two force/torque-sensed robotic arms (LEVION) with interchangeable end-effectors, integrated as first-class control actuators via a unified ROS 2 abstraction layer. On top of this software stack they build a reinforcement-learning training environment and digital twin, plus a controller exploiting the added degrees of freedom, enabling classical optimal controllers and learned policies to be swapped on the same hardware without modification.
AI.result: The integrated system, PINGU, is validated across four benchmark tasks: point-to-pose navigation (classical LQR vs. sim-to-real PPO), dynamic disturbance rejection under arm-induced center-of-mass shifts, reaction-wheel momentum stabilization, and force-controlled docking. The additions successfully extend an ATMOS-class emulator into the contact-rich regime and bridge classical optimal control and reinforcement learning on one reproducible platform.
AI.conclusion: The added reaction wheel and force/torque-sensed arms, unified under a ROS 2 abstraction layer, extend an ATMOS-class planar air-bearing emulator into the contact-rich regime and provide a reproducible platform bridging classical optimal control and reinforcement learning.

title: Few-Shot Demonstrations Elicit the Use of In-Context World Representations in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs), when acting as agents, are expected to take observed data in context, infer the latent state space underlying the world, and leverage it for downstream prediction. However, prior work demonstrated that LLMs struggle to use representations learned in context on a graph tracking task, where the model needs to construct a representation of the graph governing data generation process and use it for subsequent predictions. In this paper, we show that extending this to few-shot settings, where each demonstration is generated from a different world with either the same or different graph topologies, enhances its prediction on 6 models from 4 model families. To understand this improvement, we linearly probe a low-dimensional world representation that encodes graph information in the hidden states. Notably, we find that few-shot demonstrations relocate the world representation and increase its predictive use. Specifically, for each model, these world representations shift in directions nearly orthogonal to their original subspace, and interventions on these representations selectively impair performance more than interventions on other subspaces. Consistent with this insight, we show that few-shot demonstrations with observations from different worlds improve performance on ARC-AGI-1&2, web agent tasks, and Othello. Our findings elucidate the role and internal mechanisms of few-shot demonstrations in in-context world modeling. More broadly, our work advances our understanding of how LLM agents learn from in-context observations and provides implications for their further improvement.

AI.tldr: Extending few-shot demonstrations from different worlds (same or different graph topologies) improves LLMs' in-context world modeling on a graph tracking task, and mechanistic probing reveals that demonstrations relocate the world representation into a nearly orthogonal subspace and increase its predictive use.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are expected to infer latent world structure from in-context observations and use it for prediction, but prior work showed they fail to reuse in-context graph representations on a graph tracking task. This paper investigates whether few-shot demonstrations can remedy this and seeks to explain the underlying internal mechanism.
AI.method: The authors extend the graph tracking task to few-shot settings where each demonstration is generated from a different world with the same or different graph topologies, testing 6 models from 4 model families. They then linearly probe a low-dimensional world representation encoding graph information in hidden states and perform subspace interventions to test causal use.
AI.result: Few-shot demonstrations enhance prediction across all 6 models. Probing shows demonstrations relocate the world representation into directions nearly orthogonal to its original subspace and increase its predictive use; interventions on these representations selectively impair performance more than on other subspaces. Few-shot demonstrations with observations from different worlds also improve performance on ARC-AGI-1&2, web agent tasks, and Othello.
AI.conclusion: Few-shot demonstrations play a key role in in-context world modeling by relocating and amplifying the model's internal world representation, clarifying the internal mechanisms by which LLM agents learn from in-context observations and offering implications for their further improvement.

title: AR-WAM: A Visual-Conditioned Agent-Ready World Action Model for Robotic Manipulation
summary: As AI agents become increasingly capable, agent-driven robotic control is emerging as a compelling paradigm. However, prevailing vision-language-action (VLA) models and world action models (WAMs) still rely on natural-language instructions to specify manipulation tasks, an ill-suited interface for agent-driven control: referentially ambiguous, spatially imprecise, redundant with the agent's inherent language understanding, and entangling intent with execution. We present AR-WAM, a visual-conditioned, agent-ready world action model that replaces language with two complementary conditions: a visual grounding prompt (a bounding box of the target) denoting the interaction object and location, and a learnable operation token dictating the atomic skill to execute. Our compact 0.5B-parameter model, with a frozen pretrained visual encoder and no language encoder, predicts scene evolution within compact latent states while decoding actions, exposing the policy's intent through explicit, supervisable reasoning signals. A model-agnostic compatibility layer provides three primitives (detect, execute, and query) so that local VLMs or online agent APIs can drive the policy directly, with long-horizon memory and closed-loop error recovery delegated to the agent side. On RoboTwin 2.0, RMBench, and a real Astribot S1 dual-arm platform, AR-WAM matches the strongest baselines on standard manipulation (87.2% average success) and outperforms them on memory-dependent and real-robot long-horizon tasks, improving success rates by 5.9% and 36.7%, respectively, while maintaining the lowest inference latency (14.1 ms).

AI.tldr: AR-WAM is a visual-conditioned world action model that replaces natural-language instructions with a bounding-box grounding prompt and a learnable operation token, enabling compact agent-ready robotic control.
AI.motivation: Prevailing VLA models and world action models rely on natural-language instructions, which are an ill-suited interface for agent-driven control: referentially ambiguous, spatially imprecise, redundant with the agent's inherent language understanding, and entangling intent with execution.
AI.method: AR-WAM is a 0.5B-parameter visual-conditioned world action model with a frozen pretrained visual encoder and no language encoder. It uses two conditions: a visual grounding prompt (target bounding box) and a learnable operation token specifying the atomic skill. It predicts scene evolution in compact latent states while decoding actions, exposing intent via explicit supervisable reasoning signals. A model-agnostic compatibility layer provides detect, execute, and query primitives, letting local VLMs or online agent APIs drive the policy, with long-horizon memory and closed-loop error recovery delegated to the agent.
AI.result: On RoboTwin 2.0, RMBench, and a real Astribot S1 dual-arm platform, AR-WAM matches the strongest baselines on standard manipulation (87.2% average success) and outperforms them on memory-dependent and real-robot long-horizon tasks by 5.9% and 36.7%, respectively, with the lowest inference latency (14.1 ms).
AI.conclusion: A visual-conditioned, compact, agent-ready world action model without language encoding can match or exceed language-conditioned baselines while offering lower latency and better long-horizon performance, positioning visual grounding plus skill tokens as an effective interface for agent-driven robotic control.

title: VLM-in-Sandbox: Visual Workspaces for Agentic Visual Reasoning
summary: Sandboxed computer environments support multi-step reasoning with tools, executable programs, and persistent files, yet their extension from language models to vision-language models (VLMs) introduces a distinct state-management problem. Visual reasoning produces intermediate image-valued evidence---crops, masks, overlays, zoomed regions, and analytic renderings---that must remain addressable without accumulating unboundedly in multimodal context. We introduce VLM-in-Sandbox, a training-free framework for agentic multimodal reasoning in controlled computer environments. Its Visual Workspace registers generated artifacts in an image ledger, maintains a bounded active visual context, and lets the model explicitly promote selected evidence for subsequent inspection. This separates visual evidence generation, performed by sandbox tools, from visual evidence management. Across seven benchmarks and four base VLMs, VLM-in-Sandbox achieves the highest sample-weighted average accuracy among Vanilla VLM, Append-only Sandbox, and the proposed method. A compiler-matched $2\times2$ study on 1,260 examples further separates model-directed visibility from bounded retention: VLM-in-Sandbox reaches 66.27% accuracy with 18.6% fewer total tokens than the automatic, retain-all control. Over all 6,350 submitted GPT-4.1-mini examples, it produces 302 rescues and 142 regressions relative to Original Append-only. A local vLLM study with prefix caching confirms that the smaller request workload also reduces uncached tokens, time to first token, and end-to-end latency. These results identify explicit visual evidence state as a central abstraction for sandboxed VLM agents.

AI.tldr: VLM-in-Sandbox is a training-free framework that manages image-valued intermediate evidence in sandboxed vision-language agents via a bounded Visual Workspace with an image ledger and explicit promotion, outperforming vanilla and append-only baselines while reducing tokens and latency.
AI.motivation: Extending sandboxed tool-use environments from language models to VLMs creates a state-management problem: visual reasoning yields many intermediate image artifacts (crops, masks, overlays, zoomed regions, renderings) that must stay addressable without unboundedly growing the multimodal context.
AI.method: A training-free agentic framework for multimodal reasoning in controlled computer environments. The Visual Workspace registers generated artifacts in an image ledger, keeps a bounded active visual context, and lets the model explicitly promote selected evidence for later inspection, separating visual-evidence generation (sandbox tools) from visual-evidence management.
AI.result: Highest sample-weighted average accuracy across seven benchmarks and four base VLMs versus Vanilla VLM and Append-only Sandbox. A compiler-matched 2x2 study on 1,260 examples shows 66.27% accuracy with 18.6% fewer tokens than the retain-all control. On 6,350 GPT-4.1-mini examples: 302 rescues and 142 regressions vs. Original Append-only. Local vLLM prefix-caching study confirms fewer uncached tokens, lower time to first token, and lower end-to-end latency.
AI.conclusion: Explicit visual evidence state is a central abstraction for sandboxed VLM agents.

title: TaskAnchor: Grounding Task State in Reactive VLAs for Long-Horizon Manipulation
summary: Reactive vision--language--action (VLA) models struggle with long-horizon manipulation when visually similar observations can correspond to different actions depending on the task stage or interaction history. We refer to this ambiguity as task-state aliasing and introduce TaskAnchor, a lightweight adapter that grounds pretrained VLAs in execution history. TaskAnchor combines history-conditioned visual refinement with a milestone-supervised task-state coordinate, a scalar representing the semantic stage of execution. These signals are injected through the native visual and language interfaces, respectively, without introducing an explicit planner or modifying the action-generation mechanism. On RMBench, TaskAnchor achieves approximately 4.9--5.5$\times$ the average success rates of the published $π_{0.5}$ and X-VLA baselines, with consistent gains on RoboMemArena and real robots. The added latency is only 2.08\,ms per action chunk for $π_{0.5}$.

AI.tldr: TaskAnchor is a lightweight adapter that grounds pretrained VLA models in execution history via history-conditioned visual refinement and a milestone-supervised scalar task-state coordinate, substantially improving long-horizon manipulation success.
AI.motivation: Reactive VLA models fail at long-horizon manipulation due to task-state aliasing, where visually similar observations map to different actions depending on the task stage or interaction history.
AI.method: TaskAnchor combines history-conditioned visual refinement with a milestone-supervised task-state coordinate (a scalar encoding the semantic execution stage), injected through the native visual and language interfaces respectively, without an explicit planner or modifying the action-generation mechanism.
AI.result: On RMBench, TaskAnchor reaches roughly 4.9-5.5x the average success rates of published π0.5 and X-VLA baselines, with consistent gains on RoboMemArena and real robots; added latency is only 2.08 ms per action chunk for π0.5.
AI.conclusion: Grounding pretrained VLAs in execution history through a lightweight adapter effectively resolves task-state aliasing, yielding large and consistent long-horizon manipulation improvements at minimal computational cost.

title: Predicting Postprandial Glycemic Response from Meal Images, Clinical Variables, and Gut Microbiome Information
comment: 11 pages (9 text + 2 references). This is a paper first submitted to MICCAI 2026 MultiTab workshop prior to peer review. The final revised version will be published in Springer LNCS proceedings after the MICCAI 2026 conference
summary: Predicting postprandial glycemic response (PPGR) is fundamental to personalized nutrition and type 2 diabetes management, yet existing approaches typically rely on manually reported dietary intake, limiting their scalability in free-living settings. We propose a multimodal framework that replaces manual dietary logging with image-derived macronutrient estimates and integrates them with clinical variables and gut microbiome information for personalized PPGR prediction. The framework jointly performs image-based macronutrient estimation and glucose prediction, while an attention-based prediction module models interactions between dietary and host-specific information. We evaluate the proposed approach on a real-world dataset comprising meal images, continuous glucose monitoring, clinical variables, and gut microbiome profiles. The proposed model outperforms existing PPGR baselines using image-derived nutritional inputs and approaches the performance of methods that rely on manually reported macronutrients despite using automatically estimated nutritional information. These results demonstrate that combining image-derived nutrition with complementary clinical and gut microbiome information provides a practical foundation for scalable personalized PPGR prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multimodal framework for personalized postprandial glycemic response (PPGR) prediction that replaces manual dietary logging with image-derived macronutrient estimates, combining them with clinical variables and gut microbiome data, and jointly performs macronutrient estimation and glucose prediction via an attention-based module.
AI.motivation: Existing PPGR prediction approaches rely on manually reported dietary intake, which limits their scalability in free-living settings. This creates a need for automated dietary assessment to enable practical personalized nutrition and type 2 diabetes management.
AI.method: A multimodal framework is introduced that replaces manual dietary logging with image-derived macronutrient estimates. It integrates these with clinical variables and gut microbiome information. The framework jointly performs image-based macronutrient estimation and glucose prediction, with an attention-based prediction module modeling interactions between dietary and host-specific information. Evaluation uses a real-world dataset of meal images, continuous glucose monitoring, clinical variables, and gut microbiome profiles.
AI.result: The proposed model outperforms existing PPGR baselines that use image-derived nutritional inputs. It approaches the performance of methods relying on manually reported macronutrients, despite using automatically estimated nutritional information.
AI.conclusion: Combining image-derived nutrition with complementary clinical and gut microbiome information provides a practical foundation for scalable personalized PPGR prediction.

title: PRIMO: Prior-Informed Odometry from Human-Motion Tracking for Humanoid Robots
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures and 4 tables, Under review
summary: Simulation-trained humanoid proprioceptive odometry faces two transfer challenges: training trajectories generated by specific robot control policies intended for deployment cover only a limited range of motions, while sim-to-real mismatch can make unconstrained predictions unreliable. We address both with Prior-Informed Odometry from Human-Motion Tracking (PRIMO). On the data side, we generate odometry supervision by having the humanoid track diverse retargeted human motions in simulation, decoupling supervision from the deployment policies and broadening the training motion distribution. On the model side, a Prior-Informed estimator uses physics- and symmetry-informed priors to structure velocity and rotation prediction and a coarse raw-context pathway to preserve sensor context alongside encoded features, thereby strengthening sim-to-real generalization. Under a unified real-robot protocol, PRIMO reduces mean error by 31.6%-61.7% relative to the strongest evaluated external baseline in each domain-metric comparison. Across two locomotion-policy revisions, policy specialists exhibit symmetric crossover, whereas Tracking-Locomotion training reduces mean opposite-policy simulation error by 86.8%-94.6%. On real dynamic motion, Tracking-Locomotion training reduces mean error by 69.2%-81.7% relative to training on the union of both deployment policies. Across the tested motion compositions, the Prior-Informed estimator consistently lowers mean trajectory errors relative to its Unconstrained counterpart in both simulation and real-robot evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/Agibot-Spatial-Intelligence/PRIMO.

AI.tldr: PRIMO tackles sim-to-real transfer for humanoid proprioceptive odometry via diverse human-motion-tracking supervision and a physics/symmetry prior-informed estimator, reducing real-robot mean error by 31.6%-61.7% over the strongest baseline.
AI.motivation: Simulation-trained humanoid proprioceptive odometry faces two transfer challenges: (1) training trajectories from specific deployment policies cover only limited motions, and (2) sim-to-real mismatch makes unconstrained predictions unreliable.
AI.method: On the data side, odometry supervision is generated by having the humanoid track diverse retargeted human motions in simulation, decoupling supervision from deployment policies to broaden the training motion distribution. On the model side, a Prior-Informed estimator uses physics- and symmetry-informed priors to structure velocity and rotation prediction, plus a coarse raw-context pathway that preserves sensor context alongside encoded features to strengthen sim-to-real generalization.
AI.result: Under a unified real-robot protocol, PRIMO reduces mean error by 31.6%-61.7% versus the strongest evaluated external baseline per domain-metric comparison. Policy specialists show symmetric crossover across two locomotion-policy revisions, while Tracking-Locomotion training cuts mean opposite-policy simulation error by 86.8%-94.6%. On real dynamic motion, Tracking-Locomotion reduces mean error by 69.2%-81.7% relative to training on the union of both deployment policies. The Prior-Informed estimator consistently lowers mean trajectory errors versus its Unconstrained counterpart in both simulation and real-robot evaluation across tested motion compositions.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling odometry supervision from deployment policies via human-motion tracking broadens training distribution and, combined with prior-informed modeling and raw-context preservation, yields robust sim-to-real proprioceptive odometry with consistent accuracy gains over baselines on both simulated and real dynamic motions.

title: Fathom-Vaidya: Advancing Medical Reasoning with Rubric-Based Rewards
comment: 18 pages, 5 Figures, Correspondence to kunal.singh@fractal.ai
summary: Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in healthcare requires robust performance across two complementary dimensions - diagnostic reasoning: the convergent, evidence-driven task of inferring a patient's condition from clinical data to produce a diagnosis, and clinical healthcare reasoning: the broader, navigational judgment required to communicate, plan, and adapt across multi-turn clinical interactions where a single correct answer may not exist. Recent benchmarks such as HealthBench and MedXpertQA reveal persistent weaknesses in both areas, exposing failures in complex diagnostic scenarios and limitations in contextual, patient-centered dialogue. We introduce a sequential training framework that targets these facets using synthetic data and rubric-based reinforcement learning. First, we improve diagnostic reasoning using MedBullets-derived questions with rule- and rubric-guided Reinforcement Learning (RL). We then shift to clinical reasoning by generating 5.3k synthetic multi-turn scenarios, each paired with multi-dimensional rubrics to comprehensively assess the response. This approach yields over 10% improvement on MedXpertQA, and our 30B model achieves 50.1% accuracy on HealthBench-Hard, surpassing proprietary baselines including GPT-5 (thinking). Our results show that targeted synthetic datasets and rubric-based training can systematically improve both diagnostic and interactive clinical reasoning in medical LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a sequential training framework combining synthetic data and rubric-based RL to improve both diagnostic and clinical healthcare reasoning in medical LLMs, achieving >10% gains on MedXpertQA and 50.1% on HealthBench-Hard.
AI.motivation: Deploying LLMs in healthcare demands strong performance in two complementary dimensions: diagnostic reasoning (convergent, evidence-driven diagnosis from clinical data) and clinical healthcare reasoning (broader, navigational judgment across multi-turn interactions where no single correct answer exists). Benchmarks such as HealthBench and MedXpertQA expose persistent weaknesses in both, revealing failures in complex diagnostic scenarios and limited contextual, patient-centered dialogue.
AI.method: A sequential training framework targeting the two reasoning facets. Stage 1 improves diagnostic reasoning via MedBullets-derived questions using rule- and rubric-guided reinforcement learning (RL). Stage 2 shifts to clinical reasoning by generating 5.3k synthetic multi-turn scenarios, each paired with multi-dimensional rubrics for comprehensive response assessment.
AI.result: Over 10% improvement on MedXpertQA; the 30B model reaches 50.1% accuracy on HealthBench-Hard, surpassing proprietary baselines including GPT-5 (thinking).
AI.conclusion: Targeted synthetic datasets and rubric-based training can systematically improve both diagnostic and interactive clinical reasoning in medical LLMs.

title: CompVLA: A Variable Compliance Vision-Language-Action Model for Contact-rich Manipulation
comment: Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026
summary: Contact-rich manipulation, requiring robots to regulate not only motion but also how they yield to external forces, has emerged as the next frontier for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing VLAs output purely kinematic commands, degrading performance on real-world contact-rich tasks. In this paper, we introduce CompVLA, a unified VLA framework that jointly predicts motion and stiffness matrix from RGB and language inputs. Our approach augments the conventional architecture with a dedicated Compliance Expert, which outputs time-varying stiffness and virtual displacement profiles executed via geometric impedance control. We demonstrate that CompVLA achieves the highest average success rate across diverse contact-rich tasks, outperforming both vanilla and compliance-aware VLA baselines, with ablations confirming each component is essential.

AI.tldr: CompVLA is a unified VLA framework that jointly predicts motion and stiffness matrices from RGB and language inputs, using a Compliance Expert and geometric impedance control to boost success on contact-rich manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Contact-rich manipulation requires robots to regulate both motion and how they yield to external forces, making it the next frontier for VLA models. Existing VLAs output purely kinematic commands, which degrades performance on real-world contact-rich tasks.
AI.method: CompVLA augments the conventional VLA architecture with a dedicated Compliance Expert that outputs time-varying stiffness and virtual displacement profiles. These are executed via geometric impedance control, with the framework jointly predicting motion and stiffness matrix from RGB and language inputs.
AI.result: CompVLA achieves the highest average success rate across diverse contact-rich tasks, outperforming both vanilla and compliance-aware VLA baselines. Ablations confirm that each component is essential.
AI.conclusion: CompVLA effectively addresses the limitation of purely kinematic VLA outputs by jointly predicting motion and stiffness, demonstrating superior performance on contact-rich manipulation.

title: Not All Task Vectors Need Equal Rank: Energy-Proportional Allocation for Model Merging
summary: Model merging aims to combine multiple fine-tuned models derived from a common pretrained model into a single multi-task model without additional joint training. Recent spectral merging methods improve over simple weight averaging by exploiting low-rank structures of task-specific updates, but they commonly assign the same rank capacity to every task. This uniform allocation ignores that task vectors can have heterogeneous spectral complexity, causing the shared merging space to be used suboptimally. In this paper, we propose Spectral Energy-proportional Rank Allocation (SERA), a simple task-adaptive strategy that allocates ranks according to the singular-value energy structure of each task vector. By assigning richer spectral capacity to complex or isolated tasks and fewer directions to compact tasks, SERA extends SVD-based model merging from uniform-capacity merging to task-dependent capacity allocation. Experiments under standard vision model merging protocols show that SERA improves multi-task merging performance while preserving the same total rank budget as existing spectral merging methods. Further analysis demonstrates that task-level spectral concentration is closely related to the per-task effect of adaptive rank allocation, providing insight into when and why SERA is effective.

AI.tldr: SERA proposes allocating per-task ranks in SVD-based model merging proportional to each task vector's spectral energy, instead of uniform ranks, improving multi-task performance under the same total rank budget.
AI.motivation: Spectral model merging methods exploit low-rank task updates but assign equal rank capacity to all tasks, ignoring heterogeneous spectral complexity of task vectors. This uniform allocation underutilizes the shared merging space.
AI.method: SERA, a task-adaptive rank allocation strategy, distributes ranks according to singular-value energy structure of each task vector. It assigns richer spectral capacity to complex or isolated tasks and fewer directions to compact tasks, extending SVD-based merging from uniform-capacity to task-dependent capacity allocation.
AI.result: Under standard vision model merging protocols, SERA improves multi-task merging performance while keeping the same total rank budget as existing spectral merging methods. Analysis links task-level spectral concentration to the per-task effect of adaptive rank allocation.
AI.conclusion: Task-dependent rank allocation based on spectral energy provides a simple, budget-preserving improvement for spectral model merging, with spectral concentration explaining when and why the approach is effective.

title: Spiking Neural Network Actor-Critic Proximal Policy Optimization Control for Autonomous UAV Navigation Through Constrained Openings in Civil Infrastructure and Buildings
summary: Autonomous navigation of unmanned aerial vehicles in constrained three-dimensional environments has been a challenge in the robotics domain. The application of autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles in civil infrastructure inspection involves the use of such vehicles in bridge inspection, tunnel inspection, and structural inspection. The use of deep reinforcement learning in the autonomous navigation of unmanned aerial vehicles has been successful in constrained environments. However, the computational cost of the algorithm limits the application of the algorithm in the autonomous navigation of unmanned aerial vehicles. This paper proposes the use of the spiking neural network-based Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm in the autonomous navigation of unmanned aerial vehicles in constrained sequential environments. The proposed algorithm integrates the use of spike-based actor-critic reinforcement learning with the Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm. The proposed algorithm uses the stochastic Gaussian policy in the autonomous navigation of unmanned aerial vehicles. The proposed algorithm was implemented in the autonomous navigation of unmanned aerial vehicles in constrained 3D environments. The proposed algorithm was successful in completing 1913 episodes out of more than 3000. The proposed algorithm was successful in passing an average of 2.10 windows per episode. The proposed algorithm was successful in achieving a success rate of 63.77%. The proposed algorithm was successful in achieving success rates of more than 90% in the later stages of the algorithm.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a spiking neural network-based Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm for autonomous UAV navigation in constrained 3D environments, integrating spike-based actor-critic reinforcement learning with a stochastic Gaussian policy, achieving a 63.77% success rate and over 90% success in later stages.
AI.motivation: Autonomous navigation of UAVs in constrained 3D environments (e.g., bridge, tunnel, and structural inspection) remains challenging in robotics. While deep reinforcement learning has succeeded in constrained navigation, its computational cost limits practical deployment on UAVs. This motivates a more computationally efficient learning approach.
AI.method: The authors propose a spiking neural network-based Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm. It integrates spike-based actor-critic reinforcement learning with the PPO algorithm and employs a stochastic Gaussian policy for autonomous UAV navigation. The method is implemented and evaluated in constrained sequential 3D environments.
AI.result: The algorithm completed 1913 episodes out of more than 3000, passed an average of 2.10 windows per episode, and achieved an overall success rate of 63.77%. Success rates exceeded 90% in the later stages of training/operation.
AI.conclusion: The spiking neural network-based PPO algorithm is a viable approach for autonomous UAV navigation in constrained 3D environments, demonstrating strong late-stage performance and reduced computational burden relative to conventional deep RL.

title: The Endless Exam: Mathematical Constructions from Today's Models toward Superintelligence
comment: 51 pages, 13 figures, 25 tables
summary: We introduce the Endless Exam, a benchmark for measuring mathematical progress from today's models toward artificial superintelligence through fourteen parameterised construction families. Each submitted object is checked automatically for validity and assigned a relative quality score against a published frontier or construction baseline, without capping improvements at $1$. The families draw on open mathematical problems for long-term targets and generate new instances at larger parameters, where compact certificates keep large constructions verifiable. Across eight models evaluated on 69 distinct instances, continuous quality scores distinguish performance even though no evaluated system surpasses a published frontier. Size-quality curves show how construction quality changes as problem size increases. We release the generators, verifiers, references, model responses and analysis to support continued measurement before and beyond human frontiers.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Endless Exam, a benchmark using fourteen parameterised construction families to measure mathematical progress of today's models toward artificial superintelligence, with uncapped relative quality scores and compact certificates, evaluated across eight models on 69 instances.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks cap improvements at 1 and lack scalable, verifiable targets beyond current human frontiers, making it difficult to measure mathematical progress toward artificial superintelligence. The Endless Exam addresses this by providing parameterised families with long-term open-problem targets and unbounded quality scores.
AI.method: The benchmark employs fourteen parameterised construction families drawing on open mathematical problems for long-term targets. Each submitted object is automatically checked for validity and assigned a relative quality score against a published frontier or construction baseline without capping improvements at 1. New instances are generated at larger parameters, with compact certificates ensuring large constructions remain verifiable.
AI.result: Across eight models evaluated on 69 distinct instances, continuous quality scores distinguish performance even though no evaluated system surpasses a published frontier. Size-quality curves reveal how construction quality changes as problem size increases.
AI.conclusion: The Endless Exam supports continued measurement before and beyond human frontiers, with generators, verifiers, references, model responses, and analysis released to enable ongoing evaluation of mathematical progress toward artificial superintelligence.

title: Beyond Appearance Shifts: Task-Semantic Action Calibration for VLA Models
comment: 27 pages (10-page main text), 15 figures, 24 tables. Project page: https://nebulis-lab.com/Beyond-Appearance-Shifts
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance in embodied manipulation, but still lack a clear mechanism to balance behavioral stability with task-semantic sensitivity. We identify two complementary failure modes. Under task-preserving changes, where task semantics remain unchanged but scene appearance varies (e.g., style, illumination, clutter, or paraphrasing), policies often exhibit unnecessary action drift. Conversely, under semantic-breaking changes, where key task semantics such as the target object or constraint are altered, policies frequently fail to produce sufficiently distinct behaviors and instead follow the original trajectory. To address this gap, we propose BAS-VLA, a task-semantic action calibration framework built on top of a frozen base VLA. BAS-VLA adopts a breaking-centered calibration core as the default path, and introduces a selective evidence-gated preserving auxiliary that activates only when nuisance variation is detected while task semantics remain consistent. On the OpenPI-pi0.5 / LIBERO-Object Milk-Swap benchmark, BAS-VLA maintains high success on clean (98.0%) and semantics-preserving conditions (97.5%), while reducing clean-criterion success to 0.0% under deliberate target-object swaps, demonstrating strong stale-task suppression and task-semantic separation. On validated style-preserving shifts, it improves success from 42% to 70% without degrading clean performance. These results highlight that reliable VLA behavior requires moving beyond appearance robustness toward explicit task-semantic action calibration.

AI.tldr: BAS-VLA is a task-semantic action calibration framework built on a frozen base VLA that separates appearance robustness from task-semantic sensitivity, using a breaking-centered calibration core plus a selective evidence-gated preserving auxiliary.
AI.motivation: VLA models lack a clear mechanism to balance behavioral stability with task-semantic sensitivity. Two complementary failure modes exist: (1) unnecessary action drift under task-preserving changes (style, illumination, clutter, paraphrasing), and (2) failure to produce distinct behaviors under semantic-breaking changes (altered target object or constraint), instead following the original trajectory.
AI.method: BAS-VLA is a task-semantic action calibration framework on top of a frozen base VLA. It adopts a breaking-centered calibration core as the default path and introduces a selective evidence-gated preserving auxiliary that activates only when nuisance variation is detected while task semantics remain consistent.
AI.result: On OpenPI-pi0.5 / LIBERO-Object Milk-Swap, BAS-VLA achieves 98.0% success on clean and 97.5% on semantics-preserving conditions, while reducing clean-criterion success to 0.0% under deliberate target-object swaps, showing strong stale-task suppression and task-semantic separation. On validated style-preserving shifts, success improves from 42% to 70% without degrading clean performance.
AI.conclusion: Reliable VLA behavior requires moving beyond appearance robustness toward explicit task-semantic action calibration.

title: Ascent: An Agentic System over the Model Context Protocol for Real-World Clinical Data Analysis
summary: Answering epidemiological questions from real-world clinical data requires medical coding, schema-aware SQL, and validation of implicit choices about populations, denominators, and time. We present Ascent, an agentic system that exposes medical coding, question answering, and cohort analysis through a shared Model Context Protocol tool surface for standardized and native schemas. We introduce EpiTrap, a dataset testing whether systems avoid recognized pharmacoepidemiological errors, and compare a fixed pipeline with agents across models and orchestrators. With capable models, agents improve accuracy over the fixed pipeline by an average of 27 and 20 percentage points on native and standardized schemas, respectively. These gains require more tool calls and longer runtimes. Experience from real projects highlights the system's value for feasibility assessment, diagnostic iteration, and expert-guided analysis.

AI.tldr: Ascent is an agentic system exposing medical coding, QA, and cohort analysis through a shared MCP tool surface; evaluated on EpiTrap, agents beat a fixed pipeline by 27/20 points on native/standardized schemas at higher cost.
AI.motivation: Answering epidemiological questions from real-world clinical data is hard: it demands medical coding, schema-aware SQL, and validation of implicit choices about populations, denominators, and time. The paper motivates the need for systems that avoid recognized pharmacoepidemiological errors.
AI.method: The authors present Ascent, an agentic system that exposes medical coding, question answering, and cohort analysis through a shared Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool surface supporting both standardized and native schemas. They introduce EpiTrap, a dataset testing whether systems avoid recognized pharmacoepidemiological errors, and compare a fixed pipeline against agents across multiple models and orchestrators.
AI.result: With capable models, agents improve accuracy over the fixed pipeline by an average of 27 percentage points on native schemas and 20 percentage points on standardized schemas. These gains require more tool calls and longer runtimes.
AI.conclusion: Experience from real projects highlights the system's value for feasibility assessment, diagnostic iteration, and expert-guided analysis. The agentic approach trades increased tool calls and runtime for substantially higher accuracy, though a fixed pipeline may be preferable when resources are constrained.

title: WOLF: World Model Guided LiDAR Exploration with Predictive Frontiers
summary: LiDAR-based unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) exploration builds maps by continually selecting where to observe next. However, decisions based on the measured map provide limited foresight into spatial continuations behind occlusions, leaving potentially informative directions unrecognized. We present WOLF, a world-model-guided framework that predicts future observations to enhance autonomous exploration. In the training stage, a recurrent world model learns observation dynamics from exploration trajectories, with recurrent memory retaining the spatial context needed to interpret partial observations across successive views. Building on this context, the model combines observation history with candidate motions during exploration to predict local occupancy and visibility. To guide further sensing, a predictive frontier generation mechanism then aligns and fuses these predictions using confidence, branch agreement, and observation quality to identify promising regions. The resulting predictive frontiers join measured ones to guide geometric viewpoint selection and trajectory generation, while new scans update subsequent predictions. In simulations, our method reduces mean terminal time by 10.9% relative to EPIC in Garage at comparable coverage and increases mean coverage from 42.12% to 98.35% in Tunnel. Real-world experiments further demonstrate onboard deployment of the learned model for online inference during physical flight.

AI.tldr: WOLF, a world-model-guided framework, predicts future observations to improve LiDAR-based UAV autonomous exploration.
AI.motivation: LiDAR-based UAV exploration selects next viewpoints using the measured map, which gives limited foresight into spatial continuations behind occlusions, so potentially informative directions remain unrecognized.
AI.method: A recurrent world model is trained on exploration trajectories to learn observation dynamics, with recurrent memory preserving spatial context across successive views. It combines observation history with candidate motions to predict local occupancy and visibility. A predictive frontier generation mechanism aligns and fuses these predictions using confidence, branch agreement, and observation quality to identify promising regions. Predictive frontiers are merged with measured frontiers to guide geometric viewpoint selection and trajectory generation, and new scans update subsequent predictions.
AI.result: In simulation, the method reduces mean terminal time by 10.9% versus EPIC in Garage at comparable coverage, and raises mean coverage from 42.12% to 98.35% in Tunnel. Real-world experiments show onboard deployment of the learned model for online inference during physical flight.
AI.conclusion: Predicting future observations via a world model enhances autonomous UAV exploration, improving efficiency and coverage beyond measured-map-based approaches, and is feasible for onboard real-world flight.

title: Custom Named Entity Recognition and Topic Classification for Global Health Publications
summary: How should natural language processing models be selected and adapted for global health literature in environments where annotated data and computational resources are limited? This thesis investigates these challenges through experiments on semantic tag discovery, named entity recognition (NER), and multi-label topic classification. First, skip-gram word2vec models trained on progressively larger specialized corpora are compared with BioWordVec to assess how corpus size and domain context influence tag discovery. Vocabulary coverage and qualitative evaluation indicate that broader coverage does not necessarily yield more useful domain-specific associations.
