The analysis then turns to entity extraction, comparing convolutional spaCy models with a RoBERTa-based transformer on 1,000 annotated sentences. Under a lenient scoring protocol, the transformer achieves 0.80 micro-F1 versus 0.65-0.69 for convolutional models, but takes 82 seconds rather than 5-6 seconds. This trade-off motivates fine-tuning convolutional models and integrating a disease recognizer that achieves 81.33% test F1 on the NCBI Disease Corpus. Combined with PDF preprocessing, entity filtering, and MeSH enrichment, the resulting pipeline supports document-level indexing. To complement entity extraction with thematic annotation, MiniLM-based few-shot classification is compared with BART-MNLI zero-shot inference across 50 topics and 1,000 handcrafted test sentences. BART-MNLI achieves 95.2% single-label accuracy versus 59%; reported multi-label accuracies are 88% and 32% under partly manual assessment. However, its higher inference cost limits practical integration. The results show where domain specialization and lightweight adaptation offer practical value, and where transformer accuracy justifies higher inference costs, providing an empirical basis for building knowledge systems under resource constraints.

AI.tldr: This thesis evaluates NLP model selection and adaptation for global health literature under limited data and compute, testing semantic tag discovery, NER, and multi-label topic classification, and finds trade-offs between domain specialization, lightweight models, and transformer accuracy.
AI.motivation: Global health literature settings often lack annotated data and computational resources, raising the question of how NLP models should be selected and adapted in such constrained environments.
AI.method: Experiments cover: (1) skip-gram word2vec trained on progressively larger specialized corpora vs. BioWordVec for semantic tag discovery; (2) NER comparing convolutional spaCy models against a RoBERTa-based transformer on 1,000 annotated sentences, plus fine-tuning convolutional models and integrating a disease recognizer (81.33% test F1 on NCBI Disease Corpus) with PDF preprocessing, entity filtering, and MeSH enrichment; (3) MiniLM-based few-shot classification vs. BART-MNLI zero-shot inference across 50 topics and 1,000 handcrafted test sentences for multi-label topic classification.
AI.result: Broader vocabulary coverage did not necessarily yield more useful domain-specific associations. Under lenient scoring, the transformer reached 0.80 micro-F1 vs. 0.65-0.69 for convolutional models, but took 82s vs. 5-6s. BART-MNLI achieved 95.2% single-label accuracy vs. 59%; multi-label accuracies were 88% vs. 32% under partly manual assessment, though its higher inference cost limits integration.
AI.conclusion: Domain specialization and lightweight adaptation offer practical value in some tasks, while transformer accuracy justifies higher inference costs in others, providing an empirical basis for building knowledge systems under resource constraints.

title: UniPoint: Unified Point-Level Sensor Fusion for Humanoid Locomotion Across Challenging Terrains
comment: 8 pages, 9 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). Video: https://youtu.be/Rd9YyfOxvmY
summary: Open-world deployment requires humanoid robots to cross highly heterogeneous terrain safely, with perception that simultaneously provides wide coverage, local accuracy, and redundancy against sensor failure. Existing approaches struggle to satisfy all three: one forward depth camera or nearby height sampling covers too little; odometry-corrected elevation maps drift under aggressive motion and miss thin vertical structures; image-level encoding costs grow with camera count. We present UniPoint, a humanoid whole-body locomotion framework built on multi-source point-level sensor fusion. Measurements from a 360° light detection and ranging (LiDAR) sensor and two depth cameras are early-fused into one base-frame point set. Voxelization resamples it to a fixed number of tokens encoded by linear self-attention and proprioception-queried cross-attention, decoupling forward cost from sensor count. The point set retains standing thin barriers; a single-modality failure removes only part of the tokens, so the policy degrades gracefully. A single training run with terrain-aware rewards, perception-degradation injection, and domain randomization produces one policy for all eight terrain types, deployed on an onboard RK3588 without fine-tuning. On a DR02 humanoid, 20 trials at each of nine real-world settings over seven terrain types validate the policy on 70-cm-high platforms, 100-cm gaps, thin barriers, and sparse or narrow footholds; it also generalizes zero-shot outdoors.

AI.tldr: UniPoint is a humanoid whole-body locomotion framework that early-fuses a 360° LiDAR and two depth cameras into a single base-frame point set, encodes it with fixed-size linear/cross-attention, and trains one policy for all terrain types that runs onboard and generalizes zero-shot outdoors.
AI.motivation: Open-world humanoid deployment demands safe traversal of heterogeneous terrain with perception that delivers wide coverage, local accuracy, and redundancy against sensor failure simultaneously. Existing approaches fail on all three fronts: a single forward depth camera or nearby height sampling provides insufficient coverage; odometry-corrected elevation maps drift under aggressive motion and miss thin vertical structures; and image-level encoding cost scales with camera count.
AI.method: Multi-source point-level sensor fusion: measurements from a 360° LiDAR and two depth cameras are early-fused into one base-frame point set. Voxelization resamples this set into a fixed number of tokens, encoded via linear self-attention plus proprioception-queried cross-attention, decoupling forward cost from sensor count. A single training run uses terrain-aware rewards, perception-degradation injection, and domain randomization to yield one unified policy. Deployed onboard an RK3588 without fine-tuning.
AI.result: The point set preserves thin standing barriers, and single-modality failure removes only part of the tokens, enabling graceful degradation. On a DR02 humanoid, 20 trials at each of nine real-world settings across seven terrain types validated the policy on 70-cm-high platforms, 100-cm gaps, thin barriers, and sparse or narrow footholds, with additional zero-shot generalization outdoors.
AI.conclusion: UniPoint demonstrates that multi-source point-level fusion with fixed-token attention enables a single, sensor-count-independent policy to achieve wide-coverage, accurate, and failure-redundant perception for humanoid locomotion, validated across diverse real-world terrains and generalizing zero-shot to outdoor settings.

title: DUMA-Bench: A Dual-Control Multi-Agent Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agent Security
comment: ACL ARR 2026 March Findings
summary: LLM-based agents increasingly operate in environments where they interact with users, tools, and external systems. Yet most security evaluations assume passive users and static control, ignoring the interactive dynamics that shape real agent behavior. We introduce \textbf{DUMA-Bench}, a benchmark and evaluation protocol for measuring agent security under \emph{dual-control} interaction, where both the agent and the user can influence the shared environment state. DUMA-Bench extends $τ^2$-bench ~\cite{barres2025tau} with adversarial environments covering eight vulnerability classes, including RAG poisoning, cross-agent manipulation, and unsafe output handling. We evaluate \textbf{14 models from five model families} (OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Z.ai) across eight domains and multiple user-behavior regimes. Across our experiments, introducing dual-control interaction increases the attack success rate from \textbf{26.9\%} to \textbf{41.1\%}. These results show that agent security is not solely a property of the model but emerges from the interaction between the model, the user, and the environment. DUMA-Bench provides a missing evaluation layer for studying security in realistic agent deployments.

AI.tldr: DUMA-Bench is a benchmark and evaluation protocol measuring LLM agent security under dual-control interaction, where both agent and user affect shared environment state. Extending τ²-bench with adversarial environments across eight vulnerability classes, it evaluates 14 models from five families over eight domains and multiple user-behavior regimes. Dual-control interaction raises attack success rate from 26.9% to 41.1%, showing agent security emerges from model–user–environment interaction rather than being solely a model property.
AI.motivation: Existing security evaluations of LLM-based agents assume passive users and static control, neglecting the interactive dynamics that shape real agent behavior. Since agents increasingly interact with users, tools, and external systems, there is a need for an evaluation layer that captures security under realistic, dynamic interaction.
AI.method: The authors introduce DUMA-Bench, a benchmark and evaluation protocol for measuring agent security under dual-control interaction, in which both agent and user can influence the shared environment state. DUMA-Bench extends τ²-bench with adversarial environments covering eight vulnerability classes, including RAG poisoning, cross-agent manipulation, and unsafe output handling. They evaluate 14 models from five model families (OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Z.ai) across eight domains and multiple user-behavior regimes.
AI.result: Introducing dual-control interaction increases the attack success rate from 26.9% to 41.1% across the experiments.
AI.conclusion: Agent security is not solely a property of the model but emerges from the interaction between the model, the user, and the environment. DUMA-Bench provides a missing evaluation layer for studying security in realistic agent deployments.

title: Marginal Calibration Does Not Compose: Hidden Dependence in Modular Robot Navigation
comment: Accepted to the Rethinking Uncertainty for Modern Robotics Paradigms Workshop at IROS 2026
summary: Robotic systems are typically composed of multiple independently developed modules that work together to perceive, predict, and act in the environment. Although each module may perform reliably in isolation, composing them does not necessarily preserve uncertainty calibration at the system level. In this work, we show that well-calibrated component interfaces do not necessarily produce calibrated downstream behavior after composition. Using a moving-obstacle prediction pipeline, we demonstrate that position and velocity estimators can each appear well calibrated individually, yet differences in how their error are correlated lead to substantially different estimates of future-state uncertainty. Consequently, assuming independence can make the system either overly confident or unnecessarily conservative, directly influencing downstream planning decisions and safety. Through simulations, we show that modeling the joint covariance restores downstream calibration and improves system performance, whereas dependence-robust uncertainty bounds enhance safety at the cost of increased conservatism. Our findings reveal a fundamental limitation of independently validating robotic modules and highlight the need for interfaces that communicate dependence information or support direct system-level calibration.

AI.tldr: Well-calibrated robotic modules can still yield miscalibrated system-level uncertainty after composition; misspecified error dependence in a moving-obstacle pipeline makes the system overconfident or overconservative, and modeling joint covariance restores calibration.
AI.motivation: Robotic systems are built by composing independently developed and validated modules. The paper questions the common assumption that reliable, well-calibrated modules preserve uncertainty calibration at the system level after composition, and it highlights how error dependence between modules can break this assumption with consequences for downstream planning and safety.
AI.method: The authors study composition through a moving-obstacle prediction pipeline. They examine position and velocity estimators that each appear well calibrated in isolation, and analyze how differences in the correlation of their errors affect estimates of future-state uncertainty. They compare an independence assumption against explicitly modeling the joint covariance, and also evaluate dependence-robust uncertainty bounds, using simulations.
AI.result: Well-calibrated component interfaces do not guarantee calibrated downstream behavior after composition. Assuming independence can make the system either overly confident or unnecessarily conservative, directly affecting planning decisions and safety. Modeling the joint covariance restores downstream calibration and improves system performance, while dependence-robust uncertainty bounds enhance safety at the cost of increased conservatism.
AI.conclusion: The work exposes a fundamental limitation of independently validating robotic modules: interface calibration alone is insufficient for system-level calibration. It argues for interfaces that communicate dependence information or that support direct system-level calibration, and shows that accounting for joint error dependence is key to safe and effective composed robotic systems.

title: Beyond Endpoint Performance: Process-Level Evaluation of Self-Evolving Agents
summary: Self-evolving agents convert interaction feedback into persistent artifacts, such as memories or skills, which in turn guide subsequent decisions. As these artifacts are iteratively updated throughout an experience stream, the capabilities they support may evolve. Consequently, endpoint performance alone offers an incomplete view of self-evolution. Process-level evaluation is therefore essential to identify when a target capability emerges and whether later updates strengthen, preserve, or weaken it. Motivated by this, we propose \textsc{EvoPathBench}, a benchmark that tracks individual capabilities during artifact-level self-evolution. EvoPathBench fixes the base model, tools, freezes evolving artifacts at successive checkpoints, and evaluates the target capability on held-out episodes. This benchmark evaluates agent self-evolution using public trading data and calibrated trajectories. It tests three capabilities: generalization to unseen tasks, retention after unrelated learning, and rule adaptation to new evidence. Experimental results show that gains on similar unseen tasks often weaken under distribution shift, retention losses are concentrated in a minority of evolution paths, and no method achieves reliable rule adaptation. Moreover, while self-evolution enables agents to generate candidate artifacts with substantial held-out gains, the selected updates consistently fall short of realizing this potential. Together, these findings establish capability-level process evaluation as a foundation for analyzing self-evolution, identifying candidate evaluation and selection as key targets for improvement.

AI.tldr: EvoPathBench is a process-level benchmark that tracks individual capabilities during artifact-level self-evolution by freezing evolving artifacts at checkpoints and evaluating held-out episodes, revealing that gains weaken under distribution shift and update selection consistently underperforms its potential.
AI.motivation: Endpoint performance alone gives an incomplete view of self-evolving agents, since artifacts (memories, skills) are iteratively updated and supported capabilities may evolve over time. Process-level evaluation is needed to determine when a target capability emerges and whether later updates strengthen, preserve, or weaken it.
AI.method: EvoPathBench fixes the base model and tools, freezes evolving artifacts at successive checkpoints, and evaluates the target capability on held-out episodes. It uses public trading data and calibrated trajectories, testing three capabilities: generalization to unseen tasks, retention after unrelated learning, and rule adaptation to new evidence.
AI.result: Gains on similar unseen tasks often weaken under distribution shift; retention losses concentrate in a minority of evolution paths; no method achieves reliable rule adaptation. Self-evolution generates candidate artifacts with substantial held-out gains, but selected updates consistently fall short of realizing this potential.
AI.conclusion: Capability-level process evaluation is established as a foundation for analyzing self-evolution, with candidate evaluation and selection identified as key targets for improvement.

title: FlockDiffusion: Assignment-Conditioned Diffusion for Multi-Drone Task Allocation and Completion
summary: Autonomous multi-drone navigation requires fleets to service distributed objectives in cluttered environments under tight computational budgets. Efficient coordination depends on task bundling, where each drone visits multiple objectives along its route. Separate solvers for cost estimation, assignment, and execution incur redundant graph search and produce long, abrupt paths. We propose FlockDiffusion, a learned framework combining a scene graph encoder, an explicit allocation head, an assignment conditioned diffusion transformer, and a closed form trajectory decoder. An autoregressive teacher provides offline supervision for parallel fleet trajectory generation. PyBullet ablations show that bundling increases task completion from 50% to 100%, while our complete teacher further reduces route cost by 8.4% relative to MAGNNET with bundling. In the optimized scalability benchmark, evaluated on 100 scenes per density with ten drones, FlockDiffusion achieves 6.2 to 7.6 times faster inference and approximately 37% shorter routes than the classical pipeline. As nominal task counts increase from 20 to 40, latency rises from 7.8 to 11.1 ms, compared with 48.0 to 75.8 ms for the baseline. In a separate evaluation across five Gazebo environments, FlockDiffusion achieves 100% planner coverage and reduces planned route cost by 15.4% relative to the baseline with bundling. These results demonstrate efficient planning under increasing task density in configurations that are demanding to reproduce with physical drone fleets.

AI.tldr: FlockDiffusion is a learned framework for multi-drone navigation that unifies task bundling, assignment, and trajectory generation, achieving faster inference and shorter routes than classical pipelines.
AI.motivation: Autonomous multi-drone fleets must service distributed objectives in cluttered environments under tight computational budgets. Separate solvers for cost estimation, assignment, and execution cause redundant graph search and produce long, abrupt paths, motivating a unified learned approach with task bundling (each drone visits multiple objectives).
AI.method: FlockDiffusion combines a scene graph encoder, an explicit allocation head, an assignment-conditioned diffusion transformer, and a closed-form trajectory decoder. An autoregressive teacher provides offline supervision for parallel fleet trajectory generation.
AI.result: PyBullet ablations: bundling raises task completion from 50% to 100%; the complete teacher reduces route cost by 8.4% vs. MAGNNET with bundling. On a scalability benchmark (100 scenes per density, ten drones): 6.2–7.6x faster inference and ~37% shorter routes than the classical pipeline. As tasks increase from 20 to 40, latency rises from 7.8 to 11.1 ms vs. 48.0–75.8 ms for the baseline. Across five Gazebo environments: 100% planner coverage and 15.4% lower planned route cost vs. baseline with bundling.
AI.conclusion: FlockDiffusion enables efficient multi-drone planning under increasing task density and in configurations that are demanding to reproduce with physical drone fleets.

title: TimeLitmus: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Cross-Modal Understanding and Explanation Faithfulness in Event-Conditioned Time-Series Prediction
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to make predictions from numerical time-series histories and textual events. Yet accuracy alone cannot reveal whether correct answers reflect effective integration of the two inputs or instead arise from event polarity, unimodal priors, or superficial cues. Likewise, plausible explanations may rationalize predictions without faithfully reflecting the evidence that drives model behavior. We introduce TimeLitmus, a diagnostic benchmark for cross-modal understanding and explanation faithfulness in event-conditioned time-series prediction. TimeLitmus contains 4,856 evaluation records across Finance and Traffic, combining natural prediction with controlled counterfactual and contrastive interventions, explanation-targeted faithfulness tests, and systematic shortcut controls. Across ten representative LLMs, standard prediction accuracy substantially overstates reliable cross-modal understanding: Hard Paired Contrast (HPC) pair correctness peaks at only 19.2% in Finance and 11.7% in Traffic, and all ten models show lower-than-expected consistency on Finance series-side controls. Models often recognize scenario relations explicitly yet fail to apply them during independent prediction. Explanation faithfulness shows a similar gap: in Traffic, most models cite the manipulated temporal factor in over 90% of cases, while behavioral support remains below 22%. Human annotators outperform LLMs on matched controlled and hard-pair diagnostics, confirming that these distinctions are recoverable from the inputs. Natural-only adaptation yields selective gains in evidence selection and input sensitivity, but not consistent gains in controlled or hard-pair behavior. The benchmark, evaluation suite, and supervised adaptation data will be released publicly.

AI.tldr: TimeLitmus is a diagnostic benchmark with 4,856 records (Finance, Traffic) that tests cross-modal understanding and explanation faithfulness in event-conditioned time-series prediction using counterfactual, contrastive, and shortcut controls; ten LLMs show accuracy far overstating true cross-modal competence.
AI.motivation: Accuracy alone cannot show whether LLM predictions on time-series plus textual events reflect genuine integration of both modalities or instead rely on event polarity, unimodal priors, or superficial cues; likewise, plausible explanations may not faithfully reflect the evidence driving predictions. A diagnostic instrument is needed to separate true cross-modal understanding from shortcut-driven correctness.
AI.method: TimeLitmus comprises 4,856 evaluation records across Finance and Traffic domains, combining natural prediction tasks with controlled counterfactual and contrastive interventions, explanation-targeted faithfulness tests, and systematic shortcut controls. Ten representative LLMs are evaluated, including Hard Paired Contrast (HPC) pair correctness, series-side control consistency, explicit scenario-relation recognition versus applied prediction, and citation-versus-behavioral-support faithfulness. Human annotators serve as a recoverability baseline, and natural-only supervised adaptation is tested.
AI.result: Standard accuracy substantially overstates cross-modal understanding. HPC pair correctness peaks at only 19.2% (Finance) and 11.7% (Traffic); all ten models show lower-than-expected consistency on Finance series-side controls and often recognize scenario relations but fail to apply them. In Traffic, most models cite the manipulated temporal factor in over 90% of cases while behavioral support stays below 22%. Human annotators outperform LLMs on matched controlled and hard-pair diagnostics, confirming the distinctions are recoverable from inputs. Natural-only adaptation yields selective gains in evidence selection and input sensitivity but no consistent gains on controlled or hard-pair behavior.
AI.conclusion: Accuracy and explanation fluency are insufficient proxies for cross-modal understanding and faithfulness in event-conditioned time-series prediction. Diagnostic interventions expose a substantial gap between recognized and applied cross-modal evidence, which natural-only adaptation does not close. The benchmark, evaluation suite, and supervised adaptation data will be publicly released.

title: EgoWild2Dex: Learning Dexterous Robotic Manipulation from In-the-Wild Human Experience
summary: Egocentric human data provide a principled source of supervision for learning dexterous robot manipulation. Unlike prior approaches that often collect such data in constrained or specially constructed environments, we collect in-the-wild egocentric demonstrations in real-world settings, including homes, factories, and pharmacies, etc., where people perform their ordinary tasks while wearing head-mounted cameras. This collection protocol captures diverse workflows and hand-object interactions across long-tailed object and skill distributions, but also yields visually challenging observations due to scene clutter and head-motion-induced viewpoint changes (a mean cumulative rotation of $15.93^{\circ}$/s). To address these issues, we introduce EgoWild2Dex, which transfers in-the-wild ego-human experience to dual-arm robots with dexterous hands by jointly aligning unstable egocentric views and human motions with robot observations and actions, respectively. This work offers three benefits. First, we introduce GeoFormer, a differentiable geometric transformer that warps noisy human observations toward robot observations. Second, we design a human-robot training scheme to bridge the embodiment gap, enabling high task success with limited robot supervision. Third, we release EgoWild, a 538.9-hour in-the-wild egocentric human dataset comprising 179,049 episodes, 125,961 unique task descriptions, and 1,282 object categories. On real robots, EgoWild2Dex achieves an average success rate of 96.7% across three long-horizon bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks and an average object-level zero-shot success rate of 33.3%. The data, models, and code will be released.

AI.tldr: EgoWild2Dex transfers in-the-wild egocentric human demonstrations to dual-arm dexterous robots via joint alignment of unstable egocentric views and human motions with robot observations and actions, achieving 96.7% success on three long-horizon bimanual tasks and 33.3% zero-shot object-level success.
AI.motivation: Egocentric human data offers principled supervision for dexterous robot manipulation, but prior collection is confined to constrained or specially built environments, limiting diversity. Collecting in-the-wild (homes, factories, pharmacies) captures long-tailed object and skill distributions, yet introduces visually challenging observations from scene clutter and head-motion-induced viewpoint changes (mean cumulative rotation of 15.93°/s).
AI.method: EgoWild2Dex transfers in-the-wild egocentric human experience to dual-arm dexterous robots by jointly aligning unstable egocentric views and human motions with robot observations and actions. It introduces GeoFormer, a differentiable geometric transformer that warps noisy human observations toward robot observations, and a human-robot training scheme that bridges the embodiment gap for high task success under limited robot supervision.
AI.result: The work releases EgoWild, a 538.9-hour in-the-wild egocentric human dataset with 179,049 episodes, 125,961 unique task descriptions, and 1,282 object categories. On real robots, EgoWild2Dex attains an average 96.7% success rate across three long-horizon bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks and an average 33.3% object-level zero-shot success rate.
AI.conclusion: In-the-wild egocentric human data, when jointly aligned with robot observations and actions via GeoFormer and a human-robot training scheme, provides an effective and scalable supervision source for dual-arm dexterous manipulation. Data, models, and code will be released.

title: World State Generator
summary: Language agents solve complex tasks through plans and actions. A single step the world refuses puts the goal out of reach, and what the agent does next decides the task. Prompted planners fail at exactly this point, rewriting the refused step in new words, meeting the same refusal, and burning the attempt budget without moving. They fail because the plan was never tied to the world, so a refusal has nothing in the plan to attach to. A world is where a task runs, and it has its own rules, its own admissible actions, and its own constraints. We build synthetic worlds across 7 domains and extract training data from them. A program enforces each world's rules and grades its goal, and every world is admitted only if its goal is reachable from its initial state. Agents run inside and leave verified failures paired with repairs that carried the run to a state the world certified, a record of about 226K trajectories. On this record we train the World State Generator, a model that writes a plan as checkable states of the world and keeps that plan aligned with the world it runs in. That alignment is what a plan written in language lacks, since the world it runs in has physical limits, logical dependencies, and required orders the language never states, and the plan encounters these rules only when a state fails. WSG takes that failure as the rule the world has stated and rewrites the remaining states to obey it, so the plan bends to the world as the run goes on. Across 7 public benchmarks, WSG raises end-to-end success for two open models near 30B parameters over prompting and brings to the level of proprietary model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the World State Generator (WSG), a model trained on ~226K verified failure-repair trajectories from 7 synthetic worlds, which represents plans as checkable world states so that refusals attach to the plan and remaining states are rewritten to obey the world's rules. WSG improves end-to-end success of ~30B open models on 7 benchmarks to near-proprietary levels.
AI.motivation: Prompted planners fail when the world refuses a step: they reword the refused step, hit the same refusal, and exhaust the attempt budget. The root cause is that language plans are never tied to the world, so a refusal has nothing in the plan to attach to. Worlds have their own rules, admissible actions, and constraints—physical limits, logical dependencies, required orders—that language never states.
AI.method: Build synthetic worlds across 7 domains and extract training data. A program enforces each world's rules and grades its goal; a world is admitted only if its goal is reachable from its initial state. Agents run inside and leave verified failures paired with repairs that carried the run to a world-certified state, yielding ~226K trajectories. Train the World State Generator to write plans as checkable states of the world and keep the plan aligned with the world, treating a failed state as a stated rule and rewriting remaining states to obey it.
AI.result: Across 7 public benchmarks, WSG raises end-to-end success for two open models near 30B parameters over prompting and brings performance to the level of proprietary models.
AI.conclusion: Tying a plan to the world as checkable states, and letting failures act as rules that reshape the remaining plan, enables agents to bend to the world as the run proceeds. WSG shows that world-grounded state representation, not prompting alone, closes much of the gap between open and proprietary agents.

title: PackLab: A Comprehensive Framework for Developing, Training, and Evaluating MLLMs in Robotic Bin Packing
comment: The code, model, dataset, and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Correr-Zhou/PackLab
summary: Robotic bin packing requires long-horizon sequential decision-making, as each object placement affects the available space for subsequent packing. Existing methods primarily rely on hand-crafted geometric heuristics that optimize predefined objectives or reinforcement learning policies learned through trial and error over predefined training configurations. Despite recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for this task, their potential for closed-loop sequential decisions across heterogeneous packing configurations remains underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce PackLab, a comprehensive framework for developing, training, and evaluating MLLMs for closed-loop robotic bin packing. PackLab-Suite provides a physics-based simulation platform for scalable generation of diverse training packing trajectories and evaluation of their physical outcomes. PackLab-VLM is a packing-specialized MLLM that understands the evolving object and container states to jointly select objects and predict placements in a closed-loop manner. PackLab-Bench provides standardized packing scenarios at multiple difficulty levels for systematic evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, on average, PackLab-VLM outperforms conventional packing heuristics, traditional reinforcement learning methods, and general-purpose MLLMs across object sets and container configurations, highlighting the potential of MLLMs for long-horizon robotic packing. The code, model, dataset, and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Correr-Zhou/PackLab .

AI.tldr: PackLab is a framework for developing, training, and evaluating multimodal LLMs for closed-loop robotic bin packing, including a physics-based simulation suite, a packing-specialized MLLM, and a multi-difficulty benchmark, showing the MLLM outperforms heuristics, RL, and general-purpose MLLMs.
AI.motivation: Robotic bin packing is a long-horizon sequential decision problem where each placement changes the space available for later objects. Existing approaches depend on hand-crafted geometric heuristics or RL policies trained under fixed configurations. Although MLLMs have shown promise, their ability to make closed-loop sequential decisions across heterogeneous packing configurations is underexplored.
AI.method: The authors introduce PackLab, comprising three components: PackLab-Suite, a physics-based simulation platform for scalable generation of diverse packing trajectories and physical-outcome evaluation; PackLab-VLM, a packing-specialized MLLM that perceives evolving object and container states and jointly selects objects and predicts placements in a closed loop; and PackLab-Bench, standardized packing scenarios at multiple difficulty levels for systematic evaluation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that PackLab-VLM on average outperforms conventional packing heuristics, traditional reinforcement learning methods, and general-purpose MLLMs across object sets and container configurations.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight the potential of MLLMs for long-horizon robotic packing. Code, model, dataset, and benchmark are released at https://github.com/Correr-Zhou/PackLab.

title: Epi-Logic: A Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Runtime Control, Schema Validity Checking, and Controlled Accommodation in Autonomous AI Agents
comment: 26 pages, 1 figure, 1 table
summary:
Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed in areas where wrong decisions are hard to reverse. This paper examines schema mismatch: the condition in which an agent operates within an interpretive frame that no longer applies to the current context. Outputs produced under such a mismatch can appear internally consistent, linguistically plausible, and largely factually correct; output-quality metrics alone therefore capture the underlying loss of validity only partially.
  The paper introduces Epi-Logic, a conceptual framework for epistemic runtime control. It couples the detection of schema dissonance, a graduated reduction of autonomy, and the auditable switch to a validated schema. A schema is formalised as a tuple of variable space, expectation model, validity conditions, axioms, and metadata. The Epi-Score aggregates seven graded dimensions of epistemic dissonance; the temporal validity dimension D8, violations of the validity conditions G, and axiom violations are carried as separate categorical paths that are not offset against the aggregate.
  The architecture rests on a checking asymmetry: formalised validity conditions can be checked at runtime, whereas the correctness of many actions is established only ex post. The paper separates two architectural properties, a conditional result from sequential changepoint detection, and an empirical remainder. Eight falsifiable propositions with named baselines describe the transition to empirical validation. All propositions are empirically testable hypotheses, not established results.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Epi-Logic, a conceptual framework for epistemic runtime control in autonomous AI agents. It formalises "schema mismatch" — operating under an interpretive frame no longer valid for the current context — and proposes detection of schema dissonance, graduated autonomy reduction, and auditable schema switching via a seven-dimension Epi-Score with separate categorical paths for temporal validity, validity-condition violations, and axiom violations.
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed where wrong decisions are hard to reverse. In such settings, schema mismatch can yield outputs that are internally consistent, linguistically plausible, and largely factually correct, so output-quality metrics capture the underlying loss of validity only partially. This motivates runtime epistemic control rather than reliance on output-quality evaluation alone.
AI.method: The paper presents Epi-Logic, a conceptual framework that couples (i) detection of schema dissonance, (ii) graduated reduction of autonomy, and (iii) an auditable switch to a validated schema. A schema is formalised as a tuple of variable space, expectation model, validity conditions, axioms, and metadata. The Epi-Score aggregates seven graded dimensions of epistemic dissonance, while the temporal validity dimension D8, violations of validity conditions G, and axiom violations are carried as separate categorical paths not offset against the aggregate. The architecture rests on a checking asymmetry: formalised validity conditions are checkable at runtime, whereas the correctness of many actions is established only ex post. The paper separates two architectural properties, a conditional result from sequential changepoint detection, and an empirical remainder, and specifies eight falsifiable propositions with named baselines.
AI.result: The paper reports no established empirical results. Its contributions are conceptual and architectural: the Epi-Logic framework, the schema tuple formalisation, the Epi-Score with seven graded dimensions and three non-offset categorical paths, and a separation between a conditional result derived from sequential changepoint detection, an architectural component, and an empirical remainder. Eight falsifiable propositions with named baselines are laid out to guide the transition to empirical validation.
AI.conclusion: Epi-Logic reframes agent reliability as a problem of epistemic runtime control rather than output quality alone, using schema-dissonance detection, graduated autonomy reduction, and auditable schema switching. The framework's claims are explicitly framed as empirically testable hypotheses, not established results; the next step is empirical validation of the eight falsifiable propositions.

title: Risk-Aware Motion Planning and Control under Unknown Dynamics with Hybrid Observations
summary: We consider robotic motion planning and control under unknown dynamics with hybrid state observations, where state measurements are available only in parts of the state space. Existing work combines system identification, predicted reachability, graph search and controller synthesis in a hierarchical framework using local affine approximated models over polytopic state space partitioning, but requires state observations for identification and feedback control. Based on this framework, we address blind regions by selecting nominal dynamics and precomputing open-loop control sequences before observation is lost. Since the true dynamics may differ from the selected nominal model, the robot may exit a blind polytope through an unintended facet. We quantify this transition risk and incorporate the possible outcomes into a stochastic transition system. The high-level planning problem is formulated as a stochastic shortest path problem, whose policy guides controller synthesis. A case study demonstrates that the method guides the robot from an initial state to a target while balancing route efficiency and the risks associated with traversing blind regions.

AI.tldr: This paper extends a hierarchical motion planning framework to handle hybrid state observations, where measurements are unavailable in "blind" regions. It selects nominal dynamics, precomputes open-loop control before observation loss, and quantifies the risk of exiting blind polytopes through unintended facets, incorporating these outcomes into a stochastic transition system solved as a stochastic shortest path problem.
AI.motivation: Existing hierarchical frameworks for motion planning under unknown dynamics combine system identification, predicted reachability, graph search, and controller synthesis over polytopic partitions with local affine models. However, these methods require state observations for identification and feedback control, so they fail in blind regions where state measurements are unavailable—a realistic scenario given hybrid state observations.
AI.method: Building on the hierarchical framework, the authors handle blind regions by (1) selecting nominal dynamics and precomputing open-loop control sequences before observation is lost, (2) quantifying the risk that the true dynamics differ from the nominal model, causing the robot to exit a blind polytope through an unintended facet, and (3) incorporating these possible outcomes into a stochastic transition system. High-level planning is cast as a stochastic shortest path problem, whose policy guides controller synthesis.
AI.result: A case study shows that the method successfully guides the robot from an initial state to a target while balancing route efficiency against the risks of traversing blind regions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach enables motion planning and control under unknown dynamics with hybrid state observations by explicitly modeling transition risk in blind regions and integrating it into a stochastic shortest path formulation, yielding a policy that trades off efficiency and risk.

title: Construting Reverse Thinking: Developing Large Language Models' Reverse Thingking Ability
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: When facing complex problems, humans tend to try various ideas for different issues. Human thinking patterns exhibit remarkable flexibility in adapting to diverse scenarios. GPT-o1, GPT-o3, and DeepSeek-R1 adopt long chain-of-thought models to address complex problems by increasing reasoning depth, which default to a forward reasoning mode. We conducted statistical analysis on the accuracy of different mathematical problem datasets on models of different scales, and found five reasons for errors: Insufficient solution-space coverage, Computational mistakes, Unverified assumptions, Ignoring constraint conditions, Maximum response length limitation. To address the above issues, we proposed a backward reasoning pattern construction method aimed at enhancing the model's reverse thinking ability and dynamic adaptability. First, we constructed an easy-hard two-stage Math dataset for training large models and gradually improving their inference ability at different difficulty levels. The dataset contains forward reasoning paths as well as backward reasoning paths. And a two-stage supervised fine-tuning process is applied to progressively train the model's backward reasoning capability. Furthermore, a fine-grained reward mechanism is developed, employing smoothed reward signals to strengthen the model's ability to autonomously select thinking modes during the reasoning process, thereby avoiding reward hacking. A linear-decay balanced sampling strategy is designed to maintain a balance between forward and backward reasoning path samples during training, enabling the model to converge quickly and stably. Experimental results show that our method significantly improves reasoning efficiency and accuracy in tasks such as mathematical proofs, offering a flexible and efficient reasoning paradigm for solving complex problems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a backward reasoning pattern construction method to enhance large models' reverse thinking and dynamic adaptability, using a two-stage easy-hard math dataset, two-stage supervised fine-tuning, a fine-grained smoothed reward mechanism, and linear-decay balanced sampling, yielding significant gains in reasoning efficiency and accuracy on tasks like mathematical proofs.
AI.motivation: Current long chain-of-thought models (GPT-o1, GPT-o3, DeepSeek-R1) default to a forward reasoning mode to handle complexity by increasing reasoning depth. Statistical analysis across math datasets and model scales reveals five error sources: insufficient solution-space coverage, computational mistakes, unverified assumptions, ignoring constraint conditions, and maximum response length limitation. These shortcomings motivate a reasoning paradigm that adds reverse thinking and dynamic adaptability.
AI.method: 1) An easy-hard two-stage math dataset containing both forward and backward reasoning paths for progressive training. 2) A two-stage supervised fine-tuning process that progressively trains backward reasoning capability. 3) A fine-grained reward mechanism with smoothed reward signals to encourage autonomous selection of thinking modes and avoid reward hacking. 4) A linear-decay balanced sampling strategy to keep forward/backward reasoning samples balanced for fast, stable convergence.
AI.result: Experimental results show that the method significantly improves reasoning efficiency and accuracy in tasks such as mathematical proofs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed backward reasoning construction method offers a flexible and efficient reasoning paradigm for solving complex problems, enhancing the model's reverse thinking ability and dynamic adaptability beyond the default forward reasoning mode.

title: ContactDP: Contact-Guided Diffusion Policy for Tight Insertion Tasks
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures
summary: High-precision connector insertion remains challenging for robotic systems due to tight mechanical tolerances, partial observability during contact, and multimodal uncertainty arising from occlusion and contact ambiguity. Successful insertion requires closed-loop contact guidance that continuously integrates global alignment cues with local contact feedback to produce stable corrective actions under interaction. In this work, we present ContactDP (Contact-Guided Diffusion Policy for Tight Insertion Tasks), a multimodal diffusion-policy framework for contact-rich insertion. ContactDP jointly integrates wrist RGB observations, fingertip tactile sensing, and wrist-mounted force-torque measurements to infer contact state and generate temporally consistent corrective motions during insertion. To ensure stable execution under contact, the learned policy operates together with a hybrid position-force controller that provides compliant low-level interaction. We evaluate our approach on a suite of industrial-grade connector insertion tasks with varying connector geometries, grasp conditions, and initial misalignment. Across all tasks, ContactDP significantly outperforms vision-only diffusion policies for performance, reliability and generalization.

AI.tldr: ContactDP is a multimodal diffusion-policy framework that fuses wrist RGB, fingertip tactile, and wrist force-torque signals with a hybrid position-force controller to achieve reliable high-precision connector insertion.
AI.motivation: Tight-tolerance connector insertion is difficult for robots due to tight mechanical tolerances, partial observability during contact, and multimodal uncertainty from occlusion and contact ambiguity. Vision alone cannot resolve these ambiguities, so closed-loop contact guidance that integrates global alignment cues with local contact feedback is needed to produce stable corrective actions under interaction.
AI.method: The paper proposes ContactDP (Contact-Guided Diffusion Policy), a multimodal diffusion-policy framework that jointly integrates wrist RGB observations, fingertip tactile sensing, and wrist-mounted force-torque measurements to infer contact state and generate temporally consistent corrective motions. The learned policy is coupled with a hybrid position-force controller that provides compliant low-level interaction for stable execution under contact.
AI.result: Evaluated on a suite of industrial-grade connector insertion tasks with varying connector geometries, grasp conditions, and initial misalignment, ContactDP significantly outperforms vision-only diffusion policies in performance, reliability, and generalization.
AI.conclusion: Combining multimodal contact sensing with diffusion-based policy learning and compliant low-level force control yields a robust, generalizable solution for high-precision, contact-rich insertion tasks.

title: Convex AI Compositionality and the Governance of AI System Populations
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures, v1
summary: AI governance increasingly requires providers and public authorities to reason about multiple AI instantiations, alternative versions, and deployment configurations of multiple AI systems. Yet current regulation remains predominantly single-system-centric, acknowledging such multiplicity only sparsely without treating collections of related AI systems as governance objects. This creates an AI population governance problem: determining which instantiations can be meaningfully considered together and how their changing configurations can be represented and monitored. The first requirement has recently been addressed through trustworthiness-based accounts of AI identity. We address the second by introducing convex AI compositionality: a formal representation of the configurations generated by finite AI system populations that uses convex spaces. The core idea is that convex compositions of the operational states that a population of AI system instantiations may occupy over time are compatible with lifecycle reachability across the population and can preserve the formal identity relations between these systems. Well-known statistical and geometric constructions, such as weighted state distributions and convex hulls, become AI governance tools for distinguishing operational states, population weights, heterogeneity, and AI configuration change across different governance modes while remaining compatible, under stated conditions, with lifecycle reachability and AI identity. We illustrate our AI population governance framework through distributed healthcare deployments and controlled deployment of recruitment AI variants.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces convex AI compositionality, a convex-space formal representation of configurations generated by finite populations of related AI system instantiations, enabling AI population-level governance that is compatible with lifecycle reachability and AI identity relations.
AI.motivation: AI governance increasingly must reason about multiple AI instantiations, alternative versions, and deployment configurations across many related systems, yet current regulation remains predominantly single-system-centric. It acknowledges multiplicity only sparsely and does not treat collections of related AI systems as governance objects. This yields an AI population governance problem: deciding which instantiations can be meaningfully considered together and how their changing configurations can be represented and monitored. While the first requirement has recently been addressed via trustworthiness-based accounts of AI identity, the second remained open.
AI.method: The authors propose convex AI compositionality: a formal representation of configurations generated by finite AI system populations using convex spaces. Convex compositions of the operational states that a population of AI instantiations may occupy over time are constructed so as to be compatible with lifecycle reachability across the population and to preserve formal identity relations among the systems. Standard statistical and geometric constructions—weighted state distributions and convex hulls—are repurposed as AI governance tools for distinguishing operational states, population weights, heterogeneity, and AI configuration change across different governance modes, subject to stated conditions ensuring compatibility with lifecycle reachability and AI identity.
AI.result: The framework provides a formal account that renders population-level configurations representable and monitorable while remaining compatible, under stated conditions, with lifecycle reachability and AI identity. Weighted state distributions and convex hulls serve as governance instruments for characterizing operational states, population weights, heterogeneity, and configuration change across governance modes. The approach is illustrated through distributed healthcare deployments and controlled deployment of recruitment AI variants.
AI.conclusion: Convex AI compositionality offers a formal basis for AI population governance, extending single-system-centric regulation to populations of related AI systems by making their changing configurations representable and monitorable in a way that preserves lifecycle reachability and AI identity. The framework is demonstrated on healthcare and recruitment deployment scenarios, suggesting practical applicability to real-world multi-system governance settings.

title: Structured World-State Reasoning for Agentic Robotic Search
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, Submitted to the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027
summary: Long-horizon robotic search must resolve natural language against heterogeneous, incomplete, and often ambiguous evidence: textual information, prior maps, and observations arriving over time. The core challenge is to contextualize these streams and decide where to gather evidence before selecting a target. We present WORLDS: World-state Observation and Reasoning for Language-guided Discovery and Search, a framework that grounds reasoning in a persistent graph initialized from geospatial priors and updated by perception. Parallel Reasoners maintain competing candidate interpretations and request evidence to distinguish between them. We collect and process the requested observations with a multimodal Examiner, after which a Judge selects a grounded target or requests another pass. WORLDS achieves 51.8% navigation success across all 5,311 CityNav test episodes, the highest reported success rate, exceeding the previous published best by 15.7 percentage points under an OSM-only, high-resolution orthographic protocol. On 1,000 shared episodes, it achieves 50.0% versus 27.9% for the strongest adapted baseline using the same model, prior, sensing stack, and movement budget. Observation-based verification by the Examiner contributes 5.9 points of this success, and at a reduced reasoning-effort setting WORLDS still exceeds the adapted GeoNav baseline by 18.8 points while generating fewer tokens. We also demonstrate WORLDS on a quadrotor, which flies the generated sensing waypoints and grounds three language targets, including a vehicle absent from the map, from its onboard imagery.

AI.tldr: WORLDS is a world-state observation and reasoning framework for long-horizon, language-guided robotic search that maintains parallel candidate interpretations over a persistent geospatial-prior graph, gathers targeted evidence via a multimodal Examiner, and selects grounded targets with a Judge, achieving 51.8% success on 5,311 CityNav test episodes (a 15.7-point gain over prior best) and demonstrating on a quadrotor.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon robotic search must resolve natural language against heterogeneous, incomplete, and ambiguous evidence (text, prior maps, streaming observations). The core challenge is contextualizing these streams and deciding where to gather evidence before committing to a target.
AI.method: WORLDS grounds reasoning in a persistent graph initialized from geospatial priors and updated by perception. Parallel Reasoners maintain competing candidate interpretations and request distinguishing evidence, which is collected and processed by a multimodal Examiner; a Judge then selects a grounded target or requests another pass.
AI.result: WORLDS reaches 51.8% navigation success across all 5,311 CityNav test episodes, the highest reported rate and 15.7 points above the previous best under an OSM-only, high-resolution orthographic protocol. On 1,000 shared episodes it scores 50.0% vs. 27.9% for the strongest adapted baseline with identical model, prior, sensing, and movement budget. Examiner-based observation verification adds 5.9 points, and a reduced-effort setting still beats adapted GeoNav by 18.8 points with fewer tokens. A quadrotor demonstration flies generated sensing waypoints and grounds three language targets, including an off-map vehicle, from onboard imagery.
AI.conclusion: WORLDS shows that persistent graph-based world-state grounding combined with parallel hypothesis reasoning, targeted evidence gathering, and observation-based verification substantially improves language-guided robotic search, transfers to real quadrotor hardware, and can ground targets absent from prior maps.

title: GRUET: Quantifying Uncertainty of Agentic Reasoning-and-Acting Processes
summary: Agents have attracted considerably increasing attention due to the power of executing both Reasoning and Acting (ReAct) in open and dynamic environments. The ReAct process typically exhibits a multi-turn trajectory in which one drives Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate both reasoning chains and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner. However, agents often suffer from significant uncertainty, where identical tasks yield divergent trajectories; trajectories with higher uncertainty often produce incomprehensible behaviors, severely undermining agent credibility. This work conjectures that such trajectory-level uncertainty frequently stems from cumulative turn-level reasoning uncertainty induced by LLMs; the latter often exhibits a collection of branches of divergent reasoning chains and their resulting actions. Built upon this, we present the Graph-based Reasoning UncErtainty in Trajectories (GRUET) method for the uncertainty quantification of ReAct, comprising turn-level reasoning uncertainty quantification and trajectory-level uncertainty aggregation; the former precisely quantifies reasoning uncertainty via modeling the reasoning space spanned by potential reasoning branches as a graph and then approximating the reasoning space complexity with graph complexity, while the latter employs simple aggregation strategies for quantifying the overall trajectory credibility. Empirical evaluations across nine LLMs and five benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our proposed GRUET in terms of selective generation performance, measured by AUROC, AUPRC, and AUARC.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes GRUET, a method for quantifying uncertainty in ReAct agent trajectories by modeling turn-level reasoning uncertainty as graph complexity and aggregating it to trajectory-level uncertainty to assess agent credibility.
AI.motivation: Agents executing Reasoning and Acting (ReAct) in open dynamic environments often exhibit significant uncertainty, where identical tasks yield divergent trajectories. Trajectories with higher uncertainty produce incomprehensible behaviors, severely undermining agent credibility. The paper conjectures this trajectory-level uncertainty stems from cumulative turn-level reasoning uncertainty induced by LLMs, which manifests as divergent reasoning branches and resulting actions.
AI.method: The proposed GRUET (Graph-based Reasoning UncErtainty in Trajectories) method comprises two components: (1) turn-level reasoning uncertainty quantification, which models the reasoning space spanned by potential reasoning branches as a graph and approximates reasoning space complexity via graph complexity; and (2) trajectory-level uncertainty aggregation, which employs simple aggregation strategies to quantify overall trajectory credibility.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations across nine LLMs and five benchmarks validate GRUET's effectiveness in selective generation performance, measured by AUROC, AUPRC, and AUARC.
AI.conclusion: Modeling turn-level reasoning uncertainty via graph complexity and aggregating it to the trajectory level provides an effective means of quantifying ReAct agent uncertainty and improving agent credibility assessment.

title: Object-Centered Reconstruction for Vision-Based 3D Force Estimation
summary: Excessive force may damage tissue and increase the risk of anastomotic leakage in robotic colorectal surgery. Although the da Vinci 5 provides force sensing, this capability is unavailable on earlier da Vinci systems and many other surgical robotic platforms. In this work, we present a vision-based pipeline for estimating 3D interaction forces from soft-tissue deformation in stereo endoscopic video. We dynamically reconstruct the tissue point cloud in an object-centered coordinate frame, track tissue points with geometric constraints, and predict the 3D force vector with a neural network. We progressively evaluate the pipeline on rubber-glove phantoms, ex vivo porcine colons, and in vivo colorectal surgical video sequences. Under varying tissue orientations and positions within the endoscopic view, as well as different camera viewpoints, the proposed method achieves average root mean square error (RMSEs) of 0.77 N and 1.30 N on the phantom and porcine colon, respectively. Compared with the camera-frame representation, the object-centered representation reduces average RMSE by 51.3% and 56.7%, while geometry-constrained tracking reduces RMSE by 19.8% and 25.3% compared with CoTracker. We further qualitatively demonstrate the feasibility of vision-based force estimation on an in vivo colorectal surgical sequence, as a step toward clinical translation of vision-based, sensorless force estimation.

AI.tldr: A vision-based pipeline estimates 3D interaction forces from soft-tissue deformation in stereo endoscopic video, using an object-centered point-cloud reconstruction, geometry-constrained tracking, and a neural network, validated on phantoms, ex vivo porcine colons, and in vivo colorectal sequences.
AI.motivation: Excessive force in robotic colorectal surgery can damage tissue and increase anastomotic leakage risk. Force sensing exists only on the da Vinci 5, leaving earlier da Vinci systems and most other surgical robots without this capability, motivating a sensorless alternative.
AI.method: The pipeline dynamically reconstructs the tissue point cloud in an object-centered coordinate frame, tracks tissue points under geometric constraints, and predicts the 3D force vector with a neural network, using stereo endoscopic video.
AI.result: Average RMSEs of 0.77 N (phantom) and 1.30 N (porcine colon) were achieved across varying tissue orientations, positions, and camera viewpoints. The object-centered representation reduced average RMSE by 51.3% and 56.7% versus the camera-frame representation, and geometry-constrained tracking reduced RMSE by 19.8% and 25.3% versus CoTracker. Feasibility was qualitatively shown on an in vivo colorectal sequence.
AI.conclusion: The proposed object-centered, geometry-constrained vision pipeline enables accurate sensorless 3D force estimation and represents a step toward clinical translation for robotic colorectal surgery.

title: MedRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Medical Agents via Clinically Aligned Self-Evolution
summary: Medical agents increasingly combine general reasoning models with specialized clinical tools, yet their capabilities remain largely fixed by what clinicians and engineers design before deployment. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a different paradigm in which agents learn from their own failures and autonomously expand their capabilities, but directly applying RSI to medicine introduces fundamental safety challenges. We introduce MedRSI, the first recursive self-improvement framework for medicine, which continuously transforms diagnostic failures into new clinical capabilities through tool composition and task-specific model training. Inspired by clinical practice, MedRSI introduces two mechanisms for clinically aligned self-evolution. Clinical-cost-aware failure prioritization directs improvement toward errors according to their potential clinical consequences rather than frequency alone. Fast discovery with slow registration separates rapid capability invention from conservative adoption, allowing new tools to enter the persistent agent only after demonstrating sustained benefit across subsequent patient cohorts. Across public glaucoma and heart disease benchmarks and two private clinical tasks, MedRSI progressively develops segmentation, measurement, prediction, multimodal reasoning, and generative capabilities, surpasses manually engineered medical agents, and autonomously discovers solutions to clinical problems not anticipated by its original designers. Our results show that medical agents need not remain constrained by capabilities specified before deployment: with clinically grounded mechanisms governing what to improve and what to retain, they can continuously construct, validate, and accumulate new capabilities from diagnostic experience. Code is available at https://github.com/ImprintLab/MedRSI.

AI.tldr: MedRSI is the first recursive self-improvement framework for medicine, enabling medical agents to autonomously convert diagnostic failures into new clinical capabilities via tool composition and task-specific training, while enforcing clinical safety through cost-aware prioritization and delayed adoption.
AI.motivation: Medical agents' capabilities are largely fixed at design time by clinicians and engineers. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) could let agents learn from failures and expand capabilities autonomously, but applying RSI directly in medicine raises fundamental safety concerns.
AI.method: MedRSI continuously transforms diagnostic failures into new capabilities through tool composition and task-specific model training. Two clinically aligned mechanisms: (1) clinical-cost-aware failure prioritization, targeting errors by potential clinical consequence rather than frequency; (2) fast discovery with slow registration, separating rapid capability invention from conservative adoption, so new tools enter the persistent agent only after sustained benefit across subsequent patient cohorts.
AI.result: Across public glaucoma and heart disease benchmarks and two private clinical tasks, MedRSI progressively develops segmentation, measurement, prediction, multimodal reasoning, and generative capabilities, surpasses manually engineered medical agents, and autonomously discovers solutions to clinical problems not anticipated by its original designers.
AI.conclusion: Medical agents need not remain constrained by pre-deployment specified capabilities; with clinically grounded mechanisms governing what to improve and what to retain, they can continuously construct, validate, and accumulate new capabilities from diagnostic experience.

title: Grounded Action Model: 3D Grounding as a Foundation for Robotics
summary: Manipulation policies must know which objects matter and where they are, yet the pretrained backbones that current robot foundation models build on, from language in vision-language-action models (VLAs) to video generation in world-action models (WAMs), do not directly require this metric grounding, leaving it to be learned implicitly from robot demonstrations. We propose Grounded Action Models (GAMs), a new paradigm of robot foundation models built with 3D grounding. GAM can be conditioned using language, points, or box prompts, which are first transformed into a shared object-centric representation of the selected objects. This representation captures target-focused visual features and metric object geometry, which is mixed with robot state history through a multi-stream transformer to predict action chunks. Although GAMs can be run autonomously, they can also serve as a low-level controller that a high-level planner controls using its various input modalities, allowing for long-horizon and memory-dependent manipulation. On RoboTwin 2.0, GAM achieves an average success rate of 55.3% across 50 tasks (vs. 52.0% for Spatial Forcing), including 47.6% under scene randomization (vs. 30.4% for Abot-M0), with its action policy trained only on clean-scene demonstrations. On LIBERO-PRO, it achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate of 61% (vs. 53% for $π_{0.5}$) across 16 perturbation settings, with the largest gains when targets are relocated or newly designated. On two real robots, GAM retains 17/20 successes under visual shift on a bimanual YAM versus 4/20 for $π_{0.5}$, while its composition with a Molmo2 planner on a Franka achieves 64.7% ID and 49.8% OOD step completion on long-horizon and memory-dependent tasks.

AI.tldr: GAM is a robot foundation model built on explicit 3D grounding, using language/point/box prompts to form an object-centric representation that is fused with robot state history to predict actions, achieving strong robustness and state-of-the-art results across simulation and real-robot benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current robot foundation models (VLAs, WAMs) rely on pretrained backbones that do not require metric grounding, so the ability to identify which objects matter and where they are must be learned implicitly from robot demonstrations, limiting generalization and robustness.
AI.method: GAM conditions on language, point, or box prompts that are first transformed into a shared object-centric representation capturing target-focused visual features and metric object geometry. This representation is mixed with robot state history via a multi-stream transformer to predict action chunks. GAMs can run autonomously or serve as a low-level controller for a high-level planner, enabling long-horizon and memory-dependent manipulation.
AI.result: On RoboTwin 2.0, GAM reaches 55.3% average success across 50 tasks (vs. 52.0% for Spatial Forcing), including 47.6% under scene randomization (vs. 30.4% for Abot-M0) despite training only on clean-scene demonstrations. On LIBERO-PRO, it achieves 61% average success (vs. 53% for π_0.5) across 16 perturbation settings, with largest gains under target relocation/new designation. On two real robots, GAM retains 17/20 successes under visual shift on a bimanual YAM (vs. 4/20 for π_0.5), and composed with a Molmo2 planner on a Franka achieves 64.7% ID and 49.8% OOD step completion on long-horizon and memory-dependent tasks.
AI.conclusion: Explicit 3D grounding provides a stronger foundation than implicit grounding for robot foundation models, yielding improved robustness, generalization, and compatibility with high-level planners.

title: Extracting Arguments, Not Just Classifying Them: Instruction-Tuned LLMs for Generative Component Detection
summary: Argumentative component detection (ACD) is a core subtask of Argument(ation) Mining (AM) and one of its most challenging aspects, as it requires jointly delimiting argumentative spans and classifying them into components such as claims and premises. While research on this subtask remains relatively limited compared to other AM tasks, most existing approaches formulate it as a simplified sequence labeling problem, component classification, or a pipeline of component segmentation followed by classification. In this paper, we propose ITFACD, a novel approach based on instruction-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) using compact instruction-based prompts, and reframe ACD as a language generation task, enabling arguments to be identified directly from plain text without relying on pre-segmented components. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that our approach achieves higher performance compared to state-of-the-art systems. To the best of our knowledge, this is one of the first attempts to fully model ACD as a generative task, highlighting the potential of instruction tuning for complex AM problems. Our code and the datasets used are openly available in the following GitHub repository.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ITFACD, an instruction-tuned LLM approach that reframes argumentative component detection (ACD) as a language generation task, eliminating the need for pre-segmented components and outperforming state-of-the-art systems.
AI.motivation: ACD is a core yet challenging subtask of Argumentation Mining, requiring joint delimitation of argumentative spans and classification into components like claims and premises. Existing approaches are limited by formulating ACD as simplified sequence labeling, component classification, or a two-stage pipeline of segmentation followed by classification.
AI.method: The authors introduce ITFACD, an approach based on instruction-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) using compact instruction-based prompts, reframing ACD as a language generation task so arguments can be identified directly from plain text without pre-segmented components.
AI.result: Experiments on standard benchmarks show that ITFACD achieves higher performance compared to state-of-the-art systems.
AI.conclusion: This is one of the first attempts to fully model ACD as a generative task, highlighting the potential of instruction tuning for complex Argumentation Mining problems. Code and datasets are openly available in a GitHub repository.

title: HumynexSurg-1: A Curated Expert Liposuction Dataset
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, 13 tables. Version 0 dataset release
summary: Robot foundation models learn manipulation from large demonstration corpora, but surgery is missing from those corpora: across the 780-hour Open-H surgical collection, one dataset carries synchronized force and none covers an aesthetic procedure. Liposuction is the hard case, because the instrument works under the skin and the surgeon operates by feel and by judgment. Humynex Robotics builds curated expert datasets for this kind of procedure. HumynexSurg-1 is the first release: a master liposuction surgeon performing on porcine abdominal tissue while narrating every decision, recorded with synchronized suction pressure, six-axis hand force/torque, top-down RGB-D video, side video and a lavalier microphone -- 14 episodes, 42,738 frames, 35.6 minutes, 356 utterances of which 95% compile into a liposuction-specific label schema. The capture follows a patent-pending sensing plan organized around the quantities a policy needs, so a channel captured today by a model can be upgraded to a sensor tomorrow without changing the data format. This release captures the instrument motion as a tool-hand track in the side video and provides the force channel as state; the funded capture adds a measured 6-DoF handle pose, a validated force channel, ultrasound imaging of the fat layer, and palpation sensing. As a proof of concept, NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1.7 fine-tunes on the dataset with no custom code in under an hour per run and learns the recorded sessions; scaling probes on the same episodes show where further gains come from: every new session lowers the error on an unseen session. The dataset, its label schema, its quality-assurance reports and its evaluation protocol are the product; the next capture, many short sessions across fat regions with the sensors named here, is what the probes point to.

AI.tldr: HumynexSurg-1 is the first synchronized multimodal expert dataset for liposuction (14 episodes, 42,738 frames), captured on porcine tissue with pressure, 6-axis hand force/torque, RGB-D, side video and narrated decisions; a proof-of-concept fine-tune of NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1.7 learns the sessions, and scaling probes show cross-session error decreasing with each added session.
AI.motivation: Robot foundation models learn manipulation from large demonstration corpora, yet surgery is absent from them: across the 780-hour Open-H surgical collection, only one dataset carries synchronized force and none covers an aesthetic procedure. Liposuction is the hardest such case since the instrument acts beneath the skin and the surgeon relies on feel and judgment.
AI.method: Humynex Robotics curates expert datasets for this procedure class. HumynexSurg-1 records a master liposuction surgeon on porcine abdominal tissue while narrating every decision, with synchronized suction pressure, six-axis hand force/torque, top-down RGB-D video, side video and a lavalier microphone: 14 episodes, 42,738 frames, 35.6 minutes, 356 utterances (95% compiling into a liposuction-specific label schema). The capture follows a patent-pending sensing plan organized around the quantities a policy needs, so a channel captured today as model input can later be upgraded to a physical sensor without changing the data format. This release carries instrument motion as a tool-hand track in the side video and force as state; the funded capture adds measured 6-DoF handle pose, a validated force channel, ultrasound imaging of the fat layer, and palpation sensing. As proof of concept, NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1.7 is fine-tuned on the dataset with no custom code in under an hour per run.
AI.result: GR00T N1.7 learns the recorded sessions, and scaling probes on the same episodes show where further gains arise: every new session lowers the error on an unseen session. The dataset, its label schema, quality-assurance reports and evaluation protocol constitute the product; the probes point to a next capture of many short sessions across fat regions with the named sensors.
AI.conclusion: Surgery, and aesthetic procedures in particular, remain absent from robot foundation-model corpora, and liposuction exemplifies the under-skin, feel-and-judgment regime that current data lacks. HumynexSurg-1 addresses this with a synchronized multimodal, narration-annotated expert dataset and a sensor-plan data format designed for policy needs, demonstrating that standard foundation-model fine-tuning can learn the sessions and that added sessions generalize to unseen ones — motivating a scaled next capture of short, sensor-rich sessions.

title: Partner-Specific Affective Precision in Social Active Inference
comment: 26 pages, 6 figures. Accepted as a full paper at the 7th International Workshop on Active Inference (IWAI 2026). Code: https://github.com/har5h1l/affect_aif
summary: In multi-agent social settings, model reliability varies across relationships. Beyond inferring what others will do, an agent must calibrate how confidently those inferences should guide policy selection for each relationship. An agent may maintain a well-validated model of one partner, a fragile model of another, and a model under revision for a third; collapsing these into a single confidence estimate loses information relevant to policy selection. We therefore formalize affective precision as a relationship-specific metacognitive estimate of confidence in the current partner model.
