AI.conclusion: By fixing the diffusion policy and training only the noise policy, DSRL achieves performance-preserving fine-tuning for social navigation, and integrating multi-seed diffusion-based RL policies as the base policy further improves learning performance, with validation on a physical robot.

title: LIBERO-VPro: Benchmarking Closed-Loop Visual Robustness of Robotic Foundation Models
comment: Project:https://huiqiongli.github.io/LIBERO-VPro/
summary: Robotic foundation models achieve impressive performance on standard manipulation benchmarks, yet these evaluations typically assume clean, timely, and consistent visual observations throughout execution. We introduce LIBERO-VPro, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the closed-loop visual robustness of robotic foundation models by perturbing the visual evidence available during execution. LIBERO-VPro covers four complementary dimensions, including Visual Evidence Degradation, Camera Staleness, Visual Source Consistency, and Task-Relevant Scene Variation, spanning 12 challenge categories, 96 experimental settings, and 3,296 task-condition cases. We evaluate three vision-language-action models and three world-action models over approximately 196,000 simulated episodes, complemented by 200 real-world rollouts on a Franka Research 3. Our results reveal that strong nominal performance can mask substantial weaknesses in visual grounding and adaptation. Models often remain successful despite severe object-level occlusion, yet degrade sharply when local interaction cues are disrupted or familiar spatial priors are violated. They are also highly sensitive to stale or missing observations and struggle when changed task preconditions require behavioral adaptation. Finally, VLAs and WAMs exhibit distinct robustness profiles, showing that visual robustness is multi-dimensional and architecture-dependent. LIBERO-VPro provides a systematic diagnostic framework for developing robotic foundation models that can more reliably ground and adapt their actions under challenging visual conditions.

AI.tldr: LIBERO-VPro is a benchmark that evaluates closed-loop visual robustness of robotic foundation models by perturbing visual evidence during execution across four dimensions, 12 challenge categories, 96 settings, and 3,296 task-condition cases, revealing that strong nominal performance can mask substantial visual grounding and adaptation weaknesses.
AI.motivation: Robotic foundation models perform well on standard manipulation benchmarks, but these evaluations typically assume clean, timely, and consistent visual observations. This leaves closed-loop visual robustness under realistic perturbations largely unexamined.
AI.method: The authors introduce LIBERO-VPro, a benchmark that perturbs visual evidence available during execution. It covers four complementary dimensions: Visual Evidence Degradation, Camera Staleness, Visual Source Consistency, and Task-Relevant Scene Variation, spanning 12 challenge categories, 96 experimental settings, and 3,296 task-condition cases. Three vision-language-action (VLA) models and three world-action models (WAMs) are evaluated over approximately 196,000 simulated episodes plus 200 real-world rollouts on a Franka Research 3.
AI.result: Strong nominal performance can mask substantial weaknesses in visual grounding and adaptation. Models often remain successful despite severe object-level occlusion, yet degrade sharply when local interaction cues are disrupted or familiar spatial priors are violated. They are highly sensitive to stale or missing observations and struggle when changed task preconditions require behavioral adaptation. VLAs and WAMs exhibit distinct robustness profiles.
AI.conclusion: Visual robustness is multi-dimensional and architecture-dependent. LIBERO-VPro offers a systematic diagnostic framework for developing robotic foundation models that can more reliably ground and adapt their actions under challenging visual conditions.

title: Multi-Agent Transportation of Free-Flyers in Microgravity Via Pushing Interaction Under Human-in-the-Loop Control
summary: We propose a safety-critical framework for the cooperative transportation of passive targets in microgravity, where a team of chaser robots acts through unilateral pushing contacts to track a human-provided desired twist while ensuring safe target motion. The pushing-only nature of the interaction introduces sparse, configuration-dependent actuation constraints requiring chasers to physically relocate on the target body when the desired pushing allocation changes. To address these challenges, we formulate a delay-aware feedback control architecture leveraging Control Lyapunov Function (CLF) and Control Barrier Function (CBF) constraints within a mixed-integer thrust allocation program to enforce stability and safety of the target, respectively. The proposed framework enables reference tracking while guaranteeing obstacle avoidance with a circular obstacle despite intermittent control authority, providing a foundation for human-supervised cooperative transportation of free-flyers in space environments. The proposed framework is validated through Gazebo simulations.

AI.tldr: A delay-aware CLF/CBF-based mixed-integer thrust allocation framework enables a team of chaser robots to cooperatively transport a passive target in microgravity via unilateral pushing contacts, achieving twist tracking and obstacle avoidance despite sparse, configuration-dependent actuation.
AI.motivation: Cooperative transportation of passive targets in microgravity is safety-critical, yet pushing-only (unilateral) contact makes actuation sparse and configuration-dependent. When the desired pushing allocation changes, chasers must physically relocate on the target body, creating intermittent control authority that jeopardizes stability and safety. A framework is needed that handles these constraints while tracking a human-provided desired twist and guaranteeing safe target motion.
AI.method: The authors formulate a delay-aware feedback control architecture that embeds Control Lyapunov Function (CLF) constraints for stability and Control Barrier Function (CBF) constraints for safety within a mixed-integer thrust allocation program. This allocation explicitly accounts for the sparse, configuration-dependent actuation induced by unilateral pushing and the need for chasers to reposition on the target body when the pushing allocation changes.
AI.result: The framework enables reference (twist) tracking while guaranteeing avoidance of a circular obstacle despite intermittent control authority. Validation is performed through Gazebo simulations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed safety-critical, delay-aware CLF/CBF mixed-integer allocation framework provides a foundation for human-supervised cooperative transportation of free-flyers in space environments, ensuring both stability and safety under sparse, intermittent actuation.

title: Zeva-Ego: Egocentric Mid-Training with In-Context Causal Learning for Robot Manipulation
summary: Egocentric video offers a scalable source of physical interaction experience, yet translating it into robot-executable knowledge and enabling continual adaptation remain challenging. We introduce Zeva-Ego, a unified framework that learns physical priors from human experience and evolves through robot interaction. An Action-Centric Encoder (ACE) converts egocentric visual transitions into action-centered supervision for VLA mid-training, while In-Context Causal Learning (ICCL) enables parameter-free adaptation from action-effect feedback at deployment. Scaling Ego data to 10K hours improves RoboTwin success from 63.8% to 75.3%, matching 2K hours of robot demonstrations (74.7%), corresponding to an empirical data ratio of roughly 4-5:1. With accumulated interaction experience, ICCL further improves success from 58% to 89% within four attempts without parameter updates. These results demonstrate a scalable path toward embodied intelligence that learns from human experience and continuously improves through its own interaction.

AI.tldr: Zeva-Ego is a unified framework that learns physical priors from egocentric human video and continuously adapts via robot interaction, using an Action-Centric Encoder for VLA mid-training and In-Context Causal Learning for parameter-free deployment-time adaptation.
AI.motivation: Egocentric video is a scalable source of physical interaction experience, but translating it into robot-executable knowledge and enabling continual adaptation remain challenging. This work aims to exploit human experience at scale while allowing robots to keep improving from their own interactions.
AI.method: The framework combines two components. An Action-Centric Encoder (ACE) converts egocentric visual transitions into action-centered supervision for VLA mid-training. In-Context Causal Learning (ICCL) performs parameter-free adaptation from action-effect feedback at deployment, requiring no parameter updates.
AI.result: Scaling Ego data to 10K hours raises RoboTwin success from 63.8% to 75.3%, matching 2K hours of robot demonstrations (74.7%), an empirical data ratio of roughly 4-5:1. With accumulated interaction experience, ICCL lifts success from 58% to 89% within four attempts without parameter updates.
AI.conclusion: The results indicate a scalable path toward embodied intelligence that learns from human experience and continuously improves through its own interaction.

title: Robotic Valve Turning: Axial Misalignment Correction Using Reaction Torque Feedback
comment: 7 pages, 7 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: In this work, we propose a haptic update control law that uses reaction torques to correct axial misalignment during robotic valve manipulation. Unlike vision-based estimates, which can be affected by calibration errors, occlusion, and uncertainty in the contact geometry, reaction torques arise directly from the physical interaction between the gripper and valve. A geometric relationship exists between the error (misalignment) vector and these torques. The primary aim of this work is to propose a stable controller exploiting this geometric property. Our control law is proven to be uniformly asymptotically stable. Simulations are performed for verification. Furthermore, we experimentally test the robustness of our method using a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm for initial misalignments ranging from $-15^\circ$ to $15^\circ$ at 3 different valve positions and report the resulting data distribution. The absolute value of the median misalignment across all 18 test cases is found to be within $2.46^\circ$ and that of reaction torques within $0.23\mathrm{Nm}$.

AI.tldr: A haptic update control law using reaction torques corrects axial misalignment in robotic valve manipulation, proven uniformly asymptotically stable and validated in simulation and on a Kinova Gen3 arm with median misalignment within 2.46°.
AI.motivation: Vision-based misalignment estimates suffer from calibration errors, occlusion, and contact-geometry uncertainty, motivating a control approach that instead exploits reaction torques arising directly from physical gripper–valve interaction.
AI.method: The authors derive a geometric relationship between the misalignment (error) vector and the reaction torques, and propose a stable control law based on this geometric property, with a proof of uniform asymptotic stability, simulation verification, and experimental robustness testing using a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm.
AI.result: Initial misalignments from −15° to 15° across 3 valve positions (18 test cases) were tested; the median misalignment absolute value stayed within 2.46° and median reaction torque within 0.23 Nm.
AI.conclusion: The proposed reaction-torque-based haptic control law provides a stable and robust alternative to vision-based estimation for correcting axial misalignment in robotic valve manipulation.

title: ScaleMPA: Rethinking Scalable RRT* Acceleration With a Grid-Native Representation
summary: Real-time motion planning remains challenging in large and high-dimensional environments. Prior acceleration of RRT* follows tree-centric state organization, which reduces per-query cost but preserves superlinear end-to-end complexity and limits parallelism through structural dependencies. This paper presents ScaleMPA, a motion-planning accelerator that rethinks RRT* with a grid-native representation. By replacing hierarchical traversal with direct grid-based access, ScaleMPA reduces the planner critical path and exposes fine-grained parallelism. To make this reformulation practical under sparse high-dimensional planning, ScaleMPA further proposes a multi-resolution grid search engine and a hash-grid memory system. Implemented in 28 nm CMOS, ScaleMPA achieves millisecond-level planning latency and delivers 4.7$\times$--44.4$\times$ speedup over state-of-the-art motion-planning accelerators.

AI.tldr: ScaleMPA is a motion-planning accelerator that reformulates RRT* with a grid-native representation, using a multi-resolution grid search engine and hash-grid memory to enable fine-grained parallelism, achieving millisecond-level latency and 4.7x-44.4x speedup over SOTA accelerators in 28nm CMOS.
AI.motivation: Real-time motion planning is difficult in large, high-dimensional environments. Prior RRT* accelerators use tree-centric state organization, which lowers per-query cost but retains superlinear end-to-end complexity and restricts parallelism due to structural dependencies.
AI.method: ScaleMPA replaces hierarchical tree traversal with direct grid-based access, reducing the planner critical path and exposing fine-grained parallelism. To handle sparse high-dimensional planning, it adds a multi-resolution grid search engine and a hash-grid memory system.
AI.result: Implemented in 28 nm CMOS, ScaleMPA achieves millisecond-level planning latency and delivers 4.7x-44.4x speedup over state-of-the-art motion-planning accelerators.
AI.conclusion: A grid-native reformulation of RRT* enables lower critical path, greater parallelism, and significant latency and speedup gains, making it a promising approach for real-time high-dimensional motion planning.

title: A Monolithic Force-Proprioception Soft Acutuator Enabled by Single-Material 3D printing
summary: Pneumatic proprioceptive actuators integrate actuation and sensing for soft robots that attract interest due to functional potential. Existing approaches often suffer from assembly errors or stress concentrations caused by heterogeneous materials. In this work, we propose the Monolithic Force-Proprioception Soft (MFPS) design and fabrication method that integrates an Asymmetric Origami Bending (AOB) chamber and a Force-Proprioception Soft (FPS) sensor with single material through one-step Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) fabrication. Based on the resistance response to strain of conductive thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), we design and analyze the structure of the FPS sensor, and conduct parametric analysis on the sensing characteristics. The FDM fabrication parameters of the MFPS actuator are analyzed, followed by actuator fabrication and characterization of the actuation and proprioception performance. Experimental results show that the MFPS actuator achieves a bending angle of 40°, an output force of 12.5 N, and a resistance change of 26.9% as the applied external force increased from 0 to 45 N. A two-finger force-proprioception gripper is developed based on the MFPS actuator. The grasping and force-proprioception capabilities are experimentally validated, proving that the MFPS design method provides a new approach for the development of self-sensing actuators.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MFPS, a monolithic single-material design and one-step FDM fabrication method integrating an asymmetric origami bending chamber with a conductive TPU force-proprioception sensor, validated in a two-finger self-sensing gripper.
AI.motivation: Pneumatic proprioceptive actuators are attractive for soft robots by combining actuation and sensing, but existing approaches often suffer from assembly errors or stress concentrations caused by heterogeneous materials.
AI.method: A one-step FDM process fabricates, from a single conductive TPU material, an Asymmetric Origami Bending (AOB) chamber and a Force-Proprioception Soft (FPS) sensor exploiting resistance response to strain. The FPS structure is designed and analyzed, sensing characteristics are parametrically studied, FDM fabrication parameters are analyzed, and actuation/proprioception performance is characterized.
AI.result: The MFPS actuator achieves a 40° bending angle, 12.5 N output force, and 26.9% resistance change under external force from 0 to 45 N. A two-finger force-proprioception gripper is developed and its grasping and force-proprioception capabilities are experimentally validated.
AI.conclusion: The MFPS monolithic design and fabrication method provides a new approach for developing self-sensing soft actuators.

title: TACIT: Tactile Contact Supervision for Spatial Attention in Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Visuomotor policies trained from a few demonstrations may reproduce demonstrated trajectories without reliably following changes in object position. Existing approaches with explicit attention typically obtain spatial priors from human annotation or visual models. We introduce TACIT (tactile contact informs attention), which uses measured tactile contacts from teleoperated demonstrations to supervise spatial attention without additional point annotation. Gaussian targets over preceding camera point clouds supervise an attention head whose pooled output conditions a visuotactile diffusion policy. Targets are used only during training; tactile observations remain inputs at inference. In the primary real-robot benchmark, with ten demonstrations per task and five demonstrated placement regions, TACIT achieves 66.7% success on ball placement and 73.3% on peg insertion, compared with 10.0% and 20.0% for input-matched 3D visuotactile fusion and 20.0% and 43.3% for vision-only DP3. TACIT enters the 150 mm palm-to-object approach region within 12 seconds in all 30 trials per task; all remaining failures occur after arrival. Across three training seeds on real ball and simulated peg, TACIT outperforms input-matched fusion and an architecture-matched control without explicit attention supervision, supporting the contribution of supervision beyond branch capacity. Pre-contact and contact-time supervision show no consistent ordering. These results demonstrate that measured tactile contact provides effective spatial supervision for approach behavior from few demonstrations within the evaluated workspace.

AI.tldr: TACIT uses measured tactile contacts from teleoperated demonstrations to supervise a spatial attention head, whose pooled output conditions a visuotactile diffusion policy, improving few-shot ball placement and peg insertion on a real robot without requiring point annotations at inference.
AI.motivation: Visuomotor policies trained from few demonstrations tend to reproduce demonstrated trajectories rather than reliably adapt to changes in object position. Existing attention-based approaches rely on spatial priors from human annotation or pretrained visual models, which is costly and not always reliable. The authors seek supervision that is cheap, automatically available, and grounded in physical interaction.
AI.method: TACIT (tactile contact informs attention) derives spatial attention supervision from measured tactile contacts collected during teleoperated demonstrations, avoiding additional point annotation. Gaussian targets defined over preceding camera point clouds supervise an attention head; the pooled attention output conditions a visuotactile diffusion policy. Targets are used only during training, while tactile observations remain inputs at inference.
AI.result: On a real-robot benchmark with ten demonstrations per task and five demonstrated placement regions, TACIT reaches 66.7% success on ball placement and 73.3% on peg insertion, versus 10.0% and 20.0% for an input-matched 3D visuotactile fusion baseline and 20.0% and 43.3% for vision-only DP3. It enters the 150 mm palm-to-object approach region within 12 s in all 30 trials per task, with all remaining failures occurring after arrival. Across three training seeds on real ball and simulated peg, TACIT outperforms both input-matched fusion and an architecture-matched control lacking explicit attention supervision. Pre-contact and contact-time supervision show no consistent ordering.
AI.conclusion: Measured tactile contact provides effective, annotation-free spatial supervision for approach behavior learned from few demonstrations within the evaluated workspace. The gains reflect the supervision signal rather than branch capacity, though generalization beyond this workspace and the timing of contact supervision remain open questions.

title: InsertAnything: Generalizable Contact-Rich Precision Insertion from Simulation to Reality
summary: Contact-rich precision insertion is a key manipulation skill in robotic assembly. Tight clearances make insertion more sensitive to alignment errors and prone to collisions and jamming, while variations in geometry and clearance across parts further complicate policy reuse. We present a reinforcement learning framework that trains insertion policies entirely in simulation for direct deployment without real-world demonstrations or policy fine-tuning. By combining target poses with compact three-dimensional fingertip force feedback, the policy learns to search for alignment and correct its motion despite errors in the estimated hole position. A decoupled gated reward coordinates alignment and insertion. Force-signal smoothing and state-independent standard deviations stabilize the learning process. The resulting policies perform real-world insertion across multiple hole geometries with a minimum nominal clearance of 0.02 mm and improve success while reducing peak contact forces under hole-position errors. Cross-clearance and cross-geometry evaluations further confirm policy generalization. The system achieved the first perfect score of 20/20 on ManipulationNet's peg-in-hole benchmark under its Human-in-the-Loop protocol, with fully autonomous insertion motions. A single policy trained only on a simulated hexagonal insertion task achieved an overall success rate of 95.0% across eight unseen real-world insertion tasks. These results show that learning entirely in simulation can yield precision insertion skills that can be deployed directly and reused across real-world tasks. The project website (https://mzhsoul.github.io/InsertAnything/) provides open-source simulation and real-robot experiment scripts, assets, and trained checkpoints.

AI.tldr: A reinforcement learning framework trains contact-rich precision insertion policies entirely in simulation using target poses plus 3D fingertip force feedback, a decoupled gated reward, and stabilized learning, enabling direct real-world deployment with 0.02 mm clearance and strong generalization.
AI.motivation: Contact-rich precision insertion is a key robotic assembly skill, but tight clearances make it sensitive to alignment errors and prone to collision and jamming. Variations in geometry and clearance across parts further hinder policy reuse, and prior approaches often require real-world demonstrations or per-task fine-tuning.
AI.method: The authors train insertion policies entirely in simulation for zero-shot real deployment. The policy conditions on target poses and compact 3D fingertip force feedback to search for alignment and correct motion despite estimated hole-position errors. A decoupled gated reward coordinates alignment and insertion, while force-signal smoothing and state-independent standard deviations stabilize learning.
AI.result: The policies perform real-world insertion across multiple hole geometries with a minimum nominal clearance of 0.02 mm, improving success and reducing peak contact forces under hole-position errors. The system achieved the first perfect 20/20 score on ManipulationNet's peg-in-hole benchmark under the Human-in-the-Loop protocol with fully autonomous motions. A single policy trained only on simulated hexagonal insertion reached 95.0% overall success across eight unseen real-world insertion tasks; cross-clearance and cross-geometry evaluations confirm generalization.
AI.conclusion: Learning entirely in simulation can yield precision insertion skills that deploy directly and transfer across real-world tasks without real-world demonstrations or fine-tuning, demonstrating effective sim-to-real transfer for contact-rich manipulation.

title: Bridge3D: Enabling Vision-Language-Action Models to See and Act in 3D
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated remarkable generalization in robotic manipulation via large-scale multimodal pretraining. However, VLA models are mainly trained on 2D-centric observations, which inherently constrains their capacity for precise spatial manipulation. Previous methods enhance 3D awareness by introducing implicit spatial priors, but still lack explicit geometry guidance. In this paper, we propose Bridge3D that integrates both implicit and explicit 3D geometry guidance into pre-trained 2D VLA models, enabling them to ''see'' and ''act'' in 3D. Bridge3D introduces two strategies: 1) Implicit Fusion, which enriches visual tokens with features from 3D foundation models to improve ''seeing'' in 3D; 2) Explicit Conditioning, which integrates action denoising with an explicit 3D semantic field to achieve ''acting'' in 3D. Furthermore, we utilize the proposed layer-wise linear probing to improve learning efficiency. Experiments show that Bridge3D achieves superior performance against state-of-the-art methods. On the RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark, Bridge3D exceeds $π_0$ by 14.0 percentage points, while in real-world experiments, it outperforms Spatial Forcing by 11.7 percentage points. These results demonstrate Bridge3D's strong capabilities in high-precision and spatial-sensitive manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: Bridge3D injects both implicit and explicit 3D geometry guidance into pre-trained 2D VLA models to enable precise 3D-aware robotic manipulation, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: VLA models generalize well via large-scale multimodal pretraining but are trained mainly on 2D-centric observations, which limits precise spatial manipulation. Prior works add only implicit spatial priors and lack explicit geometry guidance.
AI.method: Bridge3D augments pre-trained 2D VLA models with (1) Implicit Fusion, enriching visual tokens with features from 3D foundation models for better 3D "seeing", and (2) Explicit Conditioning, integrating action denoising with an explicit 3D semantic field for 3D "acting". A layer-wise linear probing technique is used to improve learning efficiency.
AI.result: Bridge3D surpasses π0 by 14.0 percentage points on the RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark and outperforms Spatial Forcing by 11.7 percentage points in real-world experiments.
AI.conclusion: Integrating implicit and explicit 3D geometry guidance into 2D VLA models yields strong high-precision, spatial-sensitive manipulation capabilities.

title: Estimation and Control of Tensegrity Manipulator Kinematics based on Strut Inclination Angles
summary: Unlike conventional rigid-link robots defined by discrete joints, continuum robots pose a fundamental challenge for expressing their complex continuous bending configurations for closed-loop control. Several modelling approaches have been proposed for conventional continuum robots, but tensegrity-based continuum robots remain largely open. Moreover, many of these approaches assume a continuous elastic backbone and are therefore not directly applicable to tensegrity manipulators, whose bodies are networks of rigid struts and tensioned cables. This work presents a reduced-order model for shape and posture control of a tensegrity-based continuum manipulator. The manipulator is modelled as a serially connected parallel-link mechanism. The proposed method is formulated as an optimization problem that uses geometric constraints of the tensegrity structure together with information from the Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) sensors embedded in the strut elements. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents the first experimental demonstration of a real-time IMU-based shape estimation method on a full-scale tensegrity manipulator and demonstrates posture control using a simple Proportional-Integral (PI) controller. The results show that the proposed method can estimate the shape of both single-module tensegrity structures and multi-module tensegrity manipulators from arbitrary static configurations and achieve desired postures.

AI.tldr: This work presents a reduced-order model for real-time shape estimation and posture control of a tensegrity-based continuum manipulator, using geometric constraints and embedded IMU sensors, validated experimentally on a full-scale prototype.
AI.motivation: Continuum robots have complex continuous bending configurations that are hard to express for closed-loop control, and existing modelling approaches assume a continuous elastic backbone, making them inapplicable to tensegrity manipulators composed of rigid struts and tensioned cables.
AI.method: The manipulator is modelled as a serially connected parallel-link mechanism. The method is formulated as an optimization problem using geometric constraints of the tensegrity structure together with IMU sensor data embedded in the strut elements. Posture control is achieved with a simple PI controller.
AI.result: The method estimates the shape of both single-module tensegrity structures and multi-module tensegrity manipulators from arbitrary static configurations and achieves desired postures. This is the first experimental demonstration of a real-time IMU-based shape estimation method on a full-scale tensegrity manipulator.
AI.conclusion: The proposed reduced-order model enables real-time IMU-based shape estimation and posture control for tensegrity-based continuum manipulators, overcoming the limitations of elastic-backbone assumptions and demonstrating practical feasibility on a full-scale system.

title: MIRA: Real-Time Full-Duplex Human-Robot Interaction for Embodied Companions
summary: Real-time embodied companion interaction requires a robot to infer user intent from streaming speech, generate timely responses, and execute expressive, interruptible motions. Existing systems typically decouple dialogue orchestration from gesture synthesis, relying on offline motion generation from complete audio. This separation leaves open how a deployed robot can dynamically synchronize response content, prosodic timing, and physical safety under incremental inputs and uncertain turn boundaries. We present MIRA, a unified framework for full-duplex embodied companion interaction. Given streaming user speech, dialogue history, and vocal affect, MIRA predicts both the response text and an explicit embodiment cue. Discrete social behaviors (\eg listening, greeting) are mapped to validated robot trajectories, while open-ended speaking is paired with streaming, co-speech motion. This generative motion is governed by a predict-more-than-commit sliding window that provides temporal look-ahead for motion continuity while limiting physical commitment to a short, cancellable prefix. Crucially, we design CORTEX, a dual-timescale interaction policy that manages low-latency streaming and deliberative turn decisions, backed by a robot-side execution layer that enforces physical safety constraints at the control rate. We deploy MIRA on an Astribot S1 humanoid robot. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate competitive audio-motion alignment relative to state-of-the-art motion-generation baselines, while real-robot deployment measurements characterize streaming responsiveness and interruption handling.

AI.tldr: MIRA is a unified full-duplex framework for embodied companion interaction that jointly predicts response text and embodiment cues from streaming speech, generating interruptible co-speech motion under a dual-timescale policy and validated on an Astribot S1 humanoid.
AI.motivation: Real-time embodied companions must infer intent from streaming speech, respond promptly, and execute expressive interruptible motions. Existing systems decouple dialogue orchestration from gesture synthesis and rely on offline motion generation from complete audio, leaving unresolved how to synchronize response content, prosodic timing, and physical safety under incremental inputs and uncertain turn boundaries.
AI.method: Given streaming user speech, dialogue history, and vocal affect, MIRA predicts response text plus an explicit embodiment cue. Discrete social behaviors (e.g., listening, greeting) map to validated robot trajectories, while open-ended speaking pairs with streaming co-speech motion. A predict-more-than-commit sliding window provides temporal look-ahead for continuity but limits physical commitment to a short cancellable prefix. CORTEX, a dual-timescale interaction policy, manages low-latency streaming and deliberative turn decisions, with a robot-side execution layer enforcing physical safety at control rate.
AI.result: Deployed on an Astribot S1 humanoid, MIRA achieves competitive audio-motion alignment versus state-of-the-art motion-generation baselines; real-robot measurements characterize streaming responsiveness and interruption handling.
AI.conclusion: A unified, safety-aware full-duplex architecture can couple dialogue and motion generation in real time, enabling timely, expressive, and interruptible embodied companion behavior.

title: Smoothness as a Constraint for Stable Humanoid Locomotion
summary: Embodied AI systems, particularly humanoid robots deployed in real world scenarios require whole-body control policies that are both task-responsive and physically smooth. However, smoothness is not uniform across the body: lower body must remain sufficiently reactive, while the upper body must be tightly regulated to preserve stability. Existing reinforcement learning approaches typically impose smoothness through auxiliary terms in the reward function, which compete with task objectives, treating the body as uniform and provide no direct control over the physical quantities responsible for smooth behavior. We introduce DeCap (Decoupled Constraint-aware policy), a constrained reinforcement learning algorithm that decouples whole-body smoothness into separate upper- and lower-body constraint groups, each formulates smoothness as explicit constraints on physical motion limits. To improve constraint satisfaction near feasibility boundaries, DeCap incorporates a bounded barrier penalty that activates proactively as limits are approached and remains bounded at the constraint limit. On real-world humanoid whole-body control task, DeCap reduces upper-body action rate by 2.50x and acceleration by 2.18x relative to reward-based smoothness policies, while also improving lower-body smoothness and reducing transient motion. We demonstrate that a fixed set of smoothness constraints transfers across diverse terrains, alleviating the need of extensive reward tuning.

AI.tldr: DeCap is a constrained reinforcement learning algorithm that decouples whole-body smoothness into separate upper- and lower-body constraint groups, formulated as explicit physical motion limits with a bounded barrier penalty, achieving 2.50x lower upper-body action rate and 2.18x lower acceleration than reward-based smoothness policies on real-world humanoid control.
AI.motivation: Humanoid robots in real-world scenarios need whole-body control policies that are both task-responsive and physically smooth. However, smoothness requirements are non-uniform: the lower body must stay reactive while the upper body must be tightly regulated for stability. Existing RL methods impose smoothness via auxiliary reward terms that compete with task objectives, treat the body as uniform, and offer no direct control over the physical quantities governing smooth behavior.
AI.method: DeCap (Decoupled Constraint-aware policy) is a constrained RL algorithm that decouples whole-body smoothness into separate upper- and lower-body constraint groups, each expressing smoothness as explicit constraints on physical motion limits. It further incorporates a bounded barrier penalty that activates proactively as limits are approached and remains bounded at the constraint limit, improving constraint satisfaction near feasibility boundaries.
AI.result: On a real-world humanoid whole-body control task, DeCap reduces upper-body action rate by 2.50x and acceleration by 2.18x relative to reward-based smoothness policies, while also improving lower-body smoothness and reducing transient motion. A fixed set of smoothness constraints is shown to transfer across diverse terrains, alleviating the need for extensive reward tuning.
AI.conclusion: Formulating decoupled, constraint-based whole-body smoothness with a bounded barrier penalty outperforms reward-shaping approaches, yielding superior upper- and lower-body smoothness and terrain-transferable constraints that reduce reward-engineering effort.

title: ARSTAG: An Agentic Real2Sim2Real System for Task-Specific Robot Data Generation
comment: 12 pages, 15 figures and tables. Project webpage: https://boweili666.github.io/ARSTAG/
summary: Adapting visuomotor policies to new manipulation tasks often requires substantial manual engineering or teleoperated data collection. Simulation can provide task-specific data at scale, but constructing the scene, designing expert behavior, and configuring data generation still require significant per-task effort. We present ARSTAG, an agentic Real2Sim2Real system that turns a single RGB image and a natural-language instruction directly into robot policy-learning data. A hierarchy of language agents constructs a task-scoped simulation scene, generates robot-feasible demonstrations, and expands the training distribution through task-consistent randomization, while a coordinator agent manages cross-stage feedback and recovery. Across seven manipulation tasks spanning grasping, placement, and stacking, the ARSTAG-generated demonstrations enable sim-to-real transfer of three visuomotor policy architectures to a dual-arm robot, with pi0.5 achieving an average real-world success rate of 74.6%. Ablations show that task-consistent randomization substantially improves robustness, and policy performance increases with generated dataset size. Project webpage: https://boweili666.github.io/ARSTAG/.

AI.tldr: ARSTAG is an agentic Real2Sim2Real system that converts a single RGB image plus a natural-language instruction into robot policy-learning data via a hierarchy of language agents, achieving 74.6% average real-world success on seven manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Adapting visuomotor policies to new manipulation tasks typically demands substantial manual engineering or teleoperated data collection. Simulation can supply task-specific data at scale, but scene construction, expert behavior design, and data-generation configuration still require significant per-task effort. The paper aims to eliminate this per-task burden.
AI.method: ARSTAG is a Real2Sim2Real agentic pipeline. Given a single RGB image and a natural-language instruction, a hierarchy of language agents builds a task-scoped simulation scene, generates robot-feasible demonstrations, and expands the training distribution through task-consistent randomization. A coordinator agent manages cross-stage feedback and recovery.
AI.result: Across seven manipulation tasks covering grasping, placement, and stacking, ARSTAG-generated demonstrations enable sim-to-real transfer of three visuomotor policy architectures to a dual-arm robot, with pi0.5 reaching 74.6% average real-world success. Ablations show task-consistent randomization substantially improves robustness, and policy performance scales with generated dataset size.
AI.conclusion: ARSTAG shows that agentic Real2Sim2Real data generation from minimal input can produce effective robot policy-learning data, supporting sim-to-real transfer and improved robustness via task-consistent randomization, with performance scaling with data volume.

title: What do VLM-Based Vision-Language Navigation Models Rely on: Interpreting and Steering Policy Behavior
summary: Modern Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) models rely mostly on pre-trained large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to predict navigation actions. While this fusion of language instructions and visual observations allows multimodal reasoning, it obscures how information is routed across modalities or what mechanisms drive navigation decisions. Thus, it remains unclear whether VLN models ground their predictions in relevant semantic cues or can track task progress. In this work, we study the interpretability and steerability of VLN models. We use intervention-based metrics that measure how visual observations, instructions, and visual memory causally influence navigation decisions. Our results show that these navigation policies are sensitive to all input modalities and do not depend on a single one. We further show that these agents encode navigation progress and retain semantic structure from their VLM backbones, enabling concept-level steering through internal activations. Finally, we extract activation vectors for abstract behaviors to transfer them zero-shot to out-of-distribution real-world scenarios, improving performance without additional fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the interpretability and steerability of Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) models by using intervention-based metrics to measure how visual observations, instructions, and visual memory causally affect navigation decisions, showing that agents encode navigation progress and semantic structure that enable concept-level steering and zero-shot transfer of behavior vectors.
AI.motivation: Modern VLN models rely on pre-trained large VLMs that fuse language instructions and visual observations, but this obscures how information is routed across modalities and what mechanisms drive navigation decisions. It remains unclear whether VLN models ground predictions in relevant semantic cues or track task progress.
AI.method: The authors use intervention-based metrics that measure how visual observations, instructions, and visual memory causally influence navigation decisions. They further analyze internal activations to examine progress encoding, semantic structure, concept-level steering, and extraction of activation vectors for abstract behaviors.
AI.result: Navigation policies are sensitive to all input modalities and do not depend on a single one. The agents encode navigation progress and retain semantic structure from their VLM backbones, enabling concept-level steering through internal activations. Extracted activation vectors for abstract behaviors transfer zero-shot to out-of-distribution real-world scenarios, improving performance without additional fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: VLN models are interpretable and steerable: they causally integrate multiple input modalities, encode task progress and semantic structure, and support concept-level steering, with abstract behavior activation vectors enabling zero-shot transfer to real-world settings and improved performance without fine-tuning.

title: Learning tactile perception from high-bandwidth single-point sensing
summary:
Tactile sensing is increasingly being incorporated into learning-based robotic manipulation, yet many existing approaches rely on spatially distributed sensors. Here we introduce SpectRobot, a framework that transforms single-point tactile signals into compact time-frequency spectrograms. These spectrograms encode high-bandwidth tactile histories as fixed-size image-like representations. They can be processed by standard vision encoders and integrated into learning pipelines originally developed for vision, while preserving temporal and frequency information unavailable to conventional cameras.
  Rather than increasing spatial density through arrays of tactile elements, SpectRobot exploits the rich dynamics contained in sparse, high-bandwidth single-point measurements. In our implementation, the sensors are mounted away from the contact surface while remaining mechanically coupled to it, reducing direct exposure to wear and potentially improving robustness in harsh environments and for long-term deployment on dexterous robots.
  Our experiments demonstrate that: (1) a robot can exploit single-point vibration signals to solve a visually occluded manipulation task; (2) temporal history strongly influences policy performance, while sensing bandwidth controls the spectral information available, with measurements extending to 100~kHz; and (3) the same representation can be used across different tactile sensing technologies mediated by acceleration, force, or strain. We further show that capabilities previously associated with research-grade instrumentation can be accessed using readily available, off-the-shelf hardware. We believe that broader access to high-bandwidth tactile sensing could facilitate the integration of contact dynamics into embodied learning systems and, for some tasks, offer an alternative or complement to increasing the spatial density of tactile sensing.

AI.tldr: SpectRobot converts single-point tactile signals into time-frequency spectrograms that standard vision encoders can process, enabling learning-based manipulation without spatially dense sensor arrays.
AI.motivation: Most learning-based robotic manipulation with tactile sensing relies on spatially distributed sensor arrays, which are costly, wear-prone, and complex to integrate. The authors aim to exploit the rich dynamics of sparse, high-bandwidth single-point tactile measurements instead of increasing spatial density.
AI.method: SpectRobot transforms single-point tactile signals into compact time-frequency spectrograms, encoding high-bandwidth tactile histories as fixed-size image-like representations. These are processed by standard vision encoders and integrated into existing vision-based learning pipelines, preserving temporal and frequency information. Sensors are mounted away from the contact surface while remaining mechanically coupled to it, reducing wear exposure.
AI.result: Experiments show: (1) a robot can use single-point vibration signals to solve a visually occluded manipulation task; (2) temporal history strongly influences policy performance, and sensing bandwidth controls spectral information, with measurements extending to 100 kHz; (3) the same representation works across tactile sensing technologies based on acceleration, force, or strain. Capabilities previously requiring research-grade instrumentation are achieved with off-the-shelf hardware.
AI.conclusion: Broader access to high-bandwidth tactile sensing could facilitate integrating contact dynamics into embodied learning systems and, for some tasks, offer an alternative or complement to increasing tactile sensor spatial density.

title: Feasibility Distance Fields for Heterogeneous Constraints in Robot Configuration Space
comment: Configuration space, distance fields, Eikonal equation, feasibility, self-collision, singularity, Cartesian compliance, multi-robot systems, medial axis, safe control
summary: Robot manipulators are monitored by constraint-specific indicators whose units and gradient scales are not comparable, so they do not provide a common measure of the configuration-space motion remaining before violation. We define the feasibility distance field (FDF) as the distance, under a fixed positive-definite joint-space metric, to the union of infeasible configuration sets. Classical distance-to-set theory gives 1-Lipschitz continuity, almost-everywhere differentiability, and unit dual-gradient norm wherever the nearest projection is unique. The robotics contribution is an admissibility analysis showing when practical constraints define non-empty closed sets. We derive admissible formulations for external and self-collision, joint limits, dexterity, Cartesian and task-projected compliance, joint torque under payload, and dynamic manipulability. Since every field uses the same metric, heterogeneous constraints compose by a pointwise minimum, conditioned constraints retain a fixed distance space, and multi-robot constraints produce block-sparse gradients that identify which robots must react. We generate projection-based labels and train neural approximations with a distance loss and an Eikonal penalty. Simulations on a UR5e and a dual-arm cell evaluate seven fields using value, projection, sign, gradient, composition, and moving-obstacle diagnostics. Across 8,000 configurations, the largest feasible-side secant ratio is 0.920, mean learned gradient norms range from 0.994 to 0.998, and projection residuals range from 0.011 to 0.034 rad. Across 24 random obstacle paths, the external and composed collision fields achieve 90.4% and 91.6% success within 3 cm, with sign-error rates below 2%. The results support a common configuration-space margin and identify approximation errors near medial axes and sparsely sampled boundaries.

AI.tldr: The paper defines a feasibility distance field (FDF) that measures, under a common positive-definite joint-space metric, the distance from a robot configuration to the union of infeasible sets, allowing heterogeneous constraints to be composed uniformly and approximated by neural networks.
AI.motivation: Robot manipulators are typically monitored by constraint-specific indicators whose units and gradient scales are incomparable, so they cannot provide a common measure of remaining configuration-space motion before constraint violation. A unified, metric-consistent distance measure is needed to compose heterogeneous constraints and reason about feasibility margins.
AI.method: The FDF is defined as the distance to the union of infeasible configuration sets under a fixed positive-definite joint-space metric, inheriting 1-Lipschitz continuity, almost-everywhere differentiability, and unit dual-gradient norm where projection is unique. An admissibility analysis establishes when practical constraints define non-empty closed sets, with formulations derived for external and self-collision, joint limits, dexterity, Cartesian and task-projected compliance, joint torque under payload, and dynamic manipulability. Fields compose via pointwise minimum; conditioned constraints retain a fixed distance space, and multi-robot constraints yield block-sparse gradients. Projection-based labels train neural approximations with a distance loss and an Eikonal penalty.
AI.result: Simulations on a UR5e and a dual-arm cell evaluate seven fields via value, projection, sign, gradient, composition, and moving-obstacle diagnostics. Across 8,000 configurations, the largest feasible-side secant ratio is 0.920, mean learned gradient norms range from 0.994 to 0.998, and projection residuals range from 0.011 to 0.034 rad. Across 24 random obstacle paths, external and composed collision fields achieve 90.4% and 91.6% success within 3 cm, with sign-error rates below 2%.
AI.conclusion: The FDF provides a common configuration-space margin across heterogeneous constraints and supports neural approximation. Remaining errors concentrate near medial axes and sparsely sampled boundaries.

title: Think Like a World Model, Act Like a VLA: Distilling World-Model Representations into Compact Robot Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map observations to actions with no objective that accounts for how the world responds, so their robustness is bounded primarily by data coverage. World models carry precisely that missing objective and are better grounded for it, yet rolling the future forward costs seconds per decision and rules them out of the control loop. We show the two can be separated. What a world model knows about physical scenes lives in its \emph{internal features}; generating the future is merely the objective that produced them, so the grounding can be inherited while the generative machinery is left behind. We add one feature-alignment term to ordinary VLA training: a frozen world model is run over the training frames once and cached, and the student learns to agree with that cache. No teacher is loaded during training, the projector is discarded after it, and the deployed policy is identical to the undistilled baseline, running in $32$~ms and $1.86$~GB on a consumer RTX~5090, so every gain is attributable to the representation rather than to added capacity or test-time compute. A $0.8$B student reaches $97.9\%$ on LIBERO, improves from $48.2\%$ to $50.5\%$ on RoboCasa-GR1 humanoid manipulation, and the same objective carries over to real hardware, on both a single-arm and a bimanual platform. The gain survives changes of student scale, backbone, alignment layer, and teacher, indicating a broad representational prior rather than a fragile alignment between two particular networks. Project page: https://thaw-vla.trung-dt.com/.

AI.tldr: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models lack a world-response objective and are bounded by data coverage, while world models have that grounding but are too slow to run in the control loop. The authors decouple the two by adding a single feature-alignment term to ordinary VLA training: a frozen world model is run once over training frames, cached, and the student learns to agree with the cache, with no teacher loaded during training and the projector discarded afterward. The deployed policy is identical to the undistilled baseline (32 ms, 1.86 GB on an RTX 5090), so gains come from the representation. A 0.8B student reaches 97.9% on LIBERO and lifts RoboCasa-GR1 from 48.2% to 50.5%, transferring to real single-arm and bimanual hardware; the gain persists across student scale, backbone, alignment layer, and teacher choice.
AI.motivation: VLA models map observations to actions without any objective accounting for how the world responds, so their robustness is bounded primarily by data coverage. World models carry exactly that missing objective and are better grounded, but rolling the future forward costs seconds per decision, ruling them out of the control loop.
AI.method: The two are separated by exploiting the fact that a world model's physical knowledge lives in its internal features, and generating the future is merely the objective that produced them—so grounding can be inherited while the generative machinery is left behind. Concretely, one feature-alignment term is added to ordinary VLA training: a frozen world model is run over the training frames once and cached, and the student learns to agree with that cache. No teacher is loaded during training, the projector is discarded afterward, and the deployed policy is identical to the undistilled baseline.
AI.result: The deployed policy runs in 32 ms and 1.86 GB on a consumer RTX 5090, so every gain is attributable to the representation rather than added capacity or test-time compute. A 0.8B student reaches 97.9% on LIBERO and improves from 48.2% to 50.5% on RoboCasa-GR1 humanoid manipulation, and the same objective carries over to real hardware on both a single-arm and a bimanual platform. The gain survives changes of student scale, backbone, alignment layer, and teacher.
AI.conclusion: World-model grounding can be inherited by a VLA policy through cached feature alignment at no inference cost, yielding a broad representational prior rather than a fragile alignment between two particular networks.

title: AC-DC: Adaptive Communication for Scalable Dynamic Average Consensus in Multi-Robot Ergodic Search
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures
summary: We study scalable peer-to-peer dynamic average consensus (DC) for multi-robot systems under finite-range, finite-rate, and interference-constrained communication. We introduce Adaptive Communication for Dynamic Average Consensus (AC-DC), which jointly adapts Who communicates with whom, When, and over What parts of the consensus state, using local inputs and successfully received neighbor information. Each robot's consensus state estimates the current average of the robots' local inputs. AC-DC updates these estimates as local inputs change and averages the values exchanged between robot pairs. In AC-DC, robot pairs update without waiting for every robot to complete a communication round, and the selected-state messages carry consensus state coordinates independent of team size for a fixed state representation. We apply AC-DC to dynamic-priority multi-robot ergodic search: one consensus stream estimates team visitation for motion coordination, while the other fuses regional measurement information to update uncertainty maps and search targets. Across twelve settings with up to 80 robots and 20 paired trials per setting, AC-DC has the lowest mean (i) normalized covariance-trace area under the curve (AUC) and (ii) attempted modeled communication payload among the compared decentralized methods. Averaged across settings, AC-DC achieves paired AUC reductions of 27.5% relative to state-of-the-art baselines, with 8.7x less communication traffic. As the number of robots increases, we observe that AC-DC's communication payload approaches that of the ideal centralized baseline (one ground compute-station communicating directly with all robots): with 120 robots in a fixed 600 x 600 m scaling test, AC-DC uses 19.3 MB versus 19.2 MB for the ideal centralized baseline, while remaining peer-to-peer.

AI.tldr: AC-DC enables scalable peer-to-peer dynamic average consensus for multi-robot systems by jointly adapting who communicates with whom, when, and over what parts of the consensus state, achieving lower error and far less communication traffic than decentralized baselines.
AI.motivation: Multi-robot systems under finite-range, finite-rate, and interference-constrained communication need scalable dynamic average consensus, but existing decentralized methods struggle with communication efficiency and accuracy as team size grows. The paper aims to jointly address communication selection and consensus dynamics without a central coordinator.
AI.method: AC-DC jointly adapts Who communicates with whom, When, and over What parts of the consensus state using local inputs and successfully received neighbor information. Each robot's consensus state estimates the current average of local inputs. Robot pairs update without waiting for every robot to complete a communication round, and selected-state messages carry consensus state coordinates independent of team size for a fixed state representation. The method is applied to dynamic-priority multi-robot ergodic search, with one consensus stream estimating team visitation and another fusing regional measurement information.
AI.result: Across twelve settings with up to 80 robots and 20 paired trials per setting, AC-DC achieved the lowest mean normalized covariance-trace AUC and attempted modeled communication payload among compared decentralized methods. Averaged across settings, AC-DC obtained paired AUC reductions of 27.5% relative to state-of-the-art baselines with 8.7x less communication traffic. In a fixed 600 x 600 m scaling test with 120 robots, AC-DC used 19.3 MB versus 19.2 MB for an ideal centralized baseline while remaining peer-to-peer.
AI.conclusion: AC-DC provides a scalable, peer-to-peer approach to dynamic average consensus for multi-robot systems with stringent communication constraints. It improves both estimation accuracy and communication efficiency relative to decentralized baselines, and its communication payload approaches that of an ideal centralized baseline as team size increases, supporting scalability.

title: SPARSER: Sparse Variable Projection by Exploiting Separable Structure in Robotic Perception
summary:
Robotic perception often requires solving large nonlinear least-squares (NLS) problems. While sparsity has been widely exploited to scale solvers, a complementary and underused structure is \emph{separability}: some variables, such as visual landmarks, appear linearly in the residuals and admit a closed-form solution once the remaining variables, such as poses, are fixed. Variable projection (VarPro) exploits this structure by analytically eliminating the linear variables, yielding a reduced problem with favorable computational properties. However, its use in robotic perception has been limited by gauge symmetries, such as invariance to global translations and rotations, which introduce challenges for standard VarPro methods.
  We present SPARSER (\textbf{S}parsity \textbf{P}reserving \textbf{A}nalytic \textbf{R}eduction for \textbf{S}eparable \textbf{R}obotic \textbf{P}erception), a VarPro framework for gauge-symmetric problems that jointly exploits separability and sparsity. Our method constructs a \emph{matrix-free Schur complement operator} for efficient evaluation of reduced costs, gradients, and Hessian-vector products, enabling integration with iterative NLS solvers. We characterize the applicable problem class, identify common cases admitting further analytical simplifications, and show that IRLS-based robust costs preserve most of the exploitable structure.
  Across synthetic and real SLAM, SNL, and SfM benchmarks, SPARSER is on average $5\times$--$7\times$ faster than state-of-the-art baselines on CPU and GPU, with gains exceeding $40\times$ on individual datasets. On outlier-corrupted multi-robot SLAM data, the robust variant is $2\times$--$16\times$ faster than a state-of-the-art GNC solver. We release open-source C++ code and all datasets.

AI.tldr: SPARSER is a VarPro-based framework for gauge-symmetric robotic perception problems that jointly exploits separability and sparsity, yielding 5x-7x average speedups over state-of-the-art solvers.
AI.motivation: Robotic perception relies on large nonlinear least-squares (NLS) problems. Sparsity is widely exploited, but separability—where some variables (e.g., visual landmarks) appear linearly and admit closed-form solutions—is underused. Variable projection (VarPro) can exploit separability but struggles with gauge symmetries (global translation/rotation invariance) common in robotics.
AI.method: SPARSER constructs a matrix-free Schur complement operator to efficiently evaluate reduced costs, gradients, and Hessian-vector products, enabling integration with iterative NLS solvers. It characterizes the applicable problem class, identifies cases admitting further analytical simplifications, and shows IRLS-based robust costs preserve most exploitable structure.
AI.result: On synthetic and real SLAM, SNL, and SfM benchmarks, SPARSER is on average 5x-7x faster than state-of-the-art baselines on CPU and GPU, with gains exceeding 40x on individual datasets. On outlier-corrupted multi-robot SLAM, the robust variant is 2x-16x faster than a state-of-the-art GNC solver.
AI.conclusion: SPARSER provides an effective VarPro framework for gauge-symmetric problems that jointly exploits separability and sparsity, with open-source C++ code and datasets released.

title: Beyond Visual Quality: A Study of Test-Time Planning with World Action Models
comment: 17 pages, including appendix
summary: World action models generate actions together with visual predictions of their consequences. These paired outputs create the potential for planning by sampling multiple actions from one state, comparing their imagined outcomes, and choosing the action with the most promising predicted outcome. However, how to use imagined futures to guide action selection remains unclear. We examine this planning potential empirically. First, we estimate an oracle upper bound on selection by choosing the sampled candidate whose realised outcome is best. In a controlled same-state analysis, this choice raises success from 68.9% under uniform random selection to 79.2%. We then test selectors based on visual quality, physical consistency, and task progression as controlled interventions. Some tested selectors yield higher observed success, but the gains are uneven and the matched selectors leave much of the measured opportunity unrecovered. To investigate this gap, we examine whether sampled actions lead to different outcomes, whether these differences are visible in the predictions, and whether a score recognises them. Counterfactual branching from the same states shows that selection opportunity is concentrated in relatively few decisions in the initial candidate sets. Action spread and outcome coverage need not increase together. In a further evaluation across trajectory phases with complete action execution, the tested scores again recover little of the available improvement despite a small gain from learned value. These findings distinguish producing consequential action choices from recognising them in generated futures, motivating the evaluation of WAM predictions through their usefulness for decisions rather than visual quality alone.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically studies whether world action models (WAMs) can be used for planning by selecting among sampled candidate actions based on their imagined visual futures, and finds that although a large selection opportunity exists (oracle upper bound 79.2% vs. 68.9% random), tested selectors recover little of it.
AI.motivation: WAMs jointly generate actions and visual predictions of their consequences, which in principle enables planning: sample many actions from a state, compare imagined outcomes, and pick the most promising. However, it is unclear how, or whether, imagined futures can actually guide action selection. The paper asks whether the planning potential of WAMs is realizable in practice.
AI.method: The authors quantify planning potential via an oracle upper bound that selects the sampled candidate with the best realised outcome, evaluated in a controlled same-state analysis. They then test practical selectors as controlled interventions based on three criteria: visual quality, physical consistency, and task progression. To diagnose the gap between oracle and selector performance, they use counterfactual branching from identical states to check (i) whether sampled actions produce different outcomes, (ii) whether those differences are visible in predictions, and (iii) whether a scoring function recognises them. They further evaluate across trajectory phases with complete action execution, including a learned value baseline.
AI.result: Oracle selection raises success from 68.9% (uniform random) to 79.2%, showing substantial selection opportunity. Practical selectors based on visual quality, physical consistency, and task progression sometimes yield higher observed success, but gains are uneven and even matched selectors leave most of the measured opportunity unrecovered. Counterfactual branching reveals that selection opportunity is concentrated in relatively few decisions within the initial candidate sets, and that action spread and outcome coverage need not increase together. Across trajectory phases with full action execution, tested scores again recover little of the available improvement, despite a small gain from learned value.
AI.conclusion: The results distinguish producing consequential action choices from recognising them in generated futures: WAMs can generate diverse, outcome-relevant actions, yet current scoring/selection methods fail to identify the best ones. This motivates evaluating WAM predictions by their usefulness for decisions rather than by visual quality alone.

title: D-JEPA: A Decision-Aligned Latent World Model
comment: 26 pages, including references and appendices. Project website: https://nebulis-lab.com/D-JEPA
summary: Latent world models predict the consequences of actions, but accurate prediction does not guarantee that latent distance reflects which candidate will execute successfully. We identify a decision-local prediction gap: among the few futures competing for execution, a candidate predicted closer to the goal can produce a worse realized outcome than an available alternative. We introduce D-JEPA, a decision-aligned latent world model that learns decision-relevant relations among candidate futures from executed outcomes. A bounded, permutation-equivariant operator jointly reasons over goal-relative predictive features and ordinal evidence, refining pretrained predictive geometry where action choices are most consequential. Restricted predictor adaptation and a shared ordinal interface extend this alignment across complementary predictive geometries. D-JEPA further realizes the learned decision structure in JEPA-compatible future representations, enabling deployment through native latent-distance planning. Evaluations across latent control, manipulation, pretrained action-producing models, physical robots and autonomous driving demonstrate improved action selection, including 87.89% success on PushT, a 15.04-point average gain on RoboTwin, and a 17-point gain on physical robot tasks. These results establish decision-relevant relational structure as a direct bridge between predictive world modeling and effective control.

AI.tldr: D-JEPA is a decision-aligned latent world model that learns decision-relevant relations among candidate futures from executed outcomes, improving action selection across control, manipulation, robotics, and driving tasks.
AI.motivation: Latent world models predict the consequences of actions, but accurate prediction does not guarantee that latent distance reflects which candidate will execute successfully. This creates a decision-local prediction gap: among the few futures competing for execution, a candidate predicted closer to the goal can produce a worse realized outcome than an available alternative.
AI.method: D-JEPA learns decision-relevant relations among candidate futures from executed outcomes. A bounded, permutation-equivariant operator jointly reasons over goal-relative predictive features and ordinal evidence, refining pretrained predictive geometry where action choices matter most. Restricted predictor adaptation and a shared ordinal interface extend alignment across complementary predictive geometries. The learned decision structure is realized in JEPA-compatible future representations, enabling deployment through native latent-distance planning.
AI.result: Evaluations across latent control, manipulation, pretrained action-producing models, physical robots, and autonomous driving show improved action selection, including 87.89% success on PushT, a 15.04-point average gain on RoboTwin, and a 17-point gain on physical robot tasks.
AI.conclusion: Decision-relevant relational structure serves as a direct bridge between predictive world modeling and effective control, establishing it as a key ingredient for aligning latent world models with successful action selection.

title: A Switched Adaptive Control Framework for Aerial Manipulators Under Dynamic Transitions
summary: Aerial manipulators represent the forefront of aerial robotics. Although potentially capable of complex interaction tasks, controlling aerial manipulators throughout the dynamic transitions occurring during task execution presents significant challenges. Abrupt or discontinuous changes in system dynamics generated by the transitions suggest the use of a switched approach, yet the available aerial manipulation methods are not designed for coping with switched regimes. In addition, most available methods fall short in coping with the tight couplings between the aerial vehicle and the manipulator, as well as in coping with the state-dependent uncertainties arising from the difficulty in modeling such couplings. We propose a switched-based adaptive control framework for aerial manipulators not relying on a priori knowledge of the vehicle-manipulator couplings and of state-dependent uncertainties. To guarantee stable manipulation despite changes in system dynamics, the framework provides a class of switching signals characterizing those transition phases for which the system is guaranteed to remain stable. Comparative experiments further validate the effectiveness of the proposed switched-based framework over the state of the art.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a switched-based adaptive control framework for aerial manipulators that handles dynamic transitions during task execution without a priori knowledge of vehicle-manipulator couplings or state-dependent uncertainties, providing switching signals that guarantee stability, and validates it through comparative experiments.
AI.motivation: Aerial manipulators are at the forefront of aerial robotics and could potentially perform complex interaction tasks, but controlling them through dynamic transitions during task execution is highly challenging. Abrupt or discontinuous changes in system dynamics during transitions suggest a switched approach, yet existing aerial manipulation methods are not designed for switched regimes. Moreover, most methods fail to handle the tight couplings between the aerial vehicle and the manipulator, and the state-dependent uncertainties that arise because these couplings are difficult to model.
AI.method: The authors propose a switched-based adaptive control framework for aerial manipulators. It does not rely on a priori knowledge of the vehicle-manipulator couplings or of state-dependent uncertainties. To guarantee stable manipulation despite changes in system dynamics, the framework provides a class of switching signals characterizing the transition phases for which the system is guaranteed to remain stable.
AI.result: Comparative experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed switched-based framework over the state of the art.
AI.conclusion: The proposed switched-based adaptive control framework enables stable manipulation of aerial manipulators across dynamic transitions without requiring prior knowledge of couplings or uncertainties, and outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in comparative experiments.

title: H2RBench: A Real-to-Sim Benchmark for Evaluating Human-to-Robot Transfer
comment: 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin, TX, USA
summary: Learning robot manipulation policies from human video demonstrations constitutes a promising avenue for scalable robot learning. However, comparing different human-to-robot (H2R) transfer methods remains challenging, as existing approaches are evaluated under different settings, including differing task suites, scene layouts, object instances, and amounts of robot supervision. To address this challenge, we present H2RBench, a Real2Sim benchmark for evaluating H2R transfer methods. H2RBench provides a standardized protocol built on real human video demonstrations and simulated robot demonstrations, and includes four manipulation tasks spanning diverse interaction requirements. We evaluate multiple representative H2R transfer methods, each adopting a different strategy for bridging the embodiment gap. Using H2RBench, we systematically characterize how each method scales with the amount of human demonstrations, revealing that methods differ substantially in their ability to leverage additional human data. We further show that simulation performance is broadly predictive of real-world robot performance, with an overall Pearson correlation of r = 0.89, Spearman correlation of \r{ho} = 0.85 and Mean Maximum Rank Violation (MMRV) of 0.06 across method-task configurations. These results establish H2RBench as a practical and scalable benchmark for comparative H2R evaluation prior to real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: H2RBench is a Real2Sim benchmark for standardized comparison of human-to-robot (H2R) manipulation transfer methods, built on real human videos and simulated robot demonstrations across four tasks.
AI.motivation: Comparing H2R transfer methods is difficult because existing evaluations use inconsistent task suites, scene layouts, object instances, and robot supervision levels, preventing fair comparison. A standardized, scalable evaluation protocol is needed.
AI.method: H2RBench provides a standardized protocol based on real human video demonstrations and simulated robot demonstrations, covering four manipulation tasks with diverse interaction requirements. Multiple representative H2R methods, each using a different strategy to bridge the embodiment gap, are evaluated, including analysis of scaling with amounts of human demonstrations.
AI.result: Methods differ substantially in how well they leverage additional human data. Simulation performance is broadly predictive of real-world robot performance, with Pearson r = 0.89, Spearman rho = 0.85, and Mean Maximum Rank Violation (MMRV) of 0.06 across method-task configurations.
AI.conclusion: H2RBench is a practical and scalable benchmark for comparative H2R evaluation prior to real-world deployment.

title: Minimum Time Trajectories for a Car-Like Mobile Robot Moving with Rigid Wheels Under Non-Sliding Constraints
summary: This paper studies the minimum time trajectoriesvof a car-like mobile robot navigating in an obstacle free environment. The robot, with forward and backward speeds, is controlled by bounded front-wheels acceleration and limited front-wheels steering rate. The paper extends previous results which solved this problem for the kinematic car-like robot. However, the kinematic model assumes pure rolling at the wheels ground contacts. This assumption requires non-sliding constraints for the front and rear wheels that can only be handled by the robot dynamics. This paper formulates the non-sliding constraints based on the robot dynamics then augments the kinematic model time-optimal path primitives with three new path primitives associated with the non-sliding constraints. The three non-sliding path primitives together with the kinematic model twelve path primitives form the car-like robot time optimal trajectories. Approximate analytic solutions for the non-sliding path primitives are also provided. Examples study the time-optimal path primitives along representative maneuvers, illustrating how the non-sliding constraints influence the time optimal trajectories of the car-like robot.

AI.tldr: This paper derives minimum-time trajectories for a car-like mobile robot in an obstacle-free environment, extending prior kinematic results by incorporating dynamic non-sliding constraints at the wheels. The kinematic twelve path primitives are augmented with three new non-sliding primitives, for which approximate analytic solutions are given, and examples show their influence on time-optimal maneuvers.
AI.motivation: Previous solutions to this time-optimal trajectory problem relied on a kinematic car-like robot model assuming pure rolling (non-sliding) at the wheel-ground contacts. Because this non-sliding assumption can only be properly handled by the robot dynamics, the kinematic model is insufficient, motivating a dynamic formulation of the non-sliding constraints and an extension of the existing path primitives.
AI.method: The robot moves forward and backward with bounded front-wheel acceleration and limited front-wheel steering rate. The authors formulate the non-sliding constraints based on the robot dynamics, then augment the kinematic model's twelve time-optimal path primitives with three new path primitives associated with these non-sliding constraints. Approximate analytic solutions for the three non-sliding primitives are provided, and representative maneuvers are examined in examples.
