AI.result: The three non-sliding path primitives, combined with the twelve kinematic path primitives, constitute the car-like robot's time-optimal trajectories. Approximate analytic solutions are obtained for the non-sliding primitives, and example maneuvers illustrate how the non-sliding constraints affect the time-optimal trajectories.
AI.conclusion: The time-optimal trajectory set for the car-like robot is completed by adding three dynamic non-sliding path primitives to the twelve kinematic primitives, and the non-sliding constraints are shown to measurably influence the time-optimal trajectories.

title: PredActor: Predictive Action Diffusion for Steerable Onboard Humanoid Control
comment: Project page: https://masteryip.github.io/predactor.github.io/
summary: Diffusion models offer flexible motion generation, but translating this flexibility into feedback-responsive humanoid control remains challenging. Hierarchical systems steer motion through references that may exceed a separate tracker's capabilities, leaving recovery and physical execution largely to the tracker. Action-only diffusion generates actions directly but lacks an explicit future-state trajectory for test-time motion objectives. Joint state-action diffusion provides this representation, yet representative controllers often depend on privileged full-body states, and support for learned behavior selection and test-time motion steering remains fragmented. We present PredActor, a predictive action diffusion policy that brings these complementary steering capabilities into one directly executed policy using proprioceptive observations. Conditioned on proprioceptive history and optional task context, PredActor jointly generates executable actions and an internal future-state trajectory. Classifier-free guidance strengthens text-conditioned behavior, while classifier guidance steers predicted states toward test-time objectives. Only actions are executed, without a separate motion-reference tracker or externally estimated full-body states as policy inputs. In simulation, PredActor reaches all 15 destination targets and achieves a text retrieval score of 0.580, compared with 0.373 for conditional action diffusion, with similar observed disturbance survival. To make this guided policy practical onboard, rolling denoising and computation-preserving runtime optimizations reduce the complete callback to 16.790 ms median and 19.383 ms p95 on a Jetson Orin NX, both below the 20 ms control period. We deploy PredActor on a Unitree G1; evaluations across simulation and physical hardware demonstrate text-conditioned motion, disturbance response, joystick control, and semantic interpolation.

AI.tldr: PredActor is a predictive action diffusion policy that jointly generates executable actions and an internal future-state trajectory from proprioception, enabling text-conditioned, steerable humanoid control without a separate tracker or privileged full-body inputs, and runs in real time onboard a Unitree G1.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models allow flexible motion generation, but feedback-responsive humanoid control is hard: hierarchical systems rely on references that may exceed a tracker's ability, action-only diffusion lacks an explicit future-state trajectory for test-time objectives, and joint state-action diffusion methods often need privileged full-body states with fragmented support for learned behavior selection and test-time steering.
AI.method: PredActor conditions on proprioceptive history and optional task context to jointly diffuse executable actions and an internal future-state trajectory. It uses classifier-free guidance for text-conditioned behavior and classifier guidance to steer predicted states toward test-time objectives. Only actions are executed, requiring no separate motion-reference tracker or externally estimated full-body states. Onboard practicality is achieved via rolling denoising and computation-preserving runtime optimizations.
AI.result: In simulation, PredActor reaches all 15 destination targets and attains a text retrieval score of 0.580 versus 0.373 for conditional action diffusion, with similar disturbance survival. Optimizations reduce the complete callback to 16.790 ms median and 19.383 ms p95 on a Jetson Orin NX, both under the 20 ms control period. Deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates text-conditioned motion, disturbance response, joystick control, and semantic interpolation in simulation and on hardware.
AI.conclusion: PredActor unifies behavior selection and test-time motion steering into a single directly executed, proprioception-based diffusion policy, validating real-time, tracker-free humanoid control in both simulation and physical hardware.

title: CAST: Collision-Aware Assembly with Construction Robots using Simultaneous Trajectory Estimation and Planning
summary: Multi-robot systems have shown increasing viability in construction due to their ability to execute high-precision actions while reducing human exposure to hazardous tasks. However, these environments have high-dimensional configuration spaces and possess substantial collision-avoidance constraints, which include other robots, assembly objects, and workspace boundaries. We utilize a single factor graph for trajectory estimation and planning that incorporates measured robot states together with explicit collision and learned cable constraints. This supports changing workspaces and enables synchronized, high-dimensional robot motion planning while accounting for the stiff, vibration-induced uncertainty of heavy robotic systems. We demonstrate the success of our framework on the construction of a post-and-lintel structure using one robot arm as a timber gripper, and a second robot as a nail-fastener.

AI.tldr: A single factor graph unifies trajectory estimation and planning for multi-robot construction, embedding explicit collision and learned cable constraints to enable synchronized, high-dimensional motion planning under stiff, vibration-induced uncertainty, demonstrated by building a post-and-lintel structure with a timber-gripper arm and a nail-fastener robot.
AI.motivation: Multi-robot systems are increasingly viable in construction because they perform high-precision actions while reducing human exposure to hazardous tasks. However, construction environments involve high-dimensional configuration spaces and substantial collision-avoidance constraints from other robots, assembly objects, and workspace boundaries. Heavy robotic systems also introduce stiff, vibration-induced uncertainty that complicates planning.
AI.method: The authors use a single factor graph for trajectory estimation and planning, jointly incorporating measured robot states with explicit collision constraints and learned cable constraints. This unified formulation supports changing workspaces and enables synchronized, high-dimensional robot motion planning while accounting for vibration-induced uncertainty in heavy robotic systems.
AI.result: The framework was validated on the construction of a post-and-lintel structure, using one robot arm as a timber gripper and a second robot as a nail-fastener, demonstrating successful synchronized multi-robot assembly.
AI.conclusion: A unified factor-graph approach that fuses estimation and planning with collision and learned cable constraints is effective for high-dimensional, constraint-heavy multi-robot construction tasks, successfully coordinating heterogeneous robot roles in a real assembly scenario.

title: Range-Aided SLAM Initialization Exploiting Accurate Heading Information
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, accepted to OCEANS 2026 MTS/IEEE Conference and Exhibition
summary: This paper presents a novel initialization method for range-aided simultaneous localization and mapping (RA-SLAM). The general SLAM problem has a well-known separable structure where landmark and robot positions can be solved for in a linear fashion given known robot headings. This paper considers the case where highly accurate heading information is available, which is typical of autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) navigation, to solve for the range transponder and robot positions. The proposed approach consists of two steps. First, using a generalized trust region subproblem (GTRS), the positions of the transponders relative to the AUV are solved for given the nonlinear range measurements. Second, the relative transponder positions and the known heading of the AUV are used to estimate the transponder and AUV positions by solving a linear least-squares problem. These transponder and AUV position estimates, combined with the highly accurate heading information, provide a reliable initialization method for the general nonlinear RA-SLAM problem. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is tested on a real-world AUV dataset where long baseline (LBL) range measurements are provided in concert with highly accurate heading information provided by an inertial navigation system (INS).

AI.tldr: A two-step initialization method for range-aided SLAM that exploits accurate heading information (typical in AUV navigation) to solve for transponder and robot positions, validated on real AUV data with LBL ranges and INS headings.
AI.motivation: General SLAM has a separable structure solvable linearly given known robot headings. In AUV navigation, highly accurate heading from an INS is readily available, but the nonlinearity of range measurements makes initialization of the full nonlinear RA-SLAM problem difficult. A reliable initialization is needed to robustly bootstrap the nonlinear optimization.
AI.method: Two-step approach. Step 1: using a Generalized Trust Region Subproblem (GTRS), solve for transponder positions relative to the AUV from nonlinear range measurements. Step 2: combine these relative transponder positions with the known AUV headings to estimate transponder and AUV positions by solving a linear least-squares problem.
AI.result: The proposed initialization's effectiveness was evaluated on a real-world AUV dataset with long baseline (LBL) range measurements and highly accurate INS-provided headings, yielding a reliable initialization for the general nonlinear RA-SLAM problem.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting accurate heading information allows range-aided SLAM initialization to be decomposed into a GTRS step plus a linear least-squares step, providing a robust, reliable initialization that is demonstrated on real AUV data.

title: DualWAM: Dual-System World Action Models for Asynchronous Global Planning and Local Refinement
comment: Project page: https://steveouo.github.io/DualWAM-Web/
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly generate robot actions and predict future world states, transferring priors from video pretraining to robot control. However, future visual prediction is computationally expensive, so existing WAMs often rely on long action chunks to amortize inference cost across control steps, at the cost of closed-loop responsiveness. We present \method, a dual-system WAM that preserves broader-horizon world-action generation while enabling high-frequency closed-loop action updates by decoupling global planning and local refinement. \systwo periodically performs high-noise bidirectional denoising over a broader world-action chunk to establish a global plan, while wrist-only \sysone extracts a temporally aligned short window from the intermediate denoising state and completes low-noise refinement using the latest wrist observations, which provide action-aligned cues about local geometry, motion, and contact during interaction. The two systems operate asynchronously along a shared denoising trajectory: each global plan is reused across multiple local updates, while \sysone repeatedly incorporates fresh interaction feedback. Across zero-shot manipulation tasks on Franka and Galbot, \method improves success over the strongest evaluated baseline by 4.5 percentage points on average, while achieving a 16.6$\times$ critical-path speedup. Further studies show that role-matched egocentric and UMI data improve success by 14 percentage points, and that the decoupled design naturally supports edge--cloud deployment with substantially lower communication overhead than the baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a dual-system World Action Model that decouples global planning from local refinement, enabling high-frequency closed-loop robot control while retaining broader-horizon world-action generation, improving success and achieving large speedups.
AI.motivation: World Action Models jointly generate actions and predict future world states but future visual prediction is computationally expensive. Existing WAMs mitigate this with long action chunks that amortize inference cost, sacrificing closed-loop responsiveness. The goal is to keep broad-horizon world-action generation while restoring high-frequency closed-loop updates.
AI.method: A dual-system WAM. A slower system (\systwo) periodically performs high-noise bidirectional denoising over a broader world-action chunk to form a global plan. A faster, wrist-only system (\sysone) extracts a temporally aligned short window from the intermediate denoising state and completes low-noise refinement using the latest wrist observations, which provide action-aligned cues on local geometry, motion, and contact. The two run asynchronously along a shared denoising trajectory, with each global plan reused across multiple local updates.
AI.result: Across zero-shot manipulation tasks on Franka and Galbot, the method improves success over the strongest evaluated baseline by 4.5 percentage points on average while achieving a 16.6x critical-path speedup. Role-matched egocentric and UMI data improve success by 14 percentage points, and the decoupled design supports edge-cloud deployment with substantially lower communication overhead than the baseline.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling global planning from local refinement in a dual-system WAM preserves broad-horizon world-action generation while enabling high-frequency closed-loop control, yielding better success rates, large speedups, data-role benefits, and efficient edge-cloud deployment.

title: Steerable and Reactive Grasping Through Modular Design with a Three-Point Interface
summary: Dexterous grasping requires deciding where to grasp, reaching the target, and maintaining stable contact. We connect these stages through a compact three-point interface that separates global geometric reasoning from local contact control. Given object geometry and optional language commands, our framework samples contact triples from a precomputed grasp-affordance heatmap. A model-based reactive controller tracks the object, avoids collisions, and guides the hand toward the selected contacts. In the final centimeters, a Reinforcement Learning (RL) policy uses proprioceptive feedback to refine and stabilize the grasp despite reaching and perception errors. It observes only finger joint states and its recent actions, with no target points, visual observations, or object geometry, so a single policy is shared across objects and grasp configurations. In simulation, we compare grasp-and-lift success against squeeze and end-to-end baselines, characterize reaching convergence, and demonstrate grasp steering; hardware demonstrations on two training objects and one unseen object illustrate the full pipeline. Our modular framework uses geometry to guide the reach and local feedback to secure the grasp.

AI.tldr: A modular dexterous grasping framework decomposes the task into global geometric reasoning (contact triples sampled from a grasp-affordance heatmap) and local contact control (a proprioception-only RL policy), validated in simulation against squeeze and end-to-end baselines and on hardware for trained and unseen objects.
AI.motivation: Dexterous grasping is a multi-stage problem requiring decisions about where to grasp, reaching the target, and maintaining stable contact. Treating these stages jointly (end-to-end) or relying on simple strategies like squeezing is insufficient, motivating a decomposed approach that leverages geometry for global guidance and local feedback for stabilization.
AI.method: The framework uses a compact three-point interface separating global geometric reasoning from local contact control. Given object geometry and optional language commands, contact triples are sampled from a precomputed grasp-affordance heatmap. A model-based reactive controller tracks the object, avoids collisions, and guides the hand toward the selected contacts. In the last centimeters, an RL policy using only proprioceptive feedback (finger joint states and recent actions) refines and stabilizes the grasp, with no target points, visual observations, or object geometry, enabling a single shared policy across objects and configurations.
AI.result: In simulation, the method is compared against squeeze and end-to-end baselines on grasp-and-lift success, reaching convergence is characterized, and grasp steering is demonstrated. Hardware demonstrations cover two training objects and one unseen object, illustrating the full pipeline.
AI.conclusion: The modular framework combines geometry to guide the reach and local feedback to secure the grasp, yielding a single policy that generalizes across objects and grasp configurations without visual or geometric observations at the contact stage.

title: Learning to Drive on Mars: Visual Multimodal Traversability Estimation for Off-World Navigation
summary: Autonomous navigation on Mars requires vehicles to distinguish between traversable terrains across diverse and visually challenging environments. However, progress in learning-based navigation for off-world environments has been limited by the lack of large-scale datasets. Since landing in Jezero Crater, the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover has traversed terrain ranging from sandy dunes, rocky patches, and flat bedrocks. As a result, this paper presents a dataset spanning 500 sols and 45km of trajectories driven by both human operators and the onboard planner, ENav. Our dataset contains grayscale stereo image pairs, poses, accelerometer readings, rocker-bogie angles, and estimates of tilt and wheel slip. Building on this dataset, we introduce an uncertainty-aware traversability-estimation framework that learns terrain representations from multimodal driving experience. We compare our proposed method against existing approaches on the Mars 2020 dataset and show that our method achieves an AUROC of 0.874 and an F1 score of 0.758, outperforming the strongest baseline by 0.058 and 0.156, respectively, while also achieving the highest average precision and recall. Finally, we show that the visual representations can be integrated into path planners, such as ENav, on a physical rover test bed. Videos, code, and the M2020 dataset will be available at https://darren-chiu.github.io/learning-to-drive-on-mars.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a large-scale Mars 2020 Perseverance dataset (500 sols, 45 km) and an uncertainty-aware traversability-estimation framework that learns terrain representations from multimodal driving data, outperforming baselines on traversability prediction.
AI.motivation: Learning-based autonomous navigation for Mars is hampered by a lack of large-scale, real off-world datasets. Distinguishing traversable from non-traversable terrain in visually challenging, diverse environments is essential for rover autonomy, yet existing progress is constrained by data scarcity.
AI.method: The authors present a dataset spanning 500 sols and 45 km of trajectories driven by both human operators and the onboard planner ENav, containing grayscale stereo image pairs, poses, accelerometer readings, rocker-bogie angles, and estimates of tilt and wheel slip. On this dataset they develop an uncertainty-aware traversability-estimation framework that learns terrain representations from multimodal driving experience, and integrate the learned visual representations into path planners such as ENav on a physical rover test bed.
AI.result: Compared with existing approaches on the Mars 2020 dataset, the proposed method achieves an AUROC of 0.874 and an F1 score of 0.758, outperforming the strongest baseline by 0.058 and 0.156 respectively, while also attaining the highest average precision and recall.
AI.conclusion: The dataset, uncertainty-aware traversability framework, and planner integration demonstrate that learning-based terrain representation from multimodal rover experience improves traversability estimation and can be deployed within path planners like ENav on physical rovers. Videos, code, and the M2020 dataset are to be released.

title: MIGU: Multimodal Instruction Grounding under Uncertainty for Manipulation Planning
summary: Understanding natural human instructions is crucial for deploying robots in human-centric environments. We study multimodal instruction grounding, where language and gesture provide complementary but uncertain cues. We present MIGU, a modular framework that combines semantic and geometric evidence into a unified grounding belief and connects it to manipulation planning. MIGU constructs a 3D geometric likelihood by propagating viewing-direction and depth uncertainty through eye-finger geometry while accounting for hand-direction estimation error. A vision-language model (VLM) provides semantic priors over candidate objects and regions, which are combined with the geometric likelihood through Bayes-inspired fusion. The resulting belief supports behavior planning to either proceed directly to downstream planning or request clarification. Grounded targets then define goals for mobile manipulation and tabletop task-and-motion planning. On a real-world benchmark, MIGU outperforms all evaluated baselines, while ablations support the benefit of explicit multimodal uncertainty modeling. Project website: multimodal-instruction.github.io

AI.tldr: MIGU is a modular framework that fuses gesture-based geometric likelihood (with viewing-direction, depth, and hand-direction uncertainty) and VLM semantic priors via Bayes-inspired fusion to ground multimodal robot instructions, supporting either direct planning or clarification requests, and outperforming baselines on a real-world benchmark.
AI.motivation: Deploying robots in human-centric environments requires understanding natural human instructions. Language and gesture provide complementary but uncertain cues, so reliable grounding must handle this uncertainty rather than treat multimodal cues as exact.
AI.method: MIGU combines semantic and geometric evidence into a unified grounding belief linked to manipulation planning. It builds a 3D geometric likelihood by propagating viewing-direction and depth uncertainty through eye-finger geometry while accounting for hand-direction estimation error. A VLM supplies semantic priors over candidate objects and regions, fused with the geometric likelihood via Bayes-inspired fusion. The resulting belief drives behavior planning to proceed directly to downstream planning or request clarification, with grounded targets defining goals for mobile manipulation and tabletop task-and-motion planning.
AI.result: On a real-world benchmark, MIGU outperforms all evaluated baselines, and ablations support the benefit of explicit multimodal uncertainty modeling.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling multimodal uncertainty within a modular semantic-geometric fusion framework improves instruction grounding and enables uncertainty-aware behavior planning for robot manipulation. Project website: multimodal-instruction.github.io.

title: Learning Beyond What Humans Can Demonstrate
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026. Project website: http://guardrail-policy.github.io/
summary: Behavior cloning for robot manipulation relies on expert demonstrations. However, for tasks that require dynamic stability, precise contact timing, or dexterous coordination, human operators may find it hard or even impossible to collect data. We study this infeasible-demonstration regime and propose GLIDE: Guardrails for Learning from Infeasible Demonstrations Efficiently, a framework that infers task-specific failure modes and converts them into executable guardrails for data collection and policy deployment. Given a task description and the conditioning teleoperation code, GLIDE writes guardrails that use system states to filter teleoperation and policy commands, constrain failure-prone actions, and iteratively improve from trajectory feedback. Across three tasks, GLIDE discovers emergent guardrails that go beyond domain-expert hardcoded ones, improving data collection over naive VR teleoperation and domain-expert hardcoded guardrails. After refinement, GLIDE raises data-collection success from 0-10 percent to 70-90 percent across the three tasks. During policy execution, mixed-data guarded policies reach 70 percent, 60 percent, and 60 percent success on Tomato plate transfer, Marker handover and stand, and Wine serving tasks. These results show that GLIDE can support policy learning when direct demonstrations are infeasible. Project website: http://guardrail-policy.github.io/

AI.tldr: GLIDE infers task-specific failure modes from a task description and teleoperation code, converting them into executable guardrails that filter commands during data collection and policy deployment, enabling robot manipulation learning even when direct expert demonstrations are infeasible.
AI.motivation: Behavior cloning for robot manipulation relies on expert demonstrations, but for tasks demanding dynamic stability, precise contact timing, or dexterous coordination, human operators may find data collection hard or even impossible—an infeasible-demonstration regime that current approaches do not address.
AI.method: Given a task description and conditioning teleoperation code, GLIDE writes guardrails that use system states to filter teleoperation and policy commands, constrain failure-prone actions, and iteratively improve from trajectory feedback. It infers task-specific failure modes and converts them into executable guardrails for both data collection and policy deployment.
AI.result: Across three tasks, GLIDE discovers emergent guardrails that outperform naive VR teleoperation and domain-expert hardcoded guardrails. After refinement, data-collection success rises from 0–10% to 70–90%. During policy execution, mixed-data guarded policies reach 70%, 60%, and 60% success on Tomato plate transfer, Marker handover and stand, and Wine serving tasks, respectively.
AI.conclusion: GLIDE demonstrates that inferring and executing task-specific guardrails can support policy learning when direct demonstrations are infeasible, improving both data collection and downstream policy success.
